pages.title: Variables and Fundamental Data Types

sections.t: Step 1 of the Python on-ramp — start here. The callout above opens this entry directly; the roadmap shows the same on-ramp above Level 0, with a count of the entries you have actually run and passed. Read on if you prefer to work in your own Python 3.

Store robot measurements such as battery charge level, wheel pulse counts, and safety status flags in named Python variables, and distinguish the four fundamental data types (int, float, str, bool).
New ideas (max 2):
Storing values in named variables: Using the assignment operator (=) to evaluate the right-hand side first and store the result inside a named memory box on the left.
Fundamental data types (int, float, str, bool): Distinguishing whole numbers (int), decimal measurements (float), quoted text (str), and truth flags (bool).
New syntax: =, # comments, print(), f"{value:.2f}" formatted strings (f-strings).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Basic school arithmetic (whole numbers and decimals).
No prior programming or electronics experience required.

sections.h: Idea 1: Storing values in named variables
sections.t:
Primary resource: futurecoder.io — Chapters 1 and 3 (The Shell & Variables) [verify in-app]
What to complete: Complete Chapter 1 (The Shell) and Chapter 3 (Variables) [verify in-app].
What to skip: Skip Chapter 2 for a moment (covered in Idea 2 below) and skip Chapters 4–12.
Key takeaway: A variable is a named storage box in computer memory. In Python, the single equals sign = is the assignment action—not a math equation: Python calculates the value on the right side of = first, and copies that result into the variable name on the left (count = count + 1 increases count by 1).
Alternative resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 0 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Variables and Comments.

sections.h: Idea 2: Fundamental data types (int, float, str, bool)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 0 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Formatting Strings, Integers or int, and Float Basics.
What to skip: Skip Strings and Parameters, More on Strings, and Def.
Key takeaway: Computers treat whole numbers, decimal numbers, text, and true/false switches differently: int holds exact whole numbers (400, -5), float holds numbers with a decimal point (12.0, 0.05), str holds text inside quotation marks ("READY"), and bool holds True or False (capitalized).
Alternative resource: futurecoder.io — Chapter 2 (String Basics) and Chapter 7 (f-strings) [verify in-app] — Complete Chapter 2 (String Basics) and the f-strings page in Chapter 7 (A Bit More About Strings) [verify in-app].

In mechatronics, every value inside your program (an ordered list of instructions executed top-to-bottom) represents a physical measurement or hardware state. When you write battery_level = 12.60, the assignment operator (=) creates a variable named battery_level holding the float (floating-point decimal number) 12.60. Because Python always evaluates the right-hand side of = before storing it into the name on the left, writing wheel_ticks = wheel_ticks + 25 reads the stored int (integer whole number) in wheel_ticks, adds 25, and saves the updated total back into wheel_ticks.
Text wrapped in quotes like "ARMED" is a str (string), whereas a safety switch state like is_estop_active = False is a bool (boolean, written strictly True or False with capital first letters). Never put quotation marks around numbers you plan to use in calculations: 12 + 5 adds two integers to give 17, whereas "12" + "5" glues two strings together into "125". Finally, use a comment (#) to write human-readable unit reminders that Python ignores, and use an f-string (f"Battery: {battery_level:.2f}") inside print() to display values cleanly.

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in futurecoder.io [verify in-app] or locally via python3).
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

Tracing variable reassignment: What number is printed by these three lines of Python?
Answer
Line 1 stores 100 in ticks. Line 2 evaluates 100 + 50 (150) and stores 150 back into ticks.
Identifying data types: Name the Python data type (int, float, str, or bool) of each value: 1023, "1023", 0.0, and True.
Answer
1023 is an int (whole number with no decimal point).
"1023" is a str (text wrapped in quotes).
0.0 is a float (has a decimal point).
True is a bool (boolean truth value).
Numbers vs. strings: What is the difference between print(10 + 5) and print("10" + "5")?
Answer
print(10 + 5) adds two integers and prints 15, whereas print("10" + "5") joins two text strings side-by-side and prints 105.

A variable stores a value in memory using =, where the right-hand side is evaluated first and stored into the name on the left.
The four fundamental types are int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (quoted text), and bool (True/False).

pages.title: Computer Arithmetic and Order of Operations

sections.t:
Translate multi-step physics and circuit formulas into bug-free Python arithmetic using explicit multiplication (), division (/), exponents (), and parentheses ().
New ideas (max 2):
Computer arithmetic operators: Performing addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (), float division (/), integer floor division (//), and exponents ().
Parentheses and order of operations: Using parentheses () around numerators and denominators so multi-term engineering fractions evaluate in the exact intended order.
New syntax: +, -, , /, //, , ().
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–2.5 hours
Lesson P.1: Variables and Fundamental Data Types

Primary resource: Official Python 3 Tutorial — Section 3.1: Using Python as a Calculator [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings 3.1. Using Python as a Calculator and 3.1.1. Numbers.
What to skip: Skip 3.1.2. Text and 3.1.3. Lists (covered in Lesson P.4).
Key takeaway: In Python, multiplication always requires an explicit asterisk (never write 2x or 2(3)), standard division / always produces a decimal float (8 / 2 gives 4.0), floor division // drops the fractional remainder (1023 // 4 gives 255), and powers use a double asterisk (3 2 computes $3^2 = 9$).
Alternative resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 0 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review exact headings Integers or int and Float Basics.

sections.h: Idea 2: Parentheses and order of operations
sections.t:
Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Order of Operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Order of Operations and How Do I Remember It All ... ?.
What to skip: Skip the bottom puzzle links once the four precedence levels are clear.
Key takeaway: Python evaluates Parentheses () first, then Exponents , then Multiplication and Division / / // (from left to right), and finally Addition + and Subtraction - (from left to right). Whenever a printed fraction has a horizontal bar with multiple terms on top or bottom, you must wrap the numerator and denominator in parentheses: (top) / (bottom).
Alternative resource: Official Python 3 Tutorial — Section 3.1.1: Numbers [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review the parentheses examples under 3.1.1. Numbers.

On paper, engineers write multiplication by placing letters side by side ($d = s \cdot t$) and write fractions with a horizontal bar:
When you translate equations into computer arithmetic operators (+, -, , /, ) on a single line of code, the horizontal fraction bar disappears! You must always write explicitly for multiplication, / for floating-point division, and for exponents. If you type y_in b / a + b without parentheses, Python's order of operations (PEMDAS) performs y_in b / a first and then adds b at the very end—producing a completely wrong answer. Wrapping the denominator in parentheses (y_in (b / (a + b))) forces Python to add a + b first, just like the horizontal bar on paper.
Similarly, when squaring a speed in $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m s^2$ in Python, write 0.5 cart_mass (cart_speed 2) using for the exponent (never ^, which is a bitwise operator in Python). Whenever you are unsure which operation happens first, add parentheses ()—extra parentheses never slow down your code and make your intent unmistakable.

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in futurecoder.io [verify in-app] or locally via python3).
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

TypeError: 'int' object is not callable: You wrote implicit multiplication like 2(3 + 4) instead of 2 (3 + 4). Always write explicitly.
Using ^ instead of for exponents: In Python, 3 ^ 2 performs bitwise XOR (1), NOT $3^2 = 9$. Always write 3 2.
Missing denominator parentheses: Writing 30 / 2 3 computes (30 / 2) 3 = 45.0 instead of 30 / (2 3) = 5.0.

Order of operations bug: You want to compute $\frac{10 + 20}{2 \times 3} = 5.0$, so you type 10 + 20 / 2 3. What number does Python actually produce, and how do you fix it?
Answer
Python computes 40.0 (20 / 2 is 10.0, times 3 is 30.0, plus 10 is 40.0). Fix it with parentheses: (10 + 20) / (2 3), which gives 5.0.
Exponents and division: What value does (2 3) + (15 / 2) produce?
Answer
15.5. First 2 3 is 8, then 15 / 2 is 7.5, and 8 + 7.5 equals 15.5.
Float division / vs. floor division //: What is the difference between 1023 / 4 and 1023 // 4 in Python?
Answer
1023 / 4 returns the exact decimal float 255.75, whereas 1023 // 4 discards the decimal remainder and returns the whole int 255.

Python requires explicit for multiplication, / for decimal division, // for whole-number floor division, and for exponents.
Always wrap multi-term numerators and denominators in parentheses: (numerator) / (denominator).

pages.title: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) and Command Clamping

sections.t:
Use comparison operators and if / elif / else statements to make safety decisions in code and clamp out-of-range motor commands into a safe hardware range ([0, 255]).
New ideas (max 2):
Conditional branching (if/elif/else): Testing conditions that evaluate to True or False and running indented blocks of code only when a condition matches.
Clamping actuator commands within safe limits: Using if / elif bounds checks so a calculated command never exceeds a hardware maximum or drops below a minimum.
New syntax: ==, !=, , >=, if, elif, else, colon :, 4-space block indentation.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.1: Variables and Fundamental Data Types
Lesson P.2: Computer Arithmetic and Order of Operations

Primary resource: futurecoder.io — Chapter 5 (If Statements) [verify in-app]
What to complete: Complete Chapter 5 (If Statements) [verify in-app].
What to skip: Skip Chapter 4 (For Loops) and Chapter 6 (Lists) for now—we cover both in Lesson P.4 next.
Key takeaway: An if statement tests a comparison (, >=, == equal to, != not equal to) that evaluates to True or False. When True, Python runs the indented lines (shifted right by 4 spaces) underneath the colon :; otherwise it checks any elif ("else if") branches or falls back to else:.
Alternative resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 1 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Conditionals, if Statements, Control Flow, elif, and else, or, and and (skip Modulo and match).

sections.h: Idea 2: Clamping actuator commands within safe limits
sections.t:
Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 1 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review Control Flow, elif, and else and trace how mutually exclusive checks bound a number.
What to skip: Skip match statements.
Key takeaway: Real hardware outputs only accept a finite range of numbers—for example, a standard motor command register only accepts whole numbers from 0 to 255. Clamping (also called saturation) uses if cmd > 255: cmd = 255 and elif cmd < 0: cmd = 0 so out-of-bounds math can never wrap around or cause hardware faults.

Look closely at the difference between a single equals sign = and a double equals sign ==:
x = 255 (Assignment): Stores the number 255 into variable x.
x == 255 (Comparison): Asks the question "Is x currently equal to 255?" and produces True or False.
In Python, every if, elif, and else header ends with a colon :, and the lines that belong inside that decision branch must be indented by 4 spaces.
Why is clamping the most common if/elif pattern in robotics? Suppose your controller calculates a motor command of 310 when trying to catch a falling robot arm, or -40 when braking. If you pass 310 or -40 directly to a hardware output register that only holds 0 to 255, the register overflows (310 wraps around to 54—suddenly cutting motor power when you needed maximum effort!). Clamping the command with if motor_cmd > 255: motor_cmd = 255 and elif motor_cmd < 0: motor_cmd = 0 guarantees safe behavior at the physical limits.

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in futurecoder.io [verify in-app] or locally via python3).
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

SyntaxError: invalid syntax on if x = 5:: A single = is assignment; comparisons inside if require a double equals if x == 5:.
IndentationError: expected an indented block: Every line controlled by if, elif, or else must be indented by 4 spaces (never mix tabs and spaces).
SyntaxError: expected ':': Every if, elif, and else header line must end with a colon :.

Tracing if / elif / else: If temp_c = 85.0, what does this code print?
Answer
SHUTDOWN only. Because 85.0 >= 80.0 is True, Python runs the first branch and skips the elif and else branches completely.
Boundary check (> vs. >=): Does clamping into [0, 255] give a different result if you write if cmd >= 255: cmd = 255 instead of if cmd > 255: cmd = 255 when cmd is 255?
Answer
No—when cmd is 255, both leave cmd equal to 255.
== vs. !=: What boolean value (True or False) does 1023 != 0 evaluate to?
Answer
True, because != means "is not equal to", and 1023 is not equal to 0.

Comparison operators (==, !=, , >=) produce True or False for if / elif / else decision blocks.
Clamping bounds commands into a safe hardware interval like [0, 255] before they reach actuators.

pages.title: Ordered Lists and Repeating Actions with for Loops

sections.t:
Store sequences of sensor readings in zero-indexed Python lists ([a, b, c]) and process every item automatically using for loops and range().
New ideas (max 2):
Ordered lists with zero-based indexing: Grouping multiple values in square brackets [...] where position counting starts at index 0.
Repeating actions with for loops: Stepping through every element of a list (for item in my_list:) or a fixed number of ticks (for step in range(n):).
New syntax: [a, b, c], items[0], items.append(x), len(items), for x in items:, range(n).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours
Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Command Clamping

sections.h: Idea 1: Ordered lists with zero-based indexing
sections.t:
Primary resource: Official Python 3 Tutorial — Section 3.1.3: Lists [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading 3.1.3. Lists (creating lists with square brackets, indexing with [0], .append(), and len()).
What to skip: Skip nested lists at the very end of the section.
Key takeaway: A list stores an ordered sequence of values inside square brackets, such as distances = [12.1, 11.9, 11.8]. Python uses zero-based indexing: the first item is at index 0 (distances[0] is 12.1), the second is at index 1, and the last item in a list of length len(distances) (3) is at index 2.
Alternative resource: futurecoder.io — Chapter 6 (Lists) [verify in-app] — Complete Chapter 6 (Lists) [verify in-app].

sections.h: Idea 2: Repeating actions with for loops
sections.t:
Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 2 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings For Loops, More About Lists, and Length.
What to skip: Skip While Loops (covered in Lesson P.5), Dictionaries, and Mario.
Key takeaway: Instead of copy-pasting the same calculation ten times, a for loop (for x in items:) visits each element of a list one by one and runs its indented block. When you want to run a loop a specific number of times $N$, for step in range(N): counts step through 0, 1, 2, ..., N - 1.
Alternative resource: futurecoder.io — Chapter 4 (For Loops) [verify in-app] — Complete Chapter 4 (For Loops) [verify in-app].

Sensors on a robot produce streams of measurements over time. Instead of inventing separate variable names like s0, s1, s2, s3, we store a sequence inside a list: samples = [12.2, 12.0, 11.8, 11.6]. Because computers count offsets from the beginning of memory, zero-based indexing means:
samples[0] is the 1st item (12.2),
samples[3] is the 4th (last) item (11.6),
len(samples) returns the count of items (4), and samples.append(11.5) adds a new item to the end.
Repeating actions with for loops (for x in samples:) lets you filter, clamp, or average thousands of sensor readings in four lines of code without copy-pasting. To accumulate a running sum (for example, to compute the average of a list of sensor readings), create an accumulator variable total = 0.0 before the for loop, add each item inside the indented loop (total = total + x), and divide total / len(samples) after the loop finishes.

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in futurecoder.io [verify in-app] or locally via python3).
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

IndexError: list index out of range: In a 4-item list, valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3. Asking for index 4 crashes because index counting starts at 0.
Resetting total_cmd = 0 inside the for loop: If you put total_cmd = 0 inside the indented loop body, it erases the sum on every iteration! Always initialize accumulators above the for line.
Expecting range(5) to include 5: range(5) generates 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (5 numbers total, stopping before 5).

Zero-based indexing: Given temps = [25.0, 31.2, 42.8, 38.5], what is temps[0], what is temps[3], and what happens if you evaluate temps[4]?
Answer
temps[0] is 25.0, temps[3] is 38.5, and temps[4] raises an IndexError: list index out of range.
Counting range(n) iterations: What numbers does for k in range(4): print(k) print?
Answer
0, 1, 2, 3 (four numbers starting at 0).
Tracing a loop sum: What is the value of s after running s = 0 followed by for x in [2, 4, 6]: s = s + x?
Answer
12 (0 + 2 = 2, 2 + 4 = 6, 6 + 6 = 12).

A list ([a, b, c]) stores an ordered sequence where index 0 is the first element and len(items) is the total count.
A for loop repeats an indented block once for every element in a list or range(n).

pages.title: Reusable Functions (def/return) and while Loops

sections.t:
Package repeatable engineering calculations into named functions using def and return, and step physical simulations forward in time using while loops.
New ideas (max 2):
Reusable functions (def and return): Defining a named block of code that accepts input parameters, performs a calculation, and hands the numerical answer back via return.
Condition-controlled while loops: Repeating an indented simulation step for as long as a condition (step < total_steps) remains True.
New syntax: def func_name(param1, param2):, return value, while condition:.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Command Clamping
Lesson P.4: Ordered Lists & Repeating Actions with for Loops

Primary resource: futurecoder.io — Chapter 10 (Functions) [verify in-app]
What to complete: Complete the pages on defining functions, parameters, and returning values in Chapter 10 (Functions) [verify in-app].
What to skip: Skip Chapters 8, 9, 11, and 12.
Key takeaway: A function (def clamp_cmd(cmd):) is a reusable machine: you feed input numbers into its parameters inside the parentheses, and the return keyword hands the computed answer back to the caller so later code can store it in a variable. Never confuse return with print(): print() only displays text on screen and hands back None!
Alternative resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 0 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact heading Def.

Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 2 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading While Loops.
What to skip: Skip Dictionaries and Mario.
Key takeaway: A while loop (while step < 5:) checks its condition before every pass and repeats its indented body as long as the condition is True. You must always update the loop counter (step = step + 1) inside the while block so the loop eventually stops!

In Lesson P.3, you wrote an if / elif / else block to clamp an actuator command into [0, 255]. What if you need to clamp 20 different commands across your robot program? Instead of copy-pasting the same 6 lines 20 times, you wrap them once inside a function:
Here, cmd is the input parameter, and return sends the clamped number back to wherever clamp_cmd(...) was called. If a function uses print(cmd) instead of return cmd, Python returns the empty value None, and any math that tries to use the result will crash with a TypeError.
Functions pair naturally with while loops when simulating motion or control loops over time: as long as step < num_steps (or pos_m < target_m), the while loop calls your step function to advance position and increments step = step + 1.

A while loop repeats its indented block as long as its condition remains True.

pages.title: Loading Modules (import) and Automated Self-Checks (assert)

sections.t:
Load built-in math tools (math.sqrt, math.pi) using import math, and write automated self-checks (assert) so your code verifies its own calculations automatically.
New ideas (max 2):
Loading standard-library modules with import: Using import math at the top of a script to unlock square roots (math.sqrt), $\pi$ (math.pi), and trigonometry.
Automated self-checks with assert: Writing assert condition so Python immediately flags an AssertionError if a function returns the wrong number.
New syntax: import math, math.sqrt(x), round(val, digits), assert condition.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours
Lesson P.5: Reusable Functions (def/return) & while Loops

sections.h: Idea 1: Loading standard-library modules with import
sections.t:
Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 4 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Libraries and Random (see how import loads a module at the top of a file and calls functions using dot notation module.func()).
What to skip: Skip Command-Line Arguments, slice, Packages, and APIs.
Key takeaway: Python keeps specialized tools organized inside built-in modules (libraries). Writing import math at the top of your script loads the math module so you can call math.sqrt(25.0) ($\sqrt{25} = 5.0$) or use the constant math.pi ($\pi \approx 3.14159265$).

Primary resource: Harvard CS50P Lecture 5 Notes [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Unit Tests and assert.
What to skip: Skip pytest, Testing Strings, and Organizing Tests into Folders.
Key takeaway: Instead of checking printed numbers by eye every time you edit a script, assert condition tests your code automatically: if condition is True, Python continues silently; if False, Python stops immediately on that line with an AssertionError.

When calculating the straight-line distance from a robot's shoulder joint at $(0, 0)$ to a target at $(x, y)$, we use the Pythagorean theorem $d = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. Instead of raising to the $0.5$ power, we load Python's built-in math module at the top of our file with import math and call math.sqrt((x 2) + (y 2)).
How do professional robotics engineers make sure a bug never slips into a formula? They write unit tests right below their functions using assert. For example, we know a $3\text{–}4\text{–}5$ right triangle ($x = 3.0\text{ m}, y = 4.0\text{ m}$) has hypotenuse $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5.0\text{ m}$. Writing:
runs an automatic safety check every time the script starts. When comparing decimal float results that might have tiny rounding tails (like 0.30000000000000004), wrap the value in round(value, 4) inside your assertion (assert round(val, 4) == 0.3) so the check compares to 4 decimal places.

NameError: name 'math' is not defined: You called math.sqrt(...) without putting import math at the top of the file.
NameError: name 'sqrt' is not defined: After import math, you must write math.sqrt(x) with the math. prefix, not bare sqrt(x).
AssertionError with no message: Look at the line number printed in the traceback—the expression after assert on that line evaluated to False. Print the actual return value of your function right above the assert line to see what it computed.

What assert does when True vs. False: What happens when Python executes assert 2 + 2 == 4, and what happens when it executes assert 2 + 2 == 5?
Answer
assert 2 + 2 == 4 succeeds silently and moves to the next line. assert 2 + 2 == 5 immediately stops the program and raises an AssertionError.
Using math.sqrt: What value does math.sqrt((6.0 2) + (8.0 2)) return?
Answer
10.0 ($\sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10.0$).
Why round floats in assert? Why is assert round(0.1 + 0.2, 4) == 0.3 safer than assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3?
Answer
Because computer floating-point numbers store 0.1 + 0.2 as 0.30000000000000004, so exact == 0.3 fails! Rounding with round(..., 4) compares to 4 decimal places (0.3 == 0.3).

import math loads Python's standard math library (math.sqrt, math.pi).
assert condition automatically verifies that functions return the expected results.

pages.title: Base SI Units and Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)

sections.t:
Identify the base SI units (m, kg, s) and unit symbols (A, V, Ω) used in mechatronics, and convert values with metric prefixes (M, k, m, µ) into base units before plugging them into equations.
New ideas (max 2):
Base SI units for mechatronics: Why engineering formulas require standard base units (meters m, kilograms kg, seconds s, plus electrical unit symbols A, V, Ω).
Metric prefixes (M, k, m, µ): Scaling numbers by powers of $1{,}000$ (mega $= 10^6$, kilo $= 10^3$, milli $= 10^{-3}$, micro $= 10^{-6}$).
New syntax: Python scientific notation 1e6, 1e3, 1e-3, 1e-6.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–2.5 hours

Lesson P.2: Computer Arithmetic and Order of Operations
Lesson P.6: Loading Modules (import) & Automated Self-Checks (assert)

sections.h: Idea 1: Base SI units for mechatronics
sections.t:
Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Metric System of Measurement [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Metric System of Measurement, Meter, Kilogram, and Second.
What to skip: Skip Volume (liters) and Temperature.
Key takeaway: Every equation in physics and engineering assumes your numbers are expressed in base SI units: length in meters (m), mass in kilograms (kg), time in seconds (s), Amperes (A), Volts (V), and Ohms (Ω).

sections.h: Idea 2: Metric prefixes (M, k, m, µ)
sections.t:
Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Metric Numbers (Kilo, Mega, Milli, Micro) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Metric Numbers, Common Big and Small Numbers, and Much Bigger and Smaller.
What to skip: Skip tera, peta, exa, and femto—in beginner mechatronics you primarily use M, k, m, and µ.
Key takeaway: A metric prefix is a multiplier placed in front of a unit: mega (M) $= \times 1{,}000{,}000$ ($10^6$), kilo (k) $= \times 1{,}000$ ($10^3$), milli (m) $= \div 1{,}000$ ($10^{-3}$), and micro (µ or u) $= \div 1{,}000{,}000$ ($10^{-6}$). Always convert prefixed numbers into base SI units before multiplying or dividing!

Mixing un-converted prefixes into an equation is the #1 calculation error in beginner robotics. Every formula you will meet in this roadmap—such as distance ($d = s \cdot t$) and kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m s^2$)—strictly expects un-prefixed base SI units: meters (m), kilograms (kg), seconds (s), Amperes (A), Volts (V), and Ohms (Ω).
For example, if a datasheet says a sensor is $15\text{ mm}$ (millimeters) wide or a pulse lasts $500\ \mu\text{s}$ (microseconds) and you forget to convert to meters or seconds before multiplying, your answer will be off by a factor of $1{,}000\times$ or $1{,}000{,}000\times$! Follow a two-step habit on every problem:
Convert all inputs to base SI units on the very first line of code (so $15\text{ mA} \rightarrow 0.015\text{ A}$, $0.22\text{ k}\Omega \rightarrow 220\ \Omega$, and $250\text{ mm} \rightarrow 0.25\text{ m}$).
Run the formula purely in base SI units, and only convert back to mA, ms, or mm at the end if a display label needs it. In Python, scientific notation (1e-3 for $10^{-3} = 0.001$ and 1e-6 for $10^{-6} = 0.000001$) makes prefix conversion clean and typo-proof:

Confusing lowercase m (milli $= 10^{-3}$) with uppercase M (mega $= 10^6$): Those two letters differ by a factor of one billion ($10^9$)! A $10\text{ mm}$ spacer is $0.01\text{ m}$, whereas $10\text{ M}\Omega$ is $10{,}000{,}000\ \Omega$.
Multiplying instead of dividing for milli or micro: Ask yourself: "Is a millimeter smaller or larger than a meter?" Smaller—so $250\text{ mm} = 0.25\text{ m}$, never $250{,}000\text{ m}$.

Prefix conversion drill: Convert each measurement into its base SI unit: (a) $250\text{ mm}$ to m, (b) $4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ to Ω, and (c) $100\ \mu\text{s}$ to s.
Answer
(a) $250\text{ mm} = 250 \div 1000 = \mathbf{0.25\text{ m}}$
(b) $4.7\text{ k}\Omega = 4.7 \times 1000 = \mathbf{4{,}700\ \Omega}$
(c) $100\ \mu\text{s} = 100 \div 1{,}000{,}000 = \mathbf{0.0001\text{ s}}$ (100e-6)
Multiplying converted units: If $I = 0.5\text{ mA}$ and $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, what is the product $I \times R$ after converting both to base units (A and Ω)?
Answer
Convert first: $I = 0.5\text{ mA} = 0.0005\text{ A}$ and $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega = 10{,}000\ \Omega$. Then $0.0005 \times 10{,}000 = \mathbf{5.0\text{ V}}$.
Time conversion: How many milliseconds (ms) and how many microseconds (µs) are in $0.002\text{ s}$?
Answer
$0.002\text{ s} \times 1000 = \mathbf{2.0\text{ ms}}$, and $0.002\text{ s} \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \mathbf{2{,}000\ \mu\text{s}}$.

Always convert measurements into base SI units (m, kg, s, A, V, Ω) before plugging them into formulas.
Mega (M) $= 10^6$, kilo (k) $= 10^3$, milli (m) $= 10^{-3}$, and micro (µ) $= 10^{-6}$.

pages.title: Cycle Frequency (Hz), Period (T = 1/f) and Binary Bits (2^N)

sections.t:
Convert between a repeating signal's frequency ($f$, in Hertz Hz) and its period ($T = 1/f$, in seconds), and use powers of 2 ($2^N$) to calculate the exact integer range of an $N$-bit microcontroller register.
New ideas (max 2):
Cycle frequency (Hz) and period ($T = 1/f$): Relating how many cycles happen per second (Hz) to the time duration of a single cycle ($T = \frac{1}{f}$).
Binary bits and powers of 2 ($2^N$): Why $N$ digital bits (0 or 1) represent $2^N$ distinct integers from 0 to $2^N - 1$ (explaining 0..255 for 8-bit and 0..1023 for 10-bit).
New syntax: 1.0 / freq_hz, (2 n_bits) - 1.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson P.2: Computer Arithmetic and Order of Operations
Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)

Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Frequency and Period of a Wave [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading Frequency and Period of a Wave (specifically the reciprocal formulas $f = 1/T$ and $T = 1/f$).
What to skip: Skip the bottom pendulum/mass-on-a-spring practice questions once $T = 1/f$ is clear.
Key takeaway: Frequency ($f$, measured in Hertz Hz, where $1\text{ Hz} = 1\text{ cycle per second}$) counts how many times a control loop or switching signal repeats each second. Period ($T$, measured in seconds s) is the time duration of one cycle. They are exact reciprocals: $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and $f = \frac{1}{T}$.

sections.h: Idea 2: Binary bits and powers of 2 ($2^N$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Binary [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Why Binary?, Counting in binary, and Converting binary to decimal.
What to skip: Skip Bitwise Operators, Hexadecimal, and Two's Complement (not needed until Track 04).
Key takeaway: Digital circuits store numbers using bits (binary digits that are either 0 for OFF or 1 for ON). Each extra bit doubles the number of possible combinations, so an $N$-bit register has $2^N$ states numbered from 0 up to $2^N - 1$.
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Binary Number System [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings How do we Count using Binary? and Position (powers of 2: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \dots$).

Two sets of numbers appear in almost every microcontroller program you will ever write:
First, frequency ($f$) and period ($T$) are two ways of describing the same clock tick:
A standard hobby pulse repeats at $f = 50\text{ Hz}$, so each cycle lasts $T = \frac{1}{50\text{ Hz}} = 0.020\text{ s} = 20\text{ ms}$.
A fast robot control loop runs at $f = 1\text{ kHz}$ ($1{,}000\text{ Hz}$), so each time step is $T = \frac{1}{1000\text{ Hz}} = 0.001\text{ s} = 1.0\text{ ms}$.
Second, binary bits ($2^N$) explain why microcontrollers use seemingly strange maximum numbers like 255 and 1023 instead of 100 or 1000:
8-bit register (1 byte, used by 8-bit output commands): $2^8 = 256$ states $\rightarrow$ integers 0 to 255 ($2^8 - 1$).
10-bit register (used by 10-bit sensor inputs): $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ states $\rightarrow$ integers 0 to 1023 ($2^{10} - 1$).
12-bit register (used by 12-bit sensor inputs in later tracks): $2^{12} = 4{,}096$ states $\rightarrow$ integers 0 to 4095 ($2^{12} - 1$).
Because counting starts at 0, the maximum integer is always $2^N - 1$.

In TODO 1, 1.0 / freq_hz gives seconds, and multiplying by 1000.0 converts seconds to milliseconds (ms). In TODO 2, use for powers of 2: (2 n_bits) - 1.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Saying an 8-bit register goes up to 256 instead of 255: There are $2^8 = 256$ total values, but because 0 uses the first slot, the highest number is $256 - 1 = \mathbf{255}$.
Forgetting to convert kHz to Hz before taking $1/f$: For a $20\text{ kHz}$ switching wave, convert $20\text{ kHz} = 20{,}000\text{ Hz}$ first so $T = \frac{1}{20{,}000} = 0.00005\text{ s} = 50\ \mu\text{s}$.

Period to frequency: A control loop executes once every $T = 0.5\text{ ms}$ ($0.0005\text{ s}$). What is its frequency $f$ in Hz and in kHz?
Answer
$f = \frac{1}{0.0005\text{ s}} = \mathbf{2{,}000\text{ Hz}} = \mathbf{2.0\text{ kHz}}$.
Why 1023? In one sentence, explain why a 10-bit sensor register returns a maximum of 1023 instead of 1000.
Answer
Because a 10-bit binary register has $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ possible states, and starting the count at 0 makes the highest state $1024 - 1 = \mathbf{1023}$.
4-bit range: How many total states does a 4-bit binary number have, and what is its maximum integer value?
Answer
$2^4 = \mathbf{16\text{ states}}$, ranging from 0 to $2^4 - 1 = \mathbf{15}$.

Frequency ($f$, in Hz) and period ($T$, in s) are reciprocals: $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and $f = \frac{1}{T}$.
An $N$-bit binary register stores $2^N$ integers from 0 to $2^N - 1$ (0..255 for 8-bit, 0..1023 for 10-bit).

pages.title: Rearranging Physics Formulas and Linear Range Scaling

sections.t:
Rearrange physics formulas to isolate any unknown variable on the left side of =, and linearly map 10-bit sensor counts (0..1023) into physical units (0..5.0) or 8-bit actuator commands (0..255).
New ideas (max 2):
Rearranging three-variable physics formulas: Doing the exact same opposite operation to both sides of an equation to solve for any unknown variable ($d = s \cdot t \leftrightarrow s = d/t \leftrightarrow t = d/s$).
Linear range scaling: Converting a number from an input interval $[0, X_{\max}]$ to an output interval $[0, Y_{\max}]$ via the fraction of full scale $\left(\frac{x}{X_{\max}}\right) \times Y_{\max}$.
New syntax: None (uses Python functions and arithmetic from Lessons P.2 and P.5).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson P.5: Reusable Functions (def/return) & while Loops
Lesson P.8: Cycle Frequency (Hz), Period & Binary Bits

Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Algebra: Balance when Adding and Subtracting / Multiplying [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Solve It and Balance (applying the opposite operation to both sides of =).
What to skip: Skip multi-variable polynomial factoring links.
Key takeaway: An equation is a balanced scale: to isolate an unknown variable, undo whatever is attached to it by performing the opposite operation on both sides. If the unknown is multiplied by $t$ ($d = s \cdot t$), divide both sides by $t$ to get $s = \frac{d}{t}$; if an offset $x_0$ is added ($x_{\text{total}} = s \cdot t + x_0$), subtract $x_0$ from both sides first to get $s \cdot t = x_{\text{total}} - x_0$.

Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Proportions [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Proportions, Working With Proportions, and Using Proportions to Solve Percents.
What to skip: Skip Using Proportions to Solve Triangles at the bottom of the page.
Key takeaway: A proportion like $\frac{x}{1023} = \frac{y}{5.0}$ says that the sensor reading's fraction of full scale (x / 1023.0, a number between 0.0 and 1.0) equals the output's fraction of $5.0$. Multiplying both sides by $5.0$ gives $y = \left(\frac{x}{1023.0}\right) \times 5.0$.

In mechatronics, you do not need to memorize three separate formulas for every physical law—you only need one formula and the balance rule:
Start with distance equals speed times time: $d = s \cdot t$.
Need speed $s$? Divide both sides by $t$: $s = \frac{d}{t}$.
Need time $t$? Divide both sides by $s$: $t = \frac{d}{s}$.
What if an equation has both addition and multiplication, like a cart starting at offset $x_0$ ($x_{\text{final}} = s \cdot t + x_0$)? Undo addition/subtraction first by subtracting $x_0$ from both sides ($x_{\text{final}} - x_0 = s \cdot t$), and then divide both sides by $t$:
The exact same algebra powers linear range scaling. Whenever you map a 10-bit reading $x \in [0, X_{\max}]$ into a target range $y \in [0, Y_{\max}]$:
Divide by the input maximum to get the normalized fraction $\frac{x}{X_{\max}} \in [0.0, 1.0]$.
Multiply that fraction by the output maximum $Y_{\max}$: $y = \left(\frac{x}{X_{\max}}\right) \times Y_{\max}$.

Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Dividing before subtracting when rearranging $x_{\text{final}} = s \cdot t + x_0$: Writing $s = \frac{x_{\text{final}}}{t} - x_0$ is wrong because $t$ only multiplies $s$, not $x_0$. Subtract $x_0$ from both sides first to get $x_{\text{final}} - x_0 = s \cdot t$, then divide the entire left side by $t$: $s = \frac{x_{\text{final}} - x_0}{t}$.
Multiplying by 1023.0 / 5.0 instead of 5.0 / 1023.0: Check your endpoints! When raw_10bit = 1023, the scaled output must equal 5.0, which requires (1023 / 1023.0) 5.0 = 5.0.

Rearranging a motion equation: The velocity of an accelerating cart is $v = a \cdot t + v_0$. Rearrange this equation to solve for the acceleration $a$.
Answer
Subtract $v_0$ from both sides ($v - v_0 = a \cdot t$), then divide both sides by $t$ to get $a = \frac{v - v_0}{t}$ ((v - v0) / t).
Scaling a 10-bit reading: If a 10-bit sensor (0..1023) returns 682 on a 5.0-unit full scale, what fraction of full scale is the sensor at, and what is the scaled value?
Answer
The fraction is $\frac{682}{1023} = \mathbf{\frac{2}{3} \approx 0.6667}$ ($66.7\%$), and the scaled value is $0.6667 \times 5.0 = \mathbf{3.33}$.
Inverse scaling: Rearrange $y = \left(\frac{x}{1023}\right) \times 5.0$ to solve for $x$ when $y = 1.25$.
Answer
$x = \left(\frac{y}{5.0}\right) \times 1023 = \left(\frac{1.25}{5.0}\right) \times 1023 = 0.25 \times 1023 = \mathbf{255.75}$ (which rounds to integer count 256).

sections.h: Independence check — a week later, no formula supplied
sections.t:
The starter above hands you every expression in a comment, so it tests translation more than derivation. This one does the opposite, on different numbers, with the formula left out. Do it a week after the lesson, closed book: read the word problem, write the three unit sentences on paper, then code. If you have to open the hint or the answer to finish, mark the attempt assisted and redo it a week later without looking — that second attempt is the one that counts.
The job. A belt-driven gantry: a 200 full-step/rev stepper, a driver at 16 microsteps per full step, a 5:1 gearbox on the output, a 20-tooth pulley and a 2.0 mm belt pitch. The carriage must travel 137.5 mm, and that move takes 0.55 s at constant speed.
Before writing code, complete these three sentences with units as well as numbers:
One motor microstep turns the output shaft by ______ revolutions.
One output revolution moves the belt ______ mm.
So one microstep moves the carriage ______ mm, and one millimetre is ______ microsteps.
Now write the three functions. The docstrings must state the unit of what comes back — that sentence is part of the answer, not decoration.
Answer and the units sentence
One motor microstep is 1 / (200 × 16) = 1/3200 of a motor revolution, and the 5:1 gearbox turns that into 1/16000 of an output revolution. One output revolution pays out 20 × 2.0 = 40 mm of belt, so one microstep moves the carriage 40 / 16000 = 0.0025 mm, and one millimetre is 16000 / 40 = 400 microsteps. 137.5 mm × 400 = 55000 microsteps, and 137.5 mm / 0.55 s = 250.0 mm/s.
The units sentence that has to come first: millimetres per microstep is a length divided by a count, so it gets smaller as the gearing gets finer; microsteps per millimetre is its reciprocal and gets larger. Choosing the reciprocal by accident gives 400 mm per microstep, which the endpoint test catches: put 137.5 through 400 and the move is 0.34 mm, not 137.5.

Isolate an unknown variable by performing the opposite operation on both sides of = (undoing addition/subtraction before multiplication/division).
Linear scaling multiplies the input's fraction of full scale $\left(\frac{x}{X_{\max}}\right)$ by the target full scale $Y_{\max}$.

pages.title: Radians, Rotational Speed (rad/s) and Right-Triangle Trigonometry

sections.t:
Convert angles between degrees and radians ($\pi\text{ rad} = 180^\circ$) and motor speeds between RPM and rad/s, and use math.cos(), math.sin(), and math.atan2(y, x) to compute 2D robot arm geometry.
New ideas (max 2):
Measuring angles in radians and rotational speed (rad/s): Why one full turn ($360^\circ$) equals $2\pi\text{ radians}$, and how to convert revolutions per minute (RPM) into radians per second (rad/s).
Right-triangle trigonometry (cos, sin, atan2): Finding a robot link's horizontal reach $x = L\cos\theta$ and vertical height $y = L\sin\theta$, and recovering $\theta = \text{atan2}(y, x)$ in any quadrant.
New syntax: math.pi, math.radians(deg), math.degrees(rad), math.cos(rad), math.sin(rad), math.atan2(y, x).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.6: Loading Modules (import) & Automated Self-Checks (assert)
Lesson P.9: Rearranging Physics Formulas & Linear Range Scaling

sections.h: Idea 1: Measuring angles in radians and rotational speed (rad/s)
sections.t:
Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Radians [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Radians and Radians and Degrees.
What to skip: Skip the bottom arc-area exercises once $\pi\text{ rad} = 180^\circ$ is clear.
Key takeaway: A radian (rad) is the natural angle unit where walking 1 radius around a circle sweeps out $1\text{ radian}$ ($\approx 57.3^\circ$). Because a full circle's circumference is $2\pi r$, one full revolution ($360^\circ$) is $2\pi\text{ radians}$ ($\approx 6.283\text{ rad}$) and a half-turn ($180^\circ$) is $\pi\text{ radians}$. Consequently, converting motor speed from Revolutions Per Minute (RPM) into SI radians per second (rad/s) multiplies by $\frac{2\pi\text{ rad}}{60\text{ s}}$.
Alternative resource: BetterExplained — Intuitive Guide to Angles, Degrees and Radians [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Radians Rule, Degrees Drool, Radians: The Unselfish Choice, and Using Radians.

Primary resource: MathsIsFun — Sine, Cosine and Tangent [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Right Triangle, Sine, Cosine and Tangent, and Sohcahtoa.
What to skip: Skip Less Common Functions (secant, cosecant, cotangent).
Key takeaway: When a robot arm link of length $L$ (the hypotenuse) tilts upward by angle $\theta$ from the horizontal $x$-axis, its horizontal reach is $x = L\cos(\theta)$ and its vertical height is $y = L\sin(\theta)$. To go backward from target coordinates $(x, y)$ to joint angle $\theta$, always use four-quadrant inverse tangent math.atan2(y, x) (which takes y first, then x).
Optional extra: PhET — Trig Tour Interactive Simulation [verify in-app] — Drag the point around the circle with Radians selected [verify in-app] to watch $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ change live.

Every programming language (Python, C, C++, MATLAB) expects angles inside cos() and sin() to be in radians, never degrees! A radian measures an angle by the distance walked around a unit circle of radius $r = 1$: walking halfway around the circle ($180^\circ$) covers $\pi \approx 3.1416\text{ radians}$, and walking a full turn ($360^\circ$) covers $2\pi \approx 6.2832\text{ radians}$. Use these two conversion rules constantly:
Degrees $\leftrightarrow$ Radians: $\text{rad} = \text{deg} \times \frac{\pi}{180}$ (math.radians(deg)), and $\text{deg} = \text{rad} \times \frac{180}{\pi}$ (math.degrees(rad)).
RPM $\rightarrow$ rad/s (Angular Velocity $\omega$): Motor datasheets list rotational speed in Revolutions Per Minute (RPM), whereas physics equations need radians per second (rad/s). Since $1\text{ rev} = 2\pi\text{ rad}$ and $1\text{ minute} = 60\text{ s}$:
Across this entire roadmap, we measure a robot arm link's angle $\theta$ upward from the horizontal $x$-axis ($\theta = 0^\circ$ = horizontal pointing right; $\theta = 90^\circ = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ = pointing straight up):
Horizontal distance from pivot: $x = L \cdot \cos(\theta)$
Vertical height above pivot: $y = L \cdot \sin(\theta)$
Angle from target $(x, y)$: $\theta = \text{atan2}(y, x)$ (math.atan2(y, x) in Python, which takes y first and safely handles $x = 0$ and all four quadrants).

When all three TODOs are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
At 60.0 RPM (1 revolution per second), rpm_to_rad_s(60.0) should return $2\pi \approx 6.2832\text{ rad/s}$. In arm_tip_xy, convert rad = math.radians(angle_deg) before calling math.cos(rad) and math.sin(rad).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Passing degrees directly into math.cos(60): math.cos(60) computes the cosine of 60 radians (-0.9524), NOT $60^\circ$ (+0.5)! Always call math.radians(deg) first.
Swapping arguments in math.atan2(y, x): atan2 takes vertical y first and horizontal x second (math.atan2(y, x)), because $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{y}{x}$.

Degrees to radians: How many radians are in $360^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and $0^\circ$?
Answer
$360^\circ = \mathbf{2\pi\text{ rad}}$ ($\approx 6.283$), $180^\circ = \mathbf{\pi\text{ rad}}$ ($\approx 3.142$), $90^\circ = \mathbf{\pi/2\text{ rad}}$ ($\approx 1.571$), and $0^\circ = \mathbf{0\text{ rad}}$.
RPM to rad/s: A gearmotor shaft spins at $300\text{ RPM}$. How many revolutions per second is that, and what is its angular velocity $\omega$ in rad/s?
Answer
$\frac{300}{60} = 5\text{ rev/s}$, so $\omega = 5 \times 2\pi = 10\pi \approx \mathbf{31.42\text{ rad/s}}$.
Horizontal reach at $0^\circ$ vs. $90^\circ$: For a link of length $L = 0.25\text{ m}$ at angle $\theta$ from horizontal, what is the horizontal reach $x = L\cos\theta$ when $\theta = 0^\circ$ (horizontal) versus when $\theta = 90^\circ$ (straight up)?
Answer
At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $\cos(0) = 1$, so horizontal reach is the full length $x = \mathbf{0.25\text{ m}}$. At $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\cos(90^\circ) = 0$, so horizontal reach is $\mathbf{0.0\text{ m}}$ (the tip is directly above the pivot).

One full turn ($360^\circ$) is $2\pi\text{ radians}$, and rotational speed converts via $\omega_{\text{rad/s}} = \text{RPM} \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$.
For a link of length $L$ at angle $\theta$ from the horizontal $x$-axis, $x = L\cos\theta$, $y = L\sin\theta$, and $\theta = \text{atan2}(y, x)$.

pages.title: Reading Time-Series Graphs — Slope and Area

sections.t:
Read position-vs-time and velocity-vs-time telemetry plots by connecting slope ($\Delta y / \Delta t$) to rate of change (velocity and acceleration) and rectangle area ($v \cdot \Delta t$) to accumulated displacement.
New ideas (max 2):
Graph slope as rate of change: Computing $\text{slope} = \frac{y_{\text{now}} - y_{\text{prev}}}{\Delta t}$ to find velocity from a position graph or acceleration from a velocity graph.
Area under a curve as accumulated change: Multiplying height by time step ($v \cdot \Delta t$) to accumulate change in position (pos = pos + vel dt).
New syntax: None (uses Python for loops and functions from Lessons P.4 and P.5).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.4: Ordered Lists & Repeating Actions with for Loops
Lesson P.5: Reusable Functions (def/return) & while Loops

sections.h: Idea 1: Graph slope as rate of change
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Meaning of Slope for a p-t Graph [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading Meaning of Slope for a p-t Graph.
What to skip: Skip the bottom "Check Your Understanding" widgets if the rise-over-run example is clear.
Key takeaway: On any time-series graph (where horizontal axis = time $t$), the slope ($\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}$) is the rate of change of the vertical quantity. On a position-vs-time graph, slope is velocity ($v = \frac{x_{\text{now}} - x_{\text{prev}}}{\Delta t}$); on a velocity-vs-time graph, slope is acceleration ($a = \frac{v_{\text{now}} - v_{\text{prev}}}{\Delta t}$).
Alternative resource: The Physics Classroom — Determining the Slope on a p-t Graph [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact heading Using the Slope Equation.

sections.h: Idea 2: Area under a curve as accumulated change
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Determining the Area on a v-t Graph [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Determining the Area on a v-t Graph and Calculating the Area of a Rectangle.
What to skip: Skip Calculating the Area of a Triangle and trapezoid exercises (in computer simulations with small time step $\Delta t$, each step is a narrow rectangle vel dt).
Key takeaway: On a velocity-vs-time graph, the area of a rectangle slice of height $v$ and width $\Delta t$ equals the displacement (change in position $\Delta x = v \cdot \Delta t$) during that slice. Adding up those rectangles in a loop (pos = pos + vel dt) is how every physics simulator advances position over time!
Alternative resource: The Physics Classroom — Meaning of Shape for a v-t Graph [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings The Importance of Slope and Positive Velocity versus Negative Velocity.

Every telemetry plot in robotics puts time ($t$, in seconds) on the horizontal axis. You can read any time-series plot using just two geometric ideas—slope and rectangle area:
Slope = Rate of Change (Dividing by $\Delta t$):
Between two sensor samples separated by time step $\Delta t$, the change is $\Delta x = x_{\text{now}} - x_{\text{prev}}$ (where the triangle symbol $\Delta$, capital Greek Delta, simply means "change in").
Velocity is the slope of position: vel = (pos_now - pos_prev) / dt_s.
Acceleration is the slope of velocity: acc = (vel_now - vel_prev) / dt_s.
A flat horizontal line has slope 0 (stationary on a position graph; constant speed on a velocity graph). A downward-sloping line has a negative rate of change.
Rectangle Area = Accumulation (Multiplying by $\Delta t$):
Over one short time step $\Delta t$, a robot moving at velocity $v$ covers distance $\Delta x = v \cdot \Delta t$—the exact area ($\text{height} \times \text{width}$) of that slice under the velocity graph!
Adding each slice in a loop (pos = pos + vel dt_s) accumulates total position.

What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

sections.t: Complete slope_velocity (TODO 1) and accumulate_positions (TODO 2) to compute velocity from two position readings and accumulate position across 5 velocity steps of $\Delta t = 0.5\text{ s}$:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, subtract pos_now_m - pos_prev_m in parentheses before dividing by dt_s. In TODO 2, update pos_m = pos_m + (v dt_s) before calling history.append(round(pos_m, 2)).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Subtracting pos_prev - pos_now (backward sign): Rate of change is always new_value - old_value divided by dt_s. Reversing the subtraction flips the sign of velocity!
Forgetting to multiply by dt_s when accumulating area: Writing pos_m = pos_m + v pretends $\Delta t = 1.0\text{ s}$. Always multiply height v by width dt_s: pos_m = pos_m + (v dt_s).

Slope from a position graph: At $t = 1.0\text{ s}$, a robot is at $x = 0.20\text{ m}$. At $t = 3.0\text{ s}$, it is at $x = 1.40\text{ m}$. What is its velocity (slope) in m/s?
Answer
$v = \frac{1.40 - 0.20}{3.0 - 1.0} = \frac{1.20\text{ m}}{2.0\text{ s}} = \mathbf{0.60\text{ m/s}}$.
Signed area under a velocity graph: If a wheel moves backward at $v = -0.50\text{ m/s}$ for $\Delta t = 0.4\text{ s}$, what is its change in position $\Delta x$?
Answer
$\Delta x = (-0.50\text{ m/s}) \times 0.4\text{ s} = \mathbf{-0.20\text{ m}}$ ($20\text{ cm}$ backward).
Acceleration as the slope of velocity: A motor's speed drops from $1.60\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$ to $0.0\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 2.5\text{ s}$. What is its acceleration $a$ in $\text{m/s}^2$?
Answer
$a = \frac{0.0 - 1.60}{2.5 - 2.0} = \frac{-1.60}{0.5} = \mathbf{-3.20\text{ m/s}^2}$ (braking deceleration).

Slope ($\Delta y / \Delta t$) measures rate of change: slope of position is velocity, and slope of velocity is acceleration.
Rectangle area ($v \cdot \Delta t$) under a velocity graph measures change in position (pos = pos + vel dt_s).

pages.title: Linear Forces (F = ma) and Lever Torque (tau = m*g*L*cos(theta))

sections.t:
Calculate linear forces ($F = ma$) and gravitational weight ($W = mg$), and compute the lever torque ($\tau = F \cdot r_\perp = m g L \cos\theta$) required for a robot joint to hold a payload at any angle $\theta$ measured from the horizontal.
New ideas (max 2):
Linear force ($F = ma$) and gravitational weight ($W = mg$): Distinguishing mass (kg) from downward gravitational force in Newtons (N, $W = m \cdot 9.81$), and relating net force to acceleration ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$).
Lever torque from horizontal arm angle ($\tau = mgL\cos\theta$): Computing rotational twisting effort in Newton-meters (N·m) as downward weight $W = mg$ times the perpendicular horizontal lever arm $r_\perp = L\cos\theta$.
New syntax: None (uses math.cos(math.radians(theta_deg)) from Lesson P.10).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.10: Radians, Rotational Speed (rad/s) & Right-Triangle Trigonometry
Lesson P.11: Reading Time-Series Graphs — Slope & Area

sections.h: Idea 1: Linear force ($F = ma$) and gravitational weight ($W = mg$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Newton's Second Law [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Newton's Second Law and The BIG Equation ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$).
What to skip: Skip the bottom multi-force free-body quiz table until you read the Bridge Notes below.
Key takeaway: Mass ($m$, in kilograms kg) measures how much matter an object contains. Force ($F$, in Newtons N) is a push or pull. Newton's Second Law states that net force equals mass times acceleration ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$). On Earth, gravity pulls every mass downward with acceleration $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, creating downward weight force $W = m \cdot g$ (so a $1.0\text{ kg}$ payload weighs $9.81\text{ N}$).
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Force [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Force, Unbalanced, Newtons, and Calculations.

sections.h: Idea 2: Lever torque from horizontal arm angle ($\tau = mgL\cos\theta$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: HyperPhysics — Torque [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading Torque = Force applied x lever arm (specifically the definition that the lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot axis to the line of action of the force).
What to skip: Skip 3D vector cross-product determinant notation ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$)—in 2D planar joints, perpendicular lever arm distance is all we need!
Key takeaway: Torque ($\tau$, Greek letter tau, measured in Newton-meters N·m) is rotational twisting effort around a pivot: $\tau = \text{Force} \times \text{Perpendicular Lever Arm}$. When a robot arm of length $L$ holds a payload of weight $W = mg$ at angle $\theta$ measured from the horizontal ($0^\circ$ = horizontal, $90^\circ$ = straight up), gravity pulls straight down vertically, so the perpendicular lever arm is the horizontal reach $r_\perp = L\cos\theta$ from Lesson P.10—giving $\tau_{\text{grav}} = m \cdot g \cdot L \cos\theta$!
Optional extra: PhET — Torque Interactive Simulation [verify in-app] — Adjust the Applied Force and Radius sliders [verify in-app] to see torque scale with lever arm distance.

We use one consistent angle convention for robot arm links everywhere in this roadmap:
Arm angle $\theta$ is always measured upward from the horizontal $x$-axis ($\theta = 0^\circ$ when stretched out horizontally; $\theta = 90^\circ$ when pointing straight up).
Gravity pulls a tip payload $m$ straight down with vertical weight force $W = m \cdot g$ ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
By definition, the lever arm ($r_\perp$) is the perpendicular horizontal distance from the joint pivot to that vertical line of gravity force—which you already calculated in Lesson P.10 as the horizontal coordinate $x = L\cos\theta$!
Multiplying the downward weight $W = mg$ by the horizontal lever arm $r_\perp = L\cos\theta$ gives the gravity torque formula used across the entire roadmap:
Check the two physical extremes:
Horizontal ($\theta = 0^\circ$): $\cos(0^\circ) = 1.0$, so $r_\perp = L$ and gravity torque is at its maximum ($\tau_{\text{grav}} = mgL$).
Straight up ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $\cos(90^\circ) = 0.0$, so $r_\perp = 0$ (the weight sits directly over the pivot) and gravity torque is $0.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, multiply mass_kg 9.81. In TODO 2, convert angle_from_horiz_deg to radians with math.radians(...) before calling math.cos(...), then multiply weight_newtons(mass_kg) length_m math.cos(rad).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Using mass m (0.50 kg) directly as force without multiplying by g = 9.81 m/s²: Multiplying 0.50 kg 0.30 m gives 0.15 kg·m, which is off by nearly $10\times$! Always multiply mass by 9.81 first to get force in Newtons (N).
Forgetting to convert link length from mm or cm to meters (m): Torque is measured in Newton-meters (N·m). A $30\text{ cm}$ ($300\text{ mm}$) link must be entered as 0.30 meters.

Mass vs. weight: A robot gripper has a mass of $m = 0.20\text{ kg}$. What is its downward weight force $W$ in Newtons (N) on Earth ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$)?
Answer
$W = 0.20\text{ kg} \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2 = \mathbf{1.962\text{ N}}$.
Net force & acceleration: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ wheeled robot is pushed forward by a $6.0\text{ N}$ wheel traction force while opposed by $1.0\text{ N}$ of rolling friction ($F_{\text{net}} = 6.0 - 1.0 = 5.0\text{ N}$). What is its forward acceleration $a = F_{\text{net}} / m$?
Answer
$a = \frac{5.0\text{ N}}{2.0\text{ kg}} = \mathbf{2.5\text{ m/s}^2}$.
Horizontal vs. tilted torque: Why does holding the $0.50\text{ kg}$ mass on a $0.30\text{ m}$ link at $\theta = 60^\circ$ above horizontal require exactly half the torque ($0.7358\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) of holding it at $\theta = 0^\circ$ horizontal ($1.4715\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$)?
Answer
Because at $\theta = 60^\circ$ above horizontal, the perpendicular horizontal lever arm shrinks to $r_\perp = L\cos(60^\circ) = 0.5 L$—half the horizontal reach means half the gravity torque!

Force ($F = ma$) and weight ($W = mg$, with $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$) are measured in Newtons (N).
Measuring arm angle $\theta$ from the horizontal, the perpendicular lever arm is $r_\perp = L\cos\theta$, so gravity torque is $\tau_{\text{grav}} = m g L \cos\theta$ (in Newton-meters N·m).

pages.title: Reading a Datasheet Table — Unit Columns, Min/Typ/Max & Safe Operating Bounds

sections.t:
Read a real hardware datasheet specification table (DRV8833 vs. TB6612FNG motor driver ICs) by checking the Unit column for metric prefixes (mV, mA, kHz) and distinguishing Recommended Operating Conditions (Min / Typ / Max) from destructive Absolute Maximum Ratings.
New ideas (max 2):
Reading datasheet specification tables and unit columns: Locating the parameter symbol (VM, IOUT, fPWM), reading the Unit column (V, mA, kHz), and converting prefixed table entries into base SI units (Lesson P.7).
Recommended operating bounds (Min/Typ/Max) versus Absolute Maximum Ratings: Why a part must always be operated inside its Recommended Operating Range (for example, DRV8833 VM = 2.7 V to 10.8 V) and why running at or near the Absolute Maximum Rating (11.8 V) on a 12.0 V battery rail risks permanent silicon damage (requiring a higher-rated part such as TB6612FNG at 4.5 V to 13.5 V).
New syntax: Python dictionaries ({"min": 2.7, "max": 10.8}) for structured datasheet lookup tables.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 0.75–1.0 hours | Slow-learner: 1.5–2.0 hours

Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Command Clamping
Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)

sections.h: Idea 1: Reading datasheet specification tables and unit columns
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun Tutorials — How to Read a Schematic & Datasheet Basics [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Overview and Name Designators and Values.
What to skip: Skip PCB net-class routing details.
Key takeaway: Every electronic component datasheet contains two core specification tables near the front: Absolute Maximum Ratings and Recommended Operating Conditions. Each row lists a Parameter, a Symbol (VM, IOUT), three numerical columns (Min, Typ, Max), and a Unit column (V, mA, kHz, °C). Always check the Unit column before using a number—a quiescent draw of 2.5 in a mA column is $0.0025\text{ A}$, not $2.5\text{ A}$!
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Datasheet ("Characteristics of an electronic datasheet") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read the exact heading Product datasheet information.

sections.h: Idea 2: Recommended operating bounds (Min/Typ/Max) versus Absolute Maximum Ratings
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Safe operating area [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read the lead section, which defines the electrical operating envelope a part survives without self-damage, and the exact heading Limits of the safe operating area — the same boundary an Absolute Maximum Rating (AMR) marks, well outside the Recommended Operating Conditions (ROC) you must design inside.
What to skip: Skip military MIL-STD qualification tables.
Key takeaway: Absolute Maximum Ratings are the stress threshold beyond which permanent physical destruction occurs; manufacturers explicitly state that reliable operation is not implied at those limits. Your design must stay strictly inside the Recommended Operating Conditions (Min $\le x \le$ Max) with safety margin:

Before wiring any part in Stage 0 or Pass 1, you must read its datasheet specification table without falling for the two classic beginner traps:
Trap 1 — Confusing Absolute Maximum Ratings with Recommended Operating Conditions: Suppose you want to drive a motor from a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply rail. Looking at the DRV8833 datasheet table above, its Recommended Operating Conditions specify Min = 2.7 V and Max = 10.8 V, while its Absolute Maximum Rating is 11.8 V. Connecting a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply exceeds both the $10.8\text{ V}$ operating bound and the $11.8\text{ V}$ destruction limit! For a $6.0\text{–}9.0\text{ V}$ bench supply, DRV8833 is ideal; for a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply, reading the table tells you to select TB6612FNG (Recommended Min = 4.5 V, Max = 13.5 V, Abs Max = 15.0 V).
Trap 2 — Ignoring the Unit Column: A datasheet row often reports standby draw as Typ = 1.8, Max = 3.0 with Unit = mA, or logic timing as Typ = 250 with Unit = ns or µs. Always convert the table value using the Unit column (mA $\to \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$, kHz $\to \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$) before comparing or multiplying in Python.

Treating Absolute Maximum Rating as a normal operating point: Running a DRV8833 at $11.5\text{ V}$ or $12.0\text{ V}$ because its Absolute Maximum is $11.8\text{ V}$ leaves zero headroom for supply spikes and destroys the IC; always design strictly inside Recommended Operating Conditions (2.7 V to 10.8 V).
Missing the mA or µA prefix in the Unit column: Reading 1500 in a mA column as $1500\text{ A}$ instead of $1.50\text{ A}$ causes a $1000\times$ sizing error.

Why is DRV8833 unsafe on a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply rail even though $12.0\text{ V}$ is close to $11.8\text{ V}$?
Answer 1
Because $10.8\text{ V}$ is the maximum recommended operating bound and $11.8\text{ V}$ is the destructive Absolute Maximum Rating. At $12.0\text{ V}$, use TB6612FNG (4.5–13.5 V recommended operating range).
A sensor datasheet lists Supply Draw: Typ = 4.2, Max = 6.0, Unit = mA. Which number and base SI value should you use when sizing your supply budget?
Answer 2
Always budget for worst-case Max = 6.0 mA, converted to base SI units as $6.0 \times 10^{-3} = 0.006\text{ A}$.

I can read Min, Typ, Max, and Unit columns in a component datasheet table and convert prefixed entries to base SI units.
I can distinguish Recommended Operating Conditions from Absolute Maximum Ratings and verify why DRV8833 (2.7–10.8 V) is for $6\text{–}9\text{ V}$ rails while TB6612FNG (4.5–13.5 V) covers $12\text{ V}$.

pages.title: Track P Milestone — Gravity-Holding Robot Arm Link Simulator

sections.t:
Combine everything from Track P (variables, clamping, loops, functions, assert, metric conversions, 10-bit scaling, radians, time-series area integration, and $\tau = mgL\cos\theta$ gravity torque) into a self-testing Python simulation of a single-joint robot arm lifting a payload against gravity.
New ideas (max 2):
End-to-end sense-compute-simulate loop: Connecting a 10-bit digital command (0..1023), linear torque scaling, horizontal-angle gravity torque ($\tau_{\text{grav}} = mgL\cos\theta$), and discrete time-stepping (angle = angle + omega dt) in one script.
New syntax: None (integrates Lessons P.1 through P.14).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–2.5 hours
All Track P lessons: P.1–P.12 and P.14.

Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Determining the Area on a v-t Graph [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact heading Calculating the Area of a Rectangle.
What to skip: No new external chapters required—this milestone synthesizes the ideas you already practiced in Lessons P.1–P.12.
Key takeaway: A physical simulation is a loop that repeats three simple steps at every time slice $\Delta t$: (1) convert commands and geometry into base SI units (m, kg, s, rad, N·m), (2) compare motor torque against gravity torque $\tau_{\text{grav}} = mgL\cos\theta$, and (3) advance angle and tip $(x, y) = (L\cos\theta, L\sin\theta)$ over $\Delta t$.
Alternative resource: HyperPhysics — Torque [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review exact heading Torque = Force applied x lever arm.

Congratulations on reaching the Track P Milestone! Before moving on to electronics and microcontrollers in Stage 0, you will build a complete end-to-end sense-compute-simulate loop in Python to prove you can read, write, and debug every prerequisite concept without guessing.
Here is the physical system you are modeling using our consistent horizontal-angle convention:
A single robot arm link has length $L = 250\text{ mm}$ ($0.25\text{ m}$) and carries a tip mass $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$ ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
When the link sits at angle $\theta$ measured upward from the horizontal $x$-axis ($0^\circ$ = horizontal, $90^\circ$ = straight up), the perpendicular horizontal lever arm distance from the pivot to the vertical line of gravity force is $r_\perp = L\cos(\theta)$, so downward gravity pulls with opposing torque $\tau_{\text{grav}} = m \cdot g \cdot L \cdot \cos(\theta)$.
A 10-bit digital command cmd_10bit (0 to 1023) commands motor torque linearly from $0.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ up to $\tau_{\max} = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
You will first check whether a given command can hold the arm up against gravity at $\theta = 0^\circ$ (horizontal), and then step the arm upward at constant angular speed $\omega = 30\text{ RPM}$ over 3 steps of $\Delta t = 100\text{ ms}$ ($0.10\text{ s}$).

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (in futurecoder.io [verify in-app] or locally via python3).
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this milestone requires hardware.

Forgetting to convert 250.0 mm to 0.25 m or 100.0 ms to 0.10 s: Leaving length_m = 250.0 multiplies torque by $1{,}000\times$ (981.0 Nm), and leaving dt_s = 100.0 spins the arm by $18{,}000^\circ$ per step!

Interpreting the simulation output: Why does tau_g decrease from 0.9810 Nm at 0 deg down to 0.5766 Nm at 54.0 deg as the arm lifts upward?
Answer
As the arm rotates upward toward vertical (90 deg), the tip mass moves closer horizontally to the shoulder pivot (the perpendicular horizontal lever arm $x = L\cos\theta$ shrinks from 0.2500 m down to 0.1469 m). Shorter perpendicular lever arm distance means gravity has less leverage!
Minimum 10-bit command to hold horizontal: Since gravity torque at 0 deg is 0.9810 Nm and full scale (1023) produces 2.0 Nm, what is the smallest integer cmd_10bit (0..1023) that produces at least 0.9810 Nm?
Answer
Rearranging $\tau = \frac{\text{cmd}}{1023} \times 2.0 \ge 0.9810$ gives $\text{cmd} \ge \frac{0.9810}{2.0} \times 1023 = 501.78$. Rounding up to the next whole integer gives 502 (which produces $\frac{502}{1023} \times 2.0 \approx 0.9814\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$).
Angular displacement check: At 30 RPM ($0.5\text{ rev/s} = 180^\circ\text{/s}$), how many degrees should the arm turn in each 0.10 s (100 ms) step? Does that match Step 0: 18.0 deg, Step 1: 36.0 deg, Step 2: 54.0 deg?
Answer
$180^\circ\text{/s} \times 0.10\text{ s} = \mathbf{18.0^\circ\text{ per step}}$, which matches 18.0 -> 36.0 -> 54.0 deg!
