pages.title: Why Electricity Is Like Water Flow — Effort, Flow & Pipe Constriction

sections.t:
Build an intuitive physical mental model of electricity before opening your first circuit simulator by comparing a closed water pump-and-pipe loop to an electrical circuit using the universal Effort $\times$ Flow framework (so Track 00 Lesson 00.1 is a familiar revisit, not a cold first contact).
New ideas (max 2):
Effort (pressure or electrical push) and Flow (water stream or charge movement): Why a pump's pressure difference ($\text{Effort}$) pushes water ($\text{Flow}$) around a closed loop of pipe, and why zero pressure difference means zero flow.
Power as Effort times Flow and constriction as opposition to flow: Why narrowing a pipe restricts flow for a given push ($\text{Flow} = \text{Effort} / \text{Opposition}$), and why the rate of work delivered by any physical system is $\text{Power} = \text{Effort} \times \text{Flow}$.
New syntax: None (uses simple Python functions and arithmetic from Track P to pre-compute water/circuit flow before opening Falstad in S0.1).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 0.75–1.0 hours | Slow-learner: 1.5–2.0 hours

Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)
Lesson P.9: Rearranging Physics Formulas & Linear Range Scaling
Lesson P.14: Reading a Datasheet Table — Unit Columns & Safe Bounds

sections.h: Idea 1: Effort (pressure or electrical push) and Flow (water stream or charge movement)
sections.t:
Primary resource: HyperPhysics — Water Analogy to DC Circuits [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Water Analogy to DC Circuits comparing a water pump + return reservoir to an electrical source + return path.
What to skip: Skip sub-links to semiconductor transistor junctions.
Key takeaway: You cannot see electrons moving inside a copper wire, so engineers picture a closed water pipe loop. A pump creates a pressure difference (Effort, measured in Volts V in electricity) between its outlet and its low-pressure return tank ($0\text{ V}$ reference). That push drives a steady stream of water (Flow, measured in Amperes A in electricity) out of the pump, through the pipe, and all the way back to the return tank. If the loop is broken (a valve is shut or a wire is disconnected), Effort can still exist at the pump outlet, but Flow drops to zero!
Alternative resource: SparkFun Tutorials — What is a Circuit? ("Closed Loops") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Circuit Basics and Short and Open Circuits.

sections.h: Idea 2: Power as Effort times Flow and constriction as opposition to flow
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Hydraulic analogy ("Principal equivalents") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Equation examples and Principal equivalents (pressure difference $\leftrightarrow$ electrical push, flow rate $\leftrightarrow$ electrical flow, pipe constriction $\leftrightarrow$ electrical opposition).
What to skip: Skip acoustic wave impedance equations.
Key takeaway: A narrow constriction in a pipe opposes water movement: for the same pump push (Effort), doubling the constriction cuts the Flow in half ($\text{Flow} = \frac{\text{Effort}}{\text{Opposition}}$). Even better, across hydraulics, mechanics, and electricity, the rate of work (Power, in Watts W) is always the product of Effort and Flow:

Before you wire a single component in the Falstad simulator in Lesson S0.1, this water-pipe mental model gives you physical intuition for every electrical quantity you will meet in Stage 0 and revisit in Track 00 (Lesson 00.1):
Notice the two universal rules of Effort and Flow that govern every water loop, battery circuit, and robot joint:
Flow requires both a push (Effort) and a complete closed loop: A pump creates a pressure difference (Effort) between its high-pressure outlet and its zero-pressure return tank, driving water (Flow) through the pipe constriction (Opposition). Doubling the pump push (Effort) doubles the stream (Flow), whereas doubling the pipe constriction cuts Flow in half ($\text{Flow} = \text{Effort} / \text{Opposition}$). If a valve is shut so the loop is broken, Effort still sits waiting at the pump outlet, but Flow immediately drops to zero.
Power (Watts) is always Effort Flow: The rate of useful work delivered (or heat dissipated in a narrow pipe constriction) is always the product of Effort and Flow. A high-pressure pump with a closed valve (Effort = 9.0, Flow = 0.0) delivers $9.0 \times 0.0 = 0.0\text{ W}$ of power, just as an unplugged battery delivers $0.0\text{ W}$ until a closed circuit allows charge to flow.

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in the MechaLab Browser Runner or locally via python3) so you can predict flow and power numerically right before opening Falstad in Lesson S0.1.
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Complete compute_flow (TODO 1) and compute_effort_flow_power (TODO 2) to model how doubling pipe opposition halves flow and how Effort $\times$ Flow computes power in Watts:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, guard if opposition_ohm <= 0: raise ValueError(...), then return effort_v / opposition_ohm. A zero-opposition path is not a zero-flow condition, so the function refuses it instead of inventing an answer. In TODO 2, multiply effort flow.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Thinking "Effort flows through a wire": Water pressure (Effort) does not flow; pressure pushes across two points, while water (Flow) moves through the pipe. In the same way, Volts (V) are measured across two points, while Amperes (A) flow through a wire.
Expecting power when the loop is open: Even a high-pressure $12.0\text{ V}$ supply delivers $0\text{ W}$ of power when the switch is open because $\text{Flow} = 0$, so $\text{Effort} \times 0 = 0\text{ W}$.
Confusing a short with an open valve: zero opposition is a shorted path, not an open valve. This model cannot represent the flow a real supply would try to push through it, so compute_flow raises ValueError instead of returning 0.0; an open valve is infinite opposition, which the model also cannot represent numerically.

If you keep the pump push (Effort) constant at $9.0\text{ V}$ and double the pipe constriction from $100\ \Omega$ to $200\ \Omega$, what happens to the Flow?
Answer 1
The flow is cut in half, dropping from $9.0 / 100 = 0.090\text{ A}$ ($90\text{ mA}$) to $9.0 / 200 = 0.045\text{ A}$ ($45\text{ mA}$).
What is the power (Effort × Flow) when a $5.0\text{ V}$ push drives $0.020\text{ A}$ ($20\text{ mA}$) of flow?
Answer 2
$P = 5.0 \times 0.020 = 0.10\text{ W}$ ($100\text{ mW}$).

I can explain electrical push (Effort), charge stream (Flow), and pipe constriction (Opposition) using the closed water-loop analogy.
I can compute $\text{Flow} = \text{Effort} / \text{Opposition}$ and $\text{Power} = \text{Effort} \times \text{Flow}$ in Watts before opening Falstad in S0.1.

pages.title: Closed DC Circuits, Ground Reference (0 V) and Ohm's Law

sections.t:
Build a physical intuition for voltage (pressure), current (flow), and resistance (pipe narrowing) in a closed Direct Current (DC) loop referenced to ground (GND, $0\text{ V}$), and use Ohm's Law ($V = I \cdot R$) in Falstad to verify circuit voltage, current, and resistance.
New ideas (max 2):
Closed DC circuits and ground reference (0 V): Why electric current only flows around a complete closed loop from a higher-voltage source terminal back to ground (GND).
Ohm's Law relating voltage, current, and resistance: Using $V = I \cdot R$ (and its rearrangements $I = \frac{V}{R}$, $R = \frac{V}{I}$) in base SI units (V, A, Ω).
New syntax: Falstad File -> Import From Text... circuit netlists (v voltage source, r resistor, g ground, w wire).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)
Lesson P.9: Rearranging Physics Formulas & Linear Range Scaling
Lesson S0.0: Why Electricity Is Like Water Flow — Effort, Flow & Pipe Constriction

sections.h: Idea 1: Closed DC circuits and ground reference (0 V)
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Voltage, Current, Resistance, and Ohm's Law [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Electricity Basics, Electrical Charge, Voltage, Current, and Resistance.
What to skip: Skip Ohm's Law until Idea 2 below, and skip the bottom kit links.
Key takeaway: Think of a Direct Current (DC) circuit as a closed water pipe loop driven by a pump: voltage ($V$, in Volts V) is the pressure difference between two points, current ($I$, in Amperes A) is the flow rate of charge through the wire, and resistance ($R$, in Ohms Ω) is a narrow pipe constriction that restricts flow. Current only flows when there is an unbroken closed loop from the positive supply back to ground (GND, defined as $0.0\text{ V}$).
Alternative resource: SparkFun — What is a Circuit? [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Circuit Basics and Voltage and How it Works.

sections.h: Idea 2: Ohm's Law relating voltage, current, and resistance
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Voltage, Current, Resistance, and Ohm's Law ("Ohm's Law") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Ohm's Law and An Ohm's Law Experiment.
What to skip: Skip the bottom shopping section.
Key takeaway: Ohm's Law states that the voltage drop across a resistor equals the current flowing through it times its resistance: $V = I \cdot R$. Rearranging gives $I = \frac{V}{R}$ (doubling resistance cuts current in half) and $R = \frac{V}{I}$.
Optional interactive extra: PhET — Ohm's Law Interactive Simulation [verify in-app] — Drag the Voltage and Resistance sliders [verify in-app] to watch current in mA scale with $V$ and $1/R$.

In Stage 0, all circuits run on Direct Current (DC) standardized on a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply returning to GND (ground, the common $0.0\text{ V}$ reference point). Saying a node is at "$5.0\text{ V}$" always means "5.0 Volts higher than GND."
Remember from Lesson P.7 that Ohm's Law requires base SI units—Volts (V), Amperes (A), and Ohms (Ω):
For example, if you connect a $1.0\text{ k}\Omega$ ($1{,}000\ \Omega$) resistor across a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply and GND:
Convert $R = 1.0\text{ k}\Omega = 1{,}000\ \Omega$.
Compute current in Amperes: $I = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{1{,}000\ \Omega} = 0.005\text{ A}$.
Multiply by $1{,}000$ to express in milliamps: $0.005\text{ A} \times 1{,}000 = 5.0\text{ mA}$.
If a wire breaks anywhere in the loop, the loop becomes an open circuit ($R = \infty$), and current drops immediately to $0.0\text{ A}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.1-ohms-law.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... (or paste the Starter Code netlist below). Hover over the 1000 Ω resistor to read I = 5.00 mA, then double-click the resistor (TODO 1) to change its resistance to 250 Ω and verify I = 20.00 mA. (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and numerical mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Nothing in this lesson requires physical hardware.

sections.h: Starter Code (import into Falstad — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Copy the Falstad netlist below (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... in Falstad), verify the $1{,}000\ \Omega$ reading (5.00 mA), and then complete TODO 1 by changing the resistor line r 160 128 336 128 0 1000 from 1000 to 250:
Hovering over the resistor in Falstad before and after completing TODO 1 (plus checking $2.5\text{ mA}$ through $2.0\text{ k}\Omega$) shows:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
By Ohm's Law ($I = V / R$), $5.0\text{ V} / 1000\ \Omega = 0.005\text{ A} = 5.00\text{ mA}$. Cutting the resistance to one-fourth ($250\ \Omega$) quadruples the current to $5.0\text{ V} / 250\ \Omega = 0.020\text{ A} = 20.00\text{ mA}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, line 3 (r 160 128 336 128 0 1000) defines the resistor in Ohms. Change 1000 to 250 (or double-click the resistor in Falstad and type 250).
Full Solution

Dividing Volts by kΩ and calling the result Amperes: Dividing $5.0\text{ V}$ by $1{,}000\ \Omega$ gives $0.005\text{ A}$ ($5.0\text{ mA}$). If you divide $5.0 / 1.0 = 5.0$, remember that Volts divided by kilo-ohms gives milliamps (mA), not Amperes! Converting to base Ohms (1000.0) first avoids confusion.
No return path to GND: A single wire from +5V to a resistor with the other leg left unconnected has zero current flow because the loop is not closed back to GND.

Ohm's Law for current: A $10\text{ k}\Omega$ ($10{,}000\ \Omega$) resistor is connected between 5V and GND. How much current flows through it in Amperes (A) and in milliamps (mA)?
Answer
$I = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{10{,}000\ \Omega} = \mathbf{0.0005\text{ A}} = \mathbf{0.50\text{ mA}}$.
Ohm's Law for resistance: You measure $10.0\text{ mA}$ ($0.010\text{ A}$) flowing from a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply through an unknown resistor to GND. What is the resistor's value in Ohms (Ω)?
Answer
$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{0.010\text{ A}} = \mathbf{500\ \Omega}$.
Effect of doubling resistance: If you keep voltage fixed at $5.0\text{ V}$ and double the resistance from $500\ \Omega$ to $1{,}000\ \Omega$, what happens to the current?
Answer
Current is cut in half, dropping from $10.0\text{ mA}$ to $5.0\text{ mA}$.

Voltage ($V$) is electrical pressure difference relative to ground (GND, $0\text{ V}$), current ($I$) is charge flow rate in Amperes (A), and resistance ($R$) opposes flow in Ohms (Ω).
Ohm's Law ($V = I \cdot R$, $I = V/R$, $R = V/I$) links all three in any closed loop.

pages.title: Series vs. Parallel Resistor Networks, Voltage Dividers and Potentiometers

sections.t:
Distinguish series (end-to-end, shared current) from parallel (side-by-side, shared voltage) connections, and use the voltage divider formula ($V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$) in Falstad to scale voltages and read 3-pin potentiometers.
New ideas (max 2):
Series versus parallel circuits: Why components in series share the exact same current ($I_{\text{total}} = I_1 = I_2$, $R_{\text{series}} = R_1 + R_2$, voltages add up to $V_{\text{supply}}$), whereas components in parallel share the exact same voltage ($V_1 = V_2 = V_{\text{supply}}$, branch currents add up).
Resistive voltage dividers and 3-pin potentiometers: Using two series resistors ($R_1$ on top, $R_2$ on bottom to GND) to produce an output voltage $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, and how a rotating potentiometer wiper sweeps $V_{\text{out}}$ continuously from $0\text{ V}$ to $V_{\text{in}}$.
New syntax: Falstad voltage probe (p) element in circuit netlists.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.2: Computer Arithmetic and Order of Operations
Lesson S0.1: Closed DC Circuits, Ground Reference (0 V) & Ohm's Law

Primary resource: SparkFun — Series and Parallel Circuits [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Series Circuits, Parallel Circuits, and Calculating Equivalent Resistance.
What to skip: Skip the multi-loop series-parallel combination exercises at the very bottom.
Key takeaway: In a series circuit, components are chained end-to-end along a single path: the current is identical everywhere ($I_1 = I_2$), total resistance adds ($R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2$), and the supply voltage splits across the resistors ($V_{\text{in}} = V_1 + V_2$). In a parallel circuit, components are wired side-by-side across the same two nodes: the voltage across every branch is identical ($V_1 = V_2 = V_{\text{in}}$), and the total supply current is the sum of the branch currents ($I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2$).

sections.h: Idea 2: Resistive voltage dividers and 3-pin potentiometers
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Voltage Dividers [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Ideal Voltage Divider, Voltage Divider Equation, and Applications.
What to skip: Skip the resistor-color-code lookup table.
Key takeaway: Two series resistors ($R_1$ connected to $V_{\text{in}}$, $R_2$ connected to GND) form a voltage divider whose middle node sits at $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. A 3-pin potentiometer is simply a variable voltage divider inside a knob: its two outer pins connect to 5V and GND, and turning the knob slides the middle wiper pin smoothly from $0.0\text{ V}$ to $5.0\text{ V}$.
Alternative resource: Falstad Circuit Simulator — Potentiometer Divider [verify in-app] — Open Circuits $\rightarrow$ Basics $\rightarrow$ Potentiometer [verify in-app] and drag the Resistance slider on the right pane [verify in-app] to sweep the wiper voltage.

Let's derive the voltage divider formula in two steps from Idea 1 and Ohm's Law (Lesson S0.1):
Because $R_1$ (top resistor, connected to $V_{\text{in}}$) and $R_2$ (bottom resistor, connected to GND) are in series, their total resistance is $R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2$, so the series current is $I = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{R_1 + R_2}$.
The output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ (measured from the middle node between $R_1$ and $R_2$ down to GND) is the voltage drop across the bottom resistor $R_2$:
Notice two essential sanity checks:
Equal resistors ($R_1 = R_2$): $\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5$, so $V_{\text{out}}$ is always half of $V_{\text{in}}$ ($2.50\text{ V}$ from a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply).
Safe battery-monitoring divider ($12\text{ V} \rightarrow 3.84\text{ V}$): A $12.0\text{ V}$ motor battery will destroy a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino pin if wired directly! Using $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ on the bottom scales $12.0\text{ V}$ down to $12.0 \times \frac{4700}{10000 + 4700} \approx 3.84\text{ V}$, which is safely below the $5.0\text{ V}$ pin limit.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.2-voltage-divider.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... ($V_{\text{in}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $R_1 = 10{,}000\ \Omega$, $R_2 = 4{,}700\ \Omega$) and verify that the voltage probe reads 3.84 V (I = 0.82 mA). Then complete TODO 1 by changing the source to 5 V and both resistors to 10000 Ω (10 kΩ) to verify the 2.50 V midpoint. (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and numerical mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Mechanical wiper wear on a physical carbon-track potentiometer.

sections.h: Starter Code (import into Falstad — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Import this Falstad netlist (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text...) to verify the $12.0\text{ V} \rightarrow 3.84\text{ V}$ battery-monitor divider (R1 = 10000, R2 = 4700), and then complete TODO 1 by editing R2 (r 288 112 288 304 0 4700) to 10000 on a 5 V source (v ... 40 5 ...) to verify 2.50 V:
The Falstad voltage probe p and resistor hover readouts for both divider configurations match:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
With $V_{\text{in}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $R_1 = 10{,}000\ \Omega$, and $R_2 = 4{,}700\ \Omega$, $R_{\text{total}} = 14{,}700\ \Omega$, so $I = 12.0 / 14{,}700 \approx 0.000816\text{ A} = 0.82\text{ mA}$ and $V_{\text{out}} = 12.0 \times (4{,}700 / 14{,}700) \approx 3.84\text{ V}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
To test the $5.0\text{ V}$ equal-resistor midpoint (50% potentiometer wiper), change 12 to 5 on the v line and change 4700 to 10000 on the second r line (r 288 112 288 304 0 10000).
Full Solution

Putting $R_1$ in the numerator instead of $R_2$ ($V_{\text{in}} \cdot \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$): Because $V_{\text{out}}$ is measured from the middle node to GND, the numerator is always the resistor connected to GND ($R_2$). If you swap $R_1$ and $R_2$ on a $12\text{ V}$ battery divider ($4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ on top, $10\text{ k}\Omega$ on bottom), $V_{\text{out}}$ jumps to $8.16\text{ V}$—which exceeds a $5.0\text{ V}$ microcontroller pin limit!
Trying to power a heavy load (like a motor) from a voltage divider: A voltage divider is only for low-current sensor signals! As soon as a heavy load draws current from the middle node, the output voltage collapses.

Series vs. parallel resistors: You have two $1{,}000\ \Omega$ ($1\text{ k}\Omega$) resistors. What is their combined resistance if you wire them in series, and what is their combined resistance if you wire them in parallel?
Answer
In series: $R_{\text{series}} = 1{,}000 + 1{,}000 = \mathbf{2{,}000\ \Omega}$ ($2.0\text{ k}\Omega$).
In parallel: Two identical resistors in parallel offer twice the cross-sectional path, cutting resistance in half to $\frac{1{,}000 \times 1{,}000}{1{,}000 + 1{,}000} = \mathbf{500\ \Omega}$.
Voltage divider calculation: A $5.0\text{ V}$ supply feeds a top resistor $R_1 = 3.0\text{ k}\Omega$ in series with a bottom resistor $R_2 = 1.0\text{ k}\Omega$ to GND. What is $V_{\text{out}}$ at the middle node?
Answer
$V_{\text{out}} = 5.0\text{ V} \times \frac{1.0}{3.0 + 1.0} = 5.0 \times 0.25 = \mathbf{1.25\text{ V}}$.
Potentiometer extremes: A $10\text{ k}\Omega$ potentiometer has its outer pins connected to 5V and GND. What voltage appears on the middle wiper pin when turned all the way toward GND, halfway (50%), and all the way toward 5V?
Answer
$0.00\text{ V}$ at the GND end, $2.50\text{ V}$ at the midpoint (50%), and $5.00\text{ V}$ at the 5V end.

Series components share the same current ($R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2$); parallel components share the same voltage.
A voltage divider outputs $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, and a potentiometer is a 3-pin adjustable voltage divider.

sections.t:
You tested falstad/S0.2-voltage-divider.txt [verify in-app] in Falstad and verified 3.84 V and 2.50 V.
You can explain why a voltage divider is for signals only, never for powering motors.

pages.title: Reading Schematics, Breadboards and Short Circuits

sections.t:
Translate a circuit schematic into a physical or simulated solderless breadboard layout without accidentally shorting component legs across the same row, and visualize short circuits in Falstad.
New ideas (max 2):
Schematic symbols and breadboard internal row clips: How schematic lines represent shared electrical nodes, and how a breadboard connects 5 holes horizontally (a–e and f–j) in each row and vertically along the outer +/- power rails.
Open circuits versus short circuits: Why bridging two legs of a component (or 5V and GND) in the same 5-hole breadboard row creates a near-zero-resistance short circuit ($I = V / R_{\text{wire}}$), and why we demonstrate shorts in Falstad rather than Wokwi.
New syntax: Falstad switch (s) element in circuit netlists.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson S0.1: Closed DC Circuits, Ground Reference (0 V) & Ohm's Law
Lesson S0.2: Series vs. Parallel Resistor Networks, Voltage Dividers & Potentiometers

sections.h: Idea 1: Schematic symbols and breadboard internal row clips
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — How to Read a Schematic [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Overview, Schematic Symbols (Part 1), Reading Schematics, and Nets, Nodes and Labels.
What to skip: Skip logic-gate IC pinout history.
Key takeaway: Every continuous line on a schematic is a node—all component legs touching that node must share one metal clip on your breadboard. Inside a solderless breadboard, the outer power rails (+ red and - blue/black) run vertically down the sides, whereas the inner terminal rows connect 5 holes horizontally (a-b-c-d-e on the left, f-g-h-i-j on the right), separated by a center ravine.
Alternative resource: SparkFun — How to Use a Breadboard [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Anatomy of a Breadboard and Building Your First Breadboard Circuit (skip Binding Posts).

sections.h: Idea 2: Open circuits versus short circuits
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — What is a Circuit? ("Short and Open Circuits") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading Short and Open Circuits.
What to skip: Skip the bottom links.
Key takeaway: An open circuit is a broken loop ($R = \infty, I = 0$). A short circuit is an unintended near-zero-resistance bypass path ($R_{\text{wire}} \approx 0.05\ \Omega$) directly across a power supply or across both legs of a component. By Ohm's Law ($I = V / R_{\text{wire}}$), a $5.0\text{ V}$ short attempts to draw $I = 5.0 / 0.05 = 100\text{ A}$, starving the rest of the circuit and overheating wires!

Look at a breadboard's two rules so you never wire a hidden short circuit:
Never plug both legs of the same component into the same 5-hole horizontal row (such as row 10, hole a and row 10, hole d)! Because holes 10a–10e are pinched together by a single metal clip underneath the plastic, plugging both legs into row 10 shorts the two legs together in parallel with a $0\ \Omega$ metal bar—current takes the metal clip underneath instead of flowing through your component! Always place the two legs in two different numbered rows (e.g., row 10 and row 14) or across the center ravine (10e to 10f).
Important Simulator Fact (Wokwi vs. Falstad on Breadboard Shorts):
We checked Wokwi's breadboard and analog simulation behavior: Wokwi primarily routes digital logic states and does NOT display a smoke warning, error message, or current spike if you wire 5V directly to GND on a Wokwi breadboard.
Therefore, we always demonstrate and inspect short circuits in Falstad (falstad/S0.3-short-circuit.txt), where closing a $0.05\ \Omega$ short-circuit switch across a load visibly diverts current away from the load!

What is simulated and in which tool:
Short-circuit demonstration in Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.3-short-circuit.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text.... With the bypass switch open (s ... false), current flows normally through the load. Click the switch closed (TODO 1, s ... true) to simulate plugging both legs into the same breadboard row (0.05 Ω clip): watch all current bypass the load through the 0.05 Ω short! (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and breadboard clip logic in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Melting plastic breadboard clips or tripping a USB port's polyfuse during a real 5V-to-GND short.

Checking the three breadboard hole-pair placements (10a to 10d, 10a to 14a, and 10e to 10f across the center ravine) yields:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
Holes 10a through 10e share the exact same metal clip on the left bank of row 10 (SHORTED_SAME_CLIP), whereas 10a to 14a are in different rows (VALID_ACROSS_NODES) and 10e to 10f straddle the center ravine (VALID_ACROSS_NODES).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, line 5 (s 384 128 384 288 0 1 false) controls the parallel 0.05 Ω short-circuit switch. Change false to true (or click the switch in Falstad) to close the short.
Full Solution

Plugging both legs of a resistor into the same 5-hole strip (10a and 10e): The internal metal strip shorts the two legs together so zero current flows through the component.
Assuming Wokwi will warn you about a 5V-to-GND breadboard short: Wokwi does not flag power-to-ground breadboard shorts. Always trace power and ground wires by eye and simulate analog short behavior in Falstad.

Breadboard connectivity: A resistor's top leg is in hole 12b and its bottom leg is in hole 18b. If you want to connect another component's leg to the bottom leg of that resistor, which holes on the breadboard can you plug it into?
Answer
Any of the remaining 4 holes in that same left-side strip of row 18: 18a, 18c, 18d, or 18e (not 18f–18j, which are on the opposite side of the center ravine).
Why the center ravine exists: Why is there a gap down the middle of every breadboard between column e and column f?
Answer
So dual-row chips (DIP integrated circuits) and pushbuttons can straddle the middle gap without their left-side pins shorting to their right-side pins!
Short-circuit current calculation: If you accidentally connect a jumper wire with resistance $R_{\text{wire}} = 0.05\ \Omega$ directly between an unprotected $5.0\text{ V}$ supply and GND, how much current tries to flow according to Ohm's Law?
Answer
$I = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{0.05\ \Omega} = \mathbf{100.0\text{ A}}$!

Breadboard terminal rows connect 5 holes horizontally (a–e and f–j separated by the center ravine), while outer power rails run vertically.
Never place both legs of a component in the same 5-hole clip, and remember that Falstad (not Wokwi) visualizes analog short circuits.

pages.title: Diodes, LEDs, Forward Voltage Drop (V_f) and Resistor Power Ratings (P = VI)

sections.t:
Size a current-limiting series resistor ($R = \frac{V_{\text{supply}} - V_f}{I_{\text{target}}}$) to protect a Light-Emitting Diode (LED) on a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply in Falstad, and calculate electrical power dissipation ($P = V \cdot I = I^2 R$) so your resistors never overheat.
New ideas (max 2):
Diodes, LED polarity, and series current-limiting resistor sizing: Why a diode only conducts current in one direction (from Anode + to Cathode -) with a fixed forward voltage drop ($V_f \approx 2.0\text{ V}$ for a red LED), requiring a series resistor $R = \frac{V_{\text{supply}} - V_f}{I_{\text{target}}}$.
Electrical power dissipation ($P = V \cdot I = I^2 R$) and resistor power ratings: Computing heat generated in Watts (W) or milliwatts (mW) and applying a $2\times$ safety margin against a standard quarter-watt ($0.25\text{ W} = 250\text{ mW}$) resistor rating.
New syntax: Falstad LED (162) element in circuit netlists.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: Diodes, LED polarity, and series current-limiting resistor sizing
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Introduction, How to Use Them, 1) Polarity Matters, and Calculating Current Limiting Resistors (sizing the ballast resistor).
What to skip: Skip Types of LEDs (RGB, addressable NeoPixels, and IR LEDs).
Key takeaway: A diode is a one-way electrical check valve: current only flows when the Anode (+, longer leg) is at a higher voltage than the Cathode (-, shorter leg / flat rim) by at least its forward voltage ($V_f \approx 1.8\text{–}2.0\text{ V}$ for red, $\approx 3.0\text{–}3.3\text{ V}$ for blue/white). Once turned on, an LED has almost zero internal resistance of its own—connecting it directly across $5.0\text{ V}$ without a series current-limiting resistor destroys it instantly!

sections.h: Idea 2: Electrical power dissipation ($P = V \cdot I = I^2 R$) and resistor power ratings
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Electric Power [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings What is Electric Power?, Calculating Power, and Power Ratings.
What to skip: Skip high-voltage AC transmission line math.
Key takeaway: Electrical power ($P$, measured in Watts W or milliwatts mW) is the rate at which electrical energy turns into heat or work: $P = V \cdot I$. Substituting Ohm's Law ($V = I \cdot R$) gives $P = I^2 \cdot R = \frac{V^2}{R}$. Standard breadboard resistors are rated for $1/4\text{ W}$ ($0.25\text{ W} = 250\text{ mW}$) maximum heat; engineers always keep continuous resistor dissipation below $50\%$ of its rating ($\le 125\text{ mW}$) so it stays cool to the touch.

When a current-limiting resistor $R$ and a red LED ($V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$) are wired in series across a $V_{\text{supply}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ supply, the same current $I$ flows through both components:
Forward-biasing the LED (Anode + toward $+5.0\text{ V}$, Cathode - flat edge toward GND) drops its fixed forward voltage $V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$.
The remaining supply voltage must drop across the series resistor: $V_R = V_{\text{supply}} - V_f = 5.0\text{ V} - 2.0\text{ V} = 3.0\text{ V}$.
Applying Ohm's Law ($R = \frac{V_R}{I_{\text{target}}}$) for a desired safe LED current of $I_{\text{target}} = 15\text{ mA} = 0.015\text{ A}$ gives:
With a standard $200\ \Omega$ resistor ($I = 15.0\text{ mA}$) or $220\ \Omega$ resistor ($I = \frac{3.0\text{ V}}{220\ \Omega} \approx 13.64\text{ mA}$), we always check the electrical power turned into heat inside the resistor:
Because $45.0\text{ mW}$ is well below the $125\text{ mW}$ derated safe limit ($50\%$ of a standard $250\text{ mW}$ / $1/4\text{ W}$ resistor rating), the series resistor runs completely cool!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.4-led-resistor.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... ($5.0\text{ V}$ source, series resistor, and LED to GND). Change the resistor (TODO 1) from 220 to 200 Ohms (with LED $V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$) to verify $I = 15.0\text{ mA}$ and $P_R = 45.0\text{ mW}$. (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and numerical mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Burning a finger on an overloaded $1/4\text{ W}$ resistor or popping a physical LED connected without a series resistor.

sections.t: Import this Falstad netlist (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text...) and complete TODO 1 by changing the series resistor (r 160 128 320 128 0 220) from 220 to 200 Ohms for a $15.0\text{ mA}$ target current at $V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$:

Sizing the series resistor for $5.0\text{ V}$ supply, $V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$, and $I = 15.0\text{ mA}$, and checking power dissipation on $200\ \Omega$ ($15\text{ mA}$) vs. $100\ \Omega$ across $12\text{ V}$ ($120\text{ mA}$) gives:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
Subtract $V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$ from $V_{\text{supply}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ to get $V_R = 3.0\text{ V}$, then divide by $0.015\text{ A}$ ($15\text{ mA}$) to get $R = 200.0\ \Omega$ and $P_R = (0.015)^2 \times 200 = 0.045\text{ W} = 45.0\text{ mW}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, edit line 3 (r 160 128 320 128 0 220) so the resistance value at the end of the line is 200.
Full Solution

LED does not light up at all: Check polarity! If the LED is inserted backward (Cathode - toward +5V, Anode + toward GND), it is reverse-biased and blocks all current. Flip the LED around.
Using $V_{\text{supply}}$ instead of $(V_{\text{supply}} - V_f)$ when computing resistor power: Only $V_R = V_{\text{supply}} - V_f$ drops across the resistor; the remaining $V_f$ drops across the LED.
Putting a $100\ \Omega$ quarter-watt resistor directly across a $12.0\text{ V}$ motor battery: By $P = V^2 / R = 144 / 100 = 1.44\text{ W}$ ($1{,}440\text{ mW}$), that resistor dissipates nearly $6\times$ its $250\text{ mW}$ rating and will smoke within seconds!

White LED resistor sizing: A white LED has forward voltage $V_f = 3.2\text{ V}$ and you want $I = 10.0\text{ mA}$ ($0.010\text{ A}$) from a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino pin. What resistor value $R$ in Ohms do you need?
Answer
$R = \frac{5.0\text{ V} - 3.2\text{ V}}{0.010\text{ A}} = \frac{1.8\text{ V}}{0.010\text{ A}} = \mathbf{180\ \Omega}$.
Reversed diode: What current flows if you connect a red LED in series with a $220\ \Omega$ resistor, but connect the LED's Cathode (-) to +5V and its Anode (+) to GND?
Answer
$0.0\text{ mA}$—the diode is reverse-biased and acts like a closed one-way valve blocking flow.
Quarter-watt safety check: A $1.0\text{ k}\Omega$ ($1{,}000\ \Omega$) resistor has $12.0\text{ V}$ across it ($I = 12.0\text{ mA} = 0.012\text{ A}$). How many milliwatts (mW) of heat does it dissipate, and is a $1/4\text{ W}$ ($250\text{ mW}$) resistor safe?
Answer
$P = V \cdot I = 12.0\text{ V} \times 0.012\text{ A} = 0.144\text{ W} = \mathbf{144\text{ mW}}$. While below the absolute $250\text{ mW}$ burn-out limit, it exceeds our $50\%$ derating guideline ($125\text{ mW}$), so it will run noticeably warm (stepping up to a $2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor or a $1/2\text{ W}$ resistor is better practice).

An LED conducts only from Anode (+) to Cathode (-) with forward drop $V_f$, requiring a series resistor $R = \frac{V_{\text{supply}} - V_f}{I_{\text{target}}}$.
Electrical power ($P = V \cdot I = I^2 R$) measures heat dissipation in Watts (W); keep continuous dissipation below half of a resistor's power rating ($\le 125\text{ mW}$ for a $1/4\text{ W}$ resistor).

pages.title: Virtual Multimeters (Voltmeter vs. Ammeter) and Current-Limited (CC/CV) Bench Supplies

sections.t:
Measure circuit voltage and current in Falstad without blowing an ammeter fuse—placing voltmeters in parallel across components and ammeters in series inside the broken loop—and configure a current-limited (CC/CV) bench power supply so wiring mistakes fold voltage back safely instead of smoking parts.
New ideas (max 2):
Multimeter probing rules (voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series, ohmmeter unpowered): Why a voltmeter has mega-ohm input resistance ($R_V \approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$) and goes across two nodes, whereas an ammeter has near-zero resistance ($R_A \approx 0.05\ \Omega$) and must be inserted in series by breaking the circuit.
Bench power supply Constant-Voltage (CV) versus Constant-Current (CC) current limiting: Setting a safety current ceiling $I_{\text{limit}}$ on a power supply so that if load current reaches $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply automatically switches from Constant Voltage (CV) to Constant Current (CC) and drops its output voltage to $V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{limit}} \cdot R_{\text{load}}$.
New syntax: Falstad Ammeter (370) and Voltage Probe (p) elements.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: Multimeter probing rules (voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series, ohmmeter unpowered)
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — How to Use a Multimeter [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Measuring Voltage, Measuring Resistance, Measuring Current, and Continuity.
What to skip: Skip Changing the Fuse until you read the ammeter warning in the Bridge Notes below.
Key takeaway: A digital multimeter (DMM) combines three instruments with completely different internal circuits:
Voltmeter (V mode): Has huge internal resistance ($\approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$). Touch its red and black probes in parallel (across) the component while power is ON.
Ammeter (A / mA mode): Has near-zero internal resistance ($\approx 0.05\ \Omega$, like a bare wire!). You must break the loop and wire the ammeter in series so current flows through the meter. Touching an ammeter in parallel across 5V and GND creates a dead short circuit and blows the meter's internal fuse!
Ohmmeter (Ω / Continuity mode): Injects its own tiny test current; always turn circuit power OFF before measuring resistance or continuity.

sections.h: Idea 2: Bench power supply Constant-Voltage (CV) versus Constant-Current (CC) current limiting
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — How to Power a Project [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Overview and Variable DC Benchtop Power Supply.
What to skip: Skip solar/LiPo charging sections (covered in Track 01).
Key takeaway: Unlike a raw battery that will happily dump $50\text{ A}$ into a wiring mistake and melt your breadboard, an adjustable bench power supply lets you set two knobs before turning power on: a target voltage $V_{\text{set}}$ (e.g., $5.0\text{ V}$) and a maximum current limit $I_{\text{limit}}$ (e.g., $0.10\text{ A} = 100\text{ mA}$ for a logic breadboard). As long as your circuit draws less than $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply stays in Constant-Voltage (CV) mode at $5.0\text{ V}$. The instant a short circuit tries to draw more than $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply switches to Constant-Current (CC) mode—clamping current to $I_{\text{limit}}$ and folding output voltage down to $V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{limit}} \cdot R_{\text{load}}$!

Why does a voltmeter connect in parallel while an ammeter connects in series?
A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two nodes (V_A - V_B). Its internal resistance is huge ($\approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$), so touching its probes across a component draws almost zero current and does not disturb the circuit.
An ammeter measures the flow rate through a branch. Its internal shunt resistance is tiny ($\approx 0.05\ \Omega$, like a bare wire) so it doesn't block the current it is trying to measure. Because $R_A \approx 0.05\ \Omega$, touching an ammeter in parallel across a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply creates a dead short circuit ($I = 5.0 / 0.05 = 100\text{ A}$) that instantly blows the meter's fuse!
Similarly, a current-limited (CC/CV) bench power supply acts like an automatic safety circuit breaker during bring-up:
In Constant-Voltage (CV) mode ($I_{\text{load}} < I_{\text{limit}}$), the supply holds $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{set}}$ ($5.00\text{ V}$).
In Constant-Current (CC) mode ($V_{\text{set}} / R_{\text{load}} \ge I_{\text{limit}}$), the supply clamps current at $I = I_{\text{limit}}$ ($0.10\text{ A}$) and drops $V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{limit}} \cdot R_{\text{load}}$ ($0.05\text{ V}$ across a $0.5\ \Omega$ accidental short), saving your components from smoke!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.5-multimeter-probing.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... to see an Ammeter (370) wired in series with a $1{,}000\ \Omega$ load reading 5.00 mA and a Voltage Probe (p) wired in parallel reading 5.00 V. Complete TODO 1 by changing the load resistor (r 272 128 272 288 0 1000) to 250 Ohms to verify 20.00 mA at 5.00 V. (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and CC/CV numerical mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Blowing a physical glass $200\text{ mA}$ fuse inside a handheld multimeter by probing across a battery in mA mode.

sections.h: Starter Code (import into Falstad — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Import this Falstad netlist (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text...), observe the series ammeter (370) and parallel voltage probe (p) with the $1{,}000\ \Omega$ load, and complete TODO 1 by changing 1000 on line 4 (r 272 128 272 288 0 1000) to 250:

Evaluating a bench supply set to $V_{\text{set}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ and $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.10\text{ A}$ ($100\text{ mA}$) across a normal $250\ \Omega$ load (CV mode, 20.0 mA on the Falstad series ammeter) vs. a $0.5\ \Omega$ short (CC mode) yields:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
With $R_{\text{load}} = 250\ \Omega$ on a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply, $I = 5.0 / 250 = 0.020\text{ A} = 20.0\text{ mA} < 100\text{ mA}$, so the supply stays in CV mode at $5.00\text{ V}$. With a $0.5\ \Omega$ short, $5.0 / 0.5 = 10.0\text{ A} \ge 0.10\text{ A}$, so the supply enters CC mode at $I = 100.0\text{ mA}$ and drops $V_{\text{out}}$ to $0.10 \times 0.5 = 0.05\text{ V}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, change 1000 on line 4 (r 272 128 272 288 0 1000) to 250 so the series ammeter (370) reads 20.0 mA.
Full Solution

Leaving the red multimeter lead plugged into the A / mA current jack when switching the dial back to measure Voltage (V): Even if the dial is on V, the A jack is wired directly through a low-resistance shunt to the COM jack! Touching the probes across a battery while the red lead is in the A jack shorts the battery through the meter. Always move the red probe back to the V/Ω jack immediately after measuring current.
Measuring resistance (Ω) while the circuit is still powered on: Current from the circuit's own power supply confuses the ohmmeter and produces nonsensical readings (like negative resistance). Always disconnect power first.

Voltmeter vs. Ammeter connection: To measure the voltage across an LED, do you connect the voltmeter in series or in parallel with the LED? What about measuring the current flowing through the LED with an ammeter?
Answer
Voltmeter: Connect in parallel (across the LED's two legs).
Ammeter: Break the loop and connect in series with the LED and its resistor.
Why an ammeter across a battery blows the fuse: An ammeter has internal resistance $R_A = 0.05\ \Omega$ protected by a $0.5\text{ A}$ ($500\text{ mA}$) fuse. If you accidentally touch the ammeter probes directly across a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply in parallel, how much current tries to flow through the meter?
Answer
$I = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{0.05\ \Omega} = \mathbf{100\text{ A}}$—which is $200\times$ higher than the $0.5\text{ A}$ fuse rating, blowing the fuse instantly!
CC/CV bench supply trace: Your bench supply is set to $V_{\text{set}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ and $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.50\text{ A}$. What mode (CV or CC), voltage $V_{\text{out}}$, and current $I$ do you see when connected to (a) a $240\ \Omega$ resistor, and (b) a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor?
Answer
(a) Across $240\ \Omega$: $12.0 / 240 = 0.05\text{ A} < 0.50\text{ A}$, so CV mode, $V_{\text{out}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $I = 0.05\text{ A}$ ($50\text{ mA}$).
(b) Across $4.0\ \Omega$: $12.0 / 4.0 = 3.0\text{ A} \ge 0.50\text{ A}$, so CC mode, $I = 0.50\text{ A}$, and voltage drops to $V_{\text{out}} = 0.50\text{ A} \times 4.0\ \Omega = \mathbf{2.0\text{ V}}$.

Voltmeters ($R_V \approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$) connect in parallel; ammeters ($R_A \approx 0.05\ \Omega$) connect in series inside a broken loop; ohmmeters require power OFF.
A current-limited (CC/CV) bench supply stays at $V_{\text{set}}$ in CV mode during normal operation and folds voltage down to $I_{\text{limit}} \cdot R_{\text{load}}$ in CC mode to protect against shorts.

sections.t:

Primary resource: SparkFun — Capacitors [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Introduction, Symbols and Units, Capacitor Theory, Charging and Discharging, and Capacitor Types.
What to skip: Skip Capacitors in Series/Parallel and Application Examples -> Signal Filtering.
Key takeaway: A capacitor acts like a tiny, ultra-fast rechargeable bucket that stores electrical charge on two conductive plates separated by an insulator, measured in Farads (F)—typically microfarads (µF, $10^{-6}\text{ F}$) or nanofarads (nF, $10^{-9}\text{ F}$). Because moving charge onto the plates takes time, a capacitor's voltage cannot change instantly. When charged through a resistor $R$, the RC time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$ (in seconds) tells you the exact time needed to cover $63.2\%$ of the remaining voltage step (reaching $\approx 99.3\%$ after $5\tau$).
Alternative resource: PhET — Capacitor Lab: Basics [verify in-app] — Connect the battery to the parallel plates [verify in-app] to watch charge accumulate until $V_C = V_{\text{battery}}$.

Primary resource: SparkFun — Capacitors ("Decoupling (Bypass) Capacitors" & "Power Supply Filtering") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Application Examples, Decoupling (Bypass) Capacitors, and Power Supply Filtering.
What to skip: Skip audio crossover sections.
Key takeaway: When a heavy load or digital chip suddenly demands a burst of current, the parasitic resistance of long battery wires causes the $5.0\text{ V}$ supply rail to dip ("brown out"), which can reboot a microcontroller mid-motion. Placing a $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($100\text{ nF}$) ceramic decoupling capacitor right next to the chip's VCC and GND pins (paired with a $100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic bulk capacitor where power enters the breadboard) supplies that instant current burst locally and keeps the voltage rail rock-steady.

When a capacitor $C$ (starting at $0\text{ V}$) charges toward $V_{\text{supply}}$ through a series resistor $R$, its voltage $V_C(t)$ at time $t$ follows an exponential curve governed by the RC time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$:
Check the units carefully: multiplying Ohms ($\Omega$) by Farads ($\text{F}$) produces seconds ($\text{s}$):
If $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega = 10{,}000\ \Omega$ and $C = 100\ \mu\text{F} = 0.000100\text{ F}$, then $\tau = 10{,}000 \times 0.000100 = 1.0\text{ s}$.
At $t = 1\tau$ ($1.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63.2\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($3.16\text{ V}$ on a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply).
At $t = 2\tau$ ($2.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-2} \approx 86.5\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($4.32\text{ V}$).
At $t = 5\tau$ ($5.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-5} \approx 99.3\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($4.97\text{ V}$—effectively fully charged).
(Safety note on polarized capacitors: Small ceramic decoupling capacitors like $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ / $100\text{ nF}$ are unpolarized and can be inserted either way. Larger cylindrical aluminum electrolytic capacitors like $100\ \mu\text{F}$ are polarized: the shorter leg marked with a - stripe MUST connect to GND!)

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.6-rc-capacitor.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... ($5.0\text{ V}$ supply, $R = 10{,}000\ \Omega$, $C = 0.0001\text{ F} = 100\ \mu\text{F}$, $\tau = 1.00\text{ s}$). Complete TODO 1 by closing the charging switch (s ... 0 0 false $\rightarrow$ click closed in Falstad) and reading the capacitor voltage on the bottom oscilloscope trace at $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ (3.16 V), $2.0\text{ s}$ (4.32 V), and $5.0\text{ s}$ (4.97 V). (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and exponential charging mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Bursting a physical electrolytic capacitor by wiring its - stripe to $+12\text{ V}$.

sections.h: Starter Code (import into Falstad — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Import this Falstad netlist (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text...) and complete TODO 1 by closing the switch (s 144 128 240 128 0 0 false $\rightarrow$ click closed in Falstad) to charge the $100\ \mu\text{F}$ (0.0001 F) capacitor through the $10\text{ k}\Omega$ (10000 Ω) resistor:

With $R = 10{,}000\ \Omega$, $C = 100\ \mu\text{F}$ ($0.0001\text{ F}$), and $V_{\text{supply}} = 5.0\text{ V}$, the time constant $\tau$ and capacitor voltage $V_C(t)$ at $t = 1.0\text{ s}, 2.0\text{ s}, 5.0\text{ s}$ are:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
Convert $100\ \mu\text{F}$ to base Farads ($100 / 1{,}000{,}000 = 0.0001\text{ F}$) and multiply by $10{,}000\ \Omega$ to get $\tau = 1.00\text{ s}$. At $1\tau$, $V_C = 5.0 \times (1 - e^{-1}) \approx 3.16\text{ V}$; at $5\tau$, $V_C = 5.0 \times (1 - e^{-5}) \approx 4.97\text{ V}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, line 5 (c 352 128 352 288 0 0.0001 0 0.001) sets $C = 0.0001\text{ F}$ ($100\ \mu\text{F}$) and initial voltage 0 V, while line 3 (s ...) is the charging switch.
Full Solution

Wiring a polarized electrolytic capacitor backward (- stripe to 5V instead of GND): Reverse voltage breaks down the thin oxide layer inside an electrolytic capacitor, causing it to overheat and pop! Always connect the shorter lead with the - stripe to GND.
Placing the $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ decoupling capacitor far away from the chip on the breadboard: Long jumper wires add parasitic impedance that blocks fast current pulses; always place the $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ceramic capacitor as close as physically possible to the IC's VCC and GND pins.

Unit conversion (nF to µF): Ceramic decoupling capacitors are often labeled 100 nF (100 nanofarads). Since $1\ \mu\text{F} = 1{,}000\text{ nF}$, how many microfarads (µF) is $100\text{ nF}$?
Answer
$\frac{100\text{ nF}}{1000} = \mathbf{0.1\ \mu\text{F}}$. (100 nF and 0.1 µF are two names for the exact same capacitor!)
Calculating $1\tau$ and $5\tau$: A sensor filter uses a $1\text{ k}\Omega$ ($1{,}000\ \Omega$) resistor and a $10\ \mu\text{F}$ ($0.000010\text{ F}$) capacitor. What is the RC time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$ in milliseconds (ms), and how long does it take to reach $\approx 99.3\%$ ($5\tau$)?
Answer
$\tau = 1{,}000\ \Omega \times 0.000010\text{ F} = 0.010\text{ s} = \mathbf{10\text{ ms}}$, so $5\tau = \mathbf{50\text{ ms}}$.
Why decoupling matters in robotics: Your microcontroller runs fine when blinking an LED, but reboots every time a heavy load on the same power supply switches on. Which components across the power rails fix this brownout?
Answer
A $100\ \mu\text{F}$ bulk electrolytic capacitor across the breadboard power rails (to buffer surge current) plus a $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($100\text{ nF}$) ceramic decoupling capacitor across the microcontroller's VCC and GND pins.

A capacitor ($C$, in Farads F) stores charge and resists sudden changes in voltage ($V$), charging $63.2\%$ in one RC time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$ and $\approx 99.3\%$ in $5\tau$.
Decoupling capacitors ($0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ceramic near logic chips + $100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic on power rails) act as local charge reservoirs that prevent supply voltage dips.

pages.title: Meet the Microcontroller (Arduino Uno 5 V) — Digital I/O and INPUT_PULLUP

sections.t:
Write your first Arduino Uno (5.0 V) sketch in Wokwi using setup() and loop() to drive a digital output (pinMode, digitalWrite) and read a pushbutton reliably without floating-pin noise using the internal pull-up resistor (INPUT_PULLUP, digitalRead).
New ideas (max 2):
Microcontroller program loop (setup/loop) and digital output (pinMode/digitalWrite): How an Arduino runs setup() once at power-on and loop() forever, switching a digital pin between LOW ($0.0\text{ V}$) and HIGH ($5.0\text{ V}$, $\le 20\text{ mA}$ safe continuous limit).
Digital input (digitalRead) and active-low pushbuttons with INPUT_PULLUP: Why an unconnected input pin "floats" randomly between 0 and 1, and how enabling the internal $20\text{–}50\text{ k}\Omega$ pull-up resistor to +5V holds the pin HIGH (1) when released and LOW (0) when pressed to GND.
New syntax (C/C++ on Arduino Uno): void setup() { ... }, void loop() { ... }, int x = ...; (semicolons ; at the end of statements), pinMode(pin, mode), digitalWrite(pin, val), digitalRead(pin), Serial.begin(9600), Serial.println(...).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Command Clamping
Lesson S0.4: Diodes, LEDs, Forward Voltage Drop & Resistor Power Ratings

sections.h: Idea 1: Microcontroller program loop (setup/loop) and digital output (pinMode/digitalWrite)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wokwi Docs — wokwi-arduino-uno Reference [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Pin names (0 to 13, A0 to A5, 5V, GND, LED), Simulation features, and Simulator examples (Arduino Blink).
What to skip: Skip AREF and IOREF until Track 04.
Key takeaway: We standardize all Stage 0 microcontroller lessons on the Arduino Uno (ATmega328P, 5.0 V logic) in Wokwi because its single $5.0\text{ V}$ voltage domain, 14 digital pins (0–13), and 6 analog input pins (A0–A5) are the cleanest possible entry point. Every Arduino sketch has two functions: void setup() runs once at power-on (to configure pins with pinMode(13, OUTPUT);), and void loop() repeats forever (driving pins to $5.0\text{ V}$ with digitalWrite(13, HIGH); or $0.0\text{ V}$ with digitalWrite(13, LOW);, up to a $20\text{ mA}$ safe continuous pin limit).

sections.h: Idea 2: Digital input (digitalRead) and active-low pushbuttons with INPUT_PULLUP
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Pull-up Resistors [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings What is a Pull-up Resistor and Calculating a Pull-up Resistor Value.
What to skip: Skip open-drain I2C bus pull-up math at the bottom of the SparkFun page (covered in Track 04).
Key takeaway: If you wire a pushbutton to a digital input pin with pinMode(2, INPUT); and leave the pin unconnected when the button is not pressed, the pin floats—picking up stray electrostatic noise from the air and flipping randomly between HIGH (1) and LOW (0). Calling pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP); switches on a built-in resistor ($20\text{–}50\text{ k}\Omega$) inside the Arduino chip between Pin 2 and +5V, and you wire the button between Pin 2 and GND. That creates an active-low input:
Button released (open): Internal pull-up gently holds Pin 2 at HIGH (1, $5.0\text{ V}$).
Button pressed (closed to GND): The button connects Pin 2 directly to GND, so digitalRead(2) reads LOW (0, $0.0\text{ V}$).
Alternative resource: Wokwi Docs — wokwi-pushbutton Reference [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Pin names (1.l, 1.r, 2.l, 2.r) and Examples.

Arduino Uno sketches are written in C/C++, which uses the exact same variables, functions, and if/else decisions you learned in Track P with three small syntax rules:
Curly braces { ... } instead of indentation mark the body of every function (void setup() { ... }, void loop() { ... }) and if/else block.
Semicolons ; terminate every statement line (forgetting a ; at the end of a line is the most common C/C++ compiler error).
Explicit variable types (int, float, bool) are written in front of a variable name the first time you declare it (for example, int pin_reading = digitalRead(2);).
When wiring a pushbutton to a microcontroller input pin, never leave the pin unconnected ("floating") when the switch is open. Calling pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP); inside setup() connects an internal $20\text{–}50\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor inside the ATmega328P chip between Pin 2 and +5.0 V, while you wire the external pushbutton between Pin 2 and GND. That creates a rock-solid active-low safety input—reading HIGH (1) when released and LOW (0) when pressed:

What is simulated and in which tool:
5-Minute Falstad "See It Without Code" Twin (Always Falstad Before Arduino!): Before writing a single line of C code, open Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app] and import falstad/S0.4-led-resistor.txt [verify in-app]. Watch how a series switch + $220\ \Omega$ resistor + LED behaves purely as a physical circuit, and observe how a pull-up resistor to $+5\text{ V}$ holds a switch node at $5.0\text{ V}$ until the switch closes to GND ($0.0\text{ V}$).
In Wokwi Arduino Uno Simulator [verify in-app]: Wire a wokwi-pushbutton between Arduino Pin 2 and GND (the Uno already has a built-in LED wired to Pin 13 labeled L). Paste the Starter Code below into the Wokwi editor, complete TODO 1 and TODO 2, click the green Start Simulation play button [verify in-app], and compare the Serial Monitor output against the Expected Output below. (Automated CI compiles this sketch for arduino:avr:uno on every push via arduino-cli.)
What is real-hardware only: Physical mechanical contact bounce (microsecond chatter when metal button contacts touch).

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is in Wokwi — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Complete check_active_low_button (TODO 1) and setup() (TODO 2) in your Wokwi Arduino Uno sketch so it self-tests both button states (HIGH = released, LOW = pressed to GND) at startup and prints the exact expected verification lines to the Serial Monitor, then runs live in loop():

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed and you run the simulation in Wokwi, the Serial Monitor prints:
(And clicking the pushbutton in Wokwi while the simulation runs lights up the built-in L LED on Pin 13!)

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, remember that an active-low button (INPUT_PULLUP wired to GND) reads LOW (0) when pressed. Check if (pin_reading == LOW) and return HIGH; otherwise return LOW. In TODO 2, change pinMode(2, INPUT); to pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Using pinMode(2, INPUT) instead of pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP) without an external resistor: The input pin floats and triggers randomly when your hand gets near the wire. Always use INPUT_PULLUP for simple pushbuttons wired to GND.
Wiring the pushbutton across two pins on the same always-connected side of a 4-leg tactile switch: In Wokwi (wokwi-pushbutton), pins 1.l and 1.r are permanently connected together internally, and 2.l and 2.r are permanently connected together. Always wire Pin 2 to 1.l and GND to 2.l (or diagonally across the button) so the switch is open until pressed.

Active-low logic: When Pin 2 is configured with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP); and a button is wired between Pin 2 and GND, what does digitalRead(2) return when your finger is off the button, and what does it return when you press the button?
Answer
Finger off (switch open): HIGH (1), because the internal pull-up resistor holds the pin at $5.0\text{ V}$.
Button pressed (switch closed to GND): LOW (0), because the switch connects the pin directly to $0.0\text{ V}$ (GND).
Pull-up current when pressed: If the Arduino Uno's internal pull-up resistor is $25\text{ k}\Omega$ ($25{,}000\ \Omega$) connected to $5.0\text{ V}$, how much current flows through the button to GND while it is held down?
Answer
By Ohm's Law, $I = \frac{5.0\text{ V}}{25{,}000\ \Omega} = 0.0002\text{ A} = \mathbf{0.2\text{ mA}}$—tiny and completely safe!
Driving heavy loads: Can you connect a brushed DC motor that draws $500\text{ mA}$ directly between Arduino Pin 13 (OUTPUT) and GND?
Answer
Never! An Arduino Uno GPIO pin can safely supply at most $20\text{ mA}$ continuous ($40\text{ mA}$ absolute maximum). Drawing $500\text{ mA}$ will permanently burn out the output transistor inside the microcontroller chip; heavy loads require a dedicated high-current power driver stage (Track 01).

An Arduino Uno (5.0 V) sketch runs setup() once and loop() forever, driving OUTPUT pins to HIGH ($5.0\text{ V}$, $\le 20\text{ mA}$) or LOW ($0.0\text{ V}$).
Configuring a button pin with pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) and wiring the switch to GND eliminates floating-pin noise and produces active-low readings (HIGH when released, LOW when pressed).

pages.title: Reading Analog Sensors — The 10-Bit ADC (analogRead) and Serial Monitor

sections.t:
Read a continuous $0.0\text{–}5.0\text{ V}$ potentiometer voltage on Arduino Uno pin A0 using the 10-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (analogRead(A0) $\rightarrow$ 0..1023), convert the raw integer count back into volts, and stream live telemetry to the Serial Monitor (9600 baud).
New ideas (max 2):
10-bit Analog-to-Digital Conversion (analogRead 0..1023 at $5.0\text{ V}$): How the Arduino Uno's 10-bit ADC slices the $0.0\text{ V}$ to $5.0\text{ V}$ analog range into $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ steps (0 to 1023, $\approx 4.88\text{ mV}$ per step).
Serial UART telemetry (Serial.begin and Serial.print/println): Sending live human-readable numbers from the microcontroller to your computer at 9600 baud (bits per second) so you are never debugging blind.
New syntax (C/C++ on Arduino Uno): analogRead(A0), floating-point division 5.0 / 1023.0 (using .0 so C/C++ does not truncate integer division to 0), Serial.println(val, 2) (printing a float to 2 decimal places).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.0 hours

Lesson P.8: Cycle Frequency (Hz), Period & Binary Bits
Lesson P.9: Rearranging Physics Formulas & Linear Range Scaling
Lesson S0.2: Series vs. Parallel Resistor Networks, Voltage Dividers & Potentiometers
Lesson S0.7: Meet the Microcontroller (Arduino Uno 5 V) — Digital I/O & INPUT_PULLUP

Primary resource: SparkFun — Analog to Digital Conversion [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings The Analog World, What is the ADC?, Relating ADC Value to Voltage, and Arduino ADC Example.
What to skip: Skip AREF register reconfiguration details.
Key takeaway: Digital pins (0–13) only distinguish LOW ($0\text{ V}$) from HIGH ($5\text{ V}$). To measure a continuous analog voltage—such as a potentiometer wiper at $2.50\text{ V}$—the Arduino Uno routes pins A0 through A5 into a 10-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). As you learned in Lesson P.8, 10 bits represent $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ levels (0 to 1023), mapping $0.0\text{ V} \rightarrow 0$ and $5.0\text{ V} \rightarrow 1023$ ($\approx 4.88\text{ mV}$ per count).

sections.h: Idea 2: Serial UART telemetry (Serial.begin and Serial.print/println)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wokwi Docs — The Serial Monitor [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings The Serial Monitor, Arduino Uno and Mega, and Configuring the Serial Monitor.
What to skip: Skip custom diagram.json raw byte-stream overrides.
Key takeaway: A microcontroller has no screen of its own. Calling Serial.begin(9600); in setup() opens a text communication line at 9600 bits per second (baud) between the Arduino and Wokwi's Serial Monitor pane. Inside setup() or loop(), Serial.print(...) prints text on the current line and Serial.println(...) finishes the line with a newline (\n).

Inside the Arduino Uno (5.0 V), pins A0 through A5 connect to a 10-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). As you learned in Lesson P.8, a 10-bit binary register holds $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ distinct integer codes from 0 to 1023. Calling analogRead(A0) compares the voltage on pin A0 against the board's $5.0\text{ V}$ supply reference and returns 0 for $0.0\text{ V}$, 512 for $\approx 2.50\text{ V}$, and 1023 for $5.0\text{ V}$.
Using the linear range scaling formula from Lesson P.9, converting an Arduino Uno 10-bit ADC count $\text{adc-raw} \in [0, 1023]$ back into measured voltage $V_{\text{pin}}$ is:
Crucial C/C++ integer division warning:
In Python (Lesson P.2), 512 / 1023 automatically produces a float (0.500488...). In C/C++ on Arduino, dividing two integers (int) with / performs integer truncation—discarding everything after the decimal point so 512 / 1023 evaluates to 0! Always write 1023.0 and 5.0 with decimal points so C/C++ uses floating-point division, and print the result to 2 decimal places using Serial.print(v_pin, 2):

What is simulated and in which tool:
5-Minute Falstad "See It Without Code" Twin (Falstad Before Arduino): First open Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app] and import falstad/S0.2-voltage-divider.txt [verify in-app]. Watch the midpoint voltage divider node sit at $2.50\text{ V}$ with zero code—that exact $0.0\text{–}5.0\text{ V}$ wiper voltage is what the Arduino Uno's A0 pin measures and converts into 0..1023.
In Wokwi Arduino Uno Simulator [verify in-app]: Add a wokwi-potentiometer (+ button $\rightarrow$ Potentiometer [verify in-app]). Wire GND to Arduino GND, VCC to Arduino 5V, and the middle wiper pin SIG to A0. Paste the Starter Code below into Wokwi, complete TODO 1 and TODO 2, start the simulation, and verify that the startup self-test in the Serial Monitor matches the Expected Output below. (Automated CI compiles this sketch for arduino:avr:uno via arduino-cli.)
What is real-hardware only: $\pm 1\text{ LSB}$ thermal noise and $5\text{ V}$ USB rail sag on a physical Arduino board.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is in Wokwi — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Complete adc_to_volts (TODO 1) and adc_to_percent (TODO 2) in the Wokwi Arduino Uno sketch below. Remember to use 1023.0 and 5.0 (with .0) so C/C++ uses floating-point division!
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed and you run the simulation in Wokwi, the Serial Monitor prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In C/C++, if adc_raw is an int, writing (adc_raw / 1023) 5.0 divides two integers first (256 / 1023 == 0) and prints 0.00 V! Write (adc_raw / 1023.0) 5.0 in TODO 1 and (adc_raw / 1023.0) 100.0 in TODO 2.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

adc_to_volts prints 0.00 V for every reading except 1023: You wrote (adc_raw / 1023) 5.0 using integer 1023 instead of floating-point 1023.0. Always include .0 when dividing in C/C++.
analogRead(A0) jumps wildly when nothing is connected to A0: Just like an unconnected digital input, an unconnected analog input pin floats and acts like a tiny radio antenna. Always connect A0 to a low-impedance voltage source or voltage divider.

Step size (resolution) of the Uno ADC: What is the smallest voltage change ($1\text{ LSB}$) that the Arduino Uno's 10-bit ADC ($5.0\text{ V}$ reference, $1{,}023$ steps) can detect, in millivolts (mV)?
Answer
$\frac{5.0\text{ V}}{1023} \approx 0.004888\text{ V} \approx \mathbf{4.89\text{ mV}}$.
Predicting analogRead(A0): If a sensor outputs $3.75\text{ V}$ into A0 on a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino Uno, what integer will analogRead(A0) return?
Answer
$\frac{3.75\text{ V}}{5.0\text{ V}} \times 1023 = 0.75 \times 1023 = 767.25 \rightarrow \mathbf{767}$ (or 768).
Why Serial.begin(9600) is required: What happens in the Serial Monitor if you call Serial.println(analogRead(A0)); in loop() but forget to put Serial.begin(9600); inside setup()?
Answer
The Serial UART hardware is never initialized, so the Serial Monitor stays completely blank!

analogRead(A0) uses a 10-bit ADC (0 to 1023) to measure voltages from $0.0\text{ V}$ to $5.0\text{ V}$ ($V_{\text{pin}} = (\text{adc-raw} / 1023.0) \times 5.0$).
Serial.begin(9600) and Serial.print / Serial.println stream live measurements to the Wokwi Serial Monitor.

pages.title: Switching Power Smoothly — PWM Duty Cycle and analogWrite()

sections.t:
Control effective power delivered to a load by switching a digital pin rapidly between $0\text{ V}$ and $5.0\text{ V}$ using Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) ($V_{\text{avg}} = \text{Duty} \times 5.0\text{ V}$), inspect live PWM waveforms on Falstad's oscilloscope, and drive an LED across 4 brightness levels on Arduino Uno pin ~9 using 8-bit analogWrite(pin, 0..255) in Wokwi.
New ideas (max 2):
Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) duty cycle and average voltage ($V_{\text{avg}} = \text{Duty} \times V_{\text{cc}}$): Controlling average voltage and power using the fraction of each cycle period $T = 1/f$ that a fast digital switch stays HIGH ($T_{\text{on}} / T$).
8-bit Arduino PWM output (analogWrite 0..255) and carrier frequency: Mapping an 8-bit command ($2^8 = 256$ steps, 0 to 255) to $0\%\text{–}100\%$ duty cycle on Arduino Uno tilde (~) pins (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11).
New syntax (C/C++ on Arduino Uno): analogWrite(pwm_pin, duty_0_to_255).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.0 hours

Lesson P.8: Cycle Frequency (Hz), Period & Binary Bits
Lesson S0.8: Reading Analog Sensors — The 10-Bit ADC (analogRead) & Serial Monitor

sections.h: Idea 1: Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) duty cycle and average voltage ($V_{\text{avg}} = \text{Duty} \times V_{\text{cc}}$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Pulse Width Modulation [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings What is Pulse-width Modulation?, Duty Cycle, and Examples.
What to skip: Skip manual ATmega timer-register bit-banging—use analogWrite() in Stage 0.
Key takeaway: An Arduino Uno has no true analog voltage output (DAC); its pins can only switch between $0.0\text{ V}$ (LOW) and $5.0\text{ V}$ (HIGH). To simulate an intermediate voltage, Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) switches the pin between $0\text{ V}$ and $5\text{ V}$ hundreds of times per second. The duty cycle is the fraction (or percentage) of each period $T = 1/f$ that the signal stays HIGH ($\text{Duty} = T_{\text{on}} / T$). Because your eyes and mechanical motors average out fast pulses, a $25\%$ duty cycle acts like $0.25 \times 5.0\text{ V} = 1.25\text{ V}$, and a $50\%$ duty cycle acts like $2.50\text{ V}$!

sections.h: Idea 2: 8-bit Arduino PWM output (analogWrite 0..255) and carrier frequency
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wokwi Docs — wokwi-arduino-uno Reference ("Pin names") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact heading Pin names and note the six digital pins (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) that support hardware analogWrite PWM.
What to skip: Skip wokwi-logic-analyzer for now (see note below).
Key takeaway: On the Arduino Uno, analogWrite(pin, value) works on the six hardware PWM pins (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) and accepts an 8-bit integer (0 to 255), where 0 is always off ($0\%$), 128 is $\approx 50.2\%$ duty cycle ($2.51\text{ V}$ average), and 255 is always on ($100\%$, $5.00\text{ V}$).
Simulator waveform note (Falstad Scope vs. Wokwi Logic Analyzer): Wokwi's wokwi-logic-analyzer does not display live waveforms in the browser—it records a .vcd file that only downloads when you stop the simulation and requires installing desktop software (PulseView or GTKWave) to view. To see live PWM square waves right in your browser with zero install, we use Falstad's built-in Oscilloscope (falstad/S0.9-pwm-scope.txt)!

For any 8-bit command $\text{pwm-val} \in [0, 255]$ on a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino Uno, the duty cycle, average voltage $V_{\text{avg}}$, and pulse ON-time $T_{\text{on}}$ (at period $T = 1 / f_{\text{pwm}}$) are:
Watch out — 10-bit analogRead (0..1023) vs. 8-bit analogWrite (0..255):
analogRead(A0) returns a 10-bit number (0 to 1023).
analogWrite(9, val) expects an 8-bit number (0 to 255).
Passing 1023 directly into analogWrite(9, val) wraps around modulo 256! Always divide a 10-bit ADC reading by 4 (pwm_val = adc_raw / 4;) to map 0..1023 cleanly onto 0..255.
🔭 Looking Ahead (Stage 0 LED PWM vs. Track 01/03 Motor PWM Frequency):
On the Arduino Uno, default analogWrite() runs at ~490 Hz on pins 3, 9, 10, 11 ($T \approx 2{,}040.8\ \mu\text{s} \approx 2.04\text{ ms}$) and ~980 Hz on pins 5, 6 ($T \approx 1{,}020.4\ \mu\text{s}$). That is plenty fast enough for dimming LEDs without visible flicker (human eyes fuse flashes above $\sim 60\text{ Hz}$). However, when we drive real motors in Track 01 and Track 03, a $490\text{ Hz}$ or $980\text{ Hz}$ switching wave vibrates the motor windings right in the middle of human hearing ($20\text{ Hz–}20\text{ kHz}$), making an annoying audible whine and causing high current ripple. In Track 03, you will configure hardware timers for 20 kHz ultrasonic PWM ($T = 50\ \mu\text{s}$) so motor switching is completely silent!

What is simulated and in which tool:
Live PWM waveform on Falstad's Oscilloscope [verify in-app]: Import falstad/S0.9-pwm-scope.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... to compare $25\%$, $50\%$, and $75\%$ duty-cycle $5\text{ V}$ square waves live in the bottom scope pane.
Arduino Uno analogWrite in Wokwi [verify in-app]: Wire Arduino Pin 9 (~9) $\rightarrow$ 220 Ω resistor $\rightarrow$ LED Anode (A), and LED Cathode (C) $\rightarrow$ GND. Paste the Starter Code below, complete TODO 1 and TODO 2, run the simulation, and compare the Serial Monitor against the Expected Output below. (Automated CI compiles this sketch for arduino:avr:uno via arduino-cli.)
What is real-hardware only: Hearing audible $490\text{ Hz}$ coil whine on a physical motor vs. silent $20\text{ kHz}$ ultrasonic PWM.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In both TODO 1 and TODO 2, compute float duty = pwm_val / 255.0; using 255.0 so C/C++ performs floating-point division. In TODO 2, one cycle period in microseconds is 1000000.0 / freq_hz ($\approx 2040.816\ \mu\text{s}$ at 490.0 Hz).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Calling analogWrite() on a non-PWM pin like Pin 2, Pin 4, Pin 7, Pin 8, Pin 12, or Pin 13: On the Arduino Uno, hardware PWM only exists on the six tilde (~) pins: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11. On any other digital pin, analogWrite(pin, val) simply outputs LOW for values = 128!
Passing analogRead(A0) (0..1023) directly into analogWrite(9, val) (0..255): Values above 255 wrap around modulo 256 (256 becomes 0!). Always scale 0..1023 down to 0..255 by dividing by 4 (adc_raw / 4).

Instantaneous voltage vs. average voltage: When analogWrite(9, 128) ($\approx 50\%$ duty cycle) runs on a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino Uno, does Pin 9 ever sit at a steady $2.50\text{ V}$, or does it switch rapidly between $0.0\text{ V}$ and $5.0\text{ V}$?
Answer
It switches rapidly between $0.0\text{ V}$ and $5.0\text{ V}$ (spending $\approx 50\%$ of each $2{,}040.8\ \mu\text{s}$ cycle at $5.0\text{ V}$ and $50\%$ at $0.0\text{ V}$), which averages out to $2.51\text{ V}$.
Scaling 10-bit ADC to 8-bit PWM: If analogRead(A0) returns 768 ($75\%$ of 1023), what is 768 / 4, and what average voltage does analogWrite(9, 768 / 4) produce?
Answer
768 / 4 = 192, which produces $V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{192}{255} \times 5.0\text{ V} \approx \mathbf{3.76\text{ V}}$.
490 Hz LED PWM vs. 20 kHz Motor PWM: Why is the Arduino Uno's default $490\text{ Hz}$ analogWrite() frequency fine for dimming an LED in Stage 0, whereas motor controllers in Track 03 use $20\text{ kHz}$ PWM?
Answer
Human eyes cannot see flicker above $\sim 60\text{ Hz}$, so $490\text{ Hz}$ looks completely smooth on an LED. However, human ears hear vibrations up to $20\text{ kHz}$, so $490\text{ Hz}$ makes motor coils whine audibly and causes large current ripple, whereas $20\text{ kHz}$ is ultrasonic (silent) and keeps motor current smooth.

PWM duty cycle ($\text{Duty} = T_{\text{on}} / T$) controls average voltage $V_{\text{avg}} = \text{Duty} \times V_{\text{cc}}$ by switching rapidly between $0\text{ V}$ and $5.0\text{ V}$.
On the Arduino Uno, analogWrite(pin, 0..255) outputs 8-bit PWM on pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11.
