pages.title: Stage 0 Milestone — Potentiometer LED Dimmer with Safety Kill-Switch

sections.t:
Build and verify a complete Sense $\rightarrow$ Decide $\rightarrow$ Act embedded system on the Arduino Uno (5.0 V) in Wokwi that reads a potentiometer on A0 (0..1023), checks an active-low safety kill-switch button on Pin 2 (INPUT_PULLUP), drives an LED on Pin 9 with 8-bit PWM (0..255), and logs live telemetry to the Serial Monitor.
New ideas (max 2):
Hardware-software safety override loop (Sense $\rightarrow$ Decide $\rightarrow$ Act): Combining continuous analog sensing (analogRead(A0)), highest-priority digital kill-switch gating (digitalRead(2) == LOW), and scaled PWM output (analogWrite(9, pwm_val)) in a single loop.
New syntax: Integer scaling adc_raw / 4 in C/C++ (0..1023 $\rightarrow$ 0..255).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–2.5 hours
All Stage 0 lessons: S0.1, S0.2, S0.3, S0.4, S0.5, S0.6, S0.7, S0.8, and S0.9.

sections.h: Idea 1: Hardware-software safety override loop (Sense -> Decide -> Act)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wokwi Docs — wokwi-arduino-uno Reference [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact heading Pin names (A0, 2, 9, 5V, GND).
What to skip: No new external reading required—this milestone combines Lessons S0.7, S0.8, and S0.9.
Key takeaway: Every real mechatronic controller follows the same three-stage cycle on every tick: Sense (read the potentiometer on A0 and the kill-switch on Pin 2), Decide (if the kill-switch is pressed, force output to 0; otherwise scale 0..1023 down to 0..255), and Act & Report (write pwm_val to Pin 9 and print telemetry to the Serial Monitor).
Alternative resource: Wokwi Docs — wokwi-potentiometer Reference [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review exact heading Pin names (GND, SIG, VCC).

In this Stage 0 Milestone, you will wire three components to an Arduino Uno (5.0 V) in Wokwi:
Potentiometer (wokwi-potentiometer) on A0: VCC $\rightarrow$ 5V, GND $\rightarrow$ GND, center wiper SIG $\rightarrow$ A0. Turning the knob sweeps analogRead(A0) from 0 ($0.0\text{ V}$) to 1023 ($5.0\text{ V}$).
Safety Kill-Switch Pushbutton (wokwi-pushbutton) on Pin 2: Configured with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP); and wired between Pin 2 and GND. When released, digitalRead(2) is HIGH (1). When pressed and held, digitalRead(2) is LOW (0).
PWM Dimmer LED (wokwi-led + 220 Ω wokwi-resistor) on Pin 9: Pin 9 $\rightarrow$ 220 Ω resistor $\rightarrow$ LED Anode (A), and LED Cathode (C) $\rightarrow$ GND.
In every pass, your compute_milestone_pwm(adc_raw, button_pin) function checks the safety switch first: if button_pin == LOW, pwm_val is forced to 0 regardless of where the potentiometer knob sits! Otherwise, pwm_val is set to adc_raw / 4 (0..255).

What is simulated and in which tool:
5-Minute Falstad "See It Without Code" Twin (Falstad Before Arduino): Before running the Arduino sketch, open Falstad Circuit Simulator [verify in-app] and inspect falstad/S0.2-voltage-divider.txt [verify in-app] (potentiometer voltage divider) and falstad/S0.9-pwm-scope.txt [verify in-app] (PWM duty-cycle wave feeding an LED + ballast resistor) so you see both analog halves of the milestone without code first.
Full interactive circuit & firmware in Wokwi Arduino Uno Simulator [verify in-app]: Build the 3-part circuit described above (wokwi-potentiometer on A0, wokwi-pushbutton between Pin 2 and GND, and 220 Ω resistor + wokwi-led on Pin 9), paste the Starter Code below, complete TODO 1 and TODO 2, start the simulation, and verify that the 4 startup self-test lines in the Serial Monitor match the Expected Output below. (Automated CI compiles this sketch for arduino:avr:uno via arduino-cli.)
What is real-hardware only: Physical breadboard jumper wire resistance and mechanical button contact bounce.

sections.t: Complete compute_milestone_pwm (TODO 1 and TODO 2) in your Wokwi Arduino Uno sketch so the startup self-test verifies all 4 test cases ([0, HIGH], [512, HIGH], [1023, HIGH], and [1023, LOW] with kill-switch pressed) and loop() runs the live dimmer:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed and you run the simulation in Wokwi, the Serial Monitor prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
Check if (button_pin == LOW) first so that a pressed kill-switch always returns 0 even when adc_raw is 1023. In C/C++, dividing two int values with adc_raw / 4 performs integer floor division (1023 / 4 == 255).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Potentiometer outer pins wired to A0 instead of the middle wiper pin (SIG): If you wire SIG to 5V and one outer pin to A0, turning the knob will not divide the voltage! Always wire the two outer pins to 5V and GND, and the middle pin (SIG) to A0.
Kill-switch works backward (LED only turns on when button is held): You wrote if (button_pin == HIGH) { return 0; } instead of if (button_pin == LOW) { return 0; }. Remember: with INPUT_PULLUP, pressing the button connects the pin to GND (LOW).

Tracing the safety override: Suppose the potentiometer knob is turned to 75% (adc_raw = 768) and the user presses and holds the pushbutton on Pin 2. What values do digitalRead(2) and pwm_val take?
Answer
digitalRead(2) returns LOW (0), and the if (button_pin == LOW) safety check overrides the knob and sets pwm_val to 0, turning the LED completely off.
LED current at 50% PWM: When adc_raw = 512 (pwm_val = 128, $\approx 50\%$ duty cycle) with a red LED ($V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$) and a $220\ \Omega$ series resistor on Pin 9, what is the current during the HIGH half of each pulse, what is the current during the LOW half, and what is the average LED current?
Answer
During the HIGH ($5.0\text{ V}$) half: $I_{\text{on}} = \frac{5.0 - 2.0}{220} \approx \mathbf{13.64\text{ mA}}$.
During the LOW ($0.0\text{ V}$) half: $I_{\text{off}} = \mathbf{0.0\text{ mA}}$.
Average current over the full cycle: $13.64\text{ mA} \times \frac{128}{255} \approx \mathbf{6.85\text{ mA}}$.
Why check the safety switch before writing the output? What would happen if your code called analogWrite(9, adc_raw / 4); at the top of loop() and only checked if (button_pin == LOW) { analogWrite(9, 0); } after a delay(100);?
Answer
Even while the emergency mute button was held down, the output pin would still turn ON for 100 ms on every single loop iteration! Always compute the safe command first and call analogWrite once after all safety checks have run.

You built and verified a complete Stage 0 Arduino Uno (5.0 V) system combining a 10-bit analog sensor (A0), an active-low safety switch (D2 with INPUT_PULLUP), an 8-bit PWM actuator output (~D9), and live 9600 baud Serial Monitor telemetry.

Your Wokwi sketch prints the exact 4 expected lines in the Serial Monitor.
Turning the potentiometer in Wokwi smoothly sweeps LED brightness, and holding the pushbutton on Pin 2 immediately forces the LED off.

pages.title: Cross-Domain Power (P = Effort * Flow) and First-Order Lag

sections.t:
Connect electrical, linear mechanical, and rotational mechanical systems through the universal power law ($\text{Power} = \text{Effort} \times \text{Flow}$, measured in Watts W), and simulate a first-order lag step response in Python to see why every real sensor, thermal body, and RC circuit reaches $63.2\%$ of a step command in $1\tau$ and $99.3\%$ in $5\tau$.
New ideas (max 2):
Effort, flow, and universal instantaneous power ($P = V \cdot I = F \cdot v = \tau \cdot \omega$): Every physical energy domain pairs a "push" variable (Effort: voltage $V$, force $F$, torque $\tau$) with a "movement" variable (Flow: current $I$, linear velocity $v$, angular velocity $\omega$) whose product is instantaneous power in Watts (W).
First-order lag step response and time constant $\tau$ ($63.2\%$ at $1\tau$, $99.3\%$ at $5\tau$): How a discrete while loop updates a sluggish system whose rate of change is proportional to the remaining gap (target - y) / tau.
New syntax: None (uses Python functions, while loops, and assert from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.11: Reading Time-Series Graphs — Slope & Area
Lesson P.12: Forces, Newton's Second Law & Lever Torque
Lesson S0.4: Diodes, LEDs, Forward Voltage Drop & Resistor Power Ratings
Lesson S0.6: Capacitors — Charge Storage & Power-Rail Decoupling
Lesson S0.M: Stage 0 Milestone — Potentiometer LED Dimmer with Safety Kill-Switch

sections.h: Idea 1: Effort, flow, and universal instantaneous power ($P = V \cdot I = F \cdot v = \tau \cdot \omega$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Power [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Power and Another Formula for Power (deriving $P = F \cdot v$, Power = Force $\times$ Velocity).
What to skip: Skip the horsepower history trivia.
Key takeaway: In Stage 0 (Lesson S0.4), you learned that electrical power in Watts (W) is $P_{\text{elec}} = V \cdot I$ (Voltage push $\times$ Current flow). Mechanical systems obey the exact same law! Mechanical power for straight-line motion is $P_{\text{lin}} = F \cdot v$ (Force in N $\times$ velocity in m/s), and for rotating shafts it is $P_{\text{rot}} = \tau \cdot \omega$ (Torque in N·m $\times$ angular velocity in rad/s—always in radians per second, never RPM!). Together, these are called Effort and Flow variables: across any motor or gearbox, electrical power in equals mechanical power out plus heat loss.
Alternative resource: Math is Fun — Power [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Power and Power Formulas.

sections.h: Idea 2: First-order lag step response and time constant $\tau$ ($63.2\%$ at $1\tau$, $99.3\%$ at $5\tau$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Capacitors ("Charging and Discharging") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact heading Charging and Discharging and notice how the rate of charging slows down as the capacitor voltage approaches the target supply voltage.
What to skip: Skip series/parallel capacitor bank math.
Key takeaway: In Lesson S0.6, you saw an RC capacitor charge $63.2\%$ of the way to $5.0\text{ V}$ in one time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$ and $99.3\%$ in $5\tau$. That exact curve is called a first-order lag, and it appears everywhere in mechatronics: a temperature sensor warming up, a motor spinning up against friction, or a software smoothing filter. At every tiny time step $\Delta t$, the state $y$ steps toward target by $\Delta y = \frac{\text{target} - y}{\tau} \cdot \Delta t$.
Alternative resource: HyperPhysics — Work, Energy and Power [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Work, Energy, and Power.

Mechatronics unifies electronics and mechanics because Effort and Flow multiply to give instantaneous power in Watts (W) across every physical domain. In an electrical circuit, voltage $V$ (V) is the effort that pushes current $I$ (A), producing electrical power $P_{\text{elec}} = V \cdot I$. In straight-line motion, force $F$ (N) pushes at linear velocity $v$ (m/s), producing mechanical power $P_{\text{lin}} = F \cdot v$. In a rotating shaft, torque $\tau$ (N·m) twists at angular velocity $\omega$ (rad/s), producing rotational mechanical power $P_{\text{rot}} = \tau \cdot \omega$:
Similarly, whenever a system's rate of change (slope $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}$ from Lesson P.11) is proportional to the remaining gap between target and current value $y$, it obeys the first-order lag update rule with time constant $\tau_{\text{lag}}$ (in seconds):
Whether $y$ is capacitor voltage ($\tau_{\text{lag}} = R C$), motor housing temperature, or unloaded motor speed, stepping this rule forward from $y(0) = 0$ reaches $63.2\%$ of target at $t = 1\tau_{\text{lag}}$ and $99.3\%$ of target at $t = 5\tau_{\text{lag}}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete cross_domain_power (TODO 1) to compare electrical input power ($V \cdot I$) against rotational mechanical output power ($\tau \cdot \omega$) and efficiency, and complete simulate_first_order_lag (TODO 2) using $\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$ (1 ms) to verify the $1\tau$ ($63.2\%$) and $5\tau$ ($99.3\%$) step response milestones.
What is real-hardware only: Convective air-cooling drafts changing the thermal time constant $\tau$ of a physical motor housing.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, electrical power is volts amps (24.00 W) and rotational mechanical power is torque_nm omega_rad_s (18.00 W). In TODO 2, inside the for loop, compute rate = (target - y) / tau_s and update y = y + rate dt.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Multiplying torque $\tau$ (N·m) by speed in RPM instead of rad/s: $P = \tau \cdot \omega$ ONLY works in base SI units where $\omega$ is in radians per second (rad/s). As you learned in Lesson P.10, always convert $\text{RPM}$ to $\text{rad/s}$ first via $\omega = \text{RPM} \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$.
Choosing a simulation step size $\Delta t$ larger than the time constant $\tau_{\text{lag}}$: If $\tau_{\text{lag}} = 0.5\text{ s}$ and you pick $\Delta t = 1.0\text{ s}$, a single Euler step overshoots past $100\%$ to $200\%$! Always choose $\Delta t \le \frac{\tau_{\text{lag}}}{50}$ so the discrete loop tracks the smooth curve accurately.

Rotational mechanical power: A robot wheel delivers $\tau = 2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ of torque while spinning at $\omega = 12.0\text{ rad/s}$. How many Watts (W) of mechanical power is the wheel delivering, and what is the minimum current it must draw from a $12.0\text{ V}$ battery if the motor is $100\%$ efficient?
Answer
$P_{\text{mech}} = \tau \cdot \omega = 2.5 \times 12.0 = \mathbf{30.0\text{ W}}$. From a $12.0\text{ V}$ battery, $I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{30.0\text{ W}}{12.0\text{ V}} = \mathbf{2.5\text{ A}}$.
First-order lag settling time: A motor's speed responds to a step voltage command as a first-order lag with time constant $\tau_{\text{lag}} = 0.08\text{ s}$ ($80\text{ ms}$). How long does it take to reach $63.2\%$ of its final speed, and how long to reach $99.3\%$ ($5\tau_{\text{lag}}$)?
Answer
$63.2\%$ at $1\tau_{\text{lag}} = \mathbf{0.08\text{ s}}$ ($80\text{ ms}$).
$99.3\%$ at $5\tau_{\text{lag}} = 5 \times 0.08\text{ s} = \mathbf{0.40\text{ s}}$ ($400\text{ ms}$).

Instantaneous power (W) in any physical domain is $\text{Effort} \times \text{Flow}$: $P = V \cdot I = F \cdot v = \tau \cdot \omega$ (with $\omega$ in rad/s).
A first-order lag steps via $y_{\text{new}} = y + \frac{\text{target} - y}{\tau} \Delta t$, reaching $63.2\%$ in $1\tau$ and $99.3\%$ in $5\tau$.

pages.title: Second-Order Motion — Springs (F_s = -k*x), Dampers (F_d = -b*v) and Damping Regimes

sections.t:
Model a mass attached to a spring (Hooke's Law, $F_s = -k \cdot x$) and a viscous damper ($F_d = -b \cdot v$), and calculate its natural frequency ($\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$) and damping ratio ($\zeta$) in Python to predict whether a robot joint will ring (underdamped, $\zeta 1$).
New ideas (max 2):
Hooke's Law spring restoring force ($F_s = -k \cdot x$) and viscous damping force ($F_d = -b \cdot v$): A spring pulls back toward equilibrium proportional to position stretch $x$ (spring constant $k$ in N/m), while a damper resists motion proportional to velocity $v$ (viscous damping $b$ in N·s/m).
Natural frequency ($\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$), damping ratio ($\zeta$), and underdamped vs. critically damped vs. overdamped motion: How mass $m$ and stiffness $k$ set oscillation speed $\omega_n$, and how $\zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{m k}}$ determines whether the system overshoots and rings.
New syntax: None (math.sqrt from Lesson P.6).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: Hooke's Law spring restoring force ($F_s = -k \cdot x$) and viscous damping force ($F_d = -b \cdot v$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Motion of a Mass on a Spring [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Motion of a Mass on a Spring, Hooke's Law, and Force Analysis of a Mass on a Spring.
What to skip: Skip vertical hanging-spring equilibrium offsets for now.
Key takeaway: By Hooke's Law, stretching or compressing a spring by displacement $x$ (in meters m) creates a restoring force $F_s = -k \cdot x$ pointing back toward $x = 0$, where $k$ is the spring constant (stiffness, in N/m). Because a mass $m$ has momentum, a spring alone makes the mass coast right past $x = 0$ and oscillate back and forth forever! Adding a shock absorber provides viscous damping force $F_d = -b \cdot v$ (where $b$ is the damping coefficient in N·s/m), which opposes velocity $v$ and drains excess kinetic energy into heat.
Alternative resource: myPhysicsLab — Single Spring Simulation [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Single Spring and Physics, and drag the mass to watch position $x$ and velocity $v$ trade energy.

sections.h: Idea 2: Natural frequency ($\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$), damping ratio ($\zeta$), and underdamped vs. critically damped vs. overdamped motion
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Damping ("Oscillation cases" & "Damping ratio") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Damping, Oscillation cases (Underdamped, Critically damped, Overdamped), and Damping ratio.
What to skip: Skip logarithmic decrement and partial differential equations.
Key takeaway: Without damping ($b = 0$), a mass $m$ on a spring $k$ oscillates at its natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ (in rad/s, or $f_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi}$ in Hz). The dimensionless damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{m k}}$ compares actual damping $b$ against the critical threshold $b_{\text{crit}} = 2\sqrt{m k}$:
$\zeta < 1.0$ (Underdamped): Overshoots the target and rings with decaying oscillations.
$\zeta = 1.0$ (Critically damped): Fastest possible approach to the target with zero overshoot.
$\zeta > 1.0$ (Overdamped): Zero overshoot, but overly heavy damping makes the approach slow and sluggish.
Alternative resource: PhET — Masses and Springs: Basics [verify in-app] — Open the Bounce or Lab screen [verify in-app] and slide the Damping control from None to Lots.

Combining Newton's Second Law ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a \implies a = F_{\text{net}} / m$ from Lesson P.12) with Hooke's Law spring restoring force ($F_s = -k \cdot x$, where $k$ is the spring constant in N/m) and viscous damping ($F_d = -b \cdot v$, where $b$ is in N·s/m) gives the acceleration $a$ of a mass-spring-damper pushed by external command force $F_{\text{cmd}}$:
Here $\omega_n = \sqrt{k / m}$ is the undamped natural frequency (rad/s) and $\zeta$ is the dimensionless damping ratio that determines whether the response is underdamped ($\zeta 1$, slow and sluggish).
In a discrete Python loop with time step $\Delta t$, we update velocity $v$ first using acceleration $a$, and then update position $x$ using the new velocity $v$:
a = (f_cmd - b v - k x) / m
v = v + a dt
x = x + v dt
Updating velocity before position in each step keeps the simulated spring-mass energy accurate across thousands of time steps.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete damping_metrics (TODO 1) to calculate natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$, damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{m k}}$, and the regime label (underdamped, critically_damped, or overdamped), then complete the time-stepping loop in simulate_spring_damper (TODO 2) to compare the peak overshoot of an underdamped joint ($b = 4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$, $\zeta = 0.20$) versus a critically damped joint ($b = 20.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$, $\zeta = 1.00$).
What is real-hardware only: Dry static friction ("stiction") inside a physical rubber shock absorber seal that causes tiny deadband stick-slip near $v = 0$.

sections.t: Save as mass_spring_damper.py and run python3 mass_spring_damper.py:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, omega_n = math.sqrt(k_n_per_m / m_kg) (10.0 rad/s for $k=100, m=1$) and zeta = b_ns_per_m / (2.0 math.sqrt(m_kg k_n_per_m)). In TODO 2, compute a = (-b_ns_per_m v - k_n_per_m x) / m_kg, then v = v + a dt, then x = x + v dt.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Forgetting the minus signs on $-k \cdot x$ and $-b \cdot v$: Both the spring restoring force and viscous damping oppose displacement and velocity. If you write +b v instead of -b v, the damper pumps energy into the mass and the oscillation explodes to infinity!
Confusing natural frequency $\omega_n$ (rad/s) with cycle frequency $f_n$ (Hz): $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$ is in radians per second (rad/s). Divide by $2\pi$ ($f_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi}$) to get cycles per second (Hz).

Calculating $\omega_n$ and $f_n$: A compliant robot finger has effective mass $m = 0.25\text{ kg}$ and spring constant $k = 100.0\text{ N/m}$. What is its natural frequency $\omega_n$ in rad/s, and what is $f_n$ in Hz?
Answer
$\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{100.0}{0.25}} = \sqrt{400} = \mathbf{20.0\text{ rad/s}}$, which is $f_n = \frac{20.0}{2\pi} \approx \mathbf{3.18\text{ Hz}}$.
Choosing critical damping ($\zeta = 1.0$): For that same finger ($m = 0.25\text{ kg}$, $k = 100.0\text{ N/m}$), what damping coefficient $b$ (in N·s/m) gives critical damping ($\zeta = 1.0$) so the finger snaps back to $x = 0$ as fast as possible with zero overshoot?
Answer
Set $\zeta = 1.0 \implies b_{\text{crit}} = 2\sqrt{m \cdot k} = 2\sqrt{0.25 \times 100.0} = 2 \times 5.0 = \mathbf{10.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}}$.

Hooke's Law ($F_s = -k \cdot x$) pulls back toward equilibrium; viscous damping ($F_d = -b \cdot v$) opposes velocity.
Natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$ sets oscillation speed (rad/s), while damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{m k}}$ classifies motion as underdamped ($\zeta 1$, sluggish).

pages.title: Engineering Modeling Discipline — 4-Step Workflow, Dimensional Checks and Sign Conventions

sections.t:
Apply a repeatable 4-step engineering modeling workflow (Diagram $\rightarrow$ Symbolic Equations $\rightarrow$ Code $\rightarrow$ Sanity Check) and catch bugs before powering hardware by verifying dimensional unit consistency and extreme-case sign conventions ($\theta = 0^\circ$ vs. $90^\circ$) in Python.
New ideas (max 2):
The 4-step engineering problem-solving workflow (Diagram $\rightarrow$ Symbolic Equations $\rightarrow$ Code $\rightarrow$ Sanity Check): Never type numbers or code before drawing the coordinate axes and writing symbolic variable names with SI units.
Dimensional unit consistency and extreme-case sign checks ($\theta = 0^\circ$ vs. $90^\circ$): Verifying that the units on both sides of = match and testing equations at known boundary angles (0 rad and pi/2 rad) using assert.
New syntax: None (assert and math.cos from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)
Lesson P.9: Rearranging Physics Formulas & Linear Range Scaling
Lesson P.12: Forces, Newton's Second Law & Lever Torque
Lesson 00.1: Cross-Domain Power (P = Effort Flow) & First-Order Lag
Lesson 00.2: Second-Order Motion — Springs, Dampers & Damping Regimes

sections.h: Idea 1: The 4-step engineering problem-solving workflow (Diagram -> Symbolic Equations -> Code -> Sanity Check)
sections.t:
Primary resource: The Physics Classroom — Drawing Free-Body Diagrams [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Drawing Free-Body Diagrams and Practice.
What to skip: Skip inclined-plane friction examples for now.
Key takeaway: Professional mechatronics engineers never guess formulas by plugging raw numbers straight into code. Instead, follow a strict 4-step workflow on every problem:
Sketch a Free-Body / Circuit Diagram with a clearly labeled Sign Convention (for example: counter-clockwise +CCW is positive angle $+\theta$ and positive torque $+\tau$).
Write Symbolic Equations using descriptive SI variable names (m_kg, length_m, theta_rad) rather than magic numbers.
Translate to Code after converting all inputs to base SI units (m, kg, s, A, V, Ω, rad).
Run Automated Sanity Checks (assert) at extreme boundary cases before powering a motor.

sections.h: Idea 2: Dimensional unit consistency and extreme-case sign checks ($\theta = 0^\circ$ vs. $90^\circ$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — Metric System of Measurement [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact headings Metric System of Measurement, Meter, Kilogram, and Second.
What to skip: Skip liter volume conversions.
Key takeaway: Two fast sanity checks catch $90\%$ of robotics math bugs in seconds:
Dimensional unit consistency: Every term added or equated must have the exact same SI units. If a formula for torque (N·m) accidentally computes $m \cdot g / L$ (N/m), the units don't match—so the formula is guaranteed wrong!
Extreme-case boundary & sign checks: Test your function at $\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ ($0^\circ$, horizontal arm where gravity lever arm is full length $L$, requiring maximum positive holding torque $+m g L$) and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$ ($90^\circ$, straight up where gravity pulls straight through the pivot and holding torque is $0.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$).
Alternative resource: HyperPhysics — Torque and Equilibrium [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review exact heading Torque = Force applied x lever arm.

Why do sign convention and dimensional consistency matter so much when software meets hardware?
Suppose you mount a motor on a robot shoulder where angle $\theta$ is measured counter-clockwise (+CCW) from the horizontal $+x$ axis (Lesson P.12). Gravity pulls the arm downward (clockwise, $-\text{CW}$) with torque $\tau_{\text{gravity}} = -m \cdot g \cdot L \cdot \cos(\theta)$. Therefore, to hold the arm stationary, the motor must apply an equal and opposite upward (+CCW) holding torque:
If a programmer gets the sign convention backward (-m g L cos(theta) instead of +), the motor pushes the arm downward with gravity instead of fighting gravity—slamming the arm into the table! And if a programmer writes $\sin(\theta)$ instead of $\cos(\theta)$, testing two extreme boundary cases immediately catches the bug:
Boundary Check 1 ($\theta = 0\text{ rad}$, horizontal): $\cos(0) = 1 \implies \tau_{\text{hold}}(0) = +m g L$ (maximum positive holding torque; $\sin(0)$ would wrongly give $0$!).
Boundary Check 2 ($\theta = \pi/2\text{ rad}$, vertical): $\cos(\pi/2) = 0 \implies \tau_{\text{hold}}(\pi/2) = 0.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete holding_torque_nm (TODO 1) using base SI units (length_mm / 1000.0 and math.radians(angle_deg)) with the +CCW sign convention, and complete run_sanity_checks (TODO 2) to verify both extreme boundary cases ($\theta = 0^\circ \rightarrow +1.962\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and $\theta = 90^\circ \rightarrow 0.000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) with assert.
What is real-hardware only: Physical runaway of a robot arm when motor power leads or encoder phase wires are swapped backward without a software sign check.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Save as modeling_sanity_checks.py and run python3 modeling_sanity_checks.py:

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:
Spacing is not graded here: the three tau_hold rows line up because the labels are padded by hand ("Midpoint 60 deg : " carries twelve literal spaces) before tau_hold = +{t:.3f} Nm. The runner compares your words and numbers and ignores indentation, column padding and blank lines, so a ragged print carrying the right values still passes; the values themselves are checked by the instructor behavioral tests.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, convert length_mm to meters first (length_m = length_mm / 1000.0) so the units are kg (m/s^2) m = Nm (not Nmm, which would be $1{,}000\times$ too large!). Then convert angle_deg to radians with math.radians(angle_deg) and multiply by math.cos(theta_rad).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Plugging millimeters (400) directly into a formula expecting meters (0.400): This dimensional bug makes your computed torque $1{,}000\times$ too high (1962 N·m instead of 1.962 N·m). Always include the unit suffix in every variable name (length_mm vs. length_m).
Using $\sin(\theta)$ instead of $\cos(\theta)$ when $\theta$ is measured from horizontal: Checking $\theta = 0^\circ$ immediately catches this because a horizontal arm obviously requires maximum torque, whereas $\sin(0^\circ) = 0$.

Dimensional consistency check: A classmate proposes the formula $\omega_n = \sqrt{m / k}$ for the natural frequency of a spring-mass system (where $m$ is in kg and $k$ is in N/m = kg/s^2). Check the units of $\sqrt{m / k}$—does it give 1/s (rad/s), or is it upside down?
Answer
It is upside down! $\frac{m}{k}$ has units $\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{kg/s}^2} = \text{s}^2$, so $\sqrt{m/k}$ has units of seconds (s), not 1/s! Flipping it to $\omega_n = \sqrt{k / m}$ gives $\sqrt{\frac{\text{kg/s}^2}{\text{kg}}} = \frac{1}{\text{s}}$ (rad/s).
Sign convention check: If $+\theta$ is measured counter-clockwise (+CCW) from the horizontal $+x$ axis and the arm is at $\theta = 0^\circ$, in which direction (+CCW or -CW) does gravity pull the arm, and in which direction must the motor push to hold it still?
Answer
Gravity pulls the arm downward (-CW, negative torque), so the motor must apply an upward +CCW (positive) holding torque $+m g L$.

Follow the 4-step workflow on every engineering calculation: 1. Diagram & Sign Convention $\rightarrow$ 2. Symbolic Equations $\rightarrow$ 3. SI-Unit Code $\rightarrow$ 4. Extreme-Case Sanity Checks.
Always verify dimensional consistency (matching SI units on both sides of =) and test boundary angles ($\theta = 0^\circ$ and $\theta = 90^\circ$) with assert.

Your modeling_sanity_checks.py script passes all assert checks and prints +1.962 Nm, +0.981 Nm, and +0.000 Nm.
You can spot an upside-down formula by checking its SI units.

pages.title: Running Python, Variables, Loops, Functions & Tracebacks

sections.t: Every robot trajectory simulator, sensor parser, and motor controller test in this roadmap starts as a runnable Python script before touching microcontroller C++ or physical actuators. Learning how variables store physical measurements, how loops step time forward, and how error tracebacks pinpoint bugs lets you test control ideas safely on your computer. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Picture a clipboard checklist beside a linear slider track with a ruler taped along its edge. At the top of the page you write the starting slider position in a box labeled Position, the push speed in a box labeled Speed, and the stopwatch click interval in a box labeled Step. Each time the stopwatch clicks, you look at your checklist, multiply Speed by Step, add that distance to the number inside the Position box, erase the old Position number, and write the new one in its place. A Python script is that exact checklist executed automatically from top to bottom: variables are the labeled boxes, a while or for loop is the repeated stopwatch click, a def function is a reusable recipe card, and a traceback is the line-number pointer Python prints when an instruction asks for something impossible like dividing by zero.

Variables and Assignment (=): In Python, pos_m = 0.0 stores the floating-point number $0.0\text{ m}$ (position in meters) inside the variable pos_m. An update statement evaluates the right-hand side first and writes the result into the left-hand name:
Substituting $x_{\text{old}} = 0.25\text{ m}$ and step change $\Delta x = 0.125\text{ m}$ gives $x_{\text{new}} = 0.25\text{ m} + 0.125\text{ m} = 0.375\text{ m}$.
Functions and Time-Stepping Loops (while / for): A function def step_position(pos_m, vel_m_s, dt_s): takes current position $x$ in meters ($\text{m}$), constant velocity $v$ in meters per second ($\text{m/s}$), and time step $\Delta t$ in seconds ($\text{s}$), and returns the updated position:
Substituting $x_k = 0.0\text{ m}$, $v = 0.5\text{ m/s}$, and $\Delta t = 0.25\text{ s}$ yields $x_1 = 0.0\text{ m} + (0.5\text{ m/s})(0.25\text{ s}) = 0.125\text{ m}$.
Reading Tracebacks: When an expression divides a distance $\Delta x = 1.0\text{ m}$ by a zero time step $\Delta t = 0.0\text{ s}$ ($v = \Delta x / \Delta t$), Python halts and prints a traceback whose bottom line states the exception type (ZeroDivisionError or NameError) and the exact offending line number.
Running Your First .py Script & Worked-Example Syntax Reader:
Canonical Repository Clone & .venv Bootstrap (Core Environment — Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / Windows 11 WSL2; see resources/open-source-toolchains.md §0): Open your terminal application, clone this repository into mechalab, create and activate your local Python virtual environment .venv, save the code block below into step01.py, and run it:
Worked-Example Syntax Key:
import math loads Python's built-in mathematical library (giving access to math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9) for safe floating-point comparison).
def step_position(pos_m: float, vel_m_s: float, dt_s: float) -> float:: The : float after each parameter name and -> float before the colon are optional Python type annotations (type hints) that document that the inputs and returned result are floating-point decimal numbers (float); return sends the computed number back to the caller, and steps += 1 is shorthand for steps = steps + 1.
Scientific notation 1e-9 means $1.0 \times 10^{-9} = 0.000000001$.
assert automatically verifies that is True; if it is False, Python immediately halts with an AssertionError so bugs are caught on the exact line they occur.
try: ... except ZeroDivisionError as exc: catches an expected error cleanly so you can inspect type(exc).__name__ without crashing the script.
f"steps={steps}, pos_m={pos_m:.3f} m" is a formatted f-string that substitutes variables directly into text and formats pos_m to 3 decimal places (.3f).

Predict first (before you run it): Write down three numbers before you run the block: how far one $0.25\text{ s}$ tick moves the slider at $v = 0.5\text{ m/s}$; how many ticks the while loop needs to reach $1.0\text{ m}$ from $x_0 = 0.0\text{ m}$; and the exact exception class name printed at the bottom of the traceback for 1.0 / 0.0. Two tells that a wrong result is a mistake rather than a surprise: a final pos_m above $1.0\text{ m}$ means the loop body ran once more than the condition allowed, and any position that is not a whole multiple of the per-tick distance means dt_s or vel_m_s carried a wrong value.
A robot slider starts at $x_0 = 0.0\text{ m}$ and moves at constant velocity $v = 0.5\text{ m/s}$ with time step $\Delta t = 0.25\text{ s}$ until reaching $1.0\text{ m}$ ($8$ steps of $0.125\text{ m}$), and then tests catching a ZeroDivisionError.
Expected output:

Write a Python function battery_voltage_after_steps(v_start, drop_per_step, n_steps) that uses a for loop to subtract drop_per_step from v_start n_steps times. Verify that starting at $12.0\text{ V}$ with a drop of $0.15\text{ V}$ per step over $10$ steps returns 10.5 ($\pm 10^{-6}\text{ V}$).
If your result differs: Check that you passed range(n_steps) (which runs 10 times) rather than range(1, n_steps) (which only runs 9 times and leaves 10.65 V).

sections.h: Graded package - the loop, the traceback and the formatting
sections.t:
exercises/00-foundations.T1.00a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: step_position ($x + v\Delta t$), steps_to_target (the counted while loop), battery_voltage_after_steps (the exercise, over range(n_steps)), loop_total (the Skip test's accumulator), clamp_pwm (the one-sided ceiling), safe_divide (which reports type(exc).__name__ instead of crashing) and format_position (the .3f field). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
34 tests. The battery is checked at the exercise's $10.5\text{ V}$ and at the $10.65\text{ V}$ that nine drops give, so range(1, n_steps) fails on the exact number the module warns about; the step counter is checked at the worked example's eight ticks and at a late start's six, so returning the position instead of the count fails; the clamp is checked at the Skip test's $1.35 \to 1.0$ and exactly on the limit; the caught exception must come back named ZeroDivisionError rather than swallowed; and $2/3$ must print as 0.667. The transfer suite runs the plant's own numbers: at its $1\text{ kHz}$ tick a $0.08\text{ m/s}$ move takes exactly $1000$ ticks of $8 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}$, range(1000) accumulates $999000$, the $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ joint clamp is the same one-sided clamp, and a zero tick is refused before it can divide by zero. Five planted faults - battery_off_by_one, steps_returns_position, clamp_inverted, divide_swallows, format_ignores_precision - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Core Concepts to Review First: Variable assignment (=), for i in range(n_steps): loops, and def functions with return in ## 3. Formalization (Items 1–2) and ## 4. Worked example above.
Python Tutorial Links: Official Python Tutorial §3 (Numbers & Variables) and §4.2–4.7 (for Statements, range(), and Defining Functions).
Curriculum & Toolchain Reference: Track 00 Level 0 On-Ramp (00-foundations/README.md) and Open-Source Toolchains (resources/open-source-toolchains.md).

A loop is not a step count. step_position answers "where am I after one tick"; steps_to_target answers "how many ticks", so it needs its own counter incremented inside the body. Returning pos_m at the end is the classic mix-up - it reads 1.0 where the worked example prints 8.
range runs a number of times, not to a number. range(n_steps) yields n_steps values, so ten drops come from range(10). range(1, 10) yields nine (1 through 9), which is exactly the 10.65 V the exercise warns about: $12.0 - 9 \times 0.15$.
A traceback's bottom line names a type. type(exc).__name__ is "ZeroDivisionError"; str(exc) is the message ("float division by zero"), which is not what the exercise asks you to report.
The format field does the rounding. f"{pos_m:.3f}" turns 2/3 into "0.667", while str(2/3) gives "0.6666666666666666".
What the suite refuses. steps_to_target raises on a non-positive time step and on a velocity that is not positive (a stationary robot never arrives), step_position raises on a negative time step, battery_voltage_after_steps and loop_total raise on a negative count, and clamp_pwm raises on a non-positive ceiling - all ValueError, so a guard is part of the answer rather than defensive padding.

Printed: v_10=10.500 V | nine drops=10.650 V | ticks=8 | clamp=1.000 | error=ZeroDivisionError.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite runs this module's loop on the plant's 1 ms tick, so one 0.08 m/s step is 8e-5 m and 0.08 m is exactly 1000 ticks:

Inject the range fault the exercise hint warns about, keeping $V_{\text{start}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, drop_per_step = 0.15 V and n_steps = 10:
Inject: write for _ in range(1, n_steps): instead of for _ in range(n_steps):.
Symptom: the function returns 10.65 V instead of 10.5 V — exactly one drop_per_step high, because the loop body ran 9 times.
Diagnose: the gap is $0.15\text{ V}$, the size of a single drop, so the subtraction inside the loop is right and the count is wrong. A sign error would read $12.0 + 1.35 = 13.35\text{ V}$, and a drop typed as 0.015 would land near $11.85\text{ V}$; neither matches, which leaves the range bounds.
Fix: use range(n_steps), then confirm $12.0 - 10 \times 0.15 = 10.50\text{ V}$ to $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ V}$, and cross-check the count against the worked example's 8 ticks of $0.125\text{ m}$ for $1.0\text{ m}$.

Run the Worked example script directly with python3 step01.py in your terminal (following the canonical environment bootstrap in resources/open-source-toolchains.md §0), or open Architecture & Roadmap of the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) to inspect how discrete simulation steps drive every interactive physics plot in the browser with zero hardware.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Stage 0 (L0.3) and Track 04, the exact same while loop structure maps directly onto a microcontroller firmware loop:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: steps == 8, pos_m == 1.000 m, and caught == ZeroDivisionError.
Pass criteria: run the worked example and exercise asserts with zero errors, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/4$) on the Skip test below.

pages.title: Lists, Dictionaries, NumPy Arrays, Plotting & Git/Terminal Basics

sections.t: A 5-second test of a robot joint at $1\text{ kHz}$ records $5,000$ samples each of timestamp, angle, velocity, and motor current. You need lists, dictionaries, and vectorized arrays to compute tracking errors across thousands of samples at once, time-series plots to spot oscillations visually, and Git commits to roll back safely when a tuning change breaks your code. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Think of a Python list as a numbered row of pigeonholes starting at slot 0 where each slot holds one timestamp reading in order, and a dict (dictionary) as a labeled parts cabinet where you look up a controller setting by name ("slope" or "offset") instead of memorizing slot numbers. When you want to scale all $5,000$ pigeonholes from volts to amperes at once, a NumPy array acts like a synchronized conveyor belt that multiplies every slot simultaneously without stepping through them one by one. Finally, Git acts like a laboratory notebook with permanent ink snapshots: git status shows which pages changed today, and git commit seals a working checkpoint you can always restore.

Zero-Indexed Lists and Key-Value Dictionaries: A sequence of $N$ timestamps $t_0, t_1, \dots, t_{N-1}$ with uniform spacing $\Delta t$ in seconds ($\text{s}$) satisfies:
For $t_0 = 0.0\text{ s}$, $\Delta t = 0.1\text{ s}$, and $i = 4$ (the last element, indexed as t_s[-1]), $t_4 = 0.0\text{ s} + 4 \times 0.1\text{ s} = 0.4\text{ s}$.
Vectorized Array Scaling, Summary Statistics ($\Sigma$), zip() & Matplotlib Time-Series Plotting (plt.plot): Given sensor slope $m$ in volts per second ($\text{V/s}$) and offset $b$ in volts ($\text{V}$), the voltage array $y_i = m t_i + b$ has sample mean $\bar{y}$ (where capital Greek Sigma $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i$ means "add up $y_0 + y_1 + \dots + y_{N-1}$", written sum(y) in Python) and peak-to-peak span $\Delta y_{\text{pp}}$:
For $y = [0.5, 0.8, 1.1, 1.4, 1.7]\text{ V}$ ($N = 5$), $\bar{y} = \frac{5.5\text{ V}}{5} = 1.10\text{ V}$ and $\Delta y_{\text{pp}} = 1.7\text{ V} - 0.5\text{ V} = 1.20\text{ V}$. To iterate over two lists in parallel (such as target and measured in the Exercise below), zip(target, measured) pairs corresponding items (target[0], measured[0]), (target[1], measured[1]), .... In interactive desktop scripts, numpy arrays (np.array(t_s)) and matplotlib.pyplot (plt.plot(t_s, y_v); plt.xlabel("Time [s]"); plt.savefig("plot.png")) plot these arrays in 3 lines.
Python Virtual Environments (venv / PEP 668), Terminal & Git Workflow:
Activate Your Cloned Repository .venv & Install Scientific Packages: Modern Linux (Ubuntu 24.04) and macOS block system-wide pip install with error: externally-managed-environment (PEP 668). Inside the mechalab repository you cloned in 00-foundations.T1.00a (git clone https://github.com/TLE47/Mechatronics-Roadmap.git mechalab && cd mechalab, see resources/open-source-toolchains.md §0), activate .venv and install numpy, matplotlib, and scipy:
CLI & Git Commands: pwd prints the current folder, ls lists files, cd changes folder, python3 script.py executes the file, git status inspects modified files in your cloned mechalab repo, git diff displays line-by-line edits, and git commit -am "msg" records a versioned snapshot.

Predict first (before you run it): Before running the block, commit to three numbers: y_v[0] and y_v[-1] for "slope": 3.0 and "offset": 0.5 over $t = 0.0$ to $0.4\text{ s}$; the mean $\bar{y}$ of those five readings (decide first where the middle of an evenly spaced ramp must sit); and the peak-to-peak span. Two tells that a wrong result is a mistake rather than a surprise: a mean of 0.50 or 1.70 means an endpoint was reported instead of the average, and a span of 1.70 means min() was replaced by 0 rather than by the first reading.
Generate $N = 5$ timestamps $t = [0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]\text{ s}$, evaluate sensor readings $y = 3.0 t + 0.5\text{ V}$ using parameters stored in a dictionary, and verify the first/last elements, mean ($1.10\text{ V}$), and peak-to-peak span ($1.20\text{ V}$).
Expected output:

Given target angles target = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] rad and measured angles measured = [0.9, 2.1, 2.8, 4.2] rad, compute the per-sample error list err = [t - m for t, m in zip(target, measured)] and the Root-Mean-Square Error $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum e_i^2}$. Verify that $\text{RMSE} \approx 0.1581139\text{ rad}$ ($\sqrt{0.025}\text{ rad}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ rad}$).
If your result differs: Make sure you square each error $e_i^2$ before averaging (sum(ee for e in err) / len(err)), because averaging signed errors directly cancels $+0.1$ against $-0.1$ to give $0.0$.

sections.h: Graded package - a recorded window, an RMS error and a Git lookup
sections.t:
exercises/00-foundations.T1.00b/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: timestamps (the zero-indexed $t_0 + i\Delta t$ grid), scaled_readings (the "slope"/"offset" dictionary), mean_of, peak_to_peak, errors (paired by zip() and length-checked), rmse and git_command (the task-to-command lookup). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
31 tests. The worked trace is checked at its mean $1.10\text{ V}$ and span $1.20\text{ V}$, the Skip test's $t_{500} = 1.0\text{ s}$, and the exercise at $\text{RMSE} = 0.1581139\text{ rad}$ with a signed mean of exactly $0.0\text{ rad}$ - so an averaged signed error fails where a squared one passes. The transfer suite runs the plant's own recording: its $1\text{ kHz}$ tick for plant.TICKS is $1{,}001$ samples from $0.0$ to $1.0\text{ s}$, the 12-bit encoder's count ramp scales to $2047.5/4096$ turns, and the gravity torque over a $90^{\circ}$ sweep spans $0.318825\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Six planted faults - timestamps_off_by_one, scale_swaps_slope_offset, peak_to_peak_half_span, rmse_averages_signed_errors, errors_silently_zips, git_defaults_to_status - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Prerequisite Foundations Module: 00-foundations.T1.00a (Variables, Loops & Functions).
Core Concepts to Review First: Python list indexing, zip(target, measured), sum(samples) / len(samples), and max(samples) - min(samples) in ## 3. Formalization (Items 1–2) and ## 4. Worked example above.
Python & NumPy Study Links: Python Tutorial §3.1.3 (Lists), NumPy Absolute Beginners Tutorial (numpy.org), Matplotlib Pyplot Tutorial (matplotlib.org), and Pro Git Book Ch. 1–2 (git-scm.com).
Curriculum Reference: Track 00 Tier 1 (00-foundations/README.md) and Open-Source Toolchains (resources/open-source-toolchains.md).

Zero-index, so n samples stop one short of n. timestamps(0.0, 0.1, 5) must end at 0.4, not 0.5: range(n) gives i = 0..n-1. The Skip test's $t_{500}$ is 0.0 + 500 0.002 = 1.0 s.
The dictionary is the calibration. Both constants arrive by name in config; a KeyError on "Kp" when the key is "kp" is the module's own common-mistake row, so read config["slope"] and config["offset"] exactly.
Order the pairs before you subtract. zip(target, measured) yields (1.0, 0.9), then (2.0, 2.1); target minus measured gives +0.1, -0.1, +0.2, -0.2 rad. If your errors come back all positive, you zipped the lists in the other order.
Square before you average. sum(err) / 4 is exactly 0.0 here - the signs cancel - while sum(ee for e in err) / 4 is 0.025, and math.sqrt of that is 0.1581139 rad.
What the suite refuses. An empty trace (mean_of, peak_to_peak, rmse), a pair of traces of different lengths (errors, rmse), a timestamps call with a non-positive step or fewer than one sample, a git_command task other than the two it knows, and a scaled_readings config missing a key it needs all raise ValueError.

Printed: mean=1.10 V | span=1.20 V | signed mean=0.0 rad | RMSE=0.1581139 rad.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite builds its timestamp grid from the plant's TICKS + 1 samples at DT, which is a one-second window:

Inject the error the exercise hint warns about, on the exercise's own lists target = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] and measured = [0.9, 2.1, 2.8, 4.2]:
Inject: replace sum(e e for e in err) / len(err) with sum(err) / len(err) — average the signed errors, then take the square root as if they had been squared.
Symptom: err is [0.1, -0.1, 0.2, -0.2] rad, yet rmse prints 0.0000000 rad instead of 0.1581139 rad, because the four samples cancel in pairs and the sum is exactly 0.0.
Diagnose: a reported error of zero on four visibly non-zero samples can only mean the signs were let into the sum; a genuinely perfect controller would show err all zeros, which it does not. Squaring first gives $0.01 + 0.01 + 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.10$, then $0.10 / 4 = 0.025$ and $\sqrt{0.025} = 0.1581139$.
Fix: square each error inside the sum, sum(e e for e in err) / len(err), and confirm $\text{RMSE} = 0.1581139\text{ rad}$ to $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ rad}$ — while the mean of the signed errors, a different quantity, is the one that comes back 0.0.

pages.title: SI Units, Engineering Prefixes & Dimensional Analysis

sections.t: Real motors and power stages fail violently when units are mixed up: plugging a $1\text{ ms}$ sample period into a derivative formula as dt = 1 instead of dt = 0.001 multiplies motor torque commands by $1,000\times$, and confusing RPM with radians per second ruins back-EMF calculations. Dimensional analysis lets you catch wrong equations before running code by checking that units cancel cleanly on both sides of =. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Imagine building a table where one blueprint sheet gives leg lengths in millimeters, another gives the tabletop in meters, and a third lists weight in grams. If you add the raw numbers $500$ and $1.2$ without converting them to the same ruler first, the table collapses. In engineering code, we adopt one universal rule: convert every incoming number at the boundary of your program into standard base SI units (meters, kilograms, seconds, amperes, volts, radians), tag variable names with their unit suffix (omega_rad_s, tau_nm, dt_s), and treat unit labels like fractions where matching top and bottom labels cancel out.

Base and Derived SI Units: Store length in meters ($\text{m}$), mass in kilograms ($\text{kg}$), time in seconds ($\text{s}$), current in amperes ($\text{A}$), and plane angle in radians ($\text{rad}$). Mechanical power $P$ in watts ($\text{W} = \text{J/s} = \text{N}\cdot\text{m/s}$) is the product of torque $\tau$ in newton-meters ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) and angular velocity $\omega$ in radians per second ($\text{rad/s}$):
Substituting $\tau = 0.45\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and $\omega = 251.3274\text{ rad/s}$ gives $P = (0.45\text{ N}\cdot\text{m})(251.3274\text{ rad/s}) = 113.0973\text{ W}$.
Engineering Prefixes ($10^{3k}$): Convert prefixed datasheet quantities into base SI units on input: $\text{milli (m)} = 10^{-3}$, $\text{micro (}\mu\text{)} = 10^{-6}$, $\text{nano (n)} = 10^{-9}$, $\text{kilo (k)} = 10^{3}$, and $\text{mega (M)} = 10^{6}$. For an RC filter with resistance $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega = 10\times 10^3\,\Omega$ and capacitance $C = 100\text{ nF} = 100\times 10^{-9}\text{ F}$, the time constant $\tau_{RC}$ in seconds ($\text{s} = \Omega\cdot\text{F}$) is:
Dimensional Cancellation (RPM to $\text{rad/s}$): Given shaft speed $N$ in revolutions per minute ($\text{RPM}$), cancel revolutions and minutes using $2\pi\text{ rad} = 1\text{ rev}$ and $60\text{ s} = 1\text{ min}$:
For $N = 2400\text{ RPM}$, $\omega = 2400 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}\text{ rad/s} = 80\pi\text{ rad/s} \approx 251.3274\text{ rad/s}$.

Predict first (before you run it): Commit to three numbers before running the block: $\omega$ for $N = 2400\text{ RPM}$ (decide first whether it should sit near $40$, $250$ or $2500\text{ rad/s}$); the shaft power from $\tau = 450\text{ mN}\cdot\text{m}$ at that speed; and $\tau_{RC}$ for the $10\text{ k}\Omega$ / $100\text{ nF}$ pair, in milliseconds. Two tells that a wrong result is a mistake rather than a surprise: a power near $113\text{ kW}$ means the torque entered as 450 instead of 0.45, a factor of exactly $1000$; and a time constant of $1.0\text{ s}$ means the capacitance was read as $100\,\mu\text{F}$ ($10^{-6}$) rather than $100\text{ nF}$ ($10^{-9}$).
Convert $N = 2400\text{ RPM}$ and $\tau = 450\text{ mN}\cdot\text{m}$ into base SI units to compute mechanical shaft power $P$ in watts, and compute the time constant $\tau_{RC}$ of a $10\text{ k}\Omega$, $100\text{ nF}$ filter.
Expected output:

A $48\text{ V}$ supply delivers $I = 15\text{ A}$ through a PCB trace of resistance $R = 12\text{ m}\Omega$ ($12\times 10^{-3}\,\Omega$). Compute the voltage drop $V_{\text{drop}} = I R$ in volts ($\text{V}$) and the trace heat dissipation $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R$ in watts ($\text{W}$). Expected result: V_drop = 0.18 V and P_loss = 2.70 W (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
If your result differs: Check that you converted $12\text{ m}\Omega$ to $0.012\,\Omega$ (12e-3) before multiplying by $15^2 = 225\text{ A}^2$.

sections.h: Graded package - prefixes, the trace and the unit algebra
sections.t:
exercises/00-foundations.T1.00c/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: rpm_to_rad_s (the $2\pi/60$ factor), prefix_scale (milli, micro, nano, kilo, mega, and a refusal for a prefix that is not in the table), trace_drop_v ($IR$), trace_loss_w ($I^2R$), rc_time_constant_s ($RC$, in seconds), shaft_power_w ($\tau\omega$) and loop_period_us ($1/f$ in microseconds). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
31 tests. The conversion is checked at the worked example's $2400\text{ RPM}$, at the Skip test's $3000\text{ RPM}$ and at $60\text{ RPM} = 2\pi\text{ rad/s}$, so a factor of $60$ fails; the trace is checked at the exercise's $0.18\text{ V}$ and $2.7\text{ W}$ and at the Skip test's $100\text{ mV}$ shunt, so a loss computed as $IR$ fails; the prefix table is checked at $450\text{ mN}\cdot\text{m}$, $100\text{ nF}$ and $1\,\mu = 10^{-6}$, so nano mapped to $10^{-6}$ fails; the filter is checked at the worked example's $1\text{ ms}$; and the loop period at the Skip test's $40\,\mu\text{s}$. The transfer suite runs the plant's own constants: its $1\text{ ms}$ tick is exactly the $10\text{ k}\Omega$/$100\text{ nF}$ time constant, its $4096$-count encoder at one turn per second is $60\text{ RPM}$, its $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp is $2500\text{ mN}\cdot\text{m}$, and the clamp at $100\text{ RPM}$ delivers $26.179939\text{ W}$. Five planted faults - rpm_multiplies_by_60, nano_is_micro, loss_forgets_the_square, time_constant_in_milliseconds, period_in_milliseconds - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Prerequisite Foundations Modules: 00-foundations.T1.00a (Python Arithmetic & Functions) and 00-foundations.T1.00b (Lists & Arrays).
Core Concepts to Review First: SI prefix powers of ten ($\text{milli} = 10^{-3}, \text{micro} = 10^{-6}, \text{kilo} = 10^3$) and RPM-to-$\text{rad/s}$ factor-label cancellation ($\omega = \text{RPM} \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$) in ## 3. Formalization (Items 1–3) and ## 4. Worked example above.
SI Units & Dimensional Analysis Study Links: NIST Guide to the SI: Metric Prefixes & Unit Conversions (nist.gov) and SparkFun: Metric Prefixes & Scientific Notation Tutorial.
Curriculum Reference: Track 00 Level 0 (00-foundations/README.md) and Textbooks & Papers (resources/textbooks-and-papers.md).

Every prefixed number becomes base SI before it is used. $12\text{ m}\Omega$ is 12e-3 ohms, not 12; $450\text{ mN}\cdot\text{m}$ is 0.45 N·m. prefix_scale is that conversion in one place, and the exercise's trace is 12 1e-3.
The RPM factor is fixed, not fitted. $1\text{ rev} = 2\pi\text{ rad}$ and $1\text{ min} = 60\text{ s}$, so rpm_to_rad_s multiplies by 2math.pi/60. Using 60 instead is the planted fault: $2400 \times 60 = 144000$ rad/s instead of $251.3274$.
Two powers, two formulas. $V_{\text{drop}} = IR = 15 \times 0.012 = 0.18\text{ V}$; $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R = 225 \times 0.012 = 2.70\text{ W}$. If both come back 0.18, the square is missing from the loss.
Seconds in, microseconds out is a factor of $10^6$. $1/f$ is in seconds, so a $25\text{ kHz}$ loop's $4\times10^{-5}\text{ s}$ is 40 µs; multiplying by $10^3$ reports 0.04, which is milliseconds mislabelled.
What the suite refuses. prefix_scale refuses a prefix that is not in its table, trace_drop_v and trace_loss_w refuse a negative resistance, rc_time_constant_s refuses a non-positive resistance or capacitance, and loop_period_us refuses a non-positive frequency - each raises ValueError.

Printed: R=0.0120 ohm | V_drop=0.18 V | P_loss=2.70 W | omega=251.3274 rad/s | tau_RC=1.00 ms | T_s=40.0 us.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite checks that the plant's 1 ms tick is the RC time constant of a 10 kOhm / 100 nF filter, and prices the plant's torque clamp at 100 RPM:

Inject the ## 8. Common mistakes row about multiplying torque straight by RPM, keeping $\tau = 0.45\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and $N = 2400\text{ RPM}$:
Inject: compute power_w = tau_nm 2400.0, feeding RPM into $P = \tau\omega$ in place of the converted $\omega$.
Symptom: P = 1080.00 W instead of 113.10 W, a factor of $9.549$ too high — the table rounds it to $9.55\times$.
Diagnose: that ratio is exactly $60 / 2\pi$, the RPM-to-$\text{rad/s}$ factor itself, so the torque is right and only the speed unit is wrong. A prefix slip would be $1000\times$ off, not $9.5\times$, and a wrong radius would not leave a pure constant factor — only an unconverted $\omega$ explains it.
Fix: multiply the torque by omega_rad_s $= 2400 \times 2\pi/60 = 251.3274\text{ rad/s}$, which returns $113.10\text{ W}$ to $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ W}$ — the number the worked example asserts.

Run the worked example script in Python, then open 25 kHz PMSM FOC in the MechaLab Workbench to see how rotor speed in $\text{RPM}$ ($2800\text{ RPM}$) converts to electrical $\text{rad/s}$ and shaft power in watts.

pages.title: Linear Equations, Unit-Circle Trig, Radians, atan2 & 2D Vectors

sections.t: Robot joints rotate in angles while cameras and workpieces sit at Cartesian $(x, y)$ coordinates, and analog sensors output voltages that scale linearly with current or angle. Mastering linear calibration lines, radian angles on the unit circle, 2D vector projections, and four-quadrant atan2(y, x) prevents your robot arm from snapping $180^\circ$ into the wrong quadrant when crossing the negative $x$-axis. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Lay a rigid $40\text{ cm}$ ruler flat on your desk with one end pinned at the origin $(0,0)$ and shine a flashlight straight down from the ceiling and straight across from the right wall. As you swing the ruler counter-clockwise by an angle $\theta$, its horizontal shadow on the desk bottom edge is the cosine projection ($x$), and its vertical shadow on the left wall is the sine projection ($y$). If someone tells you only the single fraction $y/x$, you cannot tell whether the ruler points up-and-left ($x 0$) or down-and-right ($x > 0, y < 0$) because both give a negative fraction—which is why robotics code always passes both shadows separately into atan2(y, x).

Linear Calibration ($y = m x + b$): An analog sensor with output $y$ in volts ($\text{V}$), input current $x$ in amperes ($\text{A}$), sensitivity slope $m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ in $\text{V/A}$, and zero-offset $b$ in $\text{V}$ obeys:
Substituting $m = 0.20\text{ V/A}$, $x = 5.0\text{ A}$, and $b = 1.65\text{ V}$ gives $y = (0.20\text{ V/A})(5.0\text{ A}) + 1.65\text{ V} = 2.65\text{ V}$.
Radians and 2D Vector Projections: One full revolution ($360^\circ$) spans $2\pi \approx 6.2832\text{ rad}$, so $\theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\text{deg}}\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$. A link of length $L$ in meters ($\text{m}$) at angle $\theta$ in radians has tip coordinates $(x, y)$ and Euclidean norm $r$:
For $L = 0.40\text{ m}$ and $\theta = 135^\circ = 2.35619\text{ rad}$, $x = 0.40\cos(2.35619\text{ rad}) = -0.28284\text{ m}$, $y = 0.40\sin(2.35619\text{ rad}) = +0.28284\text{ m}$, and $r = \sqrt{(-0.28284\text{ m})^2 + (0.28284\text{ m})^2} = 0.40\text{ m}$.
Four-Quadrant Angle Recovery (atan2): Given tip coordinates $(x, y)$ in meters, $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)$ inspects the signs of both $y$ and $x$ to return the unique angle in $(-\pi, +\pi]\text{ rad}$:
By contrast, single-argument $\arctan(y/x) = \arctan(-1.0) = -0.78540\text{ rad} = -45.0^\circ$ (wrong quadrant by $180^\circ$).

Predict first (before you run it): Before running the block, commit to four results for $L = 0.40\text{ m}$ at $\theta = 135.0^\circ$: the sign of each tip coordinate; the Euclidean length $r$ (is it $0.40\text{ m}$, or the $|x| + |y|$ shortcut?); the degrees math.atan2(y, x) reports; and the degrees math.atan(y / x) reports instead of that. Two tells that a wrong result is a mistake rather than a surprise: a positive $x$ is impossible at $135^\circ$, since the angle sits in Quadrant II, and an atan reading of $135.0^\circ$ means the block never exercised the single-argument version at all.
Project a $L = 0.40\text{ m}$ link at $\theta = 135.0^\circ$ into $(x, y)$ coordinates, verify its length $r = 0.40\text{ m}$, and compare four-quadrant math.atan2(y, x) against math.atan(y / x).
Expected output:

A robot base at $(0, 0)$ observes a target at $(x, y) = (-0.30\text{ m}, -0.40\text{ m})$ in Quadrant III. Compute the Euclidean distance $d = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ in meters and the heading angle in degrees using math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x)). Expected result: d = 0.50 m and theta = -126.8699 deg (tolerance $\pm 0.01^\circ$).
If your result differs: Check that you passed y first and x second in math.atan2(y, x); passing atan2(x, y) swaps the axes and returns $-143.13^\circ$.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Prerequisite Foundations Modules: 00-foundations.T1.00a–00-foundations.T1.00c (Python Functions, Arrays & SI Units).
Core Concepts to Review First: 2D vector tip coordinates $(L\cos\theta, L\sin\theta)$, Euclidean norm $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and four-quadrant math.atan2(y, x) in ## 3. Formalization (Items 2–3) and ## 4. Worked example above.

sections.t: exercises/00-foundations.T1.00d/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: sensor_voltage (the calibration line), sensor_current (subtract the offset before dividing), polar_to_cartesian ($\cos$ for $x$, $\sin$ for $y$, radians), link_length (the diagonal, not $|x| + |y|$), heading_rad (four-quadrant atan2(y, x)), heading_deg and degrees_to_radians ($\pi/180$). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

The line and its inverse are two different orders. y = m x + b adds the offset last; x = (y - b)/m subtracts it first. At $V = 1.7\text{ V}$ on the $0.5\text{ V}$-at-$0\text{ A}$, $2.5\text{ V}$-at-$10\text{ A}$ sensor, the slope is (2.5 - 0.5)/(10 - 0) $= 0.2\text{ V/A}$, so the current is (1.7 - 0.5)/0.2 = 6.0 A.
The projections are a cosine and a sine, in radians. polar_to_cartesian(0.40, math.radians(135.0)) gives (-0.28284, 0.28284); passing degrees straight into math.cos is the -0.448 row in the common-mistakes table.
The norm is the diagonal. For the exercise's target, math.hypot(-0.30, -0.40) is 0.50; |-0.30| + |-0.40| = 0.70 is the taxi-cab sum, not a distance.
atan2 takes y first, and that order is the whole four-quadrant trick. math.atan2(-0.40, -0.30) is -2.2143 rad $= -126.8699^\circ$; swapping the arguments gives $-143.13^\circ$, the mirrored heading the exercise warns about.
What the suite refuses. A zero readout where sensor_current divides by the slope, a negative radius passed to polar_to_cartesian, and the origin passed to heading_rad - where no heading exists - all raise ValueError.

Printed: d=0.5000 m | theta=-126.8699 deg | atan(x, y) swap=-143.13 deg | I(V=1.7)=6.00 A.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite builds the plant's tip as this module's two projections and checks its heading against the plant's own wrap_pi:

Inject the single-argument arctan the ## 8. Common mistakes table warns about, keeping the worked example's tip at $(-0.28284\text{ m},\ +0.28284\text{ m})$:
Inject: replace math.atan2(tip[1], tip[0]) with math.atan(tip[1] / tip[0]) on those same coordinates.
Symptom: the recovered heading prints -45.0 deg instead of 135.0 deg — a $180^\circ$ error, while the tip is unchanged and the length still reads 0.40 m.
Diagnose: the projections and the norm survived, so $\cos$, $\sin$ and hypot are right and only the angle recovery is wrong. atan cannot return anything outside $(-90^\circ, +90^\circ)$, so $135^\circ$ was impossible before the code ran; the ratio $y/x = -1.0$ is identical for the correct tip and its $180^\circ$ mirror image, which is exactly the information the sign of $x$ supplies.
Fix: pass both coordinates to math.atan2(tip[1], tip[0]), which returns 135.0 deg to within $10^{-9}$ degrees, and check the exercise's target $(-0.30\text{ m},\ -0.40\text{ m})$ comes back -126.8699 deg rather than its $180^\circ$ mirror.

pages.title: Position, Velocity, Acceleration, Force, Mass, Energy & Torque in a Loop

sections.t: Before Step 1.1 (00-foundations.T1.01) compares numerical integration stability on an oscillating joint, you must connect physical push (force and torque), inertia (mass and rotational inertia), and stored energy (kinetic and spring potential energy) inside a discrete time-stepping loop. This final Level -1 module turns Newton's Second Law and Hooke's spring law into a 15-line Python simulation whose energy balance you can audit at every step. Already know this? Take the Skip test or Gate test in section 7 first.

Attach a heavy wheeled cart to a wall with a coil spring, pull the cart back by $10\text{ cm}$, and let go. At the moment of release, the cart is motionless, so all the energy you put in is stored in the stretched spring coils. The spring pulls the cart toward the wall: force causes acceleration, acceleration builds up velocity, and velocity moves the cart's position. By the time the cart passes the unstretched center mark, the spring force is zero, yet the cart is moving at peak speed—all of the spring's stored energy has sloshed into the moving mass's momentum, which then compresses the spring on the other side.

Newton's Second Law and Hooke's Spring Law: A cart of mass $m$ in kilograms ($\text{kg}$) at displacement $x$ in meters ($\text{m}$) pulled by a linear spring of stiffness $k$ in newtons per meter ($\text{N/m}$) experiences net restoring force $F_{\text{net}}$ in newtons ($\text{N}$) and acceleration $a$ in $\text{m/s}^2$:
For $m = 2.0\text{ kg}$, $k = 50.0\text{ N/m}$, and $x_0 = 0.10\text{ m}$, $F_{\text{net}} = -(50.0\text{ N/m})(0.10\text{ m}) = -5.0\text{ N}$ and $a_0 = \frac{-5.0\text{ N}}{2.0\text{ kg}} = -2.5\text{ m/s}^2$.
Rotational Analog (Torque $\tau$): A perpendicular force $F_\perp = F\sin\phi$ in newtons ($\text{N}$) applied at lever arm radius $r$ in meters ($\text{m}$) produces torque $\tau$ in newton-meters ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) on rotational inertia $J$ in $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, causing angular acceleration $\alpha$ in $\text{rad/s}^2$:
For $r = 0.25\text{ m}$, $F = 20.0\text{ N}$, and $\phi = 90^\circ$, $\tau = (0.25\text{ m})(20.0\text{ N})(1.0) = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Discrete Loop Update and Mechanical Energy ($E$): Over time step $\Delta t$ in seconds ($\text{s}$), velocity $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) and position $x$ ($\text{m}$) update sequentially (v += adt; x += vdt), while total mechanical energy $E$ in joules ($\text{J} = \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) sums kinetic and potential energy:
At release ($x_0 = 0.10\text{ m}, v_0 = 0.0\text{ m/s}$), $E_0 = 0 + 0.5(50.0\text{ N/m})(0.10\text{ m})^2 = 0.2500\text{ J}$, so peak speed at $x = 0$ is $v_{\max} = \sqrt{2 E_0 / m} = \sqrt{0.50\text{ J} / 2.0\text{ kg}} = 0.5000\text{ m/s}$.

Predict first (before you run it): With $m = 2.0\text{ kg}$, $k = 50.0\text{ N/m}$ and $\Delta t = 0.0005\text{ s}$, the $2,000$-step run covers $1.0\text{ s}$ — less than one full oscillation. Commit to three things before you run it: (1) the oscillation period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, and so what fraction of a cycle $1.0\text{ s}$ is; (2) where the cart ends up, nearer the release point $x_0 = 0.10\text{ m}$ or nearer the center $x = 0$, and which way it is moving; (3) the size of the drift in total energy, $E_{\text{final}} - E_0$ — exactly zero, a few $10^{-4}\text{ J}$, or a few $10^{-2}\text{ J}$? Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: a drift of $10^{-2}\text{ J}$ (4% of $0.2500\text{ J}$) means $\Delta t$ is far too coarse for a $1.26\text{ s}$ period, and an $E_{\text{final}}$ that matches $E_0$ to four decimals means the energy was computed before the loop rather than after it.
Simulate a $m = 2.0\text{ kg}$ mass on a $k = 50.0\text{ N/m}$ spring released from $x_0 = 0.10\text{ m}$, $v_0 = 0.0\text{ m/s}$ for $2,000$ steps of $\Delta t = 0.0005\text{ s}$ ($1.0\text{ s}$ total) and verify that total energy stays conserved at $0.2500\text{ J}$ and peak speed reaches $0.5000\text{ m/s}$.
Expected output:

Add viscous damping $F_{\text{damp}} = -b v$ with $b = 4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$ to the loop (f_net_n = -k_nm x_m - b v_ms) and run for 4000 steps ($2.0\text{ s}$). Verify that $> 95\%$ of the initial $0.25\text{ J}$ energy is dissipated as heat (e_final_j < 0.0125).
If your result differs: Check the sign on -b v_ms; writing +b v_ms injects energy (negative damping) and causes the oscillation to explode instead of decay.

sections.t:
exercises/00-foundations.T1.00e/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: spring_force (Hooke's law, with the minus sign), acceleration ($F/m$), euler_step (velocity first, then position, with the damper), mechanical_energy (both stores), peak_speed ($\sqrt{2E/m}$), torque ($r F \sin\phi$) and angular_acceleration ($\tau/J$). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
34 tests. The behaviour suite checks the worked example's $-5.0\text{ N}$, $-2.5\text{ m/s}^2$, $0.2500\text{ J}$ and $0.5000\text{ m/s}$, the exercise's 4000-step damped run (final energy under $0.0125\text{ J}$, with a 500-step coarse-step run that catches a position updated from the old velocity: forward Euler grows to $144\times$ where the new-velocity ordering stays within a few percent), and both Skip-test and Gate-test values - $5.886\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $2.20\text{ J}$, $0.198\text{ m}$ and $30\text{ rad/s}^2$. Five planted faults - spring_force_sign_dropped, damping_sign_flipped, forward_euler_position, energy_forgets_the_spring, torque_uses_cosine - each fail the test named for them. The transfer suite then runs the plant's own numbers: the submission's $r F \sin\phi$ reproduces plant.gravity_torque's cosine lever at four shoulder poses, the $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp over plant.I1 and plant.I2 gives $312.5$ and $833.3\text{ rad/s}^2$, the plant's $1\text{ ms}$ tick is $1257\times$ finer than the spring's $1.26\text{ s}$ period (so one second of the loop holds $0.25\text{ J}$), and a coasting joint decays with the plant's $I_1/B_1 = 0.2\text{ s}$ time constant.
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.00-foundations.T1.00e, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Prerequisite Foundations Modules: 00-foundations.T1.00a–00-foundations.T1.00d (Loops, SI Units & 2D Vectors).
Core Concepts to Review First: Newton's second law $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$ with viscous damping $F_{\text{damp}} = -b v$, symplectic Euler updates (v += adt; x += vdt), and total mechanical energy $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ in ## 3. Formalization (Items 1–3) and ## 4. Worked example above.
Physics & Simulation Study Links: MyPhysicsLab: Interactive Mass-Spring-Damper Simulation & Equations (myphysicslab.com) and R. H. Bishop The Mechatronics Handbook (resources/textbooks-and-papers.md).
Curriculum Reference: Track 00 Tier 1 (00-foundations/README.md#tier-1-beginner--intuitive) (Step 1.1 Calculus as while Loops).

Expected numbers (the answer): $E_0 = 0.2500\text{ J}$; the $4,000$-step damped run of $2.0\text{ s}$ ends under $0.0125\text{ J}$ (more than $95\%$ dissipated); the Skip test's $5.886\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $2.20\text{ J}$, $0.198\text{ m}$ and $30\text{ rad/s}^2$ still have to come out.

Order of the two updates. Update $v$ from the current $x$ and the current $v$, then move $x$ with the new $v$. A position updated with the old velocity is plain forward Euler: it gains energy every step instead of losing it, and at $\Delta t = 0.02\text{ s}$ it grows to $144\times$ the release energy in $500$ steps.
Why the damper is $-bv$ and not $+bv$. The damper always opposes motion, so the force changes sign with $v$; writing +bv gives the cart a tailwind and the oscillation explodes. At $x = 0$, $v = 0.5\text{ m/s}$, $b = 4.0$ and $m = 2.0\text{ kg}$ the acceleration is $-1.0\text{ m/s}^2$, so one $1\text{ ms}$ tick turns $v = 0.5$ into $0.499$.
The exercise check is an inequality. The undamped worked example conserves energy to four decimals; the damped run must lose it. The envelope decays as $e^{-(b/m)t} = e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$, so $E(2.0\text{ s}) \approx 0.25 \times 0.0183 \approx 0.0046\text{ J}$, comfortably under the $0.0125\text{ J}$ pass mark - if yours sits above it, the damper sign or the update order is wrong, not the threshold.
Units are the check. $k x$ is newtons, $b v$ is $\text{N}\cdot\text{s/m} \times \text{m/s} = \text{N}$, and dividing their sum by kilograms leaves $\text{m/s}^2$ - the right thing to add to $v$ after multiplying by $\Delta t$, and the wrong thing to add to $x$.
What the suite refuses. acceleration raises on a non-positive mass, spring_force on a negative stiffness, angular_acceleration on a non-positive inertia, peak_speed on a non-positive mass or a negative energy, mechanical_energy on a non-positive mass or a negative stiffness, torque on a negative lever arm, and euler_step on a non-positive mass or time step, a negative stiffness or a negative damping - every one a ValueError.

Printed: E0=0.2500 J | damped 2.0 s: E_final=... J, dissipated ...% | under 0.0125 J: True - the release energy, then the run's own final energy and the share of it that heating removed. The final energy sits near the $0.25e^{-4} \approx 0.0046\text{ J}$ envelope, so the last field reads True.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite prices the plant's clamp against each joint's own inertia and checks the shoulder's horizontal gravity torque:

Inject the spring_force_sign_dropped fault the graded package names, and diagnose it from the first step alone:
Inject: drop the minus sign in Hooke's law — write f_net_n = k_nm x_m instead of f_net_n = -k_nm x_m, leaving the damper, the mass and $\Delta t = 0.0005\text{ s}$ alone.
Symptom: at release the force is $+5.0\text{ N}$ and $a = +2.5\text{ m/s}^2$, so after one step $v = +0.00125\text{ m/s}$ and $x = 0.100000625\text{ m}$: the cart is pushed away from the center instead of pulled toward it. Every step adds energy, so the $2,000$-step run ends at $2,756.74\text{ J}$ — four orders of magnitude above $0.2500\text{ J}$ — and assert math.isclose(e_final_j, e_initial_j, rel_tol=1e-3) fails.
Diagnose: $E_0 = 0.2500\text{ J}$ and $v_0 = 0.0\text{ m/s}$ are both still right, so neither the initial condition nor the energy sum is at fault, and the sign appears only in the first acceleration. A spring that pushes harder the further it is stretched is a repulsive spring, not the one in ## 3. Formalization; the energy check rules the rest out, because a restoring spring trades potential for kinetic and back while a repulsive one adds energy on every step.
Fix: restore f_net_n = -k_nm x_m. The first step then gives $v = -0.00125\text{ m/s}$ and $x = 0.099999375\text{ m}$, and the run closes at $E_{\text{final}} = 0.2502\text{ J}$ with $v_{\text{peak}} = 0.5000\text{ m/s}$ — energy held within $10^{-3}$ relative, and the release energy recovered at the center.

Run the worked example in Python, then open Two-Mass & Notch Bode and Furuta Pendulum in the MechaLab Workbench to see coupled spring-mass-damper and pendulum energy loops in action.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Track 05 (Step 1.6), a closed-loop PD motor controller creates this exact spring-damper behavior electronically:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: E_init == 0.2500 J, E_final == 0.2500 J, and v_peak == 0.5000 m/s.
Pass criteria: complete the Skip test ($\ge 80\%$) to pass this module, or pass the 8-question Gate test ($\ge 80\%$) to test out of the entire Level -1 ladder (00a–00e).

pages.title: High-Current Switching — MOSFETs, Inductors (Motor Coils) and Flyback Diodes

sections.t:
Use a logic-level N-Channel MOSFET (Gate, Drain, Source) so a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino Uno pin can safely switch a high-current $12.0\text{ V}$ motor load sharing a common ground, and place a parallel flyback diode across an inductor (motor coil) in Falstad to clamp destructive turn-off voltage spikes.
New ideas (max 2):
Low-side N-Channel MOSFET switching and common ground: Using a $5.0\text{ V}$ microcontroller pin to control a voltage-controlled transistor switch on the negative (GND) side of a heavy $12.0\text{ V}$ load without exceeding the microcontroller's $20\text{ mA}$ pin limit.
Inductive kickback ($V_L = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$) and flyback diode clamping: Why a coil's magnetic field resists sudden current shutoff by generating a huge voltage spike, and how a reverse-biased diode across the coil safely recirculates the current.
New syntax: Falstad Inductor (l), Diode (d), and N-MOSFET (f) elements in circuit netlists.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.11: Reading Time-Series Graphs — Slope & Area
Lesson S0.6: Capacitors — Charge Storage (tau = RC) & Power-Rail Decoupling
