sections.h: Idea 1: Low-side N-Channel MOSFET switching and common ground
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Transistors ("Introduction" & "Applications I: Switches") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Introduction, Applications I: Switches, and Transistor Switch (focus on a small control signal switching a large load current on the low side between the load and GND).
What to skip: Skip Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) base-current amplification math ($\beta / h_{\text{FE}}$) and amplifier biasing modes—modern motor drives use voltage-controlled MOSFETs instead of BJTs!
Key takeaway: Because an Arduino Uno pin can only supply $20\text{ mA}$ at $5.0\text{ V}$ while a small motor draws $500\text{ mA}$ to $5\text{ A}$ at $12.0\text{ V}$, we place a logic-level N-Channel MOSFET (a 3-pin electronic switch with Gate G, Drain D, and Source S) between the motor's negative lead and GND. When the Arduino sets Gate = 0 V relative to Source, the MOSFET is an open switch (OFF); when Gate = 5.0 V, the MOSFET closes with tiny on-resistance ($R_{\text{DS(on)}} \approx 0.02\ \Omega$), letting motor current flow from the $+12\text{ V}$ supply through the motor and MOSFET to the shared common ground (GND).
Alternative resource: Falstad Circuit Simulator — N-MOSFET Switch [verify in-app] — Open Circuits $\rightarrow$ MOSFETs $\rightarrow$ Switch [verify in-app] and click the Gate input switch between 0 V and 5 V to watch the Drain-to-Source path open and close.

sections.h: Idea 2: Inductive kickback ($V_L = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$) and flyback diode clamping
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — Diodes ("Flyback Diodes and Voltage Spike Suppression") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Ideal Diodes, Forward Voltage, and Flyback Diodes and Voltage Spike Suppression.
What to skip: Skip Zener Diodes, Rectifiers, and Logic Gates on the Diodes page.
Key takeaway: Inside every motor is a coiled wire electromagnet called an inductor (measured in Henries H or millihenries mH), which stores energy in a magnetic field and fights any sudden change in current ($V_L = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$). If a MOSFET suddenly switches OFF a $2.0\text{ A}$ motor current in $2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ with nowhere for that current to go, the collapsing magnetic field generates a massive hundred-volt inductive kickback spike that punches straight through the MOSFET! Wiring a flyback diode in parallel across the motor coil (pointing from the MOSFET Drain upward to $+12\text{ V}$) stays off during normal running, but instantly turns on when the MOSFET opens—giving the coil current a safe loop to recirculate and clamping the Drain voltage to $V_{\text{supply}} + 0.7\text{ V} = 12.7\text{ V}$.
Alternative resource: SparkFun — Motors and Selecting the Right One [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings What Makes A Motor Move? and DC Brush Motors - The Classic.

Compare the two energy-storage components you now know:
A capacitor ($C$, Lesson S0.6) stores energy in an electric field and resists sudden changes in voltage ($V$).
An inductor ($L$, a coil of wire inside a motor or relay, measured in Henries H or mH, $10^{-3}\text{ H}$) stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden changes in current ($I$), obeying:
To switch a $12.0\text{ V}$ motor coil with a $5.0\text{ V}$ Arduino pin, we use a low-side N-Channel MOSFET:
Source (S) connects to common ground (GND)—the negative terminal of the $12\text{ V}$ battery must be tied to the Arduino's GND so the $5.0\text{ V}$ Gate signal has a shared $0\text{ V}$ reference, plus a $10\text{ k}\Omega$ gate pull-down resistor from Gate to GND so the motor stays off while the Arduino boots.
Drain (D) connects to the bottom terminal of the motor coil (whose top terminal connects to $+12.0\text{ V}$).
Flyback diode: Connected directly across the motor coil with its cathode (- stripe) at $+12.0\text{ V}$ and anode (+) at the MOSFET Drain. Without this diode, opening a $2.0\text{ A}$ current through an $L = 0.5\text{ mH}$ ($0.0005\text{ H}$) coil in $\Delta t = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ ($2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$) spikes Drain voltage to $12.0 + 0.0005 \times \frac{2.0}{0.000002} = 512.0\text{ V}$! With the flyback diode, Drain voltage is safely clamped to $12.0 + 0.7 = 12.7\text{ V}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
Inductive kickback & flyback clamping in Falstad [verify in-app]: Import ../stage-0/falstad/01.1-mosfet-flyback.txt [verify in-app] via File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text... ($12.0\text{ V}$ supply, $5\text{ mH}$ inductor, N-MOSFET driven by a $490\text{ Hz}$ $0\text{–}5\text{ V}$ PWM source, $100\ \Omega$ gate resistor, $10\text{ k}\Omega$ gate pull-down, and parallel flyback diode d). Observe on the scope (TODO 1) how the flyback diode clamps the MOSFET Drain turn-off voltage at $\approx 12.7\text{ V}$ instead of spiking to hundreds of volts! (Automated CI verifies the Falstad netlist and numerical mirror in tests/test_exercises.py.)
What is real-hardware only: Destroying an unprotected MOSFET in microseconds on a physical breadboard when switching an inductive motor or solenoid without a flyback diode.

sections.h: Starter Code (import into Falstad — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Import this Falstad netlist (File $\rightarrow$ Import From Text...) and complete TODO 1 by inspecting the MOSFET conduction drop when ON ($R_{\text{DS(on)}} = 0.02\ \Omega$, $80.0\text{ mW}$ at $2.0\text{ A}$) and the flyback diode line (d 336 224 336 112 2 default, pointing from Drain node (336, 224) upward to $+12\text{ V}$ node (336, 112)) that clamps the turn-off spike at $12.7\text{ V}$:

Comparing the MOSFET conduction heat at $I = 2.0\text{ A}$ ($R_{\text{DS(on)}} = 0.02\ \Omega$) and the peak Drain turn-off voltage ($L = 0.5\text{ mH}$, $I = 2.0\text{ A}$, $\Delta t = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ on $12.0\text{ V}$) without vs. with the flyback diode (d 336 224 336 112 2 default) yields:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
When the MOSFET is ON at $2.0\text{ A}$ with $R_{\text{DS(on)}} = 0.02\ \Omega$, heat dissipation is $P = I^2 R = 4.0 \times 0.02 = 0.08\text{ W} = 80.0\text{ mW}$. When switching OFF $2.0\text{ A}$ in $2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ through $0.5\text{ mH}$ without a flyback diode, $V_L = 0.0005 \times (2.0 / 0.000002) = 500.0\text{ V}$, so $V_{\text{Drain}} = 12.0 + 500.0 = 512.0\text{ V}$! With the flyback diode, $V_{\text{Drain}}$ is clamped to $12.0 + 0.7 = 12.7\text{ V}$.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
In the Falstad netlist, line 4 (d 336 224 336 112 2 default) wires the flyback diode with its anode at Drain (336, 224) and cathode at $+12\text{ V}$ (336, 112), while line 5 (f 208 256 256 256 32 1.5 0.02) sets the N-MOSFET threshold to 1.5 V and $R_{\text{DS(on)}} = 0.02\ \Omega$.
Full Solution

Installing the flyback diode upside down (cathode stripe pointing down to Drain instead of up to $+12\text{ V}$): During normal operation when the MOSFET turns ON, if the diode points downward from $+12\text{ V}$ to Drain (0 V), it conducts directly from $+12\text{ V}$ to GND around the motor—creating a dead short circuit that burns out both the diode and the MOSFET! The diode's cathode stripe (-) MUST connect to $+V_{\text{supply}}$, and its anode (+) to the MOSFET Drain (reverse-biased during normal operation).
Forgetting to connect Common Ground between the $12\text{ V}$ battery and the Arduino Uno: If the $12\text{ V}$ battery's negative terminal is not connected to Arduino GND, the Arduino's $5\text{ V}$ Gate signal has no return path to the MOSFET's Source pin, so the MOSFET never turns on reliably (or floats half-on and overheats).
Using a non-logic-level MOSFET (like an older IRF540N instead of a logic-level IRLZ44N): Standard MOSFETs need $10\text{ V}$ on the Gate to turn fully on; at $5.0\text{ V}$ from an Arduino Uno, they only open halfway with high resistance and overheat. Always check that the MOSFET datasheet specifies a low $R_{\text{DS(on)}}$ at $V_{\text{GS}} = 4.5\text{ V}$ or $5.0\text{ V}$ ("Logic-Level Gate Drive").

Capacitor vs. Inductor duality: A capacitor resists sudden changes in which electrical quantity ($V$ or $I$)? Which electrical quantity does an inductor (motor coil) resist changing suddenly?
Answer
A capacitor resists sudden changes in voltage ($V$).
An inductor resists sudden changes in current ($I$).
Flyback diode orientation: In a low-side N-Channel MOSFET motor switch (motor wired between $+12\text{ V}$ and MOSFET Drain), which leg of the flyback diode (Anode or Cathode stripe) connects to $+12\text{ V}$, and why doesn't current flow through the diode while the MOSFET is ON?
Answer
The Cathode (- stripe) connects to +12 V, and the Anode (+) connects to the MOSFET Drain. While the MOSFET is ON (Drain $\approx 0\text{ V}$), the diode's cathode is at $+12\text{ V}$ and its anode is at $0\text{ V}$ (reverse-biased), so the diode blocks current completely until the MOSFET switches OFF and the inductor drives the Drain voltage above $+12.7\text{ V}$.
Why use a $10\text{ k}\Omega$ Gate-to-Source pull-down resistor? During the first few milliseconds when an Arduino Uno powers up, all GPIO pins start as floating inputs (INPUT). What could happen to a MOSFET motor stage if there is no $10\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor between Gate and GND?
Answer
The floating MOSFET Gate acts like a small capacitor that can pick up stray charge and turn the motor ON unexpectedly (or hold the MOSFET half-on where it overheats) before setup() runs. A $10\text{ k}\Omega$ pull-down resistor from Gate to GND holds the Gate safely at $0.0\text{ V}$ until the Arduino actively drives the pin HIGH.

A low-side N-Channel MOSFET switches heavy $12\text{ V}$ loads on the negative (GND) side using a $5.0\text{ V}$ logic Gate signal referenced to a shared common ground.
An inductor (motor coil, in Henries H) resists sudden changes in current ($V_L = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$); a flyback diode wired across the coil (cathode to $+V_{\text{supply}}$, anode to Drain) safely clamps turn-off voltage spikes to $V_{\text{supply}} + 0.7\text{ V}$.

pages.title: Bidirectional DC Motor Control — H-Bridges, Shoot-Through and Stall Current

sections.t:
Control a brushed DC motor's direction (Forward, Reverse, Coast, Brake) and speed using a 4-switch H-Bridge without triggering a destructive shoot-through short circuit, and calculate motor back-EMF ($V_{\text{emf}} = K_e \cdot \omega$) and locked-rotor stall current ($I_{\text{stall}} = V_s / R_m$).
New ideas (max 2):
H-Bridge 4-switch topology (Forward, Reverse, Coast, Brake) and shoot-through prevention: Arranging four switches in an "H" around a motor so closing diagonal pairs reverses current direction, while never closing both top and bottom switches on the same side (shoot-through).
DC motor back-EMF ($V_{\text{emf}} = K_e \cdot \omega$) and locked-rotor stall current ($I_{\text{stall}} = V_s / R_m$): Why a spinning motor acts like a generator opposing the supply voltage, and why a stalled rotor ($\omega = 0$) draws maximum current limited only by winding resistance $R_m$.
New syntax: Driving two direction pins (IN1, IN2) and one analogWrite PWM enable pin (ENA) on the Arduino Uno in Wokwi.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: H-Bridge 4-switch topology (Forward, Reverse, Coast, Brake) and shoot-through prevention
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — H-bridge ("General" & "Operation") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings H-bridge, General, and DC motor driver (including the 4-switch S1–S4 table and shoot-through warning).
What to skip: Skip relay and inverter construction sections.
Key takeaway: A single low-side MOSFET (Lesson 01.1) can only spin a motor in one direction. To spin both Forward and Reverse, an H-Bridge places four MOSFET switches (S1, S2 on the left leg; S3, S4 on the right leg) around the motor like the letter H:
Forward (IN1 = HIGH, IN2 = LOW): Top-left S1 and bottom-right S4 close; current flows left-to-right through the motor.
Reverse (IN1 = LOW, IN2 = HIGH): Top-right S3 and bottom-left S2 close; current flows right-to-left through the motor.
Coast (IN1 = LOW, IN2 = LOW) vs. Brake (IN1 = HIGH, IN2 = HIGH): Opening all switches lets the rotor coast freely; closing both bottom switches shorts the motor terminals together so its own generated current brakes it rapidly.
Shoot-Through (S1 and S2 closed on the SAME leg): Shorts $+V_{\text{supply}}$ straight to GND without going through the motor, destroying the MOSFETs! Integrated H-bridge driver chips include built-in logic that prevents shoot-through automatically—always match the chip's Recommended Operating Supply Voltage (VM) to your motor bus: use DRV8833 only for $2.7\text{–}10.8\text{ V}$ motors ($11.8\text{ V}$ absolute max destruction limit—never connect DRV8833 to a $12\text{ V}$ supply!), TB6612FNG for $4.5\text{–}13.5\text{ V}$ ($12\text{ V}$ motors), or DRV8871 for $6.5\text{–}45\text{ V}$ ($12\text{–}24\text{ V}$ motors).
Alternative resource: SparkFun — Motors and Selecting the Right One [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings What Makes A Motor Move? and DC Brush Motors - The Classic.

sections.h: Idea 2: DC motor back-EMF ($V_{\text{emf}} = K_e \cdot \omega$) and locked-rotor stall current ($I_{\text{stall}} = V_s / R_m$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Counter-electromotive force [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Counter-electromotive force and Details (electric motor back-EMF and starting current).
What to skip: Skip AC transformer derivations.
Key takeaway: Every spinning DC motor is simultaneously a generator! As the rotor spins at angular velocity $\omega$ (rad/s), its coils cut through the permanent magnets' field and generate a reverse voltage called back-EMF ($V_{\text{emf}} = K_e \cdot \omega$) that opposes the supply voltage $V_s$. Given winding resistance $R_m$, the motor current is $I_m = \frac{V_s - K_e \cdot \omega}{R_m}$:
At stall ($\omega = 0$, startup or jammed shaft): Back-EMF is zero ($V_{\text{emf}} = 0\text{ V}$), so the motor draws its maximum stall current $I_{\text{stall}} = \frac{V_s}{R_m}$ (often $5\times$ to $10\times$ higher than normal running current!).
At fast no-load spin ($V_{\text{emf}} \approx V_s$): Back-EMF nearly cancels $V_s$, so current drops close to zero.

Inside a brushed DC motor with winding resistance $R_m$ (in $\Omega$) and back-EMF constant $K_e$ (in $\text{V}/(\text{rad/s})$), the steady-state motor current $I_m$ at supply voltage $V_s$ and shaft speed $\omega$ is governed by Ohm's Law across the remaining voltage difference $V_s - V_{\text{emf}}$:
For example, if a $12.0\text{ V}$ gearmotor has winding resistance $R_m = 4.0\ \Omega$ and $K_e = 0.10\text{ V}/(\text{rad/s})$:
Stalled ($\omega = 0\text{ rad/s}$): $V_{\text{emf}} = 0.0\text{ V} \implies I_{\text{stall}} = \frac{12.0}{4.0} = \mathbf{3.00\text{ A}}$!
Spinning at $\omega = 100.0\text{ rad/s}$: $V_{\text{emf}} = 0.10 \times 100.0 = 10.0\text{ V} \implies I_m = \frac{12.0 - 10.0}{4.0} = \mathbf{0.50\text{ A}}$.
On an Arduino Uno driving a $12\text{ V}$-rated H-bridge breakout (TB6612FNG, rated up to $13.5\text{ V}$ operating; or DRV8833 if using a $6\text{–}9\text{ V}$ motor supply $\le 10.8\text{ V}$), two digital pins (IN1 on Pin 7, IN2 on Pin 8) set the direction state, while a PWM pin (ENA on ~Pin 9) sets speed from 0 to 255:

What is simulated and in which tool:

($12.0\text{ V}$ supply, four H-bridge switches S1–S4, and a $4.0\ \Omega$ stalled motor armature drawing $+3.00\text{ A}$ in Forward and $-3.00\text{ A}$ when you toggle the diagonal switches to Reverse).
Arduino Uno H-bridge direction & stall-current firmware in Wokwi [verify in-app]: (Note: Wokwi has no brushed DC motor with mechanical inertia/back-EMF, so we test the Arduino Uno IN1/IN2/PWM driver logic and stall/running current telemetry in Wokwi below; full closed-loop motor physics runs in Python in Track 03.) Paste the Starter Code below into Wokwi, complete TODO 1 and TODO 2, run the simulation, and verify the Serial Monitor output against the Expected Output below. (Automated CI compiles this sketch for arduino:avr:uno via arduino-cli.)
What is real-hardware only: Physical brush commutator sparking and $2\times I_{\text{stall}}$ current spikes when slamming a spinning physical motor directly from full Forward into full Reverse.

In TODO 1, back-EMF is float v_emf = ke_v_per_rads omega_rads;, so current is (v_supply - v_emf) / r_ohm. In TODO 2, when signed_cmd < 0 (reverse), set in1_out = LOW; in2_out = HIGH; and make the PWM duty cycle positive with pwm_out = -signed_cmd;.

Full Solution

Sizing a motor driver or power supply for the motor's "no-load current" ($0.2\text{ A}$) instead of its stall current ($3.0\text{ A}$): Every single time a motor starts from rest ($\omega = 0$) or pushes against a heavy load, it briefly draws $I_{\text{stall}} = V_s / R_m$. Always choose an H-bridge rated above $I_{\text{stall}}$.
Passing a negative integer like -192 directly into analogWrite(9, signed_cmd): analogWrite expects an unsigned 8-bit number 0..255. Always use the sign of signed_cmd to set IN1/IN2 and pass the positive magnitude abs(signed_cmd) to analogWrite.

Calculating stall current: You measure a $6.0\text{ V}$ brushed DC gearmotor's terminal resistance with an unpowered ohmmeter (Lesson S0.5) and read $R_m = 2.0\ \Omega$. What current will this motor draw at the instant you apply $6.0\text{ V}$ while the shaft is still at rest ($\omega = 0$)?
Answer
At $\omega = 0$, $V_{\text{emf}} = 0\text{ V}$, so $I_{\text{stall}} = \frac{6.0\text{ V}}{2.0\ \Omega} = \mathbf{3.0\text{ A}}$.
Shoot-through hazard: In a 4-MOSFET H-bridge, what happens if a wiring bug turns ON the top-left switch (S1, connected to $+12\text{ V}$) and the bottom-left switch (S2, connected to GND) at the exact same time?
Answer
It creates a shoot-through short circuit directly from $+12\text{ V}$ to GND through S1 and S2 (bypassing the motor completely), destroying the MOSFETs unless the power supply current limit catches it.

An H-Bridge uses 4 switches in an "H" around a motor to drive current Forward (IN1=1, IN2=0), Reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1), Coast (0, 0), or Brake (1, 1), while preventing shoot-through.
A spinning DC motor generates back-EMF $V_{\text{emf}} = K_e \cdot \omega$ opposing the supply voltage; at $\omega = 0$, it draws peak stall current $I_{\text{stall}} = V_s / R_m$.

pages.title: Multi-Rail Robot Power — Linear (LDO) vs. Switching (Buck) Regulators and Power Budgets

sections.t:
Step a $12.0\text{ V}$ robot battery down to a clean $5.0\text{ V}$ logic rail by comparing the heat wasted in a Linear Regulator (LDO) ($P_{\text{heat}} = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) \cdot I_{\text{load}}$) against a high-efficiency Switching (Buck) Converter ($I_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}} \cdot I_{\text{out}}}{\eta \cdot V_{\text{in}}}$), and build a complete worst-case system power budget in Python.
New ideas (max 2):
Linear (LDO) regulator heat loss vs. switching (Buck) converter power conservation: Why a linear regulator burns off excess voltage as heat like a variable resistor, whereas a buck converter chops and filters with an inductor and capacitor at $85\%\text{–}95\%$ efficiency.
System worst-case power budgeting and separate motor vs. logic voltage rails: Summing peak currents across motor and logic rails so the battery fuse and regulators never brown out when motors stall.
New syntax: None (Python arithmetic and functions from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.0 hours

Lesson S0.4: Diodes, LEDs, Forward Voltage Drop & Resistor Power Ratings
Lesson S0.5: Virtual Multimeters (Voltmeter vs. Ammeter) & Current-Limited (CC/CV) Bench Supplies
Lesson 01.2: Bidirectional DC Motor Control — H-Bridges, Shoot-Through & Stall Current

sections.h: Idea 1: Linear (LDO) regulator heat loss vs. switching (Buck) converter power conservation
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Buck converter ("Theory" & "Concept") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Buck converter, Theory, and Idealised case.
What to skip: Skip discontinuous-mode inductor ripple integrals.
Key takeaway: Robots typically carry a $12.0\text{ V}$ battery for motors, but the Arduino Uno and sensors need $5.0\text{ V}$. There are two ways to step $12.0\text{ V}$ down to $5.0\text{ V}$:
Linear Regulator (LDO, like 7805 or AMS1117): Acts like an automatic variable series resistor that drops the extra $12.0 - 5.0 = 7.0\text{ V}$. Input current equals output current ($I_{\text{in}} = I_{\text{load}}$), and all the dropped voltage turns straight into heat: $P_{\text{heat}} = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) \cdot I_{\text{load}}$. Great for tiny currents ($\le 50\text{ mA}$), but at $0.50\text{ A}$ it burns $7.0 \times 0.50 = 3.50\text{ W}$ and cooks itself!
Switching Step-Down (Buck) Converter: Uses a fast PWM switch, an inductor, and a capacitor to convert high voltage at low current into low voltage at higher current with efficiency $\eta \approx 0.90$ ($90\%$): $P_{\text{in}} = \frac{P_{\text{out}}}{\eta} \implies I_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}} \cdot I_{\text{load}}}{\eta \cdot V_{\text{in}}}$.
Alternative resource: Falstad Circuit Simulator — Buck Converter [verify in-app] — Open Circuits $\rightarrow$ Power Converters $\rightarrow$ Buck Converter [verify in-app].

sections.h: Idea 2: System worst-case power budgeting and separate motor vs. logic voltage rails
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — How to Power a Project [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review how portable projects budget battery voltage and current capacity across high-draw actuators and logic electronics.
What to skip: Skip solar panel charging circuits.
Key takeaway: Never power a motor from the Arduino Uno's onboard 5V pin! Instead, split your robot into two power rails fed from the main $12.0\text{ V}$ battery:
Raw $12.0\text{ V}$ Motor Rail (VMOT): Feeds the H-bridge motor drivers directly.
Regulated $5.0\text{ V}$ Logic Rail (VCC): Stepped down from $12.0\text{ V}$ via a Buck converter to feed the Arduino and sensors cleanly.
A power budget sums the worst-case (stall) currents on every rail so you can size your regulator and main battery fuse with a safe margin.
Alternative resource: SparkFun — Electric Power [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review exact headings What is Electric Power? and Calculating Power.

Compare stepping $V_{\text{in}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ down to $V_{\text{out}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ for a $5.0\text{ V}$ logic and sensor rail drawing $I_{\text{load}} = 0.50\text{ A}$ ($P_{\text{out}} = 5.0 \times 0.50 = 2.50\text{ W}$). A Linear Regulator (LDO) passes the full load current straight from the $12.0\text{ V}$ battery ($I_{\text{in}} = I_{\text{load}} = 0.50\text{ A}$) and burns the entire $7.0\text{ V}$ voltage drop as heat ($3.50\text{ W}$). By contrast, a switching Buck Converter ($\eta = 90\%$) conserves power across its inductor-capacitor stage, drawing only $I_{\text{buck,in}} = 0.231\text{ A}$ from the $12.0\text{ V}$ battery and wasting just $0.28\text{ W}$:
To complete your robot's worst-case power budget, keep the $12.0\text{ V}$ motor rail (VMOT) separate from the $5.0\text{ V}$ logic rail (VCC) and add the buck converter's $12\text{ V}$ input current ($I_{\text{buck,in}} = 0.231\text{ A}$) to the motor's $12\text{ V}$ stall current ($I_{\text{stall}} = 3.00\text{ A}$ from Lesson 01.2) to get total peak battery current $I_{\text{batt,max}} = 3.231\text{ A}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete compare_ldo_vs_buck (TODO 1) to calculate LDO heat dissipation vs. Buck converter battery current and heat loss, and complete worst_case_battery_budget (TODO 2) to sum the $12\text{ V}$ motor stall current and Buck converter input current.
What is real-hardware only: Thermal shutdown of an un-heatsinked physical linear regulator when its silicon junction hits $150^\circ\text{C}$.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Treat that spacing as part of the answer — a single-space label has the right numbers but fails the presentation check — and the values themselves are verified by the instructor behavioral tests.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, the LDO drops v_in - v_out = 7.0 V at i_load = 0.50 A, wasting 7.0 0.50 = 3.50 W. The buck converter delivers p_out = v_out i_load = 2.50 W at 90% efficiency, so p_in = (v_out i_load) / buck_eff and i_buck_in = p_in / v_in.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Powering a hobby servo or DC motor from the Arduino Uno's onboard $5\text{ V}$ linear regulator (VIN fed by $12\text{ V}$): When the servo stalls at $1.0\text{ A}$, the tiny onboard LDO has to dissipate $(12 - 5) \times 1.0 = 7.0\text{ W}$, causing immediate thermal shutdown and rebooting the Arduino! Always use an external Buck converter for $5\text{ V}$ servos and logic.
Assuming Buck converter input current equals output current: Because a Buck converter conserves power ($V_{\text{in}} I_{\text{in}} \approx V_{\text{out}} I_{\text{out}} / \eta$), stepping $12\text{ V}$ down to $5\text{ V}$ draws less current from the $12\text{ V}$ battery than the $5\text{ V}$ load consumes!

LDO heat calculation: You power an Arduino Uno + sensors drawing $200\text{ mA}$ ($0.20\text{ A}$) at $5.0\text{ V}$ from a $9.0\text{ V}$ battery through a linear regulator (LDO). How many Watts of heat does the LDO dissipate?
Answer
$P_{\text{heat}} = (9.0\text{ V} - 5.0\text{ V}) \times 0.20\text{ A} = 4.0 \times 0.20 = \mathbf{0.80\text{ W}}$.
Why separate VMOT and VCC rails? Why do we connect the H-bridge motor supply (VMOT) directly to the $12\text{ V}$ battery while feeding the Arduino 5V rail through a separate Buck regulator?
Answer
Separating the rails keeps multi-amp motor stall surges off the $5.0\text{ V}$ regulator so the microcontroller's logic voltage stays steady at $5.0\text{ V}$ even when the motor stalls.

A Linear Regulator (LDO) wastes $P_{\text{heat}} = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) \cdot I_{\text{load}}$ as heat, whereas a Switching (Buck) Converter steps voltage down at $\sim 90\%$ efficiency ($I_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}} I_{\text{load}}}{\eta V_{\text{in}}}$).
A system power budget separates high-current motor power (VMOT) from regulated logic power (VCC) and sums worst-case stall currents to size fuses and supplies safely.

pages.title: Quiet Sensor Signals — Star Grounding and Passive RC Low-Pass Filters (f_c = 1/(2*pi*R*C))

sections.t:
Eliminate false analog sensor jumps when motors run by wiring a single-point star ground (preventing ground bounce $V_{\text{ground}} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{wire}}$), and size a passive RC low-pass filter with cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$ to pass slow sensor changes while blocking high-frequency PWM switching noise.
New ideas (max 2):
High-current ground bounce ($V_{\text{ground}} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{wire}}$) and star-ground wiring: Why routing motor return current and analog sensor ground through the same breadboard jumper wire shifts the sensor's $0\text{ V}$ reference, and how meeting at one central battery ground terminal fixes it.
Passive RC low-pass filter cutoff frequency ($f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$) and high-frequency noise attenuation: Using a resistor $R$ and capacitor $C$ so frequencies well below $f_c$ pass through ($\approx 100\%$), $f = f_c$ is reduced to $70.7\%$, and frequencies well above $f_c$ are squashed toward zero.
New syntax: None (math.pi and math.sqrt from Lesson P.6).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: High-current ground bounce ($V_{\text{ground}} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{wire}}$) and star-ground wiring
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Ground loop ("Ground currents on signal cables" & "Solutions") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Description, Ground currents on signal cables, and Solutions (single-point star grounding).
What to skip: Skip balanced audio transformer isolation.
Key takeaway: Real jumper wires are not $0.000\ \Omega$; a long thin breadboard jumper + spring clip can easily have $R_{\text{wire}} = 0.15\ \Omega$. If a $3.0\text{ A}$ motor return current and a sensitive analog sensor share that same ground wire back to the battery, Ohm's Law says the wire drops $V_{\text{ground}} = 3.0\text{ A} \times 0.15\ \Omega = 0.45\text{ V}$ (ground bounce)—making your Arduino's analogRead(A0) jump by $\sim 92$ counts every time the motor turns on! Star grounding solves this by running separate ground wires from (1) the high-current motor driver, (2) the Arduino logic board, and (3) the analog sensors so they meet at one single star point at the negative battery terminal.

sections.h: Idea 2: Passive RC low-pass filter cutoff frequency ($f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$) and high-frequency noise attenuation
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Low-pass filter ("RC filter" & "Time response") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Low-pass filter, Examples, and Time response (connecting the RC time constant $\tau = R C$ to cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$).
What to skip: Skip complex Laplace transfer functions and decibel ($\text{dB}$) logarithmic plots (covered in Pass 2).
Key takeaway: When you wire a series resistor $R$ between a noisy sensor and an Arduino ADC pin and place a capacitor $C$ from the ADC pin to GND, the capacitor acts like a fast shock absorber (Lesson S0.6). Slow sensor voltages pass straight through to the ADC pin, while fast PWM switching spikes are shorted into the capacitor before they can move the pin voltage! The boundary between "slow" and "fast" is the cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$. At input frequency $f$, the output-to-input amplitude ratio is $\frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f / f_c)^2}}$:
Slow signal ($f \ll f_c$): Ratio $\approx 1.00$ ($100\%$ passes through cleanly).
At cutoff ($f = f_c$): Ratio $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \mathbf{0.707}$ ($70.7\%$ amplitude).
Fast noise ($f = 10 \cdot f_c$): Ratio $= \frac{1}{\sqrt{101}} \approx \mathbf{0.0995}$ (over $90\%$ of the noise amplitude is wiped out!).
Alternative resource: Falstad Circuit Simulator — RC Low-Pass Filter [verify in-app] — Import falstad/01.4-rc-lowpass.txt [verify in-app] to see a $1\text{ k}\Omega$ + $1\ \mu\text{F}$ filter ($f_c = 159.15\text{ Hz}$) attenuate a cutoff sine wave to $70.7\%$.

In a noisy robot, clean analog sensing requires two defenses working together:
Star Grounding (eliminates shared ground-wire voltage drop):
If motor current $I_{\text{motor}}$ flows through a shared wire of resistance $R_{\text{shared}}$ between the sensor ground and the Arduino GND, the ADC sees a false offset error $V_{\text{ground}}-\text{bounce} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{shared}}$. Wiring a dedicated sensor ground directly to the Arduino GND pin (so $I_{\text{motor}}$ never flows through the sensor's ground wire) reduces $V_{\text{ground}}-\text{bounce}$ on the sensor reading to $0.00\text{ V}$.
Passive RC Low-Pass Filter (blocks high-frequency switching noise):
With $R = 1{,}000\ \Omega$ ($1\text{ k}\Omega$) and $C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}$ ($10^{-6}\text{ F}$), the time constant is $\tau = R C = 0.001\text{ s}$ ($1.0\text{ ms}$) and the cutoff frequency is $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 0.001\text{ s}} \approx 159.15\text{ Hz}$, with amplitude ratio $\text{Ratio}(f) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f / f_c)^2}}$. A slow $2\text{ Hz}$ knob turn passes at $99.99\%$ amplitude, while $20{,}000\text{ Hz}$ ($20\text{ kHz}$) motor PWM noise is crushed to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (20000/159.15)^2}} \approx 0.008$ ($0.8\%$—over $99\%$ blocked!).
🔭 Looking Ahead (Trig & Radians Preview — You'll Need This in the Next 2 Lessons, 02.1–02.3): You are about to start Track 02 (Kinematics), where every robot link's $(x, y)$ reach and 2-link arm solver (02.1 $\to$ 02.2 $\to$ 02.3) rely on radians (math.radians), $\cos\theta$ / $\sin\theta$, and math.atan2(y, x). Take 3 minutes right now to review Lesson P.10: Radians & Right-Triangle Trig (or run Topic 6 in the Workbench's School-Math Diagnostic) so 02.1–02.3 feels effortless!

In Python 3: Complete ground_bounce_adc_error (TODO 1) to calculate how many 10-bit Arduino ADC counts (0..1023 at $5.0\text{ V}$) are corrupted by a shared ground wire, and complete rc_lowpass_response (TODO 2) to compute cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$ and amplitude ratio at $f = f_c$ ($70.7\%$) and $f = 20\text{ kHz}$ ($0.8\%$).
What is real-hardware only: Airborne electromagnetic interference (EMI) radiated by physical motor brush sparks into unshielded sensor wires.

sections.t: Save as grounding_and_rc_filter.py and run python3 grounding_and_rc_filter.py:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, v_bounce = i_motor_a r_shared_ohm (0.45 V) and adc_count_error = (v_bounce / v_ref) 1023.0 (92.1 counts). In TODO 2, f_c = 1.0 / (2.0 math.pi r_ohm c_farad) and amplitude_ratio = 1.0 / math.sqrt(1.0 + (f_signal_hz / f_c) 2).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Picking an RC cutoff frequency $f_c$ that is too low (like $f_c = 0.5\text{ Hz}$ on a fast robot joint sensor): Remember from Lesson 00.1 that $\tau = R C = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c}$. If $f_c = 0.5\text{ Hz}$, then $\tau \approx 0.32\text{ s}$ ($5\tau \approx 1.6\text{ s}$), making your sensor reading lag behind the real arm position by over a second! Choose $f_c$ roughly $5\times\text{–}10\times$ higher than your fastest physical motion, and well below the PWM switching frequency.
Daisy-chaining sensor GND to the H-bridge motor driver GND pin: Always wire analog sensor GND directly to an Arduino GND pin, and run a separate heavy wire from the H-bridge GND straight to the battery negative terminal (star ground).

Star ground vs. daisy-chain ground: Why does a potentiometer reading on A0 jump by decenas of counts when a motor starts if the potentiometer's GND leg is plugged into the H-bridge's ground row on a breadboard?
Answer
The motor's multi-amp return current flows through the resistance of that shared breadboard ground jumper ($V_{\text{ground}} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{wire}}$), lifting the potentiometer's $0\text{ V}$ reference pin above the Arduino's GND (ground bounce).
Calculating RC cutoff frequency $f_c$: What is the cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$ of a low-pass filter built from $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ ($10{,}000\ \Omega$) and $C = 0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($10^{-7}\text{ F}$)?
Answer
$\tau = R \cdot C = 10{,}000 \times 10^{-7} = 0.001\text{ s}$, so $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 0.001} \approx \mathbf{159.15\text{ Hz}}$—the exact same cutoff frequency as $1\text{ k}\Omega$ + $1\ \mu\text{F}$!

Ground bounce ($V_{\text{ground}} = I_{\text{motor}} \cdot R_{\text{wire}}$) corrupts sensor readings when motor return current shares a ground wire with sensors; star grounding gives motor power, logic, and sensors separate ground paths meeting at the battery negative terminal.
A passive RC low-pass filter has cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$ where signal amplitude is $70.7\%$, passing slow sensor changes ($f \ll f_c$) while attenuating fast switching noise ($f \gg f_c$).

You inspected falstad/01.4-rc-lowpass.txt [verify in-app] in Falstad and ran grounding_and_rc_filter.py (92.1 ADC counts error, 159.15 Hz, 70.7%, 0.80%).
You can wire a motor + sensor system with a star ground and an RC low-pass filter.

pages.title: Voltage, Current, Resistance, Ohm's Law, KVL/KCL & Voltage Dividers

sections.t: Before wiring an H-bridge motor driver or level-shifting a $5\text{ V}$ sensor to a $3.3\text{ V}$ microcontroller in Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02), you must be able to calculate how much current flows through a resistor, how two resistors divide a voltage, and how much heat ($P = I^2 R$) a wire or resistor dissipates. Getting these three laws right prevents magic smoke on your very first breadboard build. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Picture water pumped through a closed loop of pipes. Voltage ($V$, in volts) is the water pressure difference between two points; current ($I$, in amperes) is the flow rate of charge through the pipe; and resistance ($R$, in ohms, $\Omega$) is a narrow constriction that fights the flow. Ohm's Law ($V = I R$) says that pushing more current through a constriction takes proportionally more pressure. Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) says charge never vanishes at a pipe junction (what flows in must flow out), and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) says if you walk around any closed loop and return to your starting point, the pressure rises and drops must sum to zero. When current squeezes through a resistor, the lost pressure turns directly into heat at rate $P = V I = I^2 R$.

Ohm's Law ($V = I R$): Across a resistor of resistance $R$ in ohms ($\Omega$), the voltage drop $V$ in volts ($\text{V}$) and current $I$ in amperes ($\text{A}$) obey:
Substituting $V_{\text{bat}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ across a stalled motor winding of resistance $R_m = 2.4\ \Omega$ gives stall current $I_{\text{stall}} = 12.0\text{ V} / 2.4\ \Omega = 5.0\text{ A}$.
KVL, KCL, and the Unloaded/Loaded Voltage Divider: Two series resistors $R_1$ (top, connected to $V_{\text{in}}$) and $R_2$ (bottom, connected to $\text{GND}$) share the same current $I = V_{\text{in}}/(R_1 + R_2)$ when unloaded, producing midpoint voltage:
Substituting $V_{\text{in}} = 5.0\text{ V}$, $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, and $R_2 = 20\text{ k}\Omega$ gives $V_{\text{out}} = 5.0 \times \frac{20}{30} = 3.333\text{ V}$. If a load resistor $R_L$ is connected from $V_{\text{out}}$ to $\text{GND}$, the bottom leg becomes the parallel combination $R_{2\parallel L} = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}$.
Joule Heating ($P = V I = I^2 R$): The thermal power $P$ in watts ($\text{W}$) dissipated as heat in resistance $R$ carrying current $I$ is:
Substituting $I = 5.0\text{ A}$ through $R_m = 2.4\ \Omega$ gives $P = (5.0\text{ A})^2 (2.4\ \Omega) = 60.0\text{ W}$ of heat.

Predict first (before you run it): $R_1 = 68\text{ k}\Omega$ over $R_2 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ on a $24.0\text{ V}$ rail — commit to a number now. Roughly what fraction of $24\text{ V}$ does the $10\text{ k}\Omega$ bottom leg see, is that fraction safely under $3.3\text{ V}$, and which way must $V_{\text{out}}$ move once the ADC's finite $R_L = 100\text{ k}\Omega$ loads that leg? Write it down before you scroll, then check yourself against the printout: a loaded output reading higher than the unloaded one means your parallel bottom branch is inverted.
Design a battery-voltage sensing divider that scales a $V_{\text{bat}} = 24.0\text{ V}$ supply down using $R_1 = 68\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_2 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ for a $3.3\text{ V}$ ADC pin, and compute both the unloaded output voltage and the loaded output voltage when the ADC input has finite input resistance $R_L = 100\text{ k}\Omega$.
Expected output:

Calculate the current-limiting resistor $R$ required to run a status LED ($V_{\text{LED}} = 2.1\text{ V}$, target current $I = 10\text{ mA} = 0.010\text{ A}$) from a $V_{\text{supply}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ rail using KVL ($V_R = V_{\text{supply}} - V_{\text{LED}}$), and compute the power $P_R = I^2 R$ dissipated in the resistor. Verify $R = 290.0\ \Omega$ and $P_R = 0.029\text{ W}$ ($29.0\text{ mW}$, safely within a $0.25\text{ W}$ resistor rating).
If your result differs: Make sure you subtracted $V_{\text{LED}} = 2.1\text{ V}$ from $5.0\text{ V}$ before dividing by $0.010\text{ A}$ ($2.9\text{ V} / 0.010\text{ A} = 290\ \Omega$, not $5.0 / 0.010 = 500\ \Omega$).

sections.h: Graded package - the three laws on the bench
sections.t:
exercises/01-electronics.T1.01a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: stall_current, divider_unloaded, divider_loaded, joule_power, led_series_resistor, led_current and within_derating. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
25 tests. The divider is checked unloaded, loaded and with its legs swapped ($20.9\text{ V}$ into a $3.3\text{ V}$ pin, the module's own destroyed-pin case); the loaded case must come out lower, and a shorting load must pull it to zero; the power is checked on a $5\text{ A}$ stall; the LED resistor is checked at the exercise's $2.1\text{ V} / 10\text{ mA}$ and its current round-trips back; and the derating rule is checked at 50% of a quarter-watt part, so a full-rating check fails. The transfer suite takes the plant's numbers: the shoulder damper's $B_1\dot{q}^2$ is the same $I^2R$ form at a measured peak of $0.36\text{ W}$ (a quarter-watt part is out, a one-watt part at half rating is in), the $24\text{ V}$ sensing divider must still protect a $3.3\text{ V}$ ADC when a $100\text{ k}\Omega$ input loads it, and the $20$-byte $1\text{ kHz}$ frame at 8N1 is $200\text{ kbit/s}$ - above the 115.2 kbaud link that drops frames, below the 500 kbaud one that does not. Five planted faults - divider_swaps_legs, loaded_ignores_load, power_without_square, led_resistor_divides_supply, derating_uses_full_rating - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Python Variables & Functions) and 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Prefixes $\text{k}\Omega, \text{mA}, \text{mW}$ & Joule Heating $P = I^2 R$).
Core Concepts to Review First: Ohm's law ($V = IR$), Kirchhoff's Voltage/Current Laws (KVL/KCL), and loaded voltage dividers in ## 3. Formalization (Items 1–3) and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: SparkFun Voltage Dividers Tutorial (learn.sparkfun.com), All About Circuits Vol. I (allaboutcircuits.com), and Track 01 Tier 1 (01-electronics-and-power/README.md).
The exercise above is the whole exercise: KVL for the LED's series resistor, then $P = I^2R$ for the heat it makes. Fill the seven TODOs, then compare against the full solution below.

The LED's resistor is a KVL problem, not an Ohm's-law problem. The resistor only ever sees $V_R = 5.0 - 2.1 = 2.9\text{ V}$; dividing the supply by $10\text{ mA}$ gives $500\ \Omega$, which is $210\ \Omega$ too much and dims or kills the LED.
The divider is set by the bottom leg. $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$, and a load in parallel with $R_2$ can only make the bottom leg smaller, so a loaded reading higher than the unloaded one means the parallel branch was inverted.
Heat is $I^2R$, not $IR$. For the exercise's $10\text{ mA}$ through $290\ \Omega$, $P = (0.010)^2 \times 290 = 0.029\text{ W}$ — $11.6\%$ of a quarter-watt part, so the $50\%$ derating check passes with room to spare.
Close the loop. Feed your $R$ back into led_current: $2.9\text{ V} / 290\ \Omega$ must read $10.0\text{ mA}$, so the two functions have to agree with each other.
What the suite refuses. stall_current raises on a zero winding resistance, divider_unloaded and divider_loaded on a zero leg, joule_power on a negative resistance, led_series_resistor on a supply at or below the LED's forward drop or on a zero current, and within_derating on a derating fraction of zero - all ValueError, because each one would otherwise divide by zero or report a part that cannot exist.

Printed: R_led=290.0 ohm, I_back=10.0 mA, P_R=29.0 mW, derated=True
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite measures this module's link budget on the plant's own telemetry frame:

Inject one realistic bench fault and diagnose it from the symptom alone:
Inject: swap the legs — put $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 68\text{ k}\Omega$ on the bottom, leaving everything else alone.
Symptom: the midpoint now reads $V_{\text{out}} = 24.0 \times \frac{68}{78} = 20.92\text{ V}$ — a number that would destroy the $3.3\text{ V}$ ADC pin it was meant to protect.
Diagnose: the ratio is $R_2 / (R_1 + R_2)$, so the bottom resistor sets the fraction, not the top one. A midpoint near the full supply always means the bottom leg is the larger resistor.
Fix: restore the $68\text{ k}\Omega$ / $10\text{ k}\Omega$ order, then prove the pin is safe before wiring it: $V_{\text{out}} = 3.077\text{ V} < 3.3\text{ V}$ and $P_{R_1} = (24.0 - 3.077)^2 / 68\text{ k}\Omega = 6.44\text{ mW}$.

Simulate the voltage divider and LED resistor in the browser using Falstad Circuit Simulator (resources/open-source-toolchains.md) or run the Python verification script above.
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.01-electronics.T1.01a, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.
Optional Tier 1 breadboard check (hardware_required: false): place a $68\text{ k}\Omega$ and $10\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor in series on a solderless breadboard powered from a $5.0\text{ V}$ USB rail and probe the midpoint with a digital multimeter:
Pass/fail verification: unloaded $24\text{ V}$ divider reads $3.077\text{ V} < 3.3\text{ V}$ and $P_{R1} = 6.44\text{ mW} \ll 250\text{ mW}$.

⚠️ Bench Safety Note (safety_level: low): Always verify probe placement (V/Ohm voltage port, never the 10A shunt port in parallel) and set your CC/CV bench power supply current limit ($\le 0.5\text{ A}$) before energizing any breadboard or sensor circuit.
Pass criteria: run the worked example and exercise asserts with zero errors, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test below.

[Recall] [Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] A $12.0\text{ V}$ supply drives a motor coil with resistance $R = 3.0\ \Omega$ while the rotor is stalled. Compute the stall current $I_{\text{stall}}$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Apply] [Concept: kvl_kcl_and_voltage_divider] Compute the unloaded output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) of a divider with $V_{\text{in}} = 5.0\text{ V}$, top resistor $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, and bottom resistor $R_2 = 20\text{ k}\Omega$.
[Transfer] [Concept: electrical_power_i2r_dissipation] Compute the heat power $P = I^2 R$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) dissipated in a $0.050\ \Omega$ current-sense resistor carrying $I = 10.0\text{ A}$.
[Concept: kvl_kcl_and_voltage_divider] Why can you never power a $3.3\text{ V}$ motor or microcontroller using a $10\text{ k}\Omega / 20\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor voltage divider from $5\text{ V}$?
A. Because resistors only work with AC voltages.
B. Because the load draws significant current $I_{\text{load}}$ through $R_1$, causing a massive $I_{\text{load}} R_1$ voltage drop that collapses $V_{\text{out}}$ (a voltage divider is for high-impedance signal sensing, not power delivery).
C. Because KCL does not apply when a motor is connected.
D. Because $3.3\text{ V}$ exceeds the breakdown voltage of carbon film resistors.
[Spaced review -> 00-foundations.T1.00e — Concept: spring_energy_and_power] A spring of stiffness $k = 200.0\,\text{N/m}$ is compressed by $0.050\,\text{m}$. Compute the stored energy $\tfrac12 k x^2$ in joules (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ ($80\%+$). If you missed Q1, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q2 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q3, study ## 3. Formalization item 3. If you missed Q5, review 00-foundations.T1.00e. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 01 Tier 1 bridge ladder (01-electronics.T1.01a $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01c $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01d $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01b) before Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02):
[Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] Compute the current $I$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) when $24.0\text{ V}$ is applied across an $8.0\ \Omega$ resistor.
[Concept: kvl_kcl_and_voltage_divider] Compute the unloaded output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) of a divider with $V_{\text{in}} = 15.0\text{ V}$, $R_1 = 30\text{ k}\Omega$ (top) and $R_2 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ (bottom).
[Concept: electrical_power_i2r_dissipation] Compute the heat power $P = I^2 R$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) dissipated in a $0.08\ \Omega$ wire carrying $2.5\text{ A}$.
[SAFETY] [Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] Your DMM's red lead is in the 10A jack ($R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.010\ \Omega$) and you touch the probes across a $15.0\text{ V}$ rail. Compute the short-circuit current in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Concept: breadboard_internal_bus_connectivity] A resistor's two legs are both pressed into row 12 (holes a12 and b12). What does the rest of the circuit see between those two legs?
A. A short circuit: a12–b12 are the same copper clip, so the resistor is bypassed and the node is a plain wire.
B. The full resistance, because holes in one row are isolated from each other.
C. Twice the resistance, because the clips are in series.
D. An open circuit, because the center ravine separates every row.
[Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] [Concept: capacitor_charge_storage_and_decoupling] Compute the time constant $\tau = R C$ in seconds ($\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-12}$) for $R = 2.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C = 0.10\ \mu\text{F}$.
[Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] A $5.0\text{ mH}$ coil carrying $2.0\text{ A}$ is interrupted in $2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ with no freewheeling diode. Compute the flyback spike $|V_L| = L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Concept: mosfet_low_side_rds_on_switch] Compute the conduction loss $P = I_D^2 R_{DS(\text{on})}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $I_D = 3.0\text{ A}$ and $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 25\text{ m}\Omega$.
[Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] Compute the average motor voltage $V_{\text{eff}} = D V_{\text{bus}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $V_{\text{bus}} = 18.0\text{ V}$ at $D = 0.40$.
[Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] An H-bridge runs Leg A at $D_A = 0.60$ and Leg B at $D_B = 0.20$ from $V_{\text{bus}} = 20.0\text{ V}$. Compute the average signed motor voltage $V_{AB} = (D_A - D_B)V_{\text{bus}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: esd_and_short_circuit_prevention] Before you pick up a bare motor-driver breakout on a dry winter day, what is the correct ESD precaution?
A. Touch the $3.3\text{ V}$ pin first so the static discharges through the regulator.
B. Wear a wrist strap bonded to a grounded mat, or touch a grounded metal chassis first, so your body charge equalises before it can arc into a gate oxide.
C. Hold the board by its pins to maximise contact area.
D. Nothing: CMOS inputs are protected against any static voltage.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $9/11$ overall ($80\%+$) AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on Q4 and Q11 ([SAFETY]). Remediation: Q1–Q3 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01a; Q4–Q5, Q11 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01c; Q6–Q7 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01d; Q8–Q10 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01b.

pages.title: Low-Side MOSFET Switching, PWM Duty Cycle & H-Bridge Polarity Reversal

sections.t: This is the final bridge module in the Track 01 Tier 1 ladder before Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02). A microcontroller GPIO pin can only source $\sim 20\text{ mA}$ at $3.3\text{ V}$—connecting a motor directly to it destroys the pin immediately. Power MOSFETs act as voltage-controlled electronic switches that let a tiny $3.3\text{ V}$ logic signal throttle amperes of motor current via Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) and reverse direction via a 4-switch H-Bridge. Already know this? Read ### Safety notes first, then take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7.

Think of a MOSFET as a spring-loaded water valve whose handle (the Gate) is controlled by pressure rather than flow. When the Gate voltage is $0\text{ V}$ relative to the Source ($V_{GS} = 0$), the valve is shut tight and zero current flows into the Drain. When you raise $V_{GS}$ above the threshold with a $3.3\text{ V}$ or $5\text{ V}$ logic signal, the valve snaps wide open with a tiny on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on})}$ of only a few milliohms. Instead of cracking the valve half-open (which would burn huge heat inside the valve), we flick it 100% open and 100% closed twenty thousand times per second (PWM); the motor's inductance smooths those rapid pulses into a smooth average voltage $V_{\text{eff}} = D \cdot V_{\text{bus}}$. And to spin the motor backward, an H-Bridge arranges four MOSFETs like an "H" around the motor so closing one diagonal pair pushes current left-to-right and closing the opposite diagonal pushes current right-to-left.

Low-Side N-Channel MOSFET Switch & Conduction Loss: When gate-to-source voltage $V_{GS}$ exceeds the logic-level rating, the MOSFET conducts drain current $I_D$ ($\text{A}$) with on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on})}$ ($\Omega$), dissipating conduction heat power $P_{\text{cond}}$ ($\text{W}$):
Substituting $I_D = 5.0\text{ A}$ and $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.010\ \Omega$ ($10\text{ m}\Omega$) gives $P_{\text{cond}} = 25.0 \times 0.010 = 0.25\text{ W}$ (whereas dropping $6\text{ V}$ linearly at $5\text{ A}$ would waste $30.0\text{ W}$!). A $10\text{ k}\Omega$ pull-down resistor from Gate to Source keeps $V_{GS} = 0\text{ V}$ while MCU pins float during boot.
PWM Duty Cycle ($D \in [0, 1]$): Switching $V_{\text{bus}}$ ($\text{V}$) ON for time $t_{\text{on}}$ over period $T_{\text{pwm}} = 1/f_{\text{pwm}}$ defines duty cycle $D = t_{\text{on}}/T_{\text{pwm}}$ and average effective voltage:
Substituting $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ and $D = 0.75$ ($75\%$) gives $V_{\text{eff}} = 9.0\text{ V}$.
H-Bridge Diagonal Switching, Shoot-Through & Reading a Driver Datasheet (DRV8833): Four switches $(Q_{\text{AH}}, Q_{\text{AL}})$ on leg A and $(Q_{\text{BH}}, Q_{\text{BL}})$ on leg B apply terminal voltage $V_{\text{AB}} = V_A - V_B$:
Forward: $(Q_{\text{AH}}, Q_{\text{BL}})$ ON $\implies V_{\text{AB}} = +V_{\text{bus}}$.
Reverse: $(Q_{\text{BH}}, Q_{\text{AL}})$ ON $\implies V_{\text{AB}} = -V_{\text{bus}}$.
Shoot-Through Hazard: Turning ON both switches of the same vertical leg $(Q_{\text{AH}}$ and $Q_{\text{AL}})$ simultaneously shorts $V_{\text{bus}}$ directly to $\text{GND}$ through $2 R_{DS(\text{on})}$; inserting dead-time $t_d$ (both OFF briefly during transitions) prevents shoot-through.
Canonical Walkthrough — How to Read a Component Datasheet in 5 Minutes (TI DRV8833): Whenever you meet a new IC, check four datasheet tables before wiring power: (1) Pin Configuration & Functions (maps physical pins to signals), (2) Absolute Maximum Ratings (destruction ceiling, e.g. $V_{\text{VM},\max} = 11.8\text{ V}$—never operate at this limit!), (3) Recommended Operating Conditions (safe continuous window: $V_{\text{VM}} \in [2.7\text{ V}, 10.8\text{ V}]$, $I_{\text{rms}} \le 1.5\text{ A}$), and (4) Electrical Characteristics (where combined high-side + low-side on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on}),\text{HS}+\text{LS}} \approx 0.36\ \Omega$ is specified at $25^\circ\text{C}$).
DRV8833 Breakout Pinout & Wiring Checklist:
VM & GND: Motor supply ($2.7\text{–}10.8\text{ V}$ from CC/CV bench supply) and star-ground return; place a $100\text{–}470\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic cap + $100\text{ nF}$ ceramic cap right across VM and GND.
nSLEEP (SLP): Active-low enable pin—must be tied HIGH to 3.3V to wake the chip (LOW puts the driver into sleep mode with outputs disabled!).
AIN1, AIN2: $3.3\text{ V}$ PWM/logic inputs from MCU timer pins (0,0 = Coast; 1,0 = Forward; 0,1 = Reverse; 1,1 = Dynamic Brake).
AOUT1, AOUT2: High-current H-bridge outputs wired to the two brushed DC motor leads.
nFAULT (FLT): Open-drain active-low fault output (pulls LOW on overcurrent, thermal shutdown, or undervoltage lockout).

Predict first (before you run it): Commit to two numbers. (1) The same $I_D = 4.0\text{ A}$ is either switched by a MOSFET ($R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.020\ \Omega$) or dropped linearly across the remaining $6.0\text{ V}$ at $D = 0.50$ — is the linear-drop loss tens of times or hundreds of times worse than the conduction loss? (2) Both FETs of one leg ON across $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ with $0.020\ \Omega$ each: commit to the shoot-through current in amperes. Write both down, then run the block. If your second answer sits in the tens of amperes — the same order as the $4.0\text{ A}$ load you are switching — you have let the bus voltage fall across a load instead of across two milliohm-scale on-resistances in series, and the real number is an order of magnitude larger.
Compare MOSFET conduction loss at $I_D = 4.0\text{ A}$, $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.020\ \Omega$ against linear drop loss at $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $D = 0.50$, and compute the catastrophic shoot-through current if both FETs in one leg turn on across $12.0\text{ V}$.
Expected output:

Using the Canonical TI DRV8833 Datasheet Walkthrough in ## 3. Formalization Item 3 above, (a) extract the maximum Recommended Operating supply voltage $V_{\text{VM,rec,max}}$ ($10.8\text{ V}$) vs. the Absolute Maximum destruction ceiling $V_{\text{VM,abs,max}}$ ($11.8\text{ V}$) and verify that a $V_{\text{bus}} = 9.0\text{ V}$ supply is safely inside the recommended operating window (2.7 <= 9.0 <= 10.8), and (b) extract the combined high-side + low-side path on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on, high})} + R_{DS(\text{on, low})} = 0.36\ \Omega$ to compute the total H-bridge conduction power loss $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 (R_{\text{high}} + R_{\text{low}})$ in watts ($\text{W}$) when driving $I = 1.2\text{ A}$ continuously at $D = 1.0$. Verify $P_{\text{loss}} = 0.5184\text{ W}$ ($\pm 10^{-4}\text{ W}$).
If your result differs: Remember that in an H-bridge, motor current flows through two switches in series (one high-side FET in leg A and one low-side FET in leg B), so you must multiply $I^2$ by the combined high+low resistance ($0.36\ \Omega$).

sections.h: Graded package - the switch, the duty and the leg
sections.t:
exercises/01-electronics.T1.01b/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: conduction_loss, pwm_effective_voltage, shoot_through_current (two switches, not one), h_bridge_voltage (the difference, not the sum), bridge_conduction_loss, within_recommended and duty_for_effective_voltage. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
25 tests. The loss is checked at the module's $5\text{ A} / 10\text{ m}\Omega$ and at $6\text{ A} / 15\text{ m}\Omega$; the worked example's $150\times$ advantage over a linear drop is asserted as a ratio, not a constant; the shoot-through is checked at both the worked and the Skip-test buses, so one switch fails; the H-bridge is checked forward, reverse and at equal duties, so adding the duties fails; the bridge loss is checked against one switch ($2\times$ ratio) and against the datasheet pair; a $65\%$ command must raise rather than produce $780\text{ V}$; and $11.8\text{ V}$ (the absolute maximum) must fail the recommended window. The transfer suite drives the plant at 70% duty: a square wave switching its $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp must average exactly $0.7 \times 2.5$, the schedule never exceeds the clamp, and full duty travels further than 70%; the two-switch bridge loss is exactly twice the one-switch loss. Five planted faults - conduction_without_square, shoot_through_one_switch, bridge_counts_one_switch, h_bridge_adds_duties, duty_accepts_percentage - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Clamping Functions), 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Units & Power Dissipation), and 00-foundations.T1.00e (Energy Balance).
Prerequisite Bridge Modules: 01-electronics.T1.01a (DC Circuits), 01-electronics.T1.01c (CC/CV Bench Safety), and 01-electronics.T1.01d (Capacitor/Inductor Transients).
Core Concepts to Review First: PWM average voltage $V_{\text{avg}} = D V_{\text{bus}}$, MOSFET $R_{\text{DS(on)}}$ conduction loss, H-bridge bidirectional truth table, and star-grounding in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: TI SLVA959 (Brushed DC Motor Driver H-Bridge Basics), Analog Devices MT-101 (Decoupling Techniques), and Track 01 §1.2–1.3 (01-electronics-and-power/README.md).

The exercise reads the DRV8833 datasheet twice: once for its recommended supply window, once for the pair of on-resistances the motor current actually crosses. Fill the seven TODOs, then compare against the full solution below.

Conduction loss counts the switches in the loop. In a bridge, motor current crosses one high-side FET in leg A and one low-side FET in leg B, so $P = I^2 (R_{\text{high}} + R_{\text{low}}) D$ — with a single $0.18\ \Omega$ the answer is exactly half of $0.5184\text{ W}$.
Shoot-through is two switches as well. Both FETs of one leg are in series across the bus, so with $0.020\ \Omega$ each the current is $9.0/(2 \times 0.020)$; dividing by one $R$ doubles it.
The differential drive subtracts. $V_{AB} = (D_A - D_B)V_{\text{bus}}$, so equal duties give $0\text{ V}$ (brake/coast) and $D_A = 0.25$, $D_B = 0.75$ at $24\text{ V}$ is $-12.0\text{ V}$, not $+24.0$.
Read the window, not the ceiling. $11.8\text{ V}$ is the Absolute Maximum; the Recommended Operating Conditions stop at $10.8\text{ V}$, which is why $9.0\text{ V}$ is inside and $11.8\text{ V}$ is not.
What the suite refuses. conduction_loss and h_bridge_voltage raise on a duty outside $[0, 1]$, pwm_effective_voltage raises on a percentage such as 65.0 instead of scaling it silently, duty_for_effective_voltage raises on a demand the bus cannot deliver, shoot_through_current raises on a zero resistance, and within_recommended raises on an inverted window with v_min > v_max - all ValueError.

Printed: P_loss=0.5184 W at I=1.2 A, R_high+R_low=0.36 ohm; 9.0 V recommended=True; D(9.0 V on a 12.0 V bus)=0.75; shoot-through at 9.0 V=25 A
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite switches the plant's own torque clamp at a duty cycle and measures the average it delivers:

Inject one realistic H-bridge analysis slip and diagnose it from the number alone:
Inject: recompute the exercise's conduction loss with a single switch's $R = 0.18\ \Omega$ instead of the series pair $R_{\text{high}} + R_{\text{low}} = 0.36\ \Omega$, keeping $I = 1.2\text{ A}$ at $D = 1.0$.
Symptom: $P_{\text{loss}} = (1.2\text{ A})^2 \times 0.18\ \Omega = 0.2592\text{ W}$ — exactly half the verified $0.5184\text{ W}$, which reads as a cooler, safer board than the part actually allows.
Diagnose: a clean factor of two is the tell. Conduction loss scales with the number of switches in the current loop, so trace the truth-table path (leg A high-side $\to$ motor $\to$ leg B low-side) and count the on-resistances the motor current crosses before you believe any thermal margin.
Fix: use the combined $R_{\text{high}} + R_{\text{low}} = 0.36\ \Omega$, which reproduces $P_{\text{loss}} = (1.2\text{ A})^2 \times 0.36\ \Omega = 0.5184\text{ W}$. Prove the fix by printing both loop models side by side: the ratio must be exactly the count of switches in the path (two), and any other ratio means the loop is not the one you think it is.

Simulate a low-side MOSFET PWM switch and 4-FET H-bridge in Falstad Circuit Simulator or inspect 25 kHz PMSM FOC and 3D CAD & 48V PCB in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev).
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.01-electronics.T1.01b, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.

⚠️ Mandatory Safety Briefing (safety_level: high — read before touching hardware or taking the Skip/Gate test):
Maximum Voltage & Current Limits: Keep Tier 1 breadboard motor supplies at $\le 12.0\text{ V}$ and set your bench power supply current limit to $\le 1.5\text{ A}$ before powering on (L0.1).
Shoot-Through & Short-Circuit Prevention: Never wire discrete H-bridge gates without hardware dead-time or interlock logic; a simultaneous high-side + low-side ON state across an unprotected battery can dump $>100\text{ A}$, melting breadboard strips and rupturing LiPo cells. Use integrated drivers with built-in shoot-through protection (DRV8833 in Step 1.2) and always power first from a current-limited bench supply, never directly from a LiPo battery.
Gate Pull-Down & Flyback Protection: Always include a $10\text{ k}\Omega$ Gate-to-Source pull-down resistor so the motor cannot spin unexpectedly while the MCU is in reset, and never switch an inductive coil with a single FET without a freewheeling flyback diode across the coil.

Pass criteria: read ### Safety notes, run the worked example and exercise asserts, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test ($100\%$ required on [SAFETY] items). Passing the 8-question Ladder Gate test ($\ge 80\%$, $100\%$ on [SAFETY] items) unlocks Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02).

[Recall] [Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] Compute the average effective motor voltage $V_{\text{eff}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for a $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ supply switched at duty cycle $D = 0.65$ ($65\%$).
[Apply] [Concept: mosfet_low_side_rds_on_switch] Compute the conduction heat dissipation $P_{\text{cond}} = I_D^2 R_{DS(\text{on})}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) in a MOSFET with $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.015\ \Omega$ carrying $I_D = 6.0\text{ A}$ at $100\%$ duty cycle.
[Transfer] [Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] An H-bridge powered from $V_{\text{bus}} = 24.0\text{ V}$ drives Leg A at PWM duty cycle $D_A = 0.25$ and Leg B at $D_B = 0.75$. Compute the average signed motor voltage $V_{\text{motor}} = (D_A - D_B) V_{\text{bus}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Spaced review -> 01-electronics.T1.01a — Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] [SAFETY] [Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] If both $Q_{\text{AH}}$ and $Q_{\text{AL}}$ ($R_{DS(\text{on})} = 0.020\ \Omega$ each, total series resistance $0.040\ \Omega$) turn ON simultaneously across an un-current-limited $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ battery because dead-time was omitted, compute the instantaneous shoot-through fault current $I_{\text{shoot}} = \frac{V_{\text{bus}}}{2 R_{DS(\text{on})}}$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ A}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: mosfet_low_side_rds_on_switch] Why must a discrete low-side N-MOSFET gate have a $10\text{ k}\Omega$ pull-down resistor to Source (GND)?
A. To increase the PWM frequency.
B. To bleed off gate charge and hold $V_{GS} = 0\text{ V}$ while the microcontroller GPIO pin is floating (high-Z) during boot or reset, preventing unintended motor runaway or linear-region overheating.
C. To measure motor current.
D. To boost $3.3\text{ V}$ to $12\text{ V}$.
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ overall ($80\%+$) AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on Q4 and Q5 ([SAFETY]). If you missed Q1, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; if you missed Q2 or Q5, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; if you missed Q3 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 3 and ### Safety notes. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

A. The multimeter screen will show hex numbers.
B. The $10\text{ A}$ current jack is a near-zero-ohm dead short ($\sim 0.01\ \Omega$) across the leads, short-circuiting the power supply and blowing the meter fuse or arcing at the probes.
C. It drains the multimeter's $9\text{ V}$ battery slightly faster.
D. It changes the PWM duty cycle.
[Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] [Concept: capacitor_charge_storage_and_decoupling] Compute the $-3\text{ dB}$ cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$ in $\text{Hz}$ (tolerance $\pm 0.01\text{ Hz}$) for $R = 1000\ \Omega$ and $C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}$ ($10^{-6}\text{ F}$).
[Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] Compute the inductive flyback spike magnitude $|V_L| = L \left|\frac{di}{dt}\right|$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) if a $2.0\text{ mH}$ ($0.002\text{ H}$) coil carrying $3.0\text{ A}$ is interrupted in $\Delta t = 1.0\ \mu\text{s}$ ($10^{-6}\text{ s}$) without a flyback diode.
[Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] Compute $V_{\text{eff}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $V_{\text{bus}} = 24.0\text{ V}$ at $D = 0.25$.
[SAFETY] [Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] Before powering a newly wired breadboard H-bridge for the first time, what is the mandatory bench power supply procedure?
A. Connect a fully charged 3S LiPo battery first to burn off any solder flux.
B. Verify $V_{\text{bus}}$ to $\text{GND}$ resistance is not a short with a DMM, set the bench PSU voltage to target ($6\text{–}12\text{ V}$) with the current limit set low ($0.2\text{–}0.5\text{ A}$) before enabling the output, and verify dead-time / logic states before connecting the motor.
C. Set the bench PSU current limit to $30\text{ A}$ maximum.
D. Leave the MCU ground disconnected from the motor driver ground.
Gate answer key:
