pages.title: Multimeter, Current-Limited Bench Supply, Breadboard & ESD/Short-Circuit Safety

sections.t: More beginner circuits are destroyed in the first five seconds of power-on by a breadboard row short, a multimeter lead left in the $10\text{ A}$ current jack, or an unprotected LiPo battery than by any software bug. Mastering how solderless breadboard clips are wired internally, how to measure voltage vs. current safely with a Digital Multimeter (DMM), and how to set a bench power supply's Constant-Current (CC) limit protects every board you build from Stage 0 (L0.1) through Track 08. Already know this? Read ### Safety notes first, then take the Skip test in section 7.

Imagine a solderless breadboard as an apartment building with hidden copper hallways underneath the plastic holes: the long vertical side strips (+ and -) are power elevators running the full height of the board, while each horizontal group of 5 holes (a–b–c–d–e and f–g–h–i–j, split by a center ravine) shares a single metal clip. Plugging both legs of a resistor into the same 5-hole row shorts the resistor out completely! Next, a Digital Multimeter (DMM) in Voltage mode (V) acts like an infinitely high-resistance stethoscope ($R_{\text{DMM,V}} \approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$) that you touch across two points in parallel; in Current mode (A), it acts like a near-zero-ohm pipe ($R_{\text{shunt}} \approx 0.01\ \Omega$) that must be placed in series by breaking the circuit. Finally, a current-limited bench supply is an automatic circuit breaker that smoothly folds back its output voltage the instant current exceeds your preset ceiling $I_{\text{limit}}$.

Solderless Breadboard Internal Topology:
Each 5-hole terminal row (a1, b1, c1, d1, e1) is a single electrical node ($R_{\text{clip}} \approx 0.05\ \Omega$, continuous current rating $\le 1.0\text{ A}$).
The center channel (e to f) is open circuit so dual-inline IC packages (DIP / breakout boards) straddle the gap without shorting opposite pins.
DMM Input Impedance (Parallel Voltage vs. Series Current):
Voltage mode (V jack): $R_{\text{in}} = 10\text{ M}\Omega$. Probing a $12.0\text{ V}$ rail draws only $I = 12.0 / 10^7 = 1.2\ \mu\text{A}$.
Current mode (10A jack): $R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.010\ \Omega$. Accidentally probing across a $12.0\text{ V}$ source with leads in the 10A jack attempts to draw $I_{\text{short}} = 12.0\text{ V} / 0.010\ \Omega = 1200\text{ A}$, immediately blowing the DMM fuse or arcing!
Bench Supply Constant-Voltage (CV) to Constant-Current (CC) Foldback: Given voltage setting $V_{\text{set}}$, current limit $I_{\text{limit}}$, and load resistance $R_{\text{load}}$, the actual terminal voltage is:
Substituting $V_{\text{set}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.20\text{ A}$, and a wiring short $R_{\text{load}} = 0.5\ \Omega$ folds output voltage down to $V_{\text{out}} = 0.20 \times 0.5 = 0.10\text{ V}$ and caps fault power at $P = I_{\text{limit}}^2 R_{\text{load}} = 0.020\text{ W}$ instead of $288\text{ W}$!

Predict first (before you run it): commit to three numbers before the code runs. With the limit at $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.20\text{ A}$, is the supply in "CV" or "CC" on the $R_{\text{short}} = 0.25\ \Omega$ miswire, and is the fault power nearer $0.01\text{ W}$ or $576\text{ W}$? Then estimate the DMM short current from the $0.010\ \Omega$ shunt — an order of magnitude is enough ($\approx 1\text{ A}$ or $\approx 1000\text{ A}$?). Write both down. If your two fault powers come out within a factor of $100$ of each other, you ran the battery case in "CC" as well: a $50\text{ A}$ source does not clamp at $0.25\ \Omega$. If the DMM number lands in microamps, you divided by the voltmeter's $10\text{ M}\Omega$ input instead of the current shunt.
Compare the fault power dissipated in a $R_{\text{short}} = 0.25\ \Omega$ breadboard miswire across a $12.0\text{ V}$ rail when powered by (a) a bench supply with $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.20\text{ A}$ versus (b) an unprotected $12\text{ V}$ battery capable of $50\text{ A}$, and compute the DMM current-jack short current.
Expected output:

Your circuit has normal quiescent resistance $R_{\text{idle}} = 240\ \Omega$ at $V_{\text{set}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ (drawing $50\text{ mA}$). If you set the bench supply current limit to $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.10\text{ A}$ ($100\text{ mA}$), verify using psu_output(12.0, 0.10, 240.0) that normal operation stays in "CV" mode at $12.0\text{ V}$, and compute the exact threshold resistance $R_{\text{crit}} = V_{\text{set}} / I_{\text{limit}}$ below which the supply drops into "CC" mode ($R_{\text{crit}} = 120.0\ \Omega$).
If your result differs: Divide $V_{\text{set}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ by $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.10\text{ A}$ to get $R_{\text{crit}} = 120.0\ \Omega$.

sections.h: Graded package - the supply's two modes and the DMM's two jacks
sections.t:
exercises/01-electronics.T1.01c/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: psu_output (the CC/CV foldback, returning voltage, current, power and mode), critical_resistance, dmm_voltage_loading_current, dmm_short_current, clip_power, led_current_ma and is_short. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
30 tests. The foldback is checked on both sides of the $120\ \Omega$ threshold, so a supply that ignores its limit fails; the DMM is checked in the current jack across a $0.020\ \Omega$ shunt ($1200\text{ A}$ of available fault current) and in the voltage mode across $10\text{ M}\Omega$ ($1.2\ \mu\text{A}$); the clip's heat is checked as $I^2R$ (so a missing square fails); the LED's $10\text{ mA}$ is checked; and is_short is checked either side of $10\ \Omega$, so an inverted comparison fails. The transfer suite compares the protected supply against a bare battery on the same $0.25\ \Omega$ miswire - $0.01\text{ W}$ against $576\text{ W}$ - computes the one-second run energy on the plant's own TICKS DT, and proves the foldback is memoryless at the plant's $1\text{ ms}$ tick. Five planted faults - psu_ignores_limit, critical_resistance_multiplies, dmm_uses_voltmeter_input, clip_power_without_square, is_short_inverted - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Conditional Logic) and 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Units & Power $P = VI$).
Prerequisite Bridge Module: 01-electronics.T1.01a (Ohm's Law & Short-Circuit Current).
Core Concepts to Review First: Breadboard 5-pin spring-clip topology, DMM continuity vs. current-jack hazards, and CC/CV power supply current clamping $V_{\text{out}} = \min(V_{\text{set}}, I_{\text{limit}} R_{\text{load}})$ in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: SparkFun How to Use a Breadboard, SparkFun How to Use a Multimeter, and Track 00 §0.2 (00-foundations/README.md).

The exercise is one question asked twice: is the supply still in CV at $240\ \Omega$, and where is the exact resistance at which it stops being CV? Fill the seven TODOs, then compare against the full solution below.

Foldback is a comparison, not a formula to memorise. Compute the current the load would draw at $V_{\text{set}}$; if that is above $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply gives up voltage until the current equals the limit, so $V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{limit}} R_{\text{load}}$.
The threshold is $V_{\text{set}}/I_{\text{limit}}$. $12.0/0.10 = 120\ \Omega$: at exactly $120\ \Omega$ the unclamped current equals the limit and the supply is still in CV, and $119\ \Omega$ is already in CC at $0.10 \times 119 = 11.9\text{ V}$.
Two DMM jacks, two resistances. In voltage mode the rail sees $10\text{ M}\Omega$ ($12.0/10^7 = 1.2\ \mu\text{A}$); in the current jack the rail sees the shunt ($12.0/(0.010 + 0.010) = 600\text{ A}$) — dividing by $10\text{ M}\Omega$ there gives microamps and hides the destroyed fuse.
The power-off check compares the other way. A healthy $240\ \Omega$ build must return False from is_short; only a reading below $10\ \Omega$ is the short you are hunting.
What the suite refuses. A zero current limit or zero load in psu_output, a zero power in critical_resistance, a zero or negative resistance in dmm_short_current, a negative ceiling in clip_power, a zero forward drop in led_current_ma, and an is_short threshold of zero all raise ValueError.

Printed: mode=CV, V_out=12.00 V, I_out=50.0 mA, P=600.0 mW; R_crit=120.0 ohm; 119 ohm -> CC at 11.90 V
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite puts this module's bench fault on the plant's own one-second run:

This is the classic first-power-on mistake, and it is a fault you inject on purpose so you can recognise the symptom later:
Inject: the same $R_{\text{short}} = 0.25\ \Omega$ miswire across a $12.0\text{ V}$ rail, but the current limit raised to $I_{\text{limit}} = 2.0\text{ A}$ because the $0.20\text{ A}$ setting kept folding back during bring-up.
Symptom: the supply still sits in "CC" and its voltmeter reads $V_{\text{out}} = 2.0 \times 0.25 = 0.50\text{ V}$ — but the fault now dissipates $P = I_{\text{limit}}^2 R_{\text{short}} = (2.0)^2 (0.25) = 1.0\text{ W}$, one hundred times the $0.01\text{ W}$ the protected setting allowed, through a spring clip rated for $\le 1.0\text{ A}$.
Diagnose: read the two displays together. The current reads exactly your limit ($2.0\text{ A}$) while the voltage sags far below $V_{\text{set}}$, so the supply is in Constant-Current foldback and the load is resistive — a short or a half-wired build, not an open circuit (an open would read $V_{\text{set}}$ at $0\text{ A}$). If the current sits at the limit and the clip is warm, the limit is the thing that decided how much heat you made.
Fix: drop the limit back to $0.10\text{–}0.20\text{ A}$ for logic builds, treat foldback as the signal to power off and hunt the short, and prove the fix by measuring $V_{\text{bus}}$-to-$\text{GND}$ resistance in $\Omega$ mode: $\ge 240\ \Omega$ (the healthy $R_{\text{idle}}$) means the miswire is gone, $< 10\ \Omega$ means it is still there.

Simulate a current-limited voltage source and breadboard layout in Falstad Circuit Simulator or Wokwi (resources/open-source-toolchains.md).
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.01-electronics.T1.01c, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.

⚠️ Mandatory Safety Briefing (safety_level: high — read before touching hardware or taking the Skip test):
Voltage & Current Ceilings: Keep all Tier 1 breadboard rails at $\le 12.0\text{ V}$ and $\le 1.0\text{ A}$ continuous (L0.1). Solderless breadboard spring clips overheat and melt plastic above $1.5\text{–}2.0\text{ A}$.
Power-Off Continuity Check First: Before enabling power on any new build, unplug the power supply and measure resistance between $V_{\text{bus}}$ and $\text{GND}$ with your DMM in $\Omega$ mode. If it reads $< 10\ \Omega$, find and fix the short before applying power.
DMM Lead Jack Discipline: Keep the red DMM lead in the V/Ω jack at all times. If you ever move it to the 10A or mA jack to measure series current, move it back to V/Ω the instant you finish—probing a voltage rail with the lead in 10A creates a dead short.
ESD & First Power-On Rule: Touch a grounded metal frame before handling bare CMOS MOSFETs or MCUs, and always power a new circuit from a current-limited bench supply ($I_{\text{limit}} = 0.1\text{–}0.2\text{ A}$ for logic, $0.5\text{–}1.5\text{ A}$ for small motors), never directly from a LiPo battery.
Pass criteria: read ### Safety notes, run the worked example and exercise asserts, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test ($100\%$ required on [SAFETY] questions).

[Recall] [Concept: breadboard_internal_bus_connectivity] A solderless breadboard spring clip has contact resistance $R_{\text{clip}} = 0.12\ \Omega$. If you mistakenly route $I = 5.0\text{ A}$ of motor current through that clip, compute the localized heat power $P = I^2 R_{\text{clip}}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ W}$) that melts the ABS plastic housing.
[Apply] [Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] A bench power supply is configured to $V_{\text{set}} = 12.0\text{ V}$ and current limit $I_{\text{lim}} = 0.25\text{ A}$. If you connect it across a $R_{\text{load}} = 4.0\ \Omega$ resistor, the supply enters Constant-Current (CC) foldback. Compute the clamped output voltage $V_{\text{out}} = \min(V_{\text{set}}, I_{\text{lim}} R_{\text{load}})$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Transfer] [SAFETY] [Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] If you leave the red multimeter lead plugged into the current-shunt jack ($R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.010\ \Omega$ internal resistance, $R_{\text{leads}} = 0.010\ \Omega$ probe resistance, total $0.020\ \Omega$) and touch the probes in parallel across an un-current-limited $24.0\text{ V}$ battery rail, compute the instantaneous short-circuit surge current $I_{\text{short}} = \frac{24.0}{R_{\text{shunt}} + R_{\text{leads}}}$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}\text{ A}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: esd_and_short_circuit_prevention] Before turning ON the output of your bench power supply on a freshly wired breadboard circuit, what two steps are mandatory?
A. Connect a LiPo battery in parallel and set current limit to maximum.
B. With power OFF, verify $V_{\text{bus}}$-to-$\text{GND}$ resistance is not a short using a DMM in $\Omega$ mode, and pre-configure the bench PSU to target voltage with a low Constant-Current limit ($0.1\text{–}0.2\text{ A}$).
C. Touch the $12\text{ V}$ wire to the MCU 3.3V pin to test ESD protection.
D. Remove all ground wires.
[Spaced review -> 01-electronics.T1.01a — Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] A $5.0\text{ V}$ rail powers an LED ($V_f = 2.0\text{ V}$) through a $R = 300\ \Omega$ series resistor placed across the breadboard center ravine (e10 to f10). Compute the series LED current $I = \frac{V_{\text{sup}} - V_f}{R} \times 1000$ in milliamperes ($\text{mA}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ overall ($80\%+$) AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on Q3 and Q4 ([SAFETY]). If you missed Q1 or Q5, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; if you missed Q2 or Q3, study ## 3. Formalization item 2–3; if you missed Q4, study ### Safety notes. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 01 Tier 1 bridge ladder (01-electronics.T1.01a $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01c $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01d $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01b) before Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02):
[Concept: breadboard_internal_bus_connectivity] Compute the heat $P = I^2 R_{\text{clip}}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) in a breadboard clip of $R_{\text{clip}} = 0.08\ \Omega$ carrying $3.0\text{ A}$.
[Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] A bench supply is set to $V_{\text{set}} = 15.0\text{ V}$ with $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.30\text{ A}$ and is wired across $R_{\text{load}} = 20.0\ \Omega$. Compute the clamped output voltage $V_{\text{out}} = \min(V_{\text{set}}, I_{\text{limit}} R_{\text{load}})$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] With the red lead still in the 10A jack ($R_{\text{shunt}} = 0.010\ \Omega$) and $0.008\ \Omega$ of probe lead, you probe across an $18.0\text{ V}$ battery. Compute the surge current in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: esd_and_short_circuit_prevention] Why does a grounded wrist strap protect a MOSFET gate oxide that a voltmeter never seems to damage?
A. The gate oxide is hundreds of volts thick, so only the DMM can break it.
B. A charged human body is a capacitor of roughly $100\text{ pF}$ at several kilovolts; the strap bleeds that charge to ground through a resistor before it can discharge through the gate's nanometre-thin oxide, which a $10\text{ M}\Omega$ voltmeter never stresses.
C. The strap increases the gate threshold voltage.
D. Static charge only damages bipolar transistors.
[Concept: breadboard_internal_bus_connectivity] Which statement about a solderless breadboard's internal wiring is true?
A. Every hole in a column a1–j1 is connected.
B. The two +/- side strips run the full board height as separate buses, while each row of five holes is one node and the centre ravine separates a–e from f–j.
C. All holes on the board are one node until a wire is inserted.
D. The centre ravine is a low-resistance link between the two halves.
[Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] Compute the current in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) through a $75\ \Omega$ resistor with $15.0\text{ V}$ across it.
[Concept: kvl_kcl_and_voltage_divider] Compute the unloaded midpoint voltage in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) of a $20\text{ k}\Omega$ (top) / $10\text{ k}\Omega$ (bottom) divider on a $15.0\text{ V}$ rail.
[Concept: electrical_power_i2r_dissipation] Compute the power in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) dissipated by a $0.24\ \Omega$ shunt carrying $1.5\text{ A}$.
[Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] Compute $\tau = R C$ in seconds ($\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-12}$) for $R = 3.3\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C = 22\ \mu\text{F}$.
[Concept: capacitor_charge_storage_and_decoupling] Why does a motor-driver board carry a $100\text{ nF}$ ceramic and a $470\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic across $V_{\text{bus}}$?
A. The ceramic shunts the nanosecond switching edge and the electrolytic supplies the millisecond current surge, because no single capacitor has both low inductance and large charge storage.
B. The two capacitances add to $570\text{ nF}$, which is the only value the driver accepts.
C. The electrolytic blocks DC while the ceramic passes it.
D. They are decorative; the regulator alone is sufficient.
[Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] A $3.0\text{ mH}$ winding carrying $4.0\text{ A}$ is switched off in $1.5\ \mu\text{s}$ with no freewheeling path. Compute the spike $|V_L| = L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Concept: mosfet_low_side_rds_on_switch] [Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] A low-side FET with $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 45\text{ m}\Omega$ switches $2.0\text{ A}$ at $D = 0.80$. Compute its average conduction loss $P = D I^2 R_{DS(\text{on})}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] An H-bridge runs $D_A = 0.90$ and $D_B = 0.30$ from $V_{\text{bus}} = 10.0\text{ V}$. Compute the average signed motor voltage in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).

pages.title: Capacitors, Inductors, RC Time Constants & Inductive Flyback

sections.t: Resistors respond instantaneously to voltage changes, but every real motor drive is dominated by two energy-storage components: capacitors (which store electric-field energy to stabilize power rails and filter noisy sensors) and inductors (the copper coils inside every motor, which store magnetic-field energy and unleash destructive high-voltage flyback spikes if switched off without a return path). Understanding $I_C = C\frac{dV}{dt}$ and $V_L = L\frac{dI}{dt}$ prepares you directly for PWM switching in 01-electronics.T1.01b and Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02). Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

Think of a capacitor as a rubber diaphragm stretched across a water pipe—or a tiny rechargeable pressure tank mounted right next to a thirsty valve. Voltage across a capacitor cannot jump instantaneously ($I_C = C\frac{dV}{dt}$): when a microcontroller or H-bridge suddenly gulps a spike of current, a decoupling capacitor right next to its pins supplies that instant gulp before the long supply wires can droop. Conversely, think of an inductor (a motor coil) as a heavy paddlewheel spinning inside the pipe. Because of magnetic inertia, current through an inductor cannot stop instantaneously ($V_L = L\frac{dI}{dt}$). If you slam a valve shut on a spinning paddlewheel, the water hammers against the closed valve with a massive pressure spike (inductive flyback) that bursts the pipe—unless you provide a freewheeling diode loop so the current can coast down smoothly through its own coil resistance.

Capacitor Law ($I_C = C\frac{dV}{dt}$) and Stored Energy: A capacitor of capacitance $C$ in farads ($\text{F}$) stores charge $Q = C V$ ($\text{C}$) and electric energy $E_C = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$ ($\text{J}$). To hold rail voltage droop $\Delta V$ ($\text{V}$) below a limit during a current pulse $\Delta I$ ($\text{A}$) lasting $\Delta t$ ($\text{s}$):
Substituting $\Delta I = 2.0\text{ A}$, $\Delta t = 5.0\ \mu\text{s}$, and max droop $\Delta V = 0.10\text{ V}$ requires $C \ge 100\ \mu\text{F}$.
RC Charging Time Constant ($\tau = R C$) and Cutoff Frequency ($f_c$, the $-3\text{ dB}$ Half-Power Point): Charging a capacitor $C$ through resistor $R$ ($\Omega$) from $0\text{ V}$ toward $V_{\text{in}}$ follows:
At $t = 1\tau$, $V_C(\tau) = 0.6321\,V_{\text{in}}$; at $t = 5\tau$, $V_C(5\tau) = 0.9933\,V_{\text{in}}$. For a sine-wave input at the cutoff frequency $f = f_c$, output amplitude drops to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7071$ ($70.71\%$ of input voltage, or $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = 50\%$ power, called the $-3\text{ dB}$ point on the logarithmic decibel scale $20\log_{10}(0.7071) \approx -3.01\text{ dB}$ taught inline in 07-systems.T1.07a) with $-45^\circ$ phase lag. Substituting $R = 1.0\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}$ gives $\tau = 1.0\text{ ms}$ and $f_c = 159.15\text{ Hz}$.
Inductor Law ($V_L = L\frac{dI}{dt}$), Stored Magnetic Energy & Flyback Clamp: A motor winding of inductance $L$ in henries ($\text{H}$) carrying current $I$ ($\text{A}$) stores magnetic energy $E_L = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$ ($\text{J}$) and induces voltage:
Interrupting $I = 2.0\text{ A}$ in $L = 5.0\text{ mH}$ over $\Delta t = 1.0\ \mu\text{s}$ without a diode produces $|V_L| = 0.005 \times (2.0 / 10^{-6}) = 10{,}000\text{ V}$, punching through any silicon transistor! Placing a freewheeling diode across the coil clamps the switch node to $V_{\text{bus}} + V_f$ ($\approx V_{\text{bus}} + 0.7\text{ V}$).

Predict first (before you run it): Commit to two numbers before you run the block. (1) The capacitor starts at $0\text{ V}$ and charges toward $3.3\text{ V}$ through $\tau = RC = 1.0\text{ ms}$: at $t = 1\tau$, do you expect $V_C$ to have crossed half of $3.3\text{ V}$, and roughly where between $1.6\text{ V}$ and $2.2\text{ V}$ does it actually land? (2) Opening a $L = 3.0\text{ mH}$ coil carrying $I = 2.0\text{ A}$ in $\Delta t = 0.5\ \mu\text{s}$ is a $4\ \text{A}/\mu\text{s}$ current slope: predict whether $|V_L| = L\frac{di}{dt}$ comes out near the $12.0\text{ V}$ bus, near $120\text{ V}$, or three orders of magnitude above the bus. Wrong-result signatures: a $V_C(1\tau)$ below $1.6\text{ V}$ means you evaluated $t = \tau/2$ or mis-signed the exponent, and an unclamped spike within a few volts of the bus means the micro prefix on $\Delta t$ was dropped ($0.5\text{ ms}$ instead of $0.5\ \mu\text{s}$).
Compute the RC charging curve at $t = 1\tau$ and $t = 5\tau$ for $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega, C = 0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($\tau = 1.0\text{ ms}$), and compare the unclamped inductive flyback spike of a $L = 3.0\text{ mH}$ coil carrying $I = 2.0\text{ A}$ opened in $\Delta t = 0.5\ \mu\text{s}$ against a diode-clamped switch node on a $12.0\text{ V}$ bus.
Expected output:

Calculate the minimum bulk decoupling capacitance $C_{\min}$ in microfarads ($\mu\text{F}$) needed to keep a $12.0\text{ V}$ motor bus from drooping by more than $\Delta V = 0.25\text{ V}$ during a $\Delta I = 3.0\text{ A}$ current transient lasting $\Delta t = 20\ \mu\text{s}$ ($20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$). Verify $C_{\min} = \frac{\Delta I \cdot \Delta t}{\Delta V} = 240.0\ \mu\text{F}$.
If your result differs: Check your unit conversion from farads to microfarads: $\frac{3.0 \times 20\times 10^{-6}}{0.25} = 0.00024\text{ F} = 240.0\ \mu\text{F}$.

sections.h: Graded package - the time constant, the droop and the spike
sections.t:
exercises/01-electronics.T1.01d/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: rc_time_constant, rc_voltage, rc_cutoff_hz (the $2\pi$), bulk_capacitance_f (the transient time), capacitor_energy (the half), inductor_energy and flyback_voltage ($L\Delta I/\Delta t$, in volts not millivolts). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
29 tests. The charging curve is checked at one time constant ($63.2\%$), five ($99.3\%$) and at the Break-it droop ($100\ \mu\text{F}$ sags $0.60\text{ V}$, $470\ \mu\text{F}$ $0.128\text{ V}$), so a linear ramp fails; the cutoff is checked against $1/(2\pi RC)$, so a missing $2\pi$ fails by $6.28\times$; the bulk value is checked at the exercise's $240\ \mu\text{F}$; the energies carry the $\tfrac12$; and the unclamped $12\text{ kV}$ spike is checked against a $12.7\text{ V}$ clamped node. The transfer suite puts the plant's own constants through the same laws: a $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor with $159.155\ \Omega$ has its corner exactly on the plant's $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, the shoulder's $I_1/B_1 = 0.2\text{ s}$ mechanical lag obeys the same $63.2\% / 99.3\%$ law, and the elbow's $I_2/B_2$ is quicker. Five planted faults - cutoff_forgets_2pi, charging_linear_ramp, bulk_missing_time, capacitor_energy_forgets_half, flyback_milli_dropped - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Prefixes $\mu\text{F}, \text{mH}, \text{ns}$) and 00-foundations.T1.00e (Stored Energy).
Prerequisite Bridge Modules: 01-electronics.T1.01a and 01-electronics.T1.01c.
Core Concepts to Review First: Capacitor current $I = C\frac{dV}{dt}$, RC time constant $\tau = RC$ and $-3\text{ dB}$ cutoff $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}$, and inductor voltage spike $V_L = L\frac{dI}{dt}$ with flyback clamping in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Falstad Interactive Circuit Simulator (falstad.com/circuit), All About Circuits RC & L/R Time Constants, and Track 01 §1.1–1.3 (01-electronics-and-power/README.md).
The exercise is one droop budget: how much charge the transient moves, divided by how much sag you are willing to accept. Fill the seven TODOs, then compare against the full solution below.

A capacitor is charge per volt. The transient moves $Q = \Delta I\,\Delta t = 3.0 \times 20\ \mu\text{s} = 60\ \mu\text{C}$; spreading that over a $0.25\text{ V}$ budget needs $60\ \mu\text{C} / 0.25\text{ V} = 240\ \mu\text{F}$. Dropping $\Delta t$ leaves $12\text{ F}$, which no parts bin has.
Convert once, at the end. $240\ \mu\text{F} = 240 \times 10^{-6} = 0.00024\text{ F}$; do the arithmetic in farads and multiply by $10^6$ only for the printed answer.
Droop falls as $1/C$. With the same transient, $100\ \mu\text{F}$ sags $0.60\text{ V}$ ($2.4\times$ the budget) and $470\ \mu\text{F}$ sags $0.128\text{ V}$ — so the fix is a bigger reservoir, not a slower transient.
The two energies both carry the $\tfrac12$, and the spike is a unit trap. $E_C = \tfrac12 C V^2$, $E_L = \tfrac12 L I^2$, and $V_L = L\Delta I/\Delta t$ with $\Delta t = 0.5\ \mu\text{s} = 0.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$; entering $0.5$ makes the $12\text{ kV}$ spike read $12\text{ V}$.
What the suite refuses. rc_voltage raises on a negative time, bulk_capacitance_f on a zero droop, capacitor_energy on a negative capacitance, inductor_energy on a negative inductance, flyback_voltage on a zero opening time, and rc_time_constant or rc_cutoff_hz on a non-positive part - every one a ValueError, since a negative charge store is not a smaller capacitor.

Printed: C_min=240.0 uF; 100 uF droops 0.600 V, 470 uF droops 0.128 V; tau=1.000 ms, fc=159.15 Hz
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite reads the arm's mechanical lag as the same first-order charging law:

Swap the bulk reservoir for the wrong part and diagnose the droop from the measurement alone:
Inject: build the same $12.0\text{ V}$ bus but fit the $100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic you had in the parts bin instead of the $240\ \mu\text{F}$ the droop budget demanded, leaving $\Delta I = 3.0\text{ A}$ and $\Delta t = 20\ \mu\text{s}$ unchanged.
Symptom: the loaded bus sags by $\Delta V = \frac{\Delta I \cdot \Delta t}{C} = \frac{3.0 \times 20\ \mu\text{s}}{100\ \mu\text{F}} = 0.60\text{ V}$ — that is $2.4\times$ the $0.25\text{ V}$ budget, roughly $5\%$ of a $12.0\text{ V}$ rail, and it shows up as flickering logic on the same bus, not as a hot part.
Diagnose: droop scales as $\Delta V \propto 1/C$ while the transient itself ($\Delta I$, $\Delta t$, and the $6.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ C}$ of charge it moves) has not changed, so a droop $2.4\times$ over budget means the capacitance is $100/240 \approx 0.42\times$ what the calculation required. Confirm it by measuring the sag with a scope or a fast multimeter at the driver's $V_{\text{bus}}$ pin rather than at the supply terminals — a droop that vanishes at the supply and persists at the pin is a missing local reservoir, while a droop at both is a supply-side limit.
Fix: fit at least the $240\ \mu\text{F}$ of low-ESR bulk capacitance ($470\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic is the comfortable standard substitution) in parallel with the $100\text{ nF}$ ceramic at the pins, and prove it: $\Delta V = \frac{3.0 \times 20\ \mu\text{s}}{470\ \mu\text{F}} = 0.128\text{ V}$, half the $0.25\text{ V}$ budget even before the electrolytic's worst-case tolerance and aging derating are applied.

Simulate an RC step response and an inductive coil turn-off with and without a flyback diode in Falstad Circuit Simulator (Circuits -> Inductors -> Inductive Kickback).
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.01-electronics.T1.01d, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). When wiring Electrolytic bulk capacitors ($100\text{–}470\ \mu\text{F}$) in Step 1.2 (01-electronics.T1.02), always align the negative stripe (-) with $\text{GND}$ and choose a voltage rating $\ge 2\times V_{\text{bus}}$ (e.g., $\ge 25\text{ V}$ capacitor for a $12\text{ V}$ bus):
Pass/fail verification in simulation: tau == 1.0 ms, fc == 159.15 Hz, v_flyback_unclamped == 12000 V, and v_flyback_clamped == 12.7 V.

⚠️ Bench Safety Note (safety_level: low): Always verify probe placement (V/Ohm voltage port, never the 10A shunt port in parallel) and set your CC/CV bench power supply current limit ($\le 0.5\text{ A}$) before energizing any breadboard or sensor circuit.
Pass criteria: run the worked example and exercise asserts with zero errors, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test below.

[Recall] [Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] Compute the time constant $\tau = R C$ in seconds ($\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $R = 4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ ($4700\ \Omega$) and $C = 10\ \mu\text{F}$ ($10 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$).
[Apply] [Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] What percentage of the step input voltage $V_{\text{in}}$ does an initially uncharged capacitor reach after exactly $t = 1\tau$ ($100 \times (1 - e^{-1})$, tolerance $\pm 0.01\%$)?
[Transfer] [Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] Compute the stored magnetic energy $E_L = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$ in joules ($\text{J}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) in a $L = 4.0\text{ mH}$ ($0.004\text{ H}$) motor phase winding carrying $I = 5.0\text{ A}$.
[Concept: capacitor_charge_storage_and_decoupling] Why do motor driver PCBs and breadboards place both a $100\text{ nF}$ ($0.1\ \mu\text{F}$) ceramic capacitor and a $100\text{–}470\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic bulk capacitor across $V_{\text{bus}}$ and $\text{GND}$ right at the driver IC?
A. Ceramic capacitors look nicer next to tall cylinders.
B. The small low-inductance $100\text{ nF}$ ceramic cap shunts nanosecond high-frequency switching edges, while the large $100\text{–}470\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic reservoir supplies millisecond motor current surges without bus droop.
C. Putting two capacitors in parallel divides the voltage in half.
D. The ceramic capacitor converts DC into AC.
[Spaced review -> 01-electronics.T1.01a — Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] A $12.0\,\text{V}$ rail drives $470\ \Omega$. Compute the current in milliamperes (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ ($80\%+$). If you missed Q1 or Q2, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q3, study ## 3. Formalization item 3; Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 1. If you missed Q5, review 01-electronics.T1.01a. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

[Concept: capacitor_charge_storage_and_decoupling] Compute the stored energy $E = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$ in joules ($\text{J}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) in a $470\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $12.0\text{ V}$.
[Concept: rc_time_constant_and_filtering] Compute $\tau = R C$ in seconds ($\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-12}$) for $R = 4.7\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C = 0.10\ \mu\text{F}$.
[Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] A $2.0\text{ mH}$ coil carrying $6.0\text{ A}$ is interrupted in $4.0\ \mu\text{s}$ without a freewheeling diode. Compute the peak spike $|V_L| = L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: inductor_flyback_and_freewheeling_diode] Where does a freewheeling diode go across an inductive load switched by a low-side N-MOSFET, and why there?
A. From Drain to $V_{\text{bus}}$, so the coil current keeps circulating through the diode instead of forcing the Drain node hundreds of volts above the bus.
B. From Gate to Source, so the gate capacitance discharges faster.
C. In series with the coil, so current can only flow one way.
D. From Drain to $\text{GND}$, which shorts the supply while the FET is on.
[Concept: voltage_current_resistance_ohms_law] Compute the current in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) through a $45\ \Omega$ resistor with $9.0\text{ V}$ across it.
[Concept: kvl_kcl_and_voltage_divider] Compute the unloaded midpoint voltage in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) of a $15\text{ k}\Omega$ (top) / $5.0\text{ k}\Omega$ (bottom) divider on an $18.0\text{ V}$ rail.
[Concept: electrical_power_i2r_dissipation] Compute the power in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) dissipated by a $0.06\ \Omega$ trace carrying $3.5\text{ A}$.
[Concept: breadboard_internal_bus_connectivity] You place a $100\text{ nF}$ decoupling capacitor with one leg in a10 and the other in b10. What have you built?
A. A working decoupling capacitor.
B. A short: both holes are one node, so the capacitor is bypassed and the rail is tied to whatever a10–b10 connects.
C. A $200\text{ nF}$ capacitor.
D. An open circuit, because the row is split.
[Concept: multimeter_and_current_limited_psu_safety] A supply is set to $24.0\text{ V}$ with $I_{\text{limit}} = 0.25\text{ A}$ and wired across $8.0\ \Omega$. Compute the clamped output voltage in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: esd_and_short_circuit_prevention] Why is a $10\text{ M}\Omega$ resistor built into a wrist strap's ground lead?
A. To limit the current through your body if you touch a live conductor, while still bleeding static charge away.
B. To measure your pulse through the strap.
C. To keep the strap from working at all.
D. To increase the static charge on your hands.
[Concept: mosfet_low_side_rds_on_switch] Compute the conduction loss $P = I_D^2 R_{DS(\text{on})}$ in watts ($\text{W}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $I_D = 4.0\text{ A}$ and $R_{DS(\text{on})} = 15\text{ m}\Omega$.
[Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] Compute the average voltage $V_{\text{eff}} = D V_{\text{bus}}$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $V_{\text{bus}} = 24.0\text{ V}$ at $D = 0.60$.
[Concept: h_bridge_four_switch_polarity_and_shoot_through] An H-bridge runs $D_A = 0.50$ and $D_B = 0.90$ from $V_{\text{bus}} = 12.0\text{ V}$. Compute the average signed motor voltage in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $11/13$ overall ($80\%+$) AND $1/1$ ($100\%$) on Q4 ([SAFETY]). Remediation: Q1–Q4 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization and 01-electronics.T1.01d; Q5–Q7 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01a; Q8–Q10 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01c; Q11–Q13 $\to$ 01-electronics.T1.01b.

pages.title: 2D Coordinate Frames and 1-Link Planar Arm Forward Kinematics

sections.t:
Define a 2D coordinate frame (Origin (0, 0), $+x$ right, $+y$ up, $+\theta$ counter-clockwise CCW) at a robot shoulder joint, and compute 1-link planar forward kinematics ($x = L_1 \cos\theta_1$, $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1$) and its circular workspace boundary in Python.
New ideas (max 2):
World vs. joint coordinate frames and right-hand counter-clockwise (CCW) angle sign convention: Anchoring a fixed reference grid (0, 0) at the robot base with $+x$ horizontal right, $+y$ vertical up, and $+\theta_1$ rotating counter-clockwise from $+x$.
1-link planar forward kinematics ($x = L_1 \cos\theta_1$, $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1$) and circular workspace boundary: Mapping known joint angle $\theta_1$ (rad) and link length $L_1$ (m) to tip Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ on a circle of radius $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = L_1$.
New syntax: None (math.cos, math.sin, math.radians, math.hypot from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

Lesson P.6: Importing Standard Modules (math) & Automated Verification (assert)
Lesson P.10: Radians, Right-Triangle Trig (sin, cos) & atan2(y, x)

sections.h: Idea 1: World vs. joint coordinate frames and right-hand counter-clockwise (CCW) angle sign convention
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — Cartesian Coordinates [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Cartesian Coordinates, X and Y Axis, Writing Coordinates, and Four Quadrants.
What to skip: Skip 3D (x, y, z) coordinates (covered in Pass 2).
Key takeaway: Before writing a single line of robot arm math, you must fix a coordinate frame (reference axes):
Origin (0, 0): Placed directly at the center of the stationary shoulder motor shaft.
$+x$ axis: Points horizontally to the right ($0^\circ = 0\text{ rad}$).
$+y$ axis: Points vertically straight up ($+90^\circ = +\pi/2\text{ rad}$).
Positive angle $+\theta_1$: Rotates counter-clockwise (+CCW) from $+x$ toward $+y$.

sections.h: Idea 2: 1-link planar forward kinematics ($x = L_1 \cos\theta_1$, $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1$) and circular workspace boundary
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — Sine, Cosine and Tangent [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact headings Right Triangle and Sine, Cosine and Tangent (connecting hypotenuse $L_1$ and angle $\theta_1$ to horizontal $x$ and vertical $y$).
What to skip: Skip secant/cosecant/cotangent identities.
Key takeaway: Forward Kinematics (FK) answers the question: "Given the motor's joint angle $\theta_1$, where is the tip of the arm $(x, y)$ in the world coordinate frame?" For a single rigid link of length $L_1$ rotating around the origin (0, 0), right-triangle trigonometry (Lesson P.10) gives $x = L_1 \cdot \cos(\theta_1)$ and $y = L_1 \cdot \sin(\theta_1)$. Because $\cos^2(\theta_1) + \sin^2(\theta_1) = 1$, the tip's distance from the shoulder is always $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = L_1$. The set of all points the tip can reach is called the robot's workspace—for a 1-link arm, a circle of radius $L_1$!
Alternative resource: PhET — Trig Tour [verify in-app] — Drag the unit-circle point [verify in-app] through all four quadrants to see $(x, y) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ change signs.

In robotics, Forward Kinematics (FK) always flows from joint space (the angles measured by motor encoders, like $\theta_1$) to Cartesian world space (the $(x, y)$ coordinates in meters inside the room's fixed coordinate frame). By anchoring the world origin (0, 0) at the shoulder shaft with $+x$ pointing horizontally right, $+y$ pointing vertically up, and positive angle $+\theta_1$ rotating counter-clockwise (CCW), right-triangle trigonometry gives the tip position for any link length $L_1$:
Applying the 4-step modeling discipline from Lesson 00.3, we always check the four cardinal boundary angles (0 deg, +90 deg, +180 deg, and -90 deg) for a link of length $L_1 = 0.25\text{ m}$ ($250\text{ mm}$) to confirm that the signs of $x$ and $y$ match each quadrant and that the distance from the origin is always $r = 0.250\text{ m}$:
Notice that a 1-link arm only has 1 degree of freedom (1-DOF) ($\theta_1$), so its workspace is strictly the 1D circular boundary of radius $r = L_1$; to reach inside the circle at varying radii, we will add a second link in Lesson 02.2!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete fk_1link (TODO 1) to compute $(x, y)$ from link length $L_1$ (m) and joint angle $\theta_1$ (deg), and complete verify_circular_workspace (TODO 2) using assert to confirm that $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = L_1$ at every angle.
What is real-hardware only: Mechanical hard-stop brackets and cable-wrap limits that restrict a physical shoulder joint to less than a full $360^\circ$ rotation.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, convert degrees to radians first (t1_rad = math.radians(theta1_deg)), then compute x = l1_m math.cos(t1_rad) and y = l1_m math.sin(t1_rad). In TODO 2, write assert abs(r - l1_m) < 1e-6.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Swapping $\cos$ and $\sin$ (x = L1 sin(theta1)): Check $\theta_1 = 0^\circ$! Along the horizontal $+x$ axis, $x$ must be $+L_1$ and $y$ must be $0$, which requires $x = L_1 \cos\theta_1$ and $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1$.
Measuring $\theta_1$ clockwise (CW) in one function and counter-clockwise (CCW) in another: Always stick to the right-hand standard: $+x$ right, $+y$ up, $+\theta_1$ counter-clockwise (CCW).

Quadrant II coordinates: A 1-link arm of length $L_1 = 0.20\text{ m}$ rotates counter-clockwise to $\theta_1 = +135^\circ$ (pointing up and to the left in Quadrant II). What are the signs (+ or -) of $x$ and $y$?
Answer
In Quadrant II (left of the origin, above the horizontal axis), $x$ is negative (-) ($-0.141\text{ m}$) and $y$ is positive (+) ($+0.141\text{ m}$).
Why a 1-link arm cannot reach inside its circle: Can a rigid 1-link arm of fixed length $L_1 = 0.25\text{ m}$ place its tip at $(x, y) = (0.10\text{ m}, 0.10\text{ m})$?
Answer
No! The point $(0.10, 0.10)$ is at radius $r = \sqrt{0.10^2 + 0.10^2} \approx 0.141\text{ m} \ne 0.25\text{ m}$. A 1-link arm can only reach points on its circular workspace rim $r = 0.25\text{ m}$; reaching interior radii requires a 2-link arm with an elbow joint (Lesson 02.2).

A standard 2D coordinate frame places (0, 0) at the shoulder pivot with $+x$ right, $+y$ up, and $+\theta$ counter-clockwise (CCW).
1-link forward kinematics (FK) maps joint angle $\theta_1$ to tip coordinates $(x, y) = (L_1 \cos\theta_1, L_1 \sin\theta_1)$ along a circular workspace of radius $L_1$.

pages.title: 2-Link Planar Arm Forward Kinematics (theta_1, theta_2 -> x, y)

sections.t:
Add a second link ($L_2$) and an elbow motor ($\theta_2$) to your planar robot arm, relate the relative joint angle $\theta_2$ to the forearm's absolute world angle ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$), and compute the end-effector (hand) position $(x, y)$ by chaining two tip-to-tail vectors in Python.
New ideas (max 2):
Absolute link angle ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$) from relative elbow joint angle $\theta_2$: Because the elbow motor is bolted to the end of Link 1, turning the shoulder by $\theta_1$ rotates the forearm too—so the forearm's angle relative to the world $+x$ axis is $\theta_1 + \theta_2$.
Chaining tip-to-tail vectors for 2-link forward kinematics: Adding the upper-arm vector $(L_1 \cos\theta_1, L_1 \sin\theta_1)$ and the forearm vector $(L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2), L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2))$ to locate both the elbow and the end-effector tip $(x, y)$.
New syntax: None (math.cos, math.sin, math.radians from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.10: Radians, Right-Triangle Trig (sin, cos) & atan2(y, x)
Lesson 02.1: 2D Coordinate Frames & 1-Link Planar Arm Forward Kinematics

sections.h: Idea 1: Absolute link angle ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$) from relative elbow joint angle $\theta_2$
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — Angles [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Names of Angles and Positive and Negative Angles (+CCW vs. -CW).
What to skip: Skip reflex angle naming quizzes.
Key takeaway: On a real 2-link robot arm, the elbow encoder measures the relative joint angle $\theta_2$—how much the forearm bends relative to the straight line of Link 1 ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ means the elbow is completely straight!). Because Link 1 is already tilted at angle $\theta_1$ relative to the world $+x$ axis, the forearm's absolute angle relative to the world $+x$ axis is the sum of both angles: $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$.

sections.h: Idea 2: Chaining tip-to-tail vectors for 2-link forward kinematics
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — Vectors ("Adding Vectors") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Vectors, Notation, and Adding Vectors (adding the $x$-components together and adding the $y$-components together).
What to skip: Skip vector multiplication (dot and cross products).
Key takeaway: A 2-link arm is simply two 1-link vectors chained tip-to-tail:
Shoulder to Elbow (Link 1, length $L_1$, world angle $\theta_1$): $x_{\text{elbow}} = L_1 \cos(\theta_1)$ and $y_{\text{elbow}} = L_1 \sin(\theta_1)$.
Elbow to End-Effector (Link 2, length $L_2$, world angle $\theta_1 + \theta_2$): $\Delta x_2 = L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $\Delta y_2 = L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.
Total End-Effector (hand/gripper tip) position $(x, y)$: $x = L_1 \cos(\theta_1) + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $y = L_1 \sin(\theta_1) + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.

In 2-link forward kinematics, we find the end-effector position $(x, y)$ by chaining tip-to-tail vectors: first the upper-arm vector $(L_1 \cos\theta_1, L_1 \sin\theta_1)$ from the shoulder (0, 0) to the elbow $(x_1, y_1)$, and then the forearm vector $(L_2 \cos\theta_{12}, L_2 \sin\theta_{12})$ from the elbow to the hand.
Why is the angle inside the second cosine and sine the absolute link angle $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$ instead of just the relative joint angle $\theta_2$?
Test it with an extreme-case sanity check (Lesson 00.3)! Suppose $L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.15\text{ m}$. Keep the elbow locked completely straight ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$) and raise the shoulder straight up to $\theta_1 = +90^\circ$:
With the correct formula $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ + 0^\circ = 90^\circ$, both links point straight up along $+y$, giving $(x, y) = (0.00\text{ m}, +0.30\text{ m})$.
If you forgot to add $\theta_1$ and wrote $L_2 \cos(\theta_2) = L_2 \cos(0^\circ)$, your code would claim the forearm always points horizontally right regardless of how the shoulder moves!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete fk_2link (TODO 1 and TODO 2) to compute both the elbow position $(x_1, y_1)$ and the end-effector tip position $(x, y)$ for a 2-link planar arm ($L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$, $L_2 = 0.15\text{ m}$) across 4 test postures.
What is real-hardware only: Physical link self-collision when the forearm folds past $\pm 150^\circ$ and hits the upper arm bracket.

Full Solution

Writing l2_m math.cos(t2) instead of l2_m math.cos(t1 + t2): The elbow angle $\theta_2$ is measured relative to Link 1, so its angle relative to the horizontal $+x$ world axis is always $\theta_1 + \theta_2$.
Converting $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ to radians after adding a radian and a degree: Never mix radians and degrees in t1 + t2; convert both to radians first!

Tracing Reach Diagonal ($\theta_1 = 30^\circ, \theta_2 = 60^\circ$): Why does the end-effector tip in the 4th test case (q1 = 30 deg, q2 = 60 deg) have the exact same $x$-coordinate (+0.130 m) as the elbow?
Answer
Because the forearm's absolute world angle is $\theta_{12} = 30^\circ + 60^\circ = \mathbf{90^\circ}$ (pointing straight up along $+y$!), so Link 2 adds $\Delta x_2 = L_2 \cos(90^\circ) = 0.000\text{ m}$ horizontally and $+0.150\text{ m}$ vertically!
Minimum and maximum reach of a 2-link arm: If $L_1 = 0.20\text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.12\text{ m}$, what is the farthest distance $r_{\max}$ from (0, 0) the end-effector can reach ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$), and what is the closest distance $r_{\min}$ when folded completely back ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ$)?
Answer
Maximum reach: $r_{\max} = L_1 + L_2 = 0.20 + 0.12 = \mathbf{0.32\text{ m}}$.
Minimum reach: $r_{\min} = \lvert L_1 - L_2 \rvert = 0.20 - 0.12 = \mathbf{0.08\text{ m}}$.

The elbow motor measures a relative joint angle $\theta_2$, so the forearm's absolute world angle is $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$.
2-link forward kinematics chains both link vectors tip-to-tail to locate the end-effector: $x = L_1 \cos\theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.

pages.title: 2-Link Planar Arm Inverse Kinematics (x, y -> theta_1, theta_2) and Reachability

sections.t:
Solve 2-link planar Inverse Kinematics (IK) in Python to convert a desired end-effector target $(x, y)$ into the required shoulder and elbow motor angles $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ using the Law of Cosines and math.atan2(y, x), while clamping -1.0..+1.0 at kinematic singularities ($r = L_1 + L_2$) and verifying the solution with a round-trip Forward Kinematics (FK) check.
New ideas (max 2):
Law of Cosines for elbow angle and reachability clamping: Solving the triangle formed by $L_1$, $L_2$, and target distance $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ via $\cos\theta_2 = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2 L_1 L_2}$, and clamping $\cos\theta_2 \in [-1.0, +1.0]$ so math.acos never crashes on floating-point rounding at the workspace edge.
Elbow-down vs. elbow-up geometric solutions and shoulder angle via math.atan2(y, x): Why $\theta_2 = +\arccos(\cos\theta_2)$ (elbow-down) and $\theta_2 = -\arccos(\cos\theta_2)$ (elbow-up) both reach the same $(x, y)$, and finding $\theta_1 = \text{atan2}(y, x) - \text{atan2}(L_2 \sin\theta_2, L_1 + L_2 \cos\theta_2)$.
New syntax: math.acos(val) (inverse cosine returning 0..pi radians).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.5 hours | Slow-learner: 3.0–4.0 hours

Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Command Clamping
Lesson P.10: Radians, Right-Triangle Trig (sin, cos) & atan2(y, x)
Lesson 02.2: 2-Link Planar Arm Forward Kinematics (theta_1, theta_2 -> x, y)

sections.h: Idea 1: Law of Cosines for elbow angle and reachability clamping
sections.t:
Primary resource: Math is Fun — The Law of Cosines [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings The Law of Cosines, When to Use, and Easier Version For Angles (solving for an angle when all three triangle side lengths are known).
What to skip: Skip memorization mnemonics at the bottom.
Key takeaway: When you command a robot hand to move to target $(x, y)$ at distance $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ from the shoulder (0, 0), the upper arm $L_1$, forearm $L_2$, and line $r$ form a triangle whose three side lengths are known! Applying the Law of Cosines gives the exterior elbow bend angle $\theta_2$: $\cos(\theta_2) = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2 \cdot L_1 \cdot L_2}$.
Reachability check: A target $(x, y)$ is inside the reachable workspace if and only if $\lvert L_1 - L_2 \rvert \le r \le L_1 + L_2$ (which corresponds to $-1.0 \le \cos\theta_2 \le +1.0$).
Why clamping cos_t2 into [-1.0, +1.0] is mandatory: Right on the outer kinematic singularity boundary where the arm is stretched completely straight ($r = L_1 + L_2$, $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$), tiny floating-point rounding (Lesson P.6) can make $\cos\theta_2 = 1.0000000000000002$, causing math.acos(cos_t2) to crash with ValueError: math domain error! Always clamp cos_t2 = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cos_t2)) before calling math.acos.

sections.h: Idea 2: Elbow-down vs. elbow-up geometric solutions and shoulder angle via math.atan2(y, x)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Inverse kinematics ("Analytical solutions to inverse kinematics") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Inverse kinematics, Robotics, and Analytical solutions to inverse kinematics.
What to skip: Skip Jacobian pseudoinverse matrices and 6-DOF spherical wrist sections (covered in Pass 2).
Key takeaway: Once $\theta_2 = +\arccos(\cos\theta_2)$ (elbow-down, $\theta_2 \ge 0$) or $\theta_2 = -\arccos(\cos\theta_2)$ (elbow-up, $\theta_2 \le 0$) is chosen, the shoulder angle $\theta_1$ is the target's overall ray angle $\text{atan2}(y, x)$ minus the internal triangle offset angle $\text{atan2}(L_2 \sin\theta_2, L_1 + L_2 \cos\theta_2)$, so $\theta_1 = \text{atan2}(y, x) - \text{atan2}(L_2 \sin\theta_2, L_1 + L_2 \cos\theta_2)$.
Alternative resource: Python 3 Docs — math ("Trigonometric functions") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review math.acos(x) and math.atan2(y, x) under math — Mathematical functions.

Let's trace the complete 3-step Inverse Kinematics (IK) algorithm that converts a desired Cartesian target $(x, y)$ into joint angles $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ for link lengths $L_1, L_2$:
Compute $\cos(\theta_2)$ via the Law of Cosines and apply reachability clamping to [-1.0, +1.0]:
Any reachable target $(x, y)$ satisfies $\lvert L_1 - L_2 \rvert \le \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \le L_1 + L_2$. Even when $(x, y)$ sits right on the outer kinematic singularity boundary ($r = L_1 + L_2$), floating-point roundoff can produce $\cos(\theta_2) = 1.0000000000000002$, so we always clamp $\cos(\theta_2) = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2 \cdot L_1 \cdot L_2}$ into [-1.0, +1.0] before calling math.acos.
Choose between the elbow-down ($+\arccos$) and elbow-up ($-\arccos$) geometric solutions for $\theta_2$:
Compute shoulder angle $\theta_1$ using two-argument math.atan2(y, x):
How do you prove your ik_2link(x, y) function is $100\%$ bug-free? Feed the resulting $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ right back into your fk_2link function from Lesson 02.2 and assert that the reconstructed $(x_{\text{fk}}, y_{\text{fk}})$ matches the target $(x, y)$ to within $10^{-6}\text{ m}$!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete ik_2link_elbow_down (TODO 1 and TODO 2) using the Law of Cosines, [-1.0, +1.0] clamping, math.acos, and math.atan2, then run the automated round-trip fk_2link verification across 3 target points (including the straight-out kinematic singularity at $(0.30, 0.00)\text{ m}$).
What is real-hardware only: Joint wire-harness routing that favors keeping a physical robot arm in the elbow-down posture throughout a task rather than flipping to elbow-up.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, clamp raw_cos_t2 using cos_t2 = max(-1.0, min(1.0, raw_cos_t2)) before calling t2_rad = math.acos(cos_t2). In TODO 2, subtract math.atan2(l2_m math.sin(t2_rad), l1_m + l2_m math.cos(t2_rad)) from math.atan2(y_m, x_m).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

ValueError: math domain error inside math.acos(cos_t2) when the arm stretches straight out ($r = L_1 + L_2$): Even for a valid boundary point, floating-point arithmetic can produce 1.0000000000000002. Always clamp cos_t2 into [-1.0, +1.0] before calling math.acos.
Switching randomly between elbow-down ($+\arccos$) and elbow-up ($-\arccos$) from one millisecond to the next: Pick one branch (such as elbow-down) and stick with it across the trajectory so the arm does not violently whip across the straight-arm singularity.

Elbow-down vs. Elbow-up for (0.15 m, 0.15 m): For $L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.15\text{ m}$, the elbow-down solution for target $(0.15\text{ m}, 0.15\text{ m})$ is $(\theta_1 = 0^\circ, \theta_2 = +90^\circ)$. What is the elbow-up solution ($\theta_2 = -90^\circ$)?
Answer
With $\theta_2 = -90^\circ$, $\theta_1 = \text{atan2}(0.15, 0.15) - \text{atan2}(-0.15, 0.15) = +45^\circ - (-45^\circ) = \mathbf{+90^\circ}$. That puts the elbow straight up at $(0, +0.15)$ and bends the forearm $90^\circ$ clockwise (-90 deg) to land at the exact same tip $(+0.15, +0.15)$!
What is a kinematic singularity? At $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ (arm stretched completely straight along $+x$ at $(0.30\text{ m}, 0.00\text{ m})$), why can't the tip move any farther in the $+x$ direction?
Answer
At $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$, both links are lined up along the $+x$ axis (kinematic singularity at the workspace boundary), so rotating either joint at that instant only sweeps the tip vertically ($\pm y$) and cannot extend $+x$ any farther.

2-link Inverse Kinematics (IK) uses the Law of Cosines ($\cos\theta_2 = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2 L_1 L_2}$, clamped to [-1, +1]) to find the elbow angle $\theta_2$ and math.atan2 to find the shoulder angle $\theta_1$.
Every interior workspace point has two solutions (elbow-down $+\arccos$ and elbow-up $-\arccos$) that merge at the straight-arm kinematic singularity ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$).

pages.title: Rotational Dynamics (tau_net = I_rot * alpha), Gear Ratios (N) and Reflected Inertia

sections.t:
Calculate the moment of inertia ($I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$) and angular acceleration ($\alpha = \tau_{\text{net}} / I_{\text{rot}}$) of a rotating link, and size a gear ratio ($N$) in Python by trading speed division ($\omega_{\text{out}} = \omega_{\text{in}} / N$) for torque multiplication ($\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta N \tau_{\text{in}}$) and $1/N^2$ reflected inertia.
New ideas (max 2):
Rotational Newton's Second Law ($\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$) and moment of inertia ($I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$): Why rotational inertia depends on mass $m$ times the square of distance $r$ from the pivot (kg·m^2), relating net torque $\tau_{\text{net}}$ (N·m) to angular acceleration $\alpha$ (rad/s^2).
Gear reduction ratio ($N$): torque multiplication, speed division, and $N^2$ reflected inertia: How meshing a small input gear ($N_{\text{in}}$ teeth) with a larger output gear ($N_{\text{out}}$ teeth, ratio $N = N_{\text{out}} / N_{\text{in}}$) multiplies torque by $\eta N$, divides speed by $N$, and shrinks the load's apparent inertia seen by the motor to $I_{\text{load}} / N^2$ (while introducing mechanical backlash).
New syntax: None (Python arithmetic and functions from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.10: Radians, Right-Triangle Trig (sin, cos) & atan2(y, x)
Lesson P.12: Forces, Newton's Second Law & Lever Torque
Lesson 00.1: Cross-Domain Power (P = Effort Flow) & First-Order Lag
Lesson 02.3: 2-Link Planar Arm Inverse Kinematics (x, y -> theta_1, theta_2) & Reachability

sections.h: Idea 1: Rotational Newton's Second Law ($\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$) and moment of inertia ($I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: HyperPhysics — Moment of Inertia [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Rotational-Linear Parallels and Moment of Inertia.
What to skip: Skip continuous volume integral derivations.
Key takeaway: Just as linear force accelerates a mass ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$), net rotational torque accelerates a spinning body according to Rotational Newton's Second Law $\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is angular acceleration (in rad/s^2) and $I_{\text{rot}}$ is the moment of inertia (rotational sluggishness, in kg·m^2). For a point mass $m$ at radius $r$ from the pivot, $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$. Notice the $r^2$: moving a heavy motor or gripper twice as far from the shoulder pivot makes its rotational inertia $4\times$ larger!
Alternative resource: PhET — Torque [verify in-app] — Open the Moment of Inertia tab [verify in-app] and watch how moving mass outward increases $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ and slows down angular acceleration $\alpha$.

sections.h: Idea 2: Gear reduction ratio ($N$): torque multiplication, speed division, and $N^2$ reflected inertia
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Gear train ("Gear ratio" & "Mechanical advantage") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Gear train, Gear ratio, and Mechanical advantage.
What to skip: Skip epicyclic planetary carrier velocity tables (covered in Pass 2).
Key takeaway: Small DC motors spin very fast ($3{,}000\text{–}10{,}000\text{ RPM}$) with very little torque ($\sim 0.02\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$), whereas a robot arm needs slow, smooth speed and high torque. A gearbox with gear ratio $N = \frac{N_{\text{out}}}{N_{\text{in}}}$ (for example, $N = 50:1$) trades speed for torque by conserving mechanical power ($P = \tau \cdot \omega$ from Lesson 00.1):
Speed divides by $N$: $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}$
Torque multiplies by $\eta \cdot N$: $\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta \cdot N \cdot \tau_{\text{motor}}$ (where $\eta \approx 0.85$ is gearbox efficiency)
Reflected inertia scales by $N^2$: Because the motor shaft spins $N$ times faster than the load AND has $N$ times the leverage, the load inertia felt by the motor is divided by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{reflected}} = \frac{I_{\text{load}}}{N^2}$), or equivalently the motor's rotor inertia felt at the output joint is multiplied by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{joint}} = N^2 \cdot I_{\text{rotor}}$).
Backlash: Real gear teeth need a tiny gap so they don't jam; when the motor reverses direction, that free play (typically $0.5^\circ\text{–}2^\circ$ on hobby gearboxes) is called backlash.

By Rotational Newton's Second Law, the net torque $\tau_{\text{net}}$ (N·m) acting on a joint equals its moment of inertia $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ (kg·m^2) multiplied by its angular acceleration $\alpha$ (rad/s^2). When a small, fast motor drives a heavy robot arm through a gearbox with gear reduction ratio $N = N_{\text{out}} / N_{\text{in}}$, speed division, torque multiplication, and reflected inertia follow five fundamental equations in base SI units:
Why does reflected inertia scale with $N^2$ instead of $N$?
Use kinetic energy conservation (Lesson 00.1)! A load with inertia $I_{\text{load}}$ spinning at $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}$ carries rotational kinetic energy:
Load kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} I_{\text{load}} \omega_{\text{out}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{load}} \left(\frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{I_{\text{load}}}{N^2}\right) \omega_{\text{motor}}^2$.
Thus, viewed from the fast-spinning motor shaft, the heavy arm feels $N^2$ times lighter ($I_{\text{load}} / N^2$)! Conversely, viewed from the outside world trying to push the robot arm by hand (backdriving the joint), the tiny motor rotor feels $N^2$ times heavier ($N^2 I_{\text{rotor}}$). With a $50:1$ gearbox, $N^2 = 2{,}500$!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete point_mass_inertia_and_accel (TODO 1) to compute $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ (kg·m^2) and $\alpha = \tau_{\text{net}} / I_{\text{rot}}$ (rad/s^2), and complete gearmotor_output (TODO 2) to compute output torque $\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta N \tau_{\text{motor}}$, output speed $\omega_{\text{out}} = \omega_{\text{motor}} / N$, and reflected load inertia $I_{\text{load}} / N^2$ for a $50:1$ gearmotor.
What is real-hardware only: Physical gear-tooth backlash deadband (wiggling the output shaft slightly by hand while the motor rotor is held stationary).

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, i_rot = mass_kg (radius_m 2) (0.50 0.16 = 0.080 kgm^2) and alpha_rads2 = net_torque_nm / i_rot (2.00 / 0.080 = 25.0 rad/s^2). In TODO 2, divide i_load_kgm2 by gear_ratio_n 2 (50.0 2 = 2500.0).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Forgetting to square the radius $r$ in $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$ or the gear ratio $N$ in reflected inertia: Lever torque scales with $r^1$ (Lesson P.12), but rotational inertia scales with $r^2$, and reflected inertia through a gearbox scales with $N^2$.
Mounting a heavy elbow motor at the moving elbow joint instead of near the shoulder base: Because $I_{\text{rot}} = m \cdot r^2$, putting a $0.3\text{ kg}$ motor out at the elbow ($r = 0.25\text{ m}$) burdens the shoulder with huge rotational inertia; mounting that motor near the shoulder ($r \approx 0$) and driving the elbow through a lightweight transmission (Lesson 02.5) slashes arm inertia!

Why mount heavy motors near the base? If you move a $0.4\text{ kg}$ wrist motor from $r = 0.40\text{ m}$ inward to $r = 0.10\text{ m}$ (4 times closer to the shoulder pivot), by what factor does its moment of inertia $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ around the shoulder decrease?
Answer
Because $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ depends on the square of $r$, reducing $r$ by $4\times$ reduces its moment of inertia by $4^2 = \mathbf{16\times}$!
Speed and torque through a $10:1$ reduction: A motor spins at $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 200\text{ rad/s}$ with torque $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.10\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ into an ideal ($\eta = 1.0$) $N = 10:1$ gearbox. What are $\omega_{\text{out}}$ and $\tau_{\text{out}}$?
Answer
Output speed: $\omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{200}{10} = \mathbf{20.0\text{ rad/s}}$.
Output torque: $\tau_{\text{out}} = 10 \times 0.10 = \mathbf{1.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}$.

Rotational Newton's Second Law is $\tau_{\text{net}} = I_{\text{rot}} \cdot \alpha$, where moment of inertia $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$ (kg·m^2) grows with the square of distance from the pivot.
A gear ratio $N = N_{\text{out}} / N_{\text{in}}$ divides speed by $N$, multiplies torque by $\eta N$, and scales reflected inertia by $N^2$ ($I_{\text{reflected}} = I_{\text{load}} / N^2$).

pages.title: Practical Robot Mechanisms — Double-Shear Bearings, Timing Belts and 3D-Printed Parts

sections.t:
Design reliable beginner robot joints that don't bend, wobble, or snap by supporting rotating shafts in double shear with ball bearings, sizing GT2 timing belt pulleys ($N = N_{\text{driven}} / N_{\text{driver}}$, pitch radius $r_p = \frac{N_{\text{teeth}} \cdot p}{2\pi}$) in Python, and orienting 3D-printed brackets with proper clearance fits (+0.20 mm).
New ideas (max 2):
Cantilevered vs. double-shear shaft support: Supporting both ends of a joint pin with radial ball bearings (like a 608 skate bearing) instead of hanging an arm off one unsupported (cantilevered) motor shaft.
GT2 timing belt pulley ratios and 3D-print layer-line load orientation (0.20 mm clearance): Using a $2.0\text{ mm}$-pitch toothed belt to transmit zero-backlash torque from a base-mounted motor, while orienting 3D-printed layer lines parallel to tension and adding clearance so printed holes fit real shafts.
New syntax: None (math.pi from Lesson P.6).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.0 hours

Lesson P.7: Base SI Units & Metric Prefixes (M, k, m, µ)
Lesson P.12: Forces, Newton's Second Law & Lever Torque
Lesson 02.4: Rotational Dynamics, Gear Ratios & Reflected Inertia

sections.h: Idea 1: Cantilevered vs. double-shear shaft support (why hanging a load off a bare motor shaft bends it)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Ball bearing ("Common designs" & "Deep-groove") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Ball bearing, Common designs, and Deep-groove.
What to skip: Skip axial preload life-fatigue equations (covered in Pass 2).
Key takeaway: The #1 mechanical mistake in beginner robotics is bolting a long robot arm directly onto a motor's bare $4\text{ mm}$ output shaft with nothing supporting the far end. That one-sided overhang is called a cantilevered shaft: any sideways weight or belt tension acts on a lever arm that bends the shaft and crushes the tiny internal motor bushings! Supporting the shaft on both sides of the rotating link inside two ball bearings (such as ubiquitous 608 deep-groove ball bearings: $8\text{ mm}$ inner bore, $22\text{ mm}$ outer diameter, $7\text{ mm}$ width) places the pin in double shear—splitting the load across two supports and making the joint over $16\times$ stiffer!

sections.h: Idea 2: GT2 timing belt pulley ratios and 3D-print layer-line load orientation (0.20 mm clearance)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Toothed belt ("Design and application") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Toothed belt and Design and application.
What to skip: Skip automotive camshaft history.
Key takeaway: In Lesson 02.4, we saw that keeping heavy motors near the shoulder base dramatically lowers arm inertia $I_{\text{rot}} = m r^2$. A fiberglass-reinforced GT2 timing belt (timing belt pitch $p = 2.0\text{ mm}$ between teeth) lets a base-mounted motor drive a distant elbow pulley with near-zero backlash! A driver pulley with $N_{\text{driver}}$ teeth and driven pulley with $N_{\text{driven}}$ teeth have:
Pulley Circumference: $C_{\text{pulley}} = N_{\text{teeth}} \cdot p$
Pitch Radius: $r_p = \frac{N_{\text{teeth}} \cdot p}{2\pi}$
Reduction Ratio: $N = \frac{N_{\text{driven}}}{N_{\text{driver}}}$
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Fused filament fabrication ("Process" & "Physics of the process") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Fused filament fabrication and Process to see why 3D prints are strong along continuous horizontal (X-Y) filament lines and weak between stacked vertical (Z) layers, and why melted plastic holes shrink slightly inward (requiring a +0.20 mm clearance fit for free-spinning bolts and +0.10 mm for a snug bearing press-fit).

When designing a 3D-printed robot joint driven by a GT2 timing belt ($p = 2.0\text{ mm}$ tooth pitch), always support the joint pin in double shear between two radial ball bearings rather than leaving it on a one-sided cantilevered motor shaft:
Pulley Pitch Radius & Belt Tension Force (Why Double Shear Is Essential):
A pulley with $N_{\text{teeth}}$ teeth has circumference $N_{\text{teeth}} \cdot p$, so its effective lever arm (pitch radius $r_p$) and the belt tension pull $\Delta F_{\text{belt}}$ required to transmit torque $\tau_{\text{pulley}}$ are:
For example, a $20$-tooth GT2 driver pulley ($p = 2.0\text{ mm}$) driving a $60$-tooth joint pulley gives a $N = \frac{60}{20} = 3.0:1$ reduction with driven pitch radius $r_{p,2} = \frac{60 \times 2.0}{2\pi} \approx 19.10\text{ mm}$ ($0.01910\text{ m}$), producing $\Delta F_{\text{belt}} = \frac{1.50}{0.01910} = 78.5\text{ N}$ of sideways pull that a double-shear bearing pair carries effortlessly.
3D-Printed Layer-Line Orientation & Hole Clearance Fits (0.20 mm clearance):
Print structural links flat on the bed so filament strands run parallel to tension, and add +0.20 mm diameter clearance (3.20 mm CAD hole for an M3 bolt) for a free-sliding clearance fit and +0.10 mm (22.10 mm CAD bore for a $22.00\text{ mm}$ 608 bearing) for a snug press fit.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3: Complete gt2_belt_drive (TODO 1) to calculate the reduction ratio $N$, driven pulley pitch radius $r_p$ (in mm), and belt tension force $\Delta F_{\text{belt}} = \tau_{\text{out}} / r_{p,\text{m}}$ (in N), and complete cad_hole_diameters_mm (TODO 2) to apply the +0.10 mm bearing press-fit and +0.20 mm bolt clearance-fit rules.
What is real-hardware only: Snapping a physical 3D-printed bracket along its weak Z-axis layer lines vs. testing a part printed flat on the X-Y build plate.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, the driven pulley's circumference is n_driven_teeth pitch_mm (60 2.0 = 120.0 mm), so its pitch radius is 120.0 / (2 math.pi) = 19.0986 mm (0.0190986 m). Divide tau_out_nm (1.50 Nm) by r_driven_m in meters to get 78.5 N.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Tensioning a GT2 timing belt onto an unsupported cantilevered motor shaft: Notice in our calculation above that just $1.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ of joint torque creates $78.5\text{ N}$ ($\sim 8\text{ kg}$ of sideways pull!) on the belt! Always support the pulley shaft in double shear with two bearings so that $78.5\text{ N}$ sideways pull goes into the frame bearings instead of bending the motor shaft.
Printing a long robot arm link standing vertically (Z-axis) on the 3D printer bed: Bending loads will peel the horizontal layer lines apart like a stack of crackers. Always print structural links lying flat on the X-Y build plate so continuous filament strands run the full length of the arm.

Cantilevered vs. Double Shear: Why is capturing both ends of a joint pin in two bearings (double shear) vastly stronger than supporting the pin from one side only (cantilevered)?
Answer
In double shear, radial loads are shared across two bearing supports on either side of the link with minimal bending lever arm, preventing the shaft from tilting, binding, or bending under load.
GT2 pulley pitch diameter: What is the circumference and pitch diameter ($2 r_p$) of a $40$-tooth GT2 pulley ($p = 2.0\text{ mm}$)?
Answer
Circumference: $40 \times 2.0\text{ mm} = \mathbf{80.0\text{ mm}}$.
Pitch diameter: $\frac{80.0\text{ mm}}{\pi} \approx \mathbf{25.46\text{ mm}}$ (pitch radius $r_p \approx 12.73\text{ mm}$).

Support rotating joint shafts on both ends in double shear with radial ball bearings (608) rather than hanging loads on a cantilevered motor shaft.
A GT2 timing belt ($p = 2.0\text{ mm}$ timing belt pitch) transmits low-backlash motion with ratio $N = N_{\text{driven}} / N_{\text{driver}}$ and pitch radius $r_p = \frac{N_{\text{teeth}} \cdot p}{2\pi}$; orient 3D-printed links flat on the bed and include a +0.20 mm clearance fit on bolt holes.
