pages.title: Free-Body Diagrams, Gravity Lever-Arm Torque & Gear Speed/Torque Power Scaling

sections.t: This is the bridge module before Step 1.3 (02-mechanics.T1.03). Before sizing a robot arm motor or computing $N^2$ reflected inertia in Step 1.3, you need to isolate a link in a Free-Body Diagram (FBD), calculate how gravity torque varies with shoulder angle ($\tau_g = m g L_{\text{com}} \cos\theta$), and understand how a gearbox or timing belt trades speed for torque while conserving mechanical power ($P = \tau \omega$). Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

Hold a heavy dumbbell straight out at shoulder height ($\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ horizontal): your shoulder muscles burn because gravity acts at the full horizontal lever arm $L\cos(0) = L$. Now raise your arm straight overhead ($\theta = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ vertical): the dumbbell rests directly over your shoulder pivot with zero horizontal lever arm ($L\cos(\pi/2) = 0$), requiring zero holding torque! Drawing a Free-Body Diagram (FBD) means cutting the link free from the rest of the world and drawing arrows for every force and torque acting on it so nothing is forgotten. And a gearbox with ratio $N:1$ acts as a rotary lever: much like a $10\times$ crowbar moves your hand $10\times$ farther to multiply force by $10\times$, an $N:1$ gear reducer spins the motor shaft $N$ times faster than the output joint while multiplying output torque by $N\times$.

Free-Body Diagram & Static Equilibrium ($\sum F = 0,\ \sum \tau = 0$): For a rigid body to remain stationary ($\ddot{x} = 0, \ddot{\theta} = 0$), the vector sum of external forces $\sum F_x = 0, \sum F_y = 0$ (in $\text{N}$) and the sum of torques about any pivot $\sum \tau_z = 0$ (in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) must vanish.
Planar Link Gravity Holding Torque ($\tau_g(\theta)$): For a link of mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) whose center of mass lies at distance $L_{\text{com}}$ ($\text{m}$) from the joint pivot at angle $\theta$ ($\text{rad}$) measured from the horizontal $+x$-axis, gravity $m g$ acts straight down ($-y$), creating perpendicular lever arm $r_\perp = L_{\text{com}}\cos\theta$. The joint torque required to hold the link plus a tip payload $m_{\text{tip}}$ at length $L$ is:
Substituting $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$, $L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}$, $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$, $L = 0.20\text{ m}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, and $\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ gives $\tau_{\max} = (0.04 + 0.10)(9.81)\cos(0) = 1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Gear Ratio Speed/Torque Scaling and Power Conservation: For an ideal gear or belt reduction of ratio $N = \omega_{\text{motor}} / \omega_{\text{load}} = r_{\text{load}} / r_{\text{motor}}$ with efficiency $\eta \in (0, 1]$:
Substituting $N = 8.0$, $\eta = 1.0$, $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.25\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, and $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 160\text{ rad/s}$ gives $\tau_{\text{load}} = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\omega_{\text{load}} = 20\text{ rad/s}$, and $P = 40.0\text{ W}$ on both sides.

Predict first (before you run it): The link is $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$ with its center of mass at $L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}$, the payload is $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$ at $L = 0.20\text{ m}$, and the motor sits behind an $N = 6.0$, $\eta = 0.90$ planetary gearbox. Commit to three numbers before the block runs: (1) the holding torque at the horizontal pose, in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ — nearer $1$ or nearer $2$; (2) whether the torque at $60^\circ$ is exactly half the horizontal value; (3) whether the motor torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ comes out above or below $\tau_{\text{load}}(0)/N$, and why. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: a horizontal torque near $0.9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ means the link's own mass at $L_{\text{com}}$ was left out, leaving only the payload's $0.50 \times 0.20 \times 9.81$; and a motor torque larger than the load torque means $N$ was multiplied where it should have been divided.
Size the motor torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ required to hold a horizontal single-link robot arm ($m_{\text{link}} = 0.40\text{ kg}, L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}, L = 0.20\text{ m}$) carrying a tip payload $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$ at $\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ and $\theta = \pi/3\text{ rad}$ ($60^\circ$) through an $N = 6.0$, $\eta = 0.90$ planetary gearbox.
Expected output:

A timing-belt reduction connects a motor pulley with $Z_{\text{motor}} = 16$ teeth to a joint pulley with $Z_{\text{joint}} = 72$ teeth ($\eta = 0.95$). Compute the gear ratio $N = Z_{\text{joint}} / Z_{\text{motor}}$, the output speed $\omega_{\text{joint}}$ when $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 90\text{ rad/s}$, and the output torque $\tau_{\text{joint}}$ when $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.40\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Verify $N = 4.5$, $\omega_{\text{joint}} = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$, and $\tau_{\text{joint}} = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ ($\pm 10^{-6}$).
If your result differs: Check that the driven pulley tooth count ($72$) is divided by the driving motor pulley tooth count ($16$): $72 / 16 = 4.5$, and multiply $\tau_{\text{motor}} \times N \times \eta = 0.40 \times 4.5 \times 0.95 = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

sections.h: Graded package - the lever, the gearbox and the reflected inertia
sections.t:
exercises/02-mechanics.T1.02a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: gravity_torque (the cosine lever arm, link plus tip), balance_force, gear_ratio, gear_output_speed, gear_output_torque ($\eta N \tau$), mechanical_power and reflected_inertia ($N^2$). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
29 tests. The torque is checked at the worked example, at the horizontal maximum and at vertical poses, so a sine where the cosine belongs fails; the balance force is checked at the Skip test's $60\text{ N}$; the belt drive is checked at the exercise's $4.5$, $20\text{ rad/s}$ and $1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, so an inverted ratio, a multiplied output speed or a dropped efficiency each fail; and the reflected inertia is checked at $N^2$ rather than $N$. The transfer suite runs the plant's own arm: the submission's shoulder term must reproduce plant.gravity_torque's difference between the two links at four poses, the folded elbow's full lever arm is checked (the pose that looks vertical is not the zero-torque one), the $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp is pushed back through an $8{:}1$ belt, and plant.I1 reflected through $4{:}1$ is $0.128\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Five planted faults - gravity_uses_sine, balance_divides_wrong, gear_ratio_inverted, output_speed_multiplies, torque_ignores_efficiency - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Rotational Units), 00-foundations.T1.00d (Radians, Cosine Law & math.atan2), and 00-foundations.T1.00e (Rotational Kinetic Energy).
Core Concepts to Review First: Lever torque $\tau = r F \sin\theta$, static equilibrium ($\sum F = 0, \sum \tau = 0$), gear ratio torque/speed scaling and reflected inertia $J_{\text{refl}} = N^2 J_{\text{motor}}$, and 2-link planar FK/IK in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Lynch & Park Modern Robotics Ch. 3 & Ch. 6 (hades.mech.northwestern.edu) and Track 02 Tier 1 (02-mechanics-kinematics-dynamics/README.md).

The ratio comes from the teeth, in the right order. The joint pulley is the driven one, so $N = 72/16 = 4.5$; writing $16/72$ gives $0.222$ and every downstream number inherits it.
A reducer slows and strengthens. $\omega_{\text{joint}} = 90/4.5 = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$ and $\tau_{\text{joint}} = 0.95 \times 4.5 \times 0.40 = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — speed divided by $N$, torque multiplied by $N$.
The efficiency belongs on the torque, not the speed. $\eta = 0.95$ costs $5\%$ of the torque ($1.80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ without it) and none of the speed.
Power is the check that the two sides agree. $\tau_{\text{joint}}\omega_{\text{joint}} = 1.71 \times 20.0 = 34.2\text{ W}$ equals $\eta \tau_{\text{motor}}\omega_{\text{motor}} = 0.95 \times 0.40 \times 90 = 34.2\text{ W}$; if the two differ, the speed or the torque was scaled the wrong way.
What the suite refuses. gravity_torque raises on a negative mass; balance_force raises on a lever arm at the pivot (which balances nothing); gear_ratio raises on a zero tooth count; gear_output_speed raises on a zero ratio; and gear_output_torque raises on a gear efficiency outside (0, 1]. Each of those is a ValueError.

Printed: N=4.50 | omega_joint=20.00 rad/s | tau_joint=1.7100 Nm, then P_joint=34.20 W | P_motoreta=34.20 W | J_reflected(4:1)=0.128 kgm^2.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite in exercises/02-mechanics.T1.02a/ drives the plant's own lever arms and its 2.5 N·m clamp through this module's gearbox maths:

Inject the gravity_uses_sine fault the graded package names, and diagnose it from the two poses in the worked example:
Inject: replace math.cos(theta_rad) with math.sin(theta_rad) inside arm_gravity_torque, leaving the masses, the lever arms and $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ untouched.
Symptom: the horizontal pose now reads $\tau_0 = 0.0000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — an arm that hangs out flat and needs no holding torque — while $60^\circ$ reads $1.3734 \times 0.8660 = 1.1894\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ instead of $0.6867\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, so the printed order is reversed and the motor is sized at $1.1894 / (0.90 \times 6.0) = 0.2203\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ instead of $0.2543\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Diagnose: the amplitude $1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ still appears in the output, just at the wrong angle, so $(m L_{\text{com}} + m_{\text{tip}} L)g$ and the unit chain are correct and only the angle factor can be wrong. Gravity's lever arm is the horizontal distance $L_{\text{com}}\cos\theta$ from the pivot: largest when the link lies along the horizon, zero when it points straight up. A sine factor peaks at $90^\circ$ from the horizontal — the vertical pose, where the arm balances over its own pivot — and that is the one symptom a mass error cannot produce.
Fix: put math.cos back. Then $\tau_0 = 1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\tau_{60} = 0.6867\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, and $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 1.3734 / (0.90 \times 6.0) = 0.2543\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — the worst-case gravity load the gearbox must hold, which is the number a motor is sized on.

Open URDF / MuJoCo & STO in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) to visualize how link lengths and joint angles change the horizontal moment arm of a planar robot arm.
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.02-mechanics.T1.02a, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Step 1.3 (02-mechanics.T1.03) and Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07), your gravity torque equation $\tau_g(\theta) = M g L_{\text{eff}}\cos\theta$ becomes the exact gravity feedforward compensation term added to the PID controller output:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: tau_0 == 1.3734 Nm, tau_60 == 0.6867 Nm, and tau_motor_0 == 0.2543 Nm.
Pass criteria: score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/4$) on the Skip test or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$) on the Ladder Gate test below to unlock Step 1.3 (02-mechanics.T1.03).

[Recall] [Concept: free_body_diagram_static_equilibrium] A horizontal massless beam is pivoted at $x = 0\text{ m}$. A downward load of $F_1 = 30.0\text{ N}$ acts at $x_1 = 0.20\text{ m}$. What upward force $F_2$ in newtons ($\text{N}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) must act at $x_2 = 0.10\text{ m}$ to maintain static torque equilibrium ($\sum \tau_z = 0$)?

pages.title: Quadrature Encoders (4x Counting) and 12-Bit Magnetic Angle Sensors

sections.t:
Calculate shaft angle and angular resolution from an incremental quadrature encoder (A/B channels decoded at $4\times$ edges per slot) and a 12-bit absolute magnetic encoder (AS5600, 0..4095 counts per revolution), and convert raw sensor counts into degrees and radians in Python.
New ideas (max 2):
Incremental quadrature encoders (A/B channels and $4\times$ edge counting): How two square-wave channels shifted by a quarter cycle let hardware count $4\times$ edges per disk slot ($\text{CPR} = 4 \cdot N_{\text{lines}}$) and tell clockwise from counter-clockwise rotation.
12-bit absolute magnetic encoders (AS5600 0..4095 counts to radians and degrees): How an on-axis diametric magnet above a Hall sensor IC reports instant absolute shaft angle in $2^{12} = 4096$ steps ($0.0879^\circ$ per count) right at power-on without homing.
New syntax: None (uses integer arithmetic, math.pi, and functions from Track P).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.8: Cycle Frequency, Period & Binary Bits
Lesson P.10: Radians, Rotational Speed & Right-Triangle Trig
Lesson 02.4: Rotational Inertia & Gear Ratios
Lesson 02.5: Radial Ball Bearings, GT2 Timing Belts & 3D-Printing Tolerances

sections.h: Idea 1: Incremental quadrature encoders (A/B channels and $4\times$ edge counting)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Incremental encoder ("Quadrature outputs") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Incremental encoder and Quadrature outputs.
What to skip: Skip linear glass scale interferometers.
Key takeaway: A single slotted optical sensor only tells you speed, not direction. An incremental quadrature encoder places two sensors (Channel A and Channel B) a quarter-slot apart ($90^\circ$ phase shift). When A rises before B, the shaft is turning forward (+1); when B rises before A, it is turning backward (-1). By counting rising and falling edges on both A and B ($4\times$ quadrature decoding), a disk with $N_{\text{lines}}$ slots plus a gearbox of ratio $N_{\text{gear}}$ yields $\text{CPR}_{\text{out}} = 4 \cdot N_{\text{lines}} \cdot N_{\text{gear}}$ counts per output revolution.
Alternative resource: Dynapar — Quadrature Encoder Overview [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings What is a quadrature encoder? and How does a Quadrature Encoder work?.

sections.h: Idea 2: 12-bit absolute magnetic encoders (AS5600 0..4095 counts to radians and degrees)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Rotary encoder ("Absolute encoder" & "Magnetic") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Absolute encoder and Magnetic.
What to skip: Skip Gray-code mechanical contact brushes.
Key takeaway: Because an incremental encoder only counts changes since boot, it wakes up at count = 0 no matter where the robot arm is pointing. An absolute magnetic encoder (AS5600, 12-bit 0..4095) measures the horizontal magnetic field of a diametrically magnetized cylinder magnet (North on left half, South on right half) glued to the end of the shaft. With $2^{12} = 4096$ steps per full turn, raw count $c \in [0, 4095]$ maps directly to $\theta_{\text{deg}} = \frac{c}{4096} \times 360^\circ$ and $\theta_{\text{rad}} = \frac{c}{4096} \times 2\pi$.
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Binary Number System [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review how 12 binary bits represent $2^{12} = 4096$ distinct states.

Choosing between an incremental quadrature encoder and a 12-bit absolute magnetic encoder depends on whether your joint needs instant startup pose knowledge without a mechanical homing switch. On a brushed DC gearmotor with a rear-shaft optical disk of $N_{\text{lines}} = 500$ lines and a $N_{\text{gear}} = 10:1$ gearbox, counting every rising and falling edge on both Channel A and Channel B ($4\times$ counting) gives:
By contrast, an on-axis 12-bit absolute magnetic encoder (AS5600) mounted directly on the output joint shaft divides one mechanical turn into $2^{12} = 4096$ counts (0..4095; note that the full-circle divisor is $2^{12} = 4096$ because count 4096 wraps back to 0 at $360^\circ$):
When mounting an AS5600 in your hardware build, always verify two mechanical details: first, use a diametrically magnetized cylinder magnet (North and South split across the circular face) rather than a standard axial magnet whose field does not rotate with the shaft; second, tie the DIR pin explicitly to GND or VCC so clockwise rotation always increments the angle cleanly.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete quadrature_resolution (TODO 1) and as5600_to_angle (TODO 2) to compute $4\times$ quadrature output CPR and convert 12-bit AS5600 counts into degrees and radians.
What is real-hardware only: Gluing the $6\text{ mm}$ diametric neodymium magnet centered within $1.0\text{ mm}$ air-gap above the physical AS5600 sensor chip.

Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Using an axially magnetized magnet above an AS5600: Standard fridge or craft magnets have North on the top face and South on the bottom face, so spinning the shaft does not rotate the horizontal field vector across the chip. Always buy a diametrically magnetized cylinder magnet.
Dividing a wrapped rotary encoder by 4095 instead of 4096: Unlike a linear ADC potentiometer that stops at $5.0\text{ V}$ (1023), a $360^\circ$ rotary encoder wraps around in a circle so step 4096 is the exact same angle as step 0. Quarter turns occur at exact powers of two: 1024 ($90^\circ$), 2048 ($180^\circ$), and 3072 ($270^\circ$).

$4\times$ quadrature counts: An optical encoder disk has $250\text{ lines}$ and is mounted on the motor side of a $20:1$ gearbox. How many quadrature counts ($4\times$) occur per 1 full revolution of the gearbox output shaft?
Answer
$\text{CPR}_{\text{out}} = 4 \times 250 \times 20 = \mathbf{20000\text{ counts/rev}}$.
12-bit magnetic angle step size: What is the smallest angle change (in degrees) that a 12-bit AS5600 encoder ($4096$ counts per turn) can resolve?
Answer
$\Delta \theta = \frac{360^\circ}{4096} \approx \mathbf{0.0879^\circ}$ per count.

An incremental quadrature encoder uses two $90^\circ$-shifted square waves (A/B) to detect direction and provide $\text{CPR} = 4 \cdot N_{\text{lines}} \cdot N_{\text{gear}}$ counts per revolution.
A 12-bit absolute magnetic encoder (AS5600) senses a diametrically magnetized shaft magnet to report instant absolute angle $\theta_{\text{rad}} = \frac{\text{raw}}{4096} \cdot 2\pi$ at boot.

pages.title: 3-Phase Brushless Motors, Pole Pairs and 90-Degree Electrical Torque Lead

sections.t:
Convert mechanical shaft angle $\theta_m$ into electrical angle $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$ for a brushless motor with $N_p$ pole pairs, and compute the balanced 3-phase sinusoidal coil voltages $(v_a, v_b, v_c)$ that keep the stator magnetic field locked $90^\circ$ electrical ahead of the rotor magnets for smooth maximum torque.
New ideas (max 2):
Pole pairs ($N_p$) and electrical angle versus mechanical shaft angle ($\theta_e = N_p \cdot \theta_m$): Why a rotor ring with $2 N_p$ alternating North/South magnets cycles through $N_p$ full electrical revolutions for every $1$ mechanical turn of the shaft.
3-phase sinusoidal commutation and $90^\circ$ electrical torque lead: How driving three stator coils spaced $120^\circ$ apart with sine waves at $\theta_{\text{drive}} = \theta_e + \frac{\pi}{2}$ pulls the rotor tangentially with maximum torque per Ampere.
New syntax: None (uses math.cos, math.sin, math.radians, and for loops).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: Pole pairs ($N_p$) and electrical angle versus mechanical shaft angle ($\theta_e = N_p \cdot \theta_m$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Brushless DC electric motor (" Construction" & "Variations") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Brushless DC electric motor and Implementations.
What to skip: Skip aircraft starter-generator history.
Key takeaway: Unlike a brushed DC motor whose mechanical brushes flip coil polarity automatically, a 3-phase brushless motor (BLDC) has stationary copper coils (stator) and a rotating bell lined with permanent magnets (rotor). If the rotor has $14$ alternating North and South magnets, it has $N_p = 7$ pole pairs. Every time the physical shaft rotates by $\frac{1}{7}$ of a turn ($51.43^\circ$ mechanical), the magnetic pattern repeats a full $360^\circ$ electrical angle: $\theta_e = N_p \cdot \theta_m$.
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Sine, Cosine and Tangent [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review how $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ repeat every $2\pi\text{ rad}$ ($360^\circ$).

sections.h: Idea 2: 3-phase sinusoidal commutation and $90^\circ$ electrical torque lead
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Three-phase electric power ("Principle") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Three-phase electric power and Principle (how three waveforms offset by $120^\circ = \frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ rad}$ create a smoothly rotating magnetic field).
What to skip: Skip high-voltage utility grid transformers.
Key takeaway: Imagine pulling a compass needle around a circle with a handheld magnet. If you hold your magnet directly on top of the needle ($0^\circ$ lead), the needle just pulls radially outward against its bearing with zero turning torque. To get maximum tangential pull, you must hold your stator magnetic field $90^\circ$ electrical ($\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$) ahead of the rotor's electrical angle $\theta_e$ ($\tau \propto \sin(\theta_{\text{stator}} - \theta_e) = \sin(90^\circ) = 1.0$) using three $120^\circ$-shifted phase voltages.
Alternative resource: The Physics Classroom — Magnetic Field and the Right-Hand Rule [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review closed current loops in motor windings.

In a 3-phase brushless motor with $N_p$ pole pairs, reading the mechanical shaft angle $\theta_m$ from your magnetic encoder (Lesson 03.1) immediately tells the microcontroller where the rotor magnets sit in electrical angle:
To produce smooth, ripple-free rotary torque (sinusoidal commutation, the foundation of SimpleFOC and Brushless Motor Control Lab of the MechaLab Workbench), we command a stator magnetic field angle $\theta_{\text{drive}} = \theta_e + \frac{\pi}{2}$ ($90^\circ$ electrical torque lead) across the three stator phases ($A, B, C$) spaced $120^\circ$ ($\frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ rad}$) apart:
Notice that at any angle $\theta_{\text{drive}}$, the three phase voltages remain balanced ($v_a + v_b + v_c = 0$), and because torque varies with $\sin(\Delta\theta_e)$, keeping $\Delta\theta_e = +90^\circ$ ($\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$) yields $100\%$ of the motor's available torque per Ampere whereas $\Delta\theta_e = 0^\circ$ yields $0\%$ torque and only wastes heat in the windings.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner & Brushless Motor Control Lab FOC Simulator): Complete mech_to_elec_deg (TODO 1) for an $N_p = 7$ pole-pair gimbal motor and three_phase_voltages (TODO 2) to compute balanced $(v_a, v_b, v_c)$ phase voltages with a $+90^\circ$ ($\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$) torque lead.
What is real-hardware only: Feeling the $N_p = 7$ magnetic detents per turn by hand when energizing Phase A on a physical gimbal motor.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, multiply mech_deg pole_pairs and wrap into [0, 360) with % 360.0. In TODO 2, add math.pi / 2.0 to theta_e_rad, then evaluate v_q math.cos(drive_rad), v_q math.cos(drive_rad - 2.0 math.pi / 3.0), and v_q math.cos(drive_rad - 4.0 math.pi / 3.0).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Confusing total magnet poles ($14$) with pole pairs ($N_p = 7$): Datasheets often label a motor 12N14P ($12$ stator slots, $14$ rotor magnet poles). Always divide the magnet pole count by $2$ to get $N_p = 7$ pole pairs before multiplying $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$.
Applying voltage-mode commutation (vq = 6 V) to a low-resistance drone motor ($R = 0.05\ \Omega$): Without current sensors, stalling a $0.05\ \Omega$ motor at $6\text{ V}$ draws $I = 6 / 0.05 = 120\text{ A}$! Only use open-loop/voltage-mode SimpleFOC on high-resistance gimbal motors ($R \approx 8\text{–}15\ \Omega$, where $I_{\text{stall}} \approx 0.6\text{ A}$).

Pole pairs to electrical angle: A gimbal brushless motor has $22$ permanent magnets around its rotor bell ($N_p = 11$ pole pairs). When the mechanical shaft rotates by $15^\circ$, how many electrical degrees does the magnetic field advance?
Answer
$\Delta \theta_e = 11 \times 15^\circ = \mathbf{165.0^\circ\text{ electrical}}$.
Why $0^\circ$ electrical lead fails: What happens if the stator magnetic field points at $\Delta\theta_e = 0^\circ$ (directly aligned with the rotor magnet) instead of $+90^\circ$ ahead?
Answer
It produces zero rotary torque ($\sin 0^\circ = 0$)! All coil current goes into pulling radially on the rotor bearings and heating the copper windings.

A brushless rotor with $2 N_p$ magnets has $N_p$ pole pairs, advancing through electrical angle $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$.
3-phase sinusoidal commutation drives three $120^\circ$-spaced coils with $\theta_{\text{drive}} = \theta_e + \frac{\pi}{2}$ ($90^\circ$ electrical torque lead) for smooth maximum torque.

pages.title: Track 02 + 03 Integration Micro-Lab — Read Dual Encoders to Compute 2-Link End-Effector Position

sections.t:
In this 20-minute Zero-New-Theory Integration Micro-Lab, combine Track 02 (Lesson 02.2: 2-Link Forward Kinematics) and Track 03 (Lesson 03.1: Quadrature & AS5600 Magnetic Encoders) to read raw integer counts from shoulder and elbow encoders, compute the live (x, y) end-effector coordinates of our recurring 2-DOF robot arm, and diagnose two classic R4 sensor-to-kinematics faults (a $1\times$ vs. $4\times$ CPR mismatch and an inverted encoder sign).
New ideas (max 2):
Combining quantized encoder counts with 2-link forward kinematics to compute end-effector coordinates: Chaining count -> radians conversion (Lesson 03.1) directly into $x = L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ and $y = L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ (Lesson 02.2) with zero new equations.
Diagnosing wrong encoder CPR and inverted channel-B sign faults from end-effector position errors: Recognizing why forgetting the $4\times$ quadrature factor under-reports joint angles by $4\times$ and why swapped A/B encoder wires flip the sign of $y$ (R4 fault diagnosis).
New syntax: None (pure synthesis of math.cos, math.sin, math.pi, and functions from Lessons 02.2 and 03.1).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 0.35–0.5 hours (20–30 min Micro-Lab) | Slow-learner: 0.75–1.0 hours

Lesson 02.2: 2-Link Planar Forward Kinematics (x, y Reach & Relative Elbow Angle)
Lesson 03.1: 4x Quadrature Incremental & 12-Bit AS5600 Magnetic Encoders

sections.h: Idea 1: Combining quantized encoder counts with 2-link forward kinematics to compute end-effector coordinates
sections.t:
Primary resource: Modern Robotics (Lynch & Park) — Forward Kinematics [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review Chapter 4 planar 2R chain equations.
What to skip: Skip 3D screw axes.
Key takeaway: On a real 2-DOF robot arm, forward kinematics (fk_2link) never receives floating-point degrees directly from a textbook—it receives integer counts (c1, c2) from the shoulder and elbow encoders (4096 counts/rev for a 12-bit AS5600 or $4 N_{\text{lines}} N_{\text{gear}}$ for a geared quadrature encoder). Converting each count to radians ($\theta_i = \frac{c_i}{\text{CPR}_i} \cdot 2\pi$) and feeding $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ into fk_2link(theta1_rad, theta2_rad, l1_m, l2_m) turns raw hardware sensor ticks into physical millimeter tip coordinates!
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Forward kinematics [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review planar two-link joint-to-Cartesian mapping.

sections.h: Idea 2: Diagnosing wrong encoder CPR and inverted channel-B sign faults from end-effector position errors
sections.t:
Primary resource: Dynapar — Quadrature Encoder Overview [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings How does a Quadrature Encoder work? and Achieving higher resolution with Quadrature Encoders.
What to skip: Skip NI FPGA pinout tables.
Key takeaway: When a physical robot arm's computed tip position (x, y) disagrees with a ruler measurement on the bench, two R4 bugs account for over $90\%$ of cases:
4x CPR Mismatch (cpr_4x_bug): The hardware ISR counts all $4$ quadrature edges per slot, but the kinematics code divides by lines_per_rev gear_ratio (missing the 4 factor), making the software think the arm rotated $4\times$ further than it actually did!
Inverted Encoder Sign (inverted_dir_bug): Swapping quadrature channels A and B (or mounting an AS5600 magnet upside down) negates $\theta_2 \to -\theta_2$, mirroring the elbow downward instead of upward.

This 20-minute micro-lab introduces zero new equations—instead, it gives you dedicated R2 (parameter adaptation) and R4 (fault diagnosis) practice bridging Track 02 (Mechanics) and Track 03 (Sensors) before Embedded C/C++ arrives in Track 04:
Sensor-to-Angle Stage (Lesson 03.1): Convert raw shoulder count $c_1$ and elbow count $c_2$ into joint angles in radians using each joint's true counts-per-revolution ($\text{CPR}_1, \text{CPR}_2$):
Angle-to-Cartesian Stage (Lesson 02.2): Compute cumulative global elbow angle $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$ and evaluate the 2-link end-effector position:
For our recurring 2-DOF desktop arm ($L_1 = 0.12\text{ m}, L_2 = 0.10\text{ m}$) with 12-bit AS5600 encoders ($\text{CPR} = 4096$ counts/rev), when the shoulder is at $+90^\circ$ ($c_1 = 1024$) and the elbow is bent $-90^\circ$ ($c_2 = -1024$ so $\theta_{12} = 0\text{ rad}$), the shoulder points straight up to $(0, 0.12\text{ m})$ and the forearm points horizontally right to $(0.10\text{ m}, 0.12\text{ m})$. If someone swaps the elbow encoder sign ($c_2 \to +1024$, $\theta_{12} = \pi\text{ rad}$), the tip lands at $(-0.10\text{ m}, 0.12\text{ m})$—an immediate $200\text{ mm}$ horizontal sign diagnostic!

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner) to verify encoders_to_tip_xy and diagnose_encoder_fk_fault.
What is real-hardware only: Rotating two physical AS5600 magnetic encoders over a printed millimeter grid.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)

In TODO 2, compute distance math.hypot(mx - cx, my - cy) < 1e-4 for each candidate.

Full Solution

Adding raw encoder counts (count1 + count2) when shoulder and elbow have different gear ratios (cpr1 != cpr2): Always convert each joint's count to radians using its own CPR before summing $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$.
Forgetting the $4\times$ quadrature edge factor: If a $256\text{-count}$ quarter-turn is divided by 1024 instead of 4096, the software believes the link rotated $90^\circ$ when it only rotated $22.5^\circ$.

With $\text{CPR} = 4096$, $L_1 = 0.12\text{ m}$, $L_2 = 0.10\text{ m}$, what are $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ and $(x, y)$ when count1 = 0 and count2 = 0?
Answer 1
$\theta_1 = 0\text{ rad}$ and $\theta_2 = 0\text{ rad}$, so the arm is stretched straight out along $+x$ at $(x, y) = (0.22\text{ m}, 0.00\text{ m})$.
Why does negating count2 flip the forearm to the opposite side of Link 1?
Answer 2
Because relative elbow angle $\theta_2$ is measured counter-clockwise from Link 1's direction; negating count2 changes $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ to $\theta_1 - \theta_2$ (switching elbow-up to elbow-down).

I can chain raw encoder counts (c1, c2) directly into 2-link forward kinematics to compute live end-effector (x, y) coordinates.
I can diagnose an inverted encoder direction vs. a missing $4\times$ quadrature CPR multiplier from observed tip coordinates.

pages.title: Electromagnets, Permanent Magnets, Pole Pairs, Quadrature Pulses & Faraday Back-EMF

sections.t: This is the bridge module before Step 1.4 (03-sensors.T1.04). Every electric motor is simultaneously an actuator ($\tau = K_t i$) and a generator ($v_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$), every brushless motor has $p$ magnetic pole pairs that make its electrical phase spin $p$ times faster than its physical shaft ($\theta_e = p\theta_m$), and every incremental encoder determines rotation direction from two $90^\circ$-shifted pulse channels (A and B). Mastering these three ideas makes SimpleFOC and encoder feedback in Step 1.4 click immediately. Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

Imagine a bicycle wheel with $p = 7$ pairs of North-South magnets glued around its rim, spinning past a stationary electromagnet coil on the frame. Every time the physical wheel turns by $1/7\text{th}$ of a revolution, a full North-South magnet pair sweeps past the coil—so the coil sees a complete $360^\circ$ ($2\pi\text{ rad}$) electrical cycle for every $1/7\text{th}$ of a mechanical turn ($\theta_e = p\theta_m$). When you push current $i$ into the coil, the magnetic push produces torque $\tau = K_t i$; conversely, as the magnets sweep past the coil at speed $\omega_m$, Faraday's law generates an opposing Back-EMF voltage $v_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$ that fights the supply voltage (which is why a motor draws maximum stall current at $\omega_m = 0$ and less current as it speeds up!). Finally, to know which way the wheel is turning, a quadrature encoder places two optical or Hall sensors (A and B) a quarter-slot apart: if A rises before B, the wheel is spinning forward; if B rises before A, it is spinning backward.

Motor Torque Constant ($K_t$), Back-EMF Constant ($K_e$) & Steady-State DC Motor Equation: In SI units ($\tau$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, $i$ in $\text{A}$, $v_{\text{bemf}}$ in $\text{V}$, $\omega_m$ in $\text{rad/s}$), conservation of electromechanical power ($v_{\text{bemf}} i = \tau \omega_m$) guarantees $K_t = K_e$ ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m/A} \equiv \text{V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$):
For a motor rated in $\text{KV}$ ($\text{RPM/V}$), $K_e = K_t = \frac{60}{2\pi \cdot \text{KV}}$ (for ideal phase-to-neutral scaling). Substituting $V_{\text{term}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, $R = 2.0\ \Omega$, $K_e = 0.05\text{ V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$, and $\omega_m = 100\text{ rad/s}$ gives $v_{\text{bemf}} = 5.0\text{ V}$ and current $i = (12.0 - 5.0)/2.0 = 3.5\text{ A}$.
Pole Pairs ($p$) and Electrical vs. Mechanical Angle: A rotor with $N_{\text{poles}} = 2p$ permanent magnets ($p$ North-South pole pairs) has electrical angle $\theta_e$ ($\text{rad}$) and electrical speed $\omega_e$ ($\text{rad/s}$):
Substituting $N_{\text{poles}} = 14$ ($p = 7$ pole pairs) and $\theta_m = \frac{\pi}{7}\text{ rad}$ gives $\theta_e = 7 \times \frac{\pi}{7} = \pi\text{ rad}$ ($180^\circ$ electrical).
Quadrature A/B ($4\times$) Decoding & Angle Resolution: An incremental encoder with $N_{\text{lines}}$ lines (cycles per revolution) produces $4$ quadrature edges (00 -> 10 -> 11 -> 01 -> 00) per line, yielding $\text{CPR} = 4 N_{\text{lines}}$ counts per mechanical revolution and angular resolution:
Substituting $N_{\text{lines}} = 1024$ gives $\text{CPR} = 4096\text{ counts/rev}$ and $\Delta\theta_{\text{rad}} = \frac{2\pi}{4096} \approx 0.001534\text{ rad}$ ($0.0879^\circ$).

Predict first (before you run it): The gimbal motor has $R = 4.0\ \Omega$ and $K_e = 0.06\text{ V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ on a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply with $p = 7$ pole pairs, and the decode walks $(A, B)$ through five forward edges. Commit to four numbers before the block runs: (1) the stall current $I_{\text{stall}}$ in amperes; (2) the no-load speed $\omega_{\text{no-load}}$ in $\text{rad/s}$; (3) the electrical frequency $\omega_e$ at that speed; (4) the count the five-edge walk adds. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: $\omega_e$ must come out exactly $7\times$ the mechanical speed, so any other ratio means poles and pole pairs were confused; and a quadrature total of $10$ after five edges means both edges of each transition were counted, when each forward transition contributes exactly one count.
Compute the no-load speed $\omega_{\text{no-load}}$, stall current $I_{\text{stall}}$, electrical frequency $\omega_e$ for a $14$-pole ($p=7$) gimbal motor with $R = 4.0\ \Omega, K_e = 0.06\text{ V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ driven at $V_{\text{term}} = 12.0\text{ V}$, and decode a sequence of quadrature $(A, B)$ state transitions.
Expected output:

A $2208$ gimbal BLDC motor has $12$ stator slots and $14$ rotor magnet poles (12N14P). Compute (a) the number of pole pairs $p = N_{\text{poles}} / 2$, (b) the mechanical angle $\theta_m$ in degrees corresponding to one full $360^\circ$ electrical cycle ($360^\circ / p$), and (c) the encoder angle resolution $\Delta\theta_{\text{deg}} = 360^\circ / 2^{14}$ of a 14-bit (16384 counts/rev) AS5048A magnetic encoder. Verify $p = 7$, $\theta_m = 51.4286^\circ$ ($\pm 10^{-3}$), and $\Delta\theta_{\text{deg}} = 0.02197^\circ$ ($\pm 10^{-4}$).
If your result differs: Remember that 12N14P means 12 stator teeth and 14 rotor magnets ($7$ North + $7$ South), so $p = 14 / 2 = 7$ pole pairs (not $14$).

sections.h: Graded package - back-EMF, pole pairs and the quadrature count
sections.t:
exercises/03-sensors.T1.03a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds eight holes: back_emf (Ke omega), winding_current ((V_term - Ke omega) / R, negative when generating), motor_torque, pole_pairs (N_poles / 2, not N_poles), electrical_angle (wrapped into one electrical cycle), quadrature_cpr (4 N_lines), angle_resolution and quad_step (one bit per edge, and a two-bit jump is not a step). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
49 tests. The exercise's $p = 7$, $51.4286^\circ$ and $0.02197^\circ$ are checked alongside the worked example's 3.0 A stall current, 200 rad/s no-load speed and 5-count quadrature walk, the Skip test's 2.4 A and 2000 CPR, and the Gate test's 0.36 Nm, 300 rad/s and wrapped 0.7168 rad. The transfer suite runs the plant's own encoder and actuator: its 12-bit AS5600 is exactly a 1024-line encoder decoded $4\times$ ($4096$ counts, $2\pi/4096$ rad per count), at the plant's 1 kHz tick a single count lasts only 1.534 rad/s of shaft speed while the module's 200 rad/s passes ~130 counts per tick, the plant's wrap_pi is the same angle as one pole pair, the $-0.15\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ disturbance pulse is 2.5 A of braking current inside the 3.0 A stall, and the 2.5 Nm clamp needs 41.7 A that a 12 V / 4 $\Omega$ winding cannot supply. Five planted faults - winding_current_ignores_bemf, pole_pairs_counts_poles, electrical_angle_unwrapped, cpr_equals_lines, quad_step_accepts_a_two_bit_jump - each fail the test named for them.
The package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.03-sensors.T1.03a, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00c (SI Units & RPM-to-$\text{rad/s}$), 00-foundations.T1.00d (Radians & Trigonometry), and 00-foundations.T1.00e (Electromechanical Power).
Prerequisite Bridge Module: 01-electronics.T1.01b (PWM H-Bridges).
Core Concepts to Review First: Quadrature $4\times$ decoding ($\text{CPR} = 4 N_{\text{lines}}$), SI motor constant identity $K_t = K_e$, brushed DC torque-speed line $\tau(\omega) = \tau_{\text{stall}}(1 - \omega/\omega_{\text{no-load}})$, and BLDC electrical angle $\theta_e = N_p \theta_m$ in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: SimpleFOC BLDC & Encoder Theory Docs (docs.simplefoc.com) and Track 03 Tier 1 (03-sensors-and-actuators/README.md).

Expected numbers (the answer): for 12N14P, $p = 7$; one electrical cycle spans $360^\circ/7 = 51.4286^\circ$ of shaft travel; the 14-bit encoder resolves $360^\circ/2^{14} = 0.02197^\circ$ per count, i.e. $16384$ counts per turn.

Electrical angle is the mechanical angle times $p$. $p$ counts North-South pairs, so a 12N14P rotor has $p = 14/2 = 7$, and one full $2\pi$ electrical cycle fits in $360^\circ/7 = 51.4286^\circ$ of mechanical travel. Use $14$ and every angle comes out twice too large, which also collapses the formalization's $\theta_m = \pi/7$ answer from $\pi$ to $0$ after wrapping.
Wrap, don't clip. $\theta_e = p\theta_m$ has to land in $[0, 2\pi)$, and the exercise's 14-bit answer is a mechanical resolution: $360/16384 = 0.0219727^\circ$ per count, which is spec'd from the count total, not from $p$.
One bit per edge. A valid quadrature step changes exactly one of A and B: 00 -> 10 -> 11 -> 01 -> 00 forward, the reverse cycle backwards. A jump of two bits (00 -> 11) is a glitch or a sample rate below the edge rate, so it contributes $0$ - and the worked five-edge walk must total exactly $5$, not $10$.
The winding is one subtraction. $i = (V_{\text{term}} - K_e\omega_m)/R$: at the worked $12.0\text{ V}$, $R = 4.0\ \Omega$, $K_e = 0.06$ and $\omega_m = 200\text{ rad/s}$ the back-EMF is $12.0\text{ V}$ and the current is zero, while at $\omega_m = 0$ it is the $3.0\text{ A}$ stall current.
What the suite refuses. A bad winding in winding_current; a zero or negative motor_torque constant; a zero or negative back_emf constant; an odd magnet count or no magnets at all in pole_pairs; a pole_pairs count, and therefore an electrical_angle with p <= 0, below one; an empty encoder in quadrature_cpr or angle_resolution; and a quad_step code wider than two bits all raise ValueError.

Printed: p=7 | one electrical cycle=51.4286 deg | 14-bit step=0.021973 deg (0.00038350 rad), then I_stall=3.0 A | v_bemf(200 rad/s)=12.0 V | i(200 rad/s)=0.0 A | tau(4.5 A)=0.36 Nm | walk=+5.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite in exercises/03-sensors.T1.03a/ counts the plant's 12-bit encoder and drives the same winding this module sizes:

Inject the pole_pairs_counts_poles fault the graded package names, and diagnose it from the angles alone:
Inject: set $p = N_{\text{poles}} = 14$ instead of $p = N_{\text{poles}}/2 = 7$ in the electrical-angle and electrical-speed terms, leaving $R$, $K_e$ and $V_{\text{term}}$ untouched.
Symptom: the no-load electrical frequency doubles from $1400\text{ rad/s}$ to $2800\text{ rad/s}$, and the rotor angle $\theta_m = \pi/7\text{ rad}$ from ## 3. Formalization reports $\theta_e = 14\pi/7 = 2\pi\text{ rad}$, which wraps to $0$ instead of $\pi$: the current vector is a full magnet step away from where the rotor actually is.
Diagnose: stall current and no-load speed still match, so the winding and the constants are fine; the error appears only once the shaft turns, which localises it to the angle-scaling factor rather than the electrical model. Fourteen magnets are seven North–South pairs, so one electrical cycle fits in $360^\circ/7 = 51.4286^\circ$ of shaft travel — the exercise's own answer — not in $25.7143^\circ$, and the reported angle collapsing to zero exactly where it should read $\pi$ is the half-step that gives it away.
Fix: restore $p = N_{\text{poles}}/2 = 7$. Then $\omega_e = 7 \times 200 = 1400\text{ rad/s}$ and $\theta_m = \pi/7$ maps to $\theta_e = \pi\text{ rad}$, half an electrical cycle, where the five-edge walk still adds $5$ counts.

Open 25 kHz PMSM FOC in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) to see how mechanical rotor angle $\theta_m$ multiplies by pole pairs $p$ into electrical commutation angle $\theta_e = p\theta_m$.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Step 1.4 (03-sensors.T1.04), you can verify pole pairs $p$ on a real BLDC motor by Energizing Phase A to $+1.5\text{ V}$ (current-limited to $0.5\text{ A}$) and Phase B/C to $\text{GND}$, rotating the rotor by hand through one full $360^\circ$ mechanical turn, and counting the $p$ magnetic detent lock positions:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: i_stall == 3.0 A, w_noload == 200.0 rad/s, we_noload == 1400.0 rad/s, and count == 5.
Pass criteria: score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$) on the Ladder Gate test below to unlock Step 1.4 (03-sensors.T1.04).

[Recall] [Concept: lorentz_force_and_back_emf_constants] A DC motor with winding resistance $R = 2.5\ \Omega$ and back-EMF constant $K_e = 0.10\text{ V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ spins at $\omega_m = 40.0\text{ rad/s}$ while driven from $V_{\text{term}} = 10.0\text{ V}$. Compute the winding current $i = (V_{\text{term}} - K_e\omega_m)/R$ in amperes ($\text{A}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Apply] [Concept: mechanical_vs_electrical_angle_pole_pairs] A 24N28P outrunner motor has $28$ permanent magnet poles ($14$ North, $14$ South). Compute its number of pole pairs $p$ and its electrical speed $\omega_e = p\omega_m$ in $\text{rad/s}$ when $\omega_m = 10.0\text{ rad/s}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Transfer] [Concept: quadrature_ab_gray_code_direction] An optical quadrature encoder disc has $N_{\text{lines}} = 500$ lines per revolution and is decoded in $4\times$ quadrature mode (counting rising and falling edges of both channels A and B). Compute the total counts per mechanical revolution ($\text{CPR} = 4 N_{\text{lines}}$, exact integer, tolerance $\pm 0$).
[Concept: quadrature_ab_gray_code_direction] Why does a quadrature encoder require two channels (A and B shifted by $90^\circ$ electrical) instead of a single pulse channel A?
A. Because a single channel can only count up to 100.
B. Because a single pulse channel tells you speed (edge rate) but cannot distinguish clockwise from counter-clockwise rotation when the motor reverses direction.
C. To double the supply voltage.
D. Because channel B carries power.
[Spaced review -> 01-electronics.T1.01b — Concept: pwm_duty_cycle_effective_voltage] A $24.0\,\text{V}$ supply is chopped at $25\%$ duty. Compute the average voltage across the load in volts (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ ($80\%+$). If you missed Q1, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q2, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q3 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 3. If you missed Q5, review 01-electronics.T1.01b. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 03 Tier 1 bridge ladder (03-sensors.T1.03a) before Step 1.4 (03-sensors.T1.04):
[Concept: lorentz_force_and_back_emf_constants] Compute the electromagnetic torque $\tau = K_t i$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) produced by a motor with $K_t = 0.08\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/A}$ carrying $i = 4.5\text{ A}$.
[Concept: lorentz_force_and_back_emf_constants] Compute the theoretical no-load speed $\omega_{\text{no-load}} = V_{\text{term}} / K_e$ in $\text{rad/s}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) when $V_{\text{term}} = 24.0\text{ V}$ and $K_e = 0.08\text{ V}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ (ignoring friction).
[Concept: lorentz_force_and_back_emf_constants] Why does a DC or BLDC motor draw its highest current when stalled ($\omega_m = 0$) and much lower current when spinning fast under light load?
A. Because winding resistance $R$ increases by $100\times$ when spinning.
B. Because spinning generates opposing back-EMF $v_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$, leaving less net voltage $(V_{\text{term}} - K_e\omega_m)$ to push current through $R$.
C. Because the battery disconnects at high speed.
D. Because inductance $L$ blocks DC current.
[Concept: mechanical_vs_electrical_angle_pole_pairs] For a motor with $p = 7$ pole pairs, compute the wrapped electrical angle $\theta_e = (p\theta_m) \bmod (2\pi)$ in radians (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) when mechanical angle is $\theta_m = 1.0\text{ rad}$.
[Concept: mechanical_vs_electrical_angle_pole_pairs] How many full $2\pi$ electrical cycles occur during one full $2\pi$ mechanical revolution of a $p = 11$ pole-pair motor?
[Concept: quadrature_ab_gray_code_direction] Compute the angular resolution $\Delta\theta = \frac{2\pi}{4096}$ in radians (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) of a 12-bit (4096 CPR) encoder.
[Concept: quadrature_ab_gray_code_direction] In $4\times$ quadrature Gray code (00 -> 10 -> 11 -> 01), how many bits of (A, B) are allowed to change on a valid single-step edge transition?
[Concept: quadrature_ab_gray_code_direction] If a quadrature decoder observes an immediate jump from 00 to 11 (both bits flipped in one sample), what does that indicate?
A. Normal half-speed rotation.
B. An invalid/missed transition (glitch or sample rate too slow for the shaft speed).
C. Zero velocity.
D. Index pulse detected.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $7/8$ ($80\%+$). Remediation: Q1–Q3 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q4–Q5 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q6–Q8 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 3.

pages.title: Fixed-Width C/C++ Types (uint16_t), volatile ISR Flags and 1 kHz Timer Loops

sections.t:
Bridge from Python to microcontroller C/C++ by computing roll-over-safe tick differences with fixed-width integers (uint16_t) and replacing blocking delay() loops with a deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) using a volatile flag.
New ideas (max 2):
Fixed-width C/C++ integers (uint8_t, uint16_t, int16_t) and modular rollover subtraction: How microcontroller C variables occupy a fixed bit width (0..65535 for uint16_t) and why unsigned subtraction (now - prev) & 0xFFFF measures exact elapsed ticks even when the counter wraps past 65535 to 0.
Hardware timer Interrupt Service Routines ($1\text{ kHz}$ ISR), volatile flags, and why delay() ruins $\Delta t$: How a hardware timer peripheral fires an ISR every $1.000\text{ ms}$ ($1\text{ kHz}$) and why any variable shared between an ISR and loop() must be declared volatile.
New syntax: C/C++ fixed-width types (uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t), volatile bool, and Python bitwise mask & 0xFFFF.
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.8: Cycle Frequency, Period & Binary Bits
Lesson S0.7: Arduino Uno Digital I/O & INPUT_PULLUP
Lesson 03.2: 3-Phase Brushless Motors, Pole Pairs & 90-Degree Electrical Torque Lead
Lesson 03.3: Track 02 + 03 Integration Micro-Lab — Read Dual Encoders to Compute 2-Link End-Effector Position

sections.h: Idea 1: Fixed-width C/C++ integers (uint8_t, uint16_t, int16_t) and modular rollover subtraction
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Integer (computer science) ("Standard integer types") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Integer (computer science) and Value and representation.
What to skip: Skip 128-bit mainframe formats.
Key takeaway: In Python, integers grow to any size automatically, but in microcontroller C/C++ (#include ) every variable has a fixed hardware bit width: uint8_t holds $0..255$ ($1\text{ byte}$), uint16_t holds $0..65535$ ($2\text{ bytes}$), and signed int16_t holds $-32768..+32767$. Like a 4-wheel mechanical odometer that rolls from 65535 back to 0, unsigned subtraction modulo $2^{16}$ ((uint16_t)(now - prev) in C, or (now - prev) & 0xFFFF in Python) always gives the exact elapsed ticks across a rollover ((4 - 65530) & 0xFFFF == 10).
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Binary Number System [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review $2^{16} = 65536$.

sections.h: Idea 2: Hardware timer Interrupt Service Routines ($1\text{ kHz}$ ISR), volatile flags, and why delay() ruins $\Delta t$
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Interrupt ("Overview" & "Interrupt handler") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Interrupt and Overview.
What to skip: Skip PCIe message-signaled interrupts.
Key takeaway: Calling delay(1) + Serial.println() inside loop() stretches your loop period $\Delta t$ from $1.0\text{ ms}$ to $6.0+\text{ ms}$ whenever the serial buffer fills up, causing velocity estimates $\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}$ to spike wildly! Instead, a hardware timer peripheral counts clock pulses in silicon and triggers an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) at an exact $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$). Any flag shared between an ISR and loop() (volatile bool tick_1khz = false;) must use the C keyword volatile so the compiler never caches the variable in a CPU register and always reads fresh SRAM.
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Volatile (computer programming) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Volatile (computer programming) and In C and C++.

When transitioning from Python to embedded C/C++ firmware, keep this side-by-side translation table in mind for fixed-width integers (uint16_t), volatile ISR flags, and hardware timer ISR loops:
Why does delay(1) ruin control loops? Suppose a motor rotates steadily by $\Delta \theta = 0.020\text{ rad}$ every millisecond. In a deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer ISR ($\Delta t = 0.0010\text{ s}$), measured velocity is $\omega = \frac{0.020}{0.0010} = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$ on every single tick. By contrast, if a slow Serial.println() stalls loop() so actual elapsed time stretches to $\Delta t_{\text{actual}} = 0.0050\text{ s}$ while your code still divides by nominal $\Delta t_{\text{nom}} = 0.0010\text{ s}$ after the shaft moved $5\times$ farther ($\Delta \theta = 0.100\text{ rad}$), the computed velocity explodes to $100.0\text{ rad/s}$ ($5\times$ false spike!). Keep your ISR short, mark shared flags volatile, and never call blocking serial prints inside a real-time loop.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete uint16_tick_delta (TODO 1) to verify rollover-safe 16-bit timer subtraction, velocity_from_step (TODO 2) to quantify blocking serial jitter vs. a $1\text{ kHz}$ timer ISR, and diagnose_uint8_wrap_bug (TODO 3, R4 debug exercise: classic uint8_t loop/packet counter wrapping at 255 -> 0 when counting past 255).
What is real-hardware only: Probing the $1000.0\ \mu\text{s}$ rising edges of a microcontroller debug pin with a hardware logic analyzer.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Save as c_types_and_timer_isr.py and run python3 c_types_and_timer_isr.py:

When TODO 1, TODO 2, and TODO 3 are completed, running the script prints:
Spacing is not graded here: the expected lines line their numbers up because the print statements pin each field to a fixed width ({prev_t:5d}, {now_t:5d}, {dt_ticks:3d}), so the -> delta= column starts in the same place whether the counter reads 1250 or wraps back to 4. The runner ignores indentation, column padding and blank lines and compares your words and numbers, so dropping those widths keeps a correct solution passing; the rollover arithmetic itself is checked by the instructor behavioral tests.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, mask the difference with & 0xFFFF so negative differences wrap modulo $65536$ just like a C uint16_t. In TODO 2, compute d_theta = true_omega_rad_s actual_dt_s and divide by assumed_dt_s.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Forgetting volatile on a variable modified inside an ISR: If you write bool tick_1khz = false; without volatile, the C++ compiler's -O2 optimizer sees that while (!tick_1khz) never changes tick_1khz inside loop() and caches false in a CPU register forever—hanging your robot at startup! Always write volatile bool tick_1khz = false;.
Calling Serial.println() or delay() inside an ISR: An ISR must finish in a few microseconds. Never put slow serial prints or delay() inside the interrupt handler; set a volatile flag or copy data into a buffer and let loop() handle low-priority logging.

16-bit unsigned rollover: A 16-bit hardware microsecond timer (uint16_t, range 0..65535) was at prev = 65500 and is now at now = 64 after wrapping around once. How many microseconds elapsed?
Answer
(64 - 65500) & 0xFFFF $= 65536 - 65500 + 64 = \mathbf{100\text{ ticks}}$ ($100\ \mu\text{s}$).
Why volatile is mandatory: What bug occurs in C/C++ if an ISR sets flag = true and main() checks if (flag) on a variable declared without volatile?
Answer
The compiler may optimize away memory reads in main() by caching the old value (false) in a CPU register, so main() never sees the ISR update.

Microcontroller C/C++ uses fixed-width integers (uint8_t, uint16_t, int16_t, uint32_t), where unsigned modular subtraction (now - prev) & 0xFFFF is immune to counter wrap-around.
A $1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer ISR guarantees an exact $\Delta t = 1.000\text{ ms}$ control step, and shared ISR variables must be declared volatile.

pages.title: Packed Binary Telemetry Structs (struct.pack), CRC-8 & UART Bandwidth Budgets

sections.t:
Pack and unpack a compact binary telemetry struct between microcontroller C/C++ (struct __attribute__((packed))) and Python (struct.pack / struct.unpack), verify 8N1 UART serial bandwidth budgets ($10\text{ bits/byte}$), and protect each frame with a 0xAA sync byte and a true polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) checksum that catches multi-bit errors that fool a simple XOR checksum.
New ideas (max 2):
Packed binary C structs (__attribute__((packed)) and Python struct.pack/unpack) and 8N1 UART bandwidth budgets: Why sending raw binary numbers (<BHHfB, $10\text{ bytes} = 100\text{ bits}$ at 8N1) is $5\times$ smaller than ASCII text, and why a $20\text{-byte}$ frame at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($200\text{ kbit/s}$) overflows a $115.2\text{ kbaud}$ link and requires $\ge 230.4\text{ kbaud}$ (or $500\text{ kbaud}$).
Sync headers (0xAA), byte-wise XOR checksums, and polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) for corrupted-frame rejection: Why a naive byte-wise XOR checksum (xor_chk ^= b) is blinded when the same bit flips in two different bytes, and how a shift-register CRC-8 (0x07 polynomial) catches both single-bit and paired two-byte bit flips.
New syntax: Python import struct, struct.pack("<BHHf", ...), struct.unpack("<BHHfB", ...), and bitwise shift/XOR (<<, ^).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: Packed binary C structs (__attribute__((packed)) and Python struct.pack/unpack) and 8N1 UART bandwidth budgets
sections.t:
Primary resource: Python 3 Documentation — struct — Interpret bytes as packed binary data [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Functions and Exceptions and Format Characters (< little-endian, B=uint8_t, H=uint16_t, f=float).
What to skip: Skip native @ pointer alignment tables.
Key takeaway: On a standard 8N1 UART serial link, every byte requires $10\text{ bits}$ on the wire ($1\text{ start bit} + 8\text{ data bits} + 1\text{ stop bit}$). At rate $f_{\text{tx}}\text{ Hz}$, a frame of $N_{\text{bytes}}$ demands a minimum raw wire bit rate of $R_{\text{req}} = 10 \cdot N_{\text{bytes}} \cdot f_{\text{tx}}$. At $1\text{ kHz}$, a $10\text{-byte}$ binary struct requires $100\text{ kbit/s}$ (fitting inside $115{,}200\text{ baud}$ at $86.8\%$ utilization), whereas a $20\text{-byte}$ binary struct at $1\text{ kHz}$ requires $200\text{ kbit/s}$—which exceeds $115{,}200\text{ baud}$ ($173.6\%$ utilization, guaranteeing TX buffer overflow and dropped frames) and therefore requires $\ge 230{,}400\text{ baud}$ or $500{,}000\text{ baud}$!
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — C data types ("Basic types") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Compare byte widths of uint8_t, uint16_t, and float.

sections.h: Idea 2: Sync headers (0xAA), byte-wise XOR checksums, and polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) for corrupted-frame rejection
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Cyclic redundancy check ("Computation") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Introduction and Computation.
What to skip: Skip Galois field ring proofs.
Key takeaway: A simple byte-wise XOR checksum (xor_chk ^= b) catches any single-bit flip, but if motor PWM noise flips the same bit position in two different bytes (b[3] ^= 1 and b[5] ^= 1), the two XOR flips cancel out (1 ^ 1 = 0) and the corrupted frame slips through! A true polynomial CRC-8 (crc8_ccitt with generator polynomial $x^8 + x^2 + x + 1 \implies \text{0x07}$) shifts and mixes bits across every byte position, catching single-bit flips, burst errors, and paired two-byte bit flips.
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Checksum ("Simple checksums") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Contrast simple longitudinal parity (XOR) checksums with cyclic redundancy checks.

In C/C++ firmware on an ESP32 or STM32, marking a struct with __attribute__((packed)) prevents the compiler from inserting hidden alignment padding bytes between fields, so its memory layout in SRAM matches Python's little-endian struct.pack("<BHHfB", ...) format string (< = little-endian byte order, B = uint8_t, H = uint16_t, f = 32-bit IEEE-754 float) byte-for-byte:
Before claiming "zero dropped frames" at $f_{\text{tx}} = 1000\text{ Hz}$, always check the 8N1 UART bandwidth budget ($10\text{ bits/byte}$ including start and stop bits) so the serial wire rate stays safely below your configured baud rate:
A $10\text{-byte}$ binary struct at $1\text{ kHz}$ requires $100\text{ kbit/s}$ ($86.8\%$ of $115{,}200\text{ baud}$, taking $868.1\ \mu\text{s}$ per frame), whereas a $20\text{-byte}$ binary struct at $1\text{ kHz}$ requires $200\text{ kbit/s}$ ($173.6\%$ of $115{,}200\text{ baud}$), which continuously overflows the transmit ring buffer unless you increase the UART speed to $\ge 230{,}400\text{ baud}$ or $500{,}000\text{ baud}$. Finally, while a simple byte-wise XOR checksum (chk ^= b) catches single-bit errors, appending a shift-register polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) (crc8_ccitt) mixes bit positions across every payload byte so paired two-byte bit flips are immediately rejected.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete crc8_ccitt (TODO 1), pack_telemetry_10b (TODO 2), and uart_bandwidth_ok (TODO 3) to verify a 10-byte <BHHfB frame, prove that crc8_ccitt catches a paired 2-byte bit flip that fools an XOR checksum, and check 8N1 UART bandwidth limits at $1\text{ kHz}$.
What is real-hardware only: Electrical crosstalk from unshielded motor phase wires flipping physical bits on a $3.3\text{ V}$ UART line.

sections.t: Save as packed_telemetry_and_crc.py and run python3 packed_telemetry_and_crc.py:
When TODO 1, TODO 2, and TODO 3 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, XOR each byte into crc, then shift left 8 times, XORing with 0x07 whenever bit 7 (crc & 0x80) is 1. In TODO 2, pack "<BHHf" and append struct.pack("<B", crc8_ccitt(body)). In TODO 3, multiply frame_bytes 10 rate_hz for 8N1 serial framing.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Calling a simple byte-wise XOR (crc ^= b) a "CRC-8": A byte-wise XOR is a longitudinal parity checksum—if the same bit flips in two bytes, the errors cancel out (1 ^ 1 = 0). Use a shift-register polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) so bit positions mix across bytes.
Streaming a 20-byte frame at $1\text{ kHz}$ over $115{,}200\text{ baud}$: At 8N1 ($10\text{ bits/byte}$), $20\text{ bytes} \times 10 \times 1000\text{ Hz} = 200{,}000\text{ bit/s}$, which exceeds $115{,}200\text{ baud}$ and continuously drops frames! Use $\ge 230{,}400\text{ baud}$ or $500{,}000\text{ baud}$.

8N1 UART wire bit rate: What minimum raw bit rate (in $\text{bit/s}$) is required to transmit a $20\text{-byte}$ binary telemetry packet at $1\text{ kHz}$ over an 8N1 serial link ($10\text{ bits/byte}$), and why does $115{,}200\text{ baud}$ drop frames?
Answer
$20\text{ bytes} \times 10\text{ bits/byte} \times 1000\text{ Hz} = \mathbf{200{,}000\text{ bit/s}}$ ($200\text{ kbit/s}$). Because $200{,}000 > 115{,}200$, the TX ring buffer fills faster than the UART shift register can drain it, dropping $>40\%$ of frames unless the baud rate is raised to $\ge 230{,}400$ or $500{,}000\text{ baud}$.
XOR checksum vs. polynomial CRC-8 (0x07): Why does flipping bit 0 in byte 3 AND bit 0 in byte 5 fool xor_checksum, while crc8_ccitt catches it?
Answer
In a byte-wise XOR checksum, bit 0 of every byte is XORed into the same column (1 ^ 1 = 0), so paired bit flips cancel out. In crc8_ccitt, each byte is shifted left 8 times and mixed with generator polynomial 0x07, spreading a bit flip in byte 3 across different bit positions before byte 5 arrives.

Packed binary C structs (__attribute__((packed)) and Python struct.pack("<BHHfB", ...)) cut serial payload size by $5\times$ compared to ASCII text, and checking the 8N1 UART bandwidth budget ($10\text{ bits/byte}$) prevents TX buffer overflows.
Pairing a 0xAA sync header with a polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) catches both single-bit noise and multi-byte paired bit flips that fool a naive XOR checksum.

pages.title: Python-to-C Bridge (Part 3) — C Structs as Labeled Boxes & Pointers as Box Addresses

sections.t:
Complete our 3-part Python-to-C Bridge (04.1 Fixed-Width Ints + Overflow $\to$ 04.2 Bitwise Masks + CRC-8 $\to$ 04.3 Structs + Pointers) by using only two mental pictures: a C struct is a labeled box that holds a joint's variables together, and a pointer (JointState p = &joint) is the memory address of that box so a function can update the original box in place (p->pos_rad = ...) without copying it—and diagnose the classic R4 pass-by-value bug where a C function modifies a temporary copy that vanishes upon return.
New ideas (max 2):
C structs as labeled multi-field boxes for grouping joint state: Grouping enc_count, pos_rad, vel_rad_s, and fault_flags inside struct JointState instead of scattering loose global variables (q1_pos, q1_vel, q2_pos, q2_vel).
Pointers (, &, ->) as box addresses for in-place updates and pass-by-value bug diagnosis: Why void update_joint(JointState j) in C modifies a throwaway copy (leaving the caller's struct frozen at 0.0), while passing the box's address void update_joint(JointState j) with &joint1 updates the original box in place via j->pos_rad.
New syntax: C struct JointState { ... };, address-of &box, pointer parameter JointState p, and arrow field access p->field (mirrored in Python via a dict/object reference vs. shallow copy).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: C structs as labeled multi-field boxes for grouping joint state
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — struct (C programming language)) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Declaration and Pointers.
What to skip: Skip bit-field compiler packing subtleties.
Key takeaway: When a robot has 2, 4, or 6 joints, creating separate variables (joint1_count, joint1_pos, joint2_count, joint2_pos...) quickly turns into copy-paste spaghetti. A C struct is simply a labeled box with named compartments (joint1.enc_count, joint1.pos_rad, joint1.vel_rad_s, joint1.cmd_nm). You define the box blueprint once (struct JointBox), and stamp out one box per robot joint (JointBox shoulder; JointBox elbow;).
Alternative resource: Python 3 Documentation — Data Structures ("Dictionaries") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Compare named key lookup in Python dicts to fixed-offset field access (box.pos_rad) in a C struct.

sections.h: Idea 2: Pointers (, &, ->) as box addresses for in-place updates and pass-by-value bug diagnosis
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Pointer (computer programming) ("C and C++")) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Formal description and C and C++.
What to skip: Skip dynamic malloc/free heap allocation—in real-time embedded control we never allocate heap memory inside a $1\text{ kHz}$ loop!
Key takeaway: You never need mysterious pointer arithmetic in beginner firmware—you only need three symbols:
&box ("Address of box"): Hands a function the street address where box lives in RAM instead of photocopying the entire box.
JointBox p ("Pointer parameter"): Declares that p holds the address of a JointBox.
p->pos_rad ("Follow the address arrow into the box"): Opens the original box at address p and reads or writes its pos_rad compartment in place!

Why do C/C++ robotics drivers use pointers (JointBox p) whenever a function updates a joint's state? Because by default, C passes structs by value—meaning it makes a temporary photocopy of the box and hands that copy to the function:
Keep these three rules in mind whenever you read or write embedded C/C++ joint drivers:
Direct struct variable (.) vs. struct pointer (->): When you hold the labeled box directly (JointBox shoulder;), access its compartments with a dot (shoulder.pos_rad). When a function receives the memory address of the box via a pointer parameter (JointBox p = &shoulder), follow the address arrow into the box using p->pos_rad.
Zero-copy speed inside a $1\text{ kHz}$ loop: Passing &shoulder copies only a single memory address ($4\text{ bytes}$ on a 32-bit STM32 or ESP32) instead of copying every float and integer field on the stack.
R4 Pass-by-Value Bug Diagnosis: If your joint struct stays frozen at 0.0 in loop() even though the math inside update_joint(...) is right, check the function header first: writing JointBox b instead of JointBox p means your function updated a temporary photocopy that vanished on return!

What is simulated and in which tool: Runs 100% in Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner) to model a C JointBox struct, contrast the R4 pass-by-value copy bug against in-place pointer-style updates, and update a 2-joint arm state array.
What is real-hardware only: Inspecting raw SRAM addresses (0x20000100) in an STM32 debugger watch window.

Forgetting in a C function parameter (void update(JointBox b) instead of void update(JointBox p)): C copies the entire struct on entry and discards the copy on return, leaving the caller's struct unchanged.
Using . instead of -> on a C struct pointer (p.pos_rad instead of p->pos_rad): In C/C++, p->field dereferences the pointer p and accesses field in one step.

In C, if JointBox shoulder; is a struct variable and void reset_joint(JointBox p) expects a pointer to a JointBox, how do you call reset_joint?
Answer 1
Pass the address of shoulder using the & operator: reset_joint(&shoulder);.
Inside void reset_joint(JointBox p), how do you set the pos_rad compartment inside the caller's box to 0.0f?
Answer 2
Use the arrow operator: p->pos_rad = 0.0f;.

pages.title: From Python to C/Arduino: Fixed-Width Types, Bitwise Masks, Structs & Pointers

sections.t: Python integers grow arbitrarily large and never overflow, but microcontroller C/C++ variables occupy a fixed number of bits (uint8_t, int16_t, uint32_t, float) in hardware registers. Before writing real-time timer interrupts and binary serial telemetry in Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05), you must know how fixed-width integers wrap around, how bitwise masks (|, &, ~, <<) flip single register bits without corrupting neighbors, and how struct pointers pass data with zero copy overhead. Already know this? Take the Skip test in section 7 first.

When you transition from desktop Python to microcontroller firmware, you first meet the Arduino / Wiring execution model (void setup() runs once at power-on to configure pins with pinMode(pin, OUTPUT); void loop() repeats forever calling digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) or analogWrite(pin, pwm)). Imagine moving from an infinite notepad (Python) to a mechanical odometer with only four digit wheels (uint16_t, which holds 0 to 65535). If your odometer is at 65535 and clicks forward by 1, it doesn't add a fifth wheel—it wraps cleanly back to 0 (integer wrap-around). Next, when packing status flags or configuration bits into an 8-bit or 32-bit C integer, think of that integer as a row of individual toggle switches: you use a bitwise stencil (mask) 1U << n with bitwise OR (|), AND (&), and NOT (~) to set, clear, or test one flag bit without disturbing its neighbors. Finally, a C struct is a molded tray that holds several related variables side-by-side in memory, and a pointer () passes the address of that tray on a sticky note instead of copying the entire tray on every function call.

C-for-Python Syntax Bridge, Arduino Execution Model (setup() / loop()) & Fixed-Width Integer Types ():
C/C++ Syntax for Python Programmers:
Explicit Types & Semicolons (;): Every variable declaration states its fixed hardware type (uint16_t count = 0;, float vel = 3.25f;), and every statement ends with ;.
Braces ({ ... }) & Comments (//): Code blocks use curly braces { ... } instead of indentation; comments start with //.
Functions & Loops: int32_t add(int32_t a, int32_t b) { return a + b; } declares return and argument types; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { ... } is the C equivalent of for i in range(N):.
Firmware Entry (setup() / loop()) & Integer Bounds: Firmware entry starts at reset, runs void setup() once, and repeats void loop() forever. Unlike Python's arbitrary-precision integers, an $N$-bit unsigned C integer uintN_t stores values in $[0, 2^N - 1]$, and a two's-complement signed integer intN_t stores $[-2^{N-1}, 2^{N-1} - 1]$:
uint8_t: $[0, 255]$ ($1\text{ byte}$); int16_t: $[-32768, 32767]$ ($2\text{ bytes}$); uint32_t: $[0, 4294967295]$ ($4\text{ bytes}$); float: IEEE-754 single precision ($4\text{ bytes}$).
Computing unsigned tick difference (uint16_t)(now - prev) modulo $2^{16} = 65536$: substituting now = 4 and prev = 65530 yields (4 - 65530) & 0xFFFF = 10 ticks elapsed across rollover.
Bitwise Masks and Shifts (|, &, ~, >): For bit index $n \in \{0, \dots, 31\}$ in an unsigned status or configuration word $W$:
Set bit $n$ to 1: $W \leftarrow W \mid (1\text{U} \ll n)$.
Clear bit $n$ to 0: $W \leftarrow W \mathbin{\&} \sim(1\text{U} \ll n)$.
Toggle bit $n$: $W \leftarrow W \oplus (1\text{U} \ll n)$.
Test bit $n$: $\text{is-set} = (W \gg n) \mathbin{\&} 1\text{U}$.
Substituting $W = \text{0x01}$ (0b00000001), setting bit $3$ ($1 \ll 3 = 8 = \text{0x08}$) gives $W = \text{0x09}$ (0b00001001).
Structs and Pass-by-Pointer ( and ->): Grouping fields in struct MotorState { int16_t count; float vel_rad_s; }; and passing MotorState s passes a single memory address (4 or 8 bytes) so s->count += 1 (-> dereferences a struct pointer, equivalent to (s).count) mutates the caller's struct in-place and packs cleanly into binary frames (struct.pack("<Hhf", ...)).

Predict first (before you run it): The block starts a uint16_t counter at 65530 and reads 4 after the rollover, starts a register at 0b0000_0001, sets bit 3, then clears bit 0, and packs (1000, -512, 3.25) with struct.pack("<Hhf", ...). Commit before you run it: (1) how many ticks elapsed across the wrap; (2) the register's decimal value after those two edits, and what the bit-3 test returns; (3) the packed frame's length in bytes, and whether 1000, -512 and 3.25 survive the round trip. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: an elapsed count of $-65526$ is the raw Python difference before the $2^{16}$ mask, which is exactly the bug elapsed_unsigned exists to catch; and a register value of $9$ after the clear means the ~ was dropped, leaving reg &= (1 << 0) as a no-op.
Simulate 16-bit encoder counter wrap-around, bitwise GPIO register set/clear operations, and packing an 8-byte C telemetry struct (<Hhf: uint16_t, int16_t, float) using Python's struct module.
Expected output:

Start with register value reg = 0x5A (0b01011010). Write a Python expression that sets bit 6 (1 << 6) and clears bit 3 (~(1 << 3)), and verify the resulting integer is 0x52 (82 in decimal, 0b01010010). Bit 6 is already set in 0x5A, so setting it changes nothing - the read-modify-write form has to keep that neighbour, not toggle it.
If your result differs: Check that bit indices are 0-based from the least-significant (rightmost) bit: bit 0 has weight $2^0 = 1$, bit 3 has weight $2^3 = 8$, and bit 6 has weight $2^6 = 64$.

sections.h: Graded package - the width, the mask and the frame
sections.t:
exercises/04-embedded.T1.04a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: int_range (the signed and unsigned bounds), wrap_uint (the width mask), elapsed_unsigned (subtract, then mask), apply_bits ($W \mid \text{set} \mathbin{\&} \sim\text{clear}$), bit_is_set, and pack_telemetry/unpack_telemetry for the 8-byte <Hhf frame. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
38 tests. The register edit is checked at the exercise's 0x5A -> 0x52 and the Skip test's 0x0F -> 11, the rollover at the worked example's 10 and the Skip test's 9, the frame at its exact little-endian bytes (e8 03 00 fe 00 00 50 40), and every guard at the boundary one past its own range. The transfer suite runs the plant's own numbers: its 12-bit encoder wraps at 4096 counts and the difference across that wrap is 16 counts, its 1 kHz tick is a uint16 millisecond counter where the 1000-tick run is 1000 ms, its $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp is 2500 mN$\cdot$m inside an int16_t, and a config word keeps its neighbours when only the low twelve bits move. Five planted faults - elapsed_no_mask, clear_forgets_the_tilde, int_range_signed_off_by_one, wrap_masks_a_byte, pack_big_endian - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Variables, Loops & Functions) and 00-foundations.T1.00b (Arrays & Indexing).
Core Concepts to Review First: Fixed-width integer types (uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t), bitwise set/clear/toggle/extract idioms (|= (1U << n), &= ~(1U << n)), and C structs/pointers in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
