sections.h: Four sittings - do not take this page in one go
sections.t:
The 3.5 hours are one page but four different skills, and the jump inside it is the largest in Track 04 Tier 1: a new language, a fixed width, a register and a wire frame. Keep every topic; split the sitting. Each row is 40-50 minutes and ends with a green test subset, so stopping between rows is a finished state rather than an abandoned one. The workbench entry keeps every TODO, and the four commands below run the same suite in slices - -k matches a test class, so no file is copied and every slice still runs from the same starter.
Sitting 3 has no Python hole because C's compiler, not CPython, owns that fact. Put this in frame.cpp and run g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Werror frame.cpp -o frame && ./frame:
It prints 8 12 8 and PaddedState count at 8, offsetof(MotorState, vel_rad_s) = 4: H h f needs no padding because 2 + 2 lands the float on its own 4-byte boundary, while H f h loses two bytes before the float and two more at the end - and the packed frame stays 8 either way. That is the whole of §8's second Common-mistakes row, seen rather than memorised: the field order is what decides the padding, which is why the Python package packs "<Hhf" by hand instead of trusting a native layout.

Expected numbers (the answer): 0x5A with bit 6 set and bit 3 cleared is 0x52 (82); the Skip test's 0x0F with bit 2 cleared is 11; (uint16_t)(4 - 65530) = 10; the 12-bit encoder's 8 - 4088 is 16 counts; the <Hhf frame of (1000, -512, 3.25) is 8 bytes, e8 03 00 fe 00 00 50 40.

Width first, value second. uint16_t holds 0..65535 and int16_t holds -32768..32767; both bounds come from bits alone, so write them as shifts of 1, not as remembered constants.
The mask is the width. 216 - 1 is 0xFFFF and 212 - 1 is 0x0FFF, so & (2bits - 1) keeps exactly the bits a uintN_t keeps - hard-coding 0xFF makes the 12-bit encoder 4096 come back as 0.
Subtract before you mask. 4 - 65530 is -65526 in Python; -65526 & 0xFFFF is the 10 ticks that actually elapsed. Masking each reading first and then subtracting gives the same 10, but subtracting and never masking gives -65526.
Clearing is an AND with an inverted mask. ~(1 << 3) is 0xF7, so 0x5A & 0xF7 keeps bits 1, 4, 6 and clears only bit 3 - 0x5A & 0x08 instead keeps bit 3 and wipes the rest.
What the suite refuses. A width of zero, or past 64 bits, in int_range and a zero-width elapsed_unsigned; a negative mask in apply_bits; a bit index past 31 in bit_is_set; a tick past 65535 or a count past 32767 in pack_telemetry, which has no room for them; and an unpack_telemetry frame that is not exactly 8 bytes - each raises ValueError instead of masking the overflow away.

Printed: reg=0x52 (bit6=1, bit3=0) | skip reg=11 | u16 delta=10 | 12-bit encoder delta=16, then frame=e8 03 00 fe 00 00 50 40 | tick=1000 count=-512 vel=3.25 rad/s.
On the shared arm. The package's Transfer suite runs the same wrapping on the plant's own encoder and clamp:

Inject the clear_forgets_the_tilde fault the graded package names, and diagnose it from the register value alone:
Inject: drop the ~ — write reg &= (1 << 3) to clear bit 3 of the exercise's reg = 0x5A (0b01011010) instead of reg &= ~(1 << 3).
Symptom: the register reads 0x5A & 0x08 = 0x08 — decimal 8, not 82 — so bit 3 is still set and the other three set bits (1, 4, 6) have been wiped out. On a live peripheral register the same line silently clears every other configuration bit in the word.
Diagnose: the symptom is always "too many bits changed", never "the wrong bit". & (1 << n) keeps bit $n$ and discards the rest, while & ~(1 << n) keeps everything except bit $n$; an answer in the single digits where a two-digit value was expected therefore means the mask was never inverted, and it rules out a wrong bit index, which would disturb exactly one bit and leave the others alone.
Fix: restore reg &= ~(1 << 3), which gives 0x5A & 0xF7 = 0x52 = 82, with the bit-6 neighbour still set and bit 3 cleared — the exercise's assertion passing, and the same guarantee a live read-modify-write needs.

Test the C equivalent directly in the browser on the Wokwi ESP32/STM32 Simulator (resources/open-source-toolchains.md), run the Python bit-exact verification script above, or compile and run native C++20 on your workstation using the canonical host g++ command (taught once here and used for all C++ labs):
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05), the exact struct.pack("<Hhf", ...) layout matches the __attribute__((packed)) C struct transmitted over the microcontroller's USB-UART bridge (flashed via pio run -t upload in 04-embedded-and-realtime/README.md §1.2):

pages.title: Non-Blocking millis()/micros() State Machines, Hardware Interrupts (ISRs) & volatile

sections.t: This is the final bridge module in the Track 04 Tier 1 ladder before Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05). Calling delay(100) freezes the CPU for $100\text{ ms}$—during that time your robot is blind to encoder pulses, limit switches, and PID loops. Replacing delay() with a non-blocking tick scheduler (now_us - last_us >= PERIOD_US), an enum finite state machine, and a hardware timer Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) with volatile shared variables gives your robot deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ reflexes. Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

Imagine a chef cooking three dishes at once. A delay() loop is like staring at a pot of water for 10 minutes with your eyes glued to it while the toast burns and the doorbell goes unanswered. A non-blocking tick scheduler (micros() - last_us >= 1000) is glancing at the wall clock on every pass through the kitchen: if $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ has elapsed, you stir the pot for $5\ \mu\text{s}$ and immediately check the next station. A hardware interrupt (ISR) is a smoke alarm wired directly to your reflex nervous system—the instant the hardware timer hits zero, the CPU pauses whatever background line it was running, executes the short ISR function in a few microseconds, sets a flag on a shared whiteboard, and resumes the background loop. Marking that flag volatile tells the C++ compiler: "Do not cache this variable in a register—another context (the ISR) can change it behind your back at any nanosecond!"

Non-Blocking Rollover-Safe Tick Scheduler: Given unsigned 32-bit microsecond timer now_us and period PERIOD_US = 1000 ($1\text{ kHz}$), the condition:
executes without blocking and without cumulative phase drift. Substituting $t_{\text{last}} = 2000\ \mu\text{s}$, $T_{\text{period}} = 1000\ \mu\text{s}$, and $t_{\text{now}} = 3015\ \mu\text{s}$ triggers execution and advances $t_{\text{last}}$ to $3000\ \mu\text{s}$ (preserving the exact $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ grid).
Finite State Machine (enum + switch): An actuator controller defines explicit states enum class State { IDLE, HOMING, RUN, FAULT }; and transitions cleanly on each tick (e.g., FAULT forces pwm = 0.0 immediately if current exceeds $I_{\max}$ or E-stop is pressed).
Hardware Timer ISR Budget & volatile: If a timer ISR fires at frequency $f_{\text{isr}} = 1/T_{\text{isr}}$ and takes execution time $t_{\text{exec}}$, its CPU utilization fraction is:
Substituting $t_{\text{exec}} = 45\ \mu\text{s}$ at $f_{\text{isr}} = 1000\text{ Hz}$ ($T_{\text{isr}} = 1000\ \mu\text{s}$) gives $U_{\text{isr}} = 45 / 1000 = 4.5\%$. Any variable written inside an ISR and read in loop() must be declared volatile.

Predict first (before you run it): The loop below runs $10{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$ of a $1\text{ kHz}$ control task and a $100\text{ Hz}$ telemetry task, with the state machine starting at IDLE and pos_rad = -0.05, gaining $0.01$ on every HOMING tick. Before you run it, commit to three numbers: how many control runs and how many telemetry runs fire in that window, and which tick carries the HOMING -> RUN switch. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: the control count must be the window divided by the $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ period and not one more, so $11$ means the deadline at $t = 0$ was counted as a run, and the telemetry count cannot be the same as the control count because its period is ten times longer; and the switch to RUN cannot happen in the same pass that leaves IDLE, so a RUN on the first tick means two transitions ran in one pass.
Simulate $10\text{ ms}$ ($10{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$) of a microcontroller running a $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1000\ \mu\text{s}$) control task and a $100\text{ Hz}$ ($10{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$) telemetry task concurrently alongside an IDLE -> HOMING -> RUN -> FAULT state machine with zero delay() calls.
Expected output:

Calculate the maximum allowable ISR execution time $t_{\text{exec,max}}$ in microseconds ($\mu\text{s}$) if a $f_{\text{isr}} = 10\text{ kHz}$ ($T_{\text{isr}} = 100\ \mu\text{s}$) current-loop ISR must consume no more than $U_{\max} = 25\%$ ($0.25$) of total CPU time so that $75\%$ remains for telemetry and state machines. Verify $t_{\text{exec,max}} = 25.0\ \mu\text{s}$.
If your result differs: Multiply the period $T_{\text{isr}} = 10^6 / 10000 = 100\ \mu\text{s}$ by $0.25$ ($100 \times 0.25 = 25.0\ \mu\text{s}$).

sections.h: Graded package - the scheduler, the ISR budget and the latched fault
sections.t:
exercises/04-embedded.T1.04b/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds eight holes: elapsed_us (subtract first, then mask to the timer width), tick_due, next_deadline_us (advance on the grid, never resynchronise to now), isr_utilization_pct (the $10^{-6}$), max_isr_exec_us, fault_latency_us, ticks_in and fsm_step (FAULT latches and forces pwm = 0). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
45 tests. The elapsed time is checked at the $3015 - 2000 = 1015\ \mu\text{s}$ worked example and across both wraps ($12 - 65520$ is $28$ on a 16-bit counter and $4294901788$ on a 32-bit one), so a difference taken without the mask fails; the deadline is checked at exactly one period, so > instead of >= loses that tick; the $45\ \mu\text{s}$/$1\text{ kHz}$ utilization, the $3.5\%$ Skip test, the $25\ \mu\text{s}$ exercise budget and the $150\ \mu\text{s}$ debounce latency each fail on a dropped $10^{-6}$ or a percentage read as a fraction; and the FSM is checked at IDLE -> HOMING -> RUN, at the current limit itself (no fault) and after the current recovers, so a FAULT that clears itself fails. The transfer suite runs the plant's own clock: plant.DT is the $1\text{ kHz}$ period, one second is plant.TICKS ticks, a $10\text{ kHz}$ loop fits ten times per tick with $975\ \mu\text{s}$ left over, and the uint32 wrap lands back on the same $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ grid. Five planted faults - rollover_not_masked, tick_due_uses_greater_than, isr_microseconds_dropped, isr_budget_ignores_percent, fsm_fault_not_latched - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a–00-foundations.T1.00c (Loops, Arrays & SI Timing Units).
Prerequisite Bridge Modules: 01-electronics.T1.01b (PWM Control) and 04-embedded.T1.04a (Bitwise Masks & volatile).
Core Concepts to Review First: Non-blocking timer ISR execution vs. delay(), enum finite-state machines (IDLE, HOMING, CLOSED_LOOP, FAULT_STOP), and packed binary telemetry (struct.pack/unpack + XOR checksum) in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Python struct Binary Packing Docs (docs.python.org), Samek Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, and Track 04 §1.1–1.3 (04-embedded-and-realtime/README.md).

Expected numbers (the answer): $t_{\text{exec,max}} = 25.0\ \mu\text{s}$ at $25\%$ of a $10\text{ kHz}$ period; a $45\ \mu\text{s}$ ISR at $1\text{ kHz}$ costs $4.5\%$ ($3.5\%$ at $30\ \mu\text{s}$); three samples at $20\text{ kHz}$ debounce in $150\ \mu\text{s}$; $3015 - 2000 = 1015\ \mu\text{s}$; the same $12 - 65520$ difference is $28$ on a 16-bit counter and $4294901788$ on a 32-bit one.

Mask after subtracting, not before. 12 - 65520 is -65508; -65508 & 0xFFFF is 28, and -65508 & 0xFFFFFFFF is 4294901788. The mask belongs to the counter width, so bits is an argument, not a constant 32.
A deadline advances on its own grid. next_deadline_us(1000, 1000) is 2000, not now + period: resynchronising to the late reading is what lets a 1 kHz loop drift to 999 Hz.
Percentages and microseconds cancel cleanly. $100 \times t_{\text{exec}}/T_{\text{isr}} = 100 \times t_{\text{exec}}\times 10^{-6}\times f_{\text{isr}}$; the budget comes back with u_max_pct / 100 because 25 means $0.25$.
FAULT is latched. Once current_a > i_max_a has set it, the next tick - current recovered, PWM requested - still returns ("FAULT", 0.0). Only HOMING waits on pos_rad < 0.0; the others advance.
What the suite refuses. A zero period in tick_due, next_deadline_us or ticks_in; a timer width outside 1..32 bits in elapsed_us; a submission budget outside 0..100 percent in max_isr_exec_us; an isr_utilization_pct whose ISR is longer than its period, or whose frequency is zero; a zero debounce in fault_latency_us; an unknown state or a duty above one in fsm_step; and a negative duration anywhere - each raises ValueError.

Printed: budget=25.0 us at 10 kHz (25%) | util(45 us @ 1 kHz)=4.5% | debounce(3 @ 20 kHz)=150 us, then elapsed(3015-2000)=1015 us | 16-bit wrap(12-65520)=28 | IDLE->HOMING | over-limit->FAULT.
On the shared arm. The package's Transfer suite schedules the plant's own clock:

Inject: replace the rollover-safe comparison with an absolute one, if now_us >= last_us + 1000:, keeping last_us += 1000 and the $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ period.
Symptom: everything is correct for the first $2^{32}\ \mu\text{s} = 4294.97\ \text{s} \approx 71.6\ \text{min}$, then the control task stops dead: with last_us = 4_294_966_000 and the counter wrapped to now_us = 1200, the two stamps are $2496\ \mu\text{s}$ apart, yet 1200 >= 4294967000 is false, so the task goes silent for the rest of that $71.6\ \text{min}$ window.
Diagnose: the failure starts at one specific moment since boot and only when the two timestamps straddle the wrap, so the period, the ISR and the state machine are all ruled out; the comparison assumes micros() never wraps, which holds for the first $71.6$ minutes and then stops holding.
Fix: subtract first in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, if ((now_us - last_us) & 0xFFFFFFFF) >= 1000:, and advance last_us by the period. The pair $4{,}294{,}966{,}000 \to 1200$ then reads $2496\ \mu\text{s}$, fires, and moves the deadline to $4{,}294{,}967{,}000$, so the $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ grid survives the wrap and a $10{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$ window still yields the ten control ticks the worked example asserts.

Open Real-Time Concurrency & ISR Preemption in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) or run a non-blocking micros() sketch on the Wokwi Simulator.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). When you transition to physical microcontroller hardware in Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05), follow the canonical First-Use PlatformIO Build/Flash (pio run -t upload), Linux udev Serial Permissions & Python struct.unpack Telemetry Walkthrough in 04-embedded-and-realtime/README.md (§1.1–1.3) and resources/open-source-toolchains.md (§0). There you will toggle a physical GPIO pin at entry and exit of the $1\text{ kHz}$ timer ISR on an ESP32 or STM32 Nucleo and measure pulse width $t_{\text{exec}}$ and period $T_{\text{isr}} = 1000\ \mu\text{s}$ with a logic analyzer (PulseView):
Pass/fail verification in simulation: ctrl_runs == 10, telem_runs == 1, and final_state == "FAULT".
Pass criteria: score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test to pass this module, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$) on the Ladder Gate test below to unlock Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05).

[Recall] [Concept: non_blocking_tick_scheduler] If a main loop calls delay(50) ($50\text{ ms}$) for an LED blink and delay(20) ($20\text{ ms}$) for a sensor wait, what is the maximum loop execution frequency $f_{\text{loop}} = \frac{1}{0.050 + 0.020}$ in $\text{Hz}$ (tolerance $\pm 0.01\text{ Hz}$)?
[Apply] [Concept: hardware_isr_and_volatile_contract] Compute the CPU utilization percentage $U_{\text{isr}}\% = 100 \times \frac{t_{\text{exec}}}{T_{\text{isr}}}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$) for a $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1000\ \mu\text{s}$) timer ISR that takes $t_{\text{exec}} = 35\ \mu\text{s}$.
[Transfer] [Concept: finite_state_machine_switch_enum] An actuator FSM running inside a $f_{\text{isr}} = 20\text{ kHz}$ ($T_{\text{isr}} = 50\ \mu\text{s}$) timer ISR transitions from RUN to FAULT (forcing pwm_cmd = 0.0) after $N_{\text{debounce}} = 3$ consecutive overcurrent samples. Compute the total fault-detection latency $t_{\text{fault}} = N_{\text{debounce}} / f_{\text{isr}}$ in microseconds ($\mu\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: hardware_isr_and_volatile_contract] Why must a global flag bool tick_ready written inside a hardware timer ISR and polled inside main() be declared volatile bool tick_ready in C/C++?
A. To make the variable use flash memory instead of RAM.
B. To prevent the compiler optimizer (-O2/-O3) from caching tick_ready in a CPU register and turning while (!tick_ready) into an infinite loop.
C. To automatically disable interrupts during math operations.
D. To convert the boolean into a 32-bit float.
[Spaced review -> 04-embedded.T1.04a — Concept: bitwise_masks_and_shifts] Compute the mask 1U << 5 as a decimal integer (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).

Covers the complete Track 04 Tier 1 bridge ladder (04-embedded.T1.04a $\to$ 04-embedded.T1.04b) before Step 1.5 (04-embedded.T1.05):
[Concept: c_fixed_width_integer_types_and_overflow] Compute the unsigned 16-bit elapsed tick difference (now - prev) & 0xFFFF when now = 12 and prev = 65520.
[Concept: c_fixed_width_integer_types_and_overflow] How many bytes does a packed struct { uint32_t tick_ms; int16_t enc_count; int16_t pwm_cmd; } occupy in memory?
[Concept: bitwise_masks_and_shifts] Starting with reg = 0x00, compute the decimal value of reg after setting bits 1 and 4 (reg |= (1 << 1) | (1 << 4)).
[Concept: bitwise_masks_and_shifts] Starting with reg = 0xFF (255), compute the decimal value of reg after clearing bit 7 (reg &= ~(1 << 7)).
[Concept: c_structs_and_pointers_pass_by_reference] Why do embedded C functions accept const TelemetryPacket pkt instead of passing TelemetryPacket pkt by value?
A. Passing a pointer copies only a 4-byte memory address instead of copying the entire struct onto the stack, while const prevents accidental modification.
B. C does not allow structs to be returned or passed by value.
C. Pointers automatically encrypt serial data.
D. Pointers run at twice the clock frequency.
[Concept: non_blocking_tick_scheduler] Why is last_us += PERIOD_US preferred over last_us = now_us in a periodic tick scheduler?
A. Because last_us += PERIOD_US advances the target deadline on an exact phase grid without accumulating positive timing drift when now_us is checked a few microseconds late.
B. Because = is slower than +=.
C. Because now_us is a floating-point number.
D. Because last_us = now_us causes a division by zero.
[Concept: finite_state_machine_switch_enum] Compute the number of $1\text{ kHz}$ control ticks executed over $0.25\text{ s}$ ($250{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$).
[Concept: hardware_isr_and_volatile_contract] Why must you never call Serial.println() or delay() inside a $1\text{ kHz}$ hardware timer ISR?
A. Because Serial.println() and delay() block for milliseconds (exceeding the $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ ISR period), starving the main loop and causing missed control ticks or watchdog resets.
B. Because ISRs can only use float variables.
C. Because timer ISRs run on the GPU.
D. Because Serial.println() resets the encoder counter to zero.

pages.title: PID Virtual Spring-Damper Control and Integrator Anti-Windup Clamping

sections.t:
Simulate a closed-loop PID controller on a gravity-loaded robot arm joint, connecting Proportional ($K_p$) and Derivative ($K_d$) gains to a physical virtual spring and viscous damper, and adding anti-windup clamping to the Integral ($K_i$) accumulator so actuator saturation never causes violent windup overshoot.
New ideas (max 2):
PD control as a virtual mechanical spring ($K_p$) and virtual viscous damper ($K_d$): How $u_{\text{PD}} = K_p(r - q) - K_d \dot{q}$ turns a motor into a programmable spring ($K_p$) with shock-absorber damping ($K_d$), and why pure PD sags by $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$ under a steady gravity torque $\tau_g$.
Integral gravity sag elimination ($K_i$) and anti-windup clamping under actuator saturation: How accumulating error $I_{\text{new}} = I + K_i e \Delta t$ eliminates steady-state gravity sag, and why clamping $I \in [-u_{\max}, +u_{\max}]$ stops integrator windup when the motor hits its voltage or torque limit.
New syntax: None (uses Python time-stepping for loops, min/max clamping, and assert).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.3: Conditional Decisions (if/elif/else) & Clamping
Lesson 00.2: Second-Order Motion — Springs, Dampers & Damping Regimes
Lesson 04.2: Packed Binary Telemetry Structs & 8-Bit XOR Checksums
Lesson 04.3: Python-to-C Bridge (Part 3) — C Structs as Labeled Boxes & Pointers as Box Addresses

sections.h: Idea 1: PD control as a virtual mechanical spring ($K_p$) and virtual viscous damper ($K_d$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Proportional-integral-derivative controller ("Control loop example" & "Controller theory") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Fundamental operation, Proportional term, and Derivative term.
What to skip: Skip Laplace transfer function pole-zero derivations.
Key takeaway: In Lesson 00.2, a physical spring and damper pulled a mass toward equilibrium with $F = -kx - bv$. A PD controller creates that exact spring and shock absorber in software around any target angle $r$: the Proportional term $K_p(r - q)$ pulls toward $r$ like a virtual spring, while the Derivative term $-K_d \dot{q}$ pushes against velocity like viscous honey so the arm stops smoothly without ringing. Under a constant gravity load $\tau_g$, a pure virtual spring stretches until $K_p e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g$, leaving a steady-state droop $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$.
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Damping ("Critical damping") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review how critical damping ($K_d = 2\sqrt{J K_p}$) prevents overshoot.

sections.h: Idea 2: Integral gravity sag elimination ($K_i$) and anti-windup clamping under actuator saturation
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Integral windup ("Occurrence" & "Solutions") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Integral windup, Occurrence, and Solutions.
What to skip: Skip multi-loop chemical process cascades.
Key takeaway: Adding the Integral term ($I \leftarrow I + K_i e \Delta t$) steadily builds up holding torque until gravity sag $e_{\text{ss}}$ reaches $0.000\text{ rad}$. However, every real motor driver saturates at a maximum effort $\pm u_{\max}$. During a large step move while the motor is already maxed out at $+u_{\max}$, an unclamped integrator keeps ballooning (integrator windup), forcing the arm to overshoot violently past the target! Anti-windup clamping freezes or clamps the integral accumulator whenever the actuator is saturated in the direction of the error.
Alternative resource: Åström & Murray — Feedback Systems (fbsbook.org) — Chapter 11 covers PID physical intuition and anti-windup. The host answers 500 to scripts as of 2026-10-19 (site outage), so open it in a browser.

Inside your $1\text{ kHz}$ timer ISR (Lesson 04.1), a PID controller computes tracking error $e = r - q$ and combines a virtual mechanical spring ($K_p$), a virtual viscous damper ($K_d$) applied directly to velocity $\dot{q}$ (so sudden step changes in $r$ never cause a derivative kick), and an integral accumulator ($I$) with anti-windup clamping against actuator limit $\pm u_{\max}$:
Why does anti-windup clamping matter so much on hardware? When lifting a robot arm against gravity torque $\tau_g = 0.60\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ with actuator limit $u_{\max} = 1.20\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$:
Pure PD ($K_i = 0$): Settles cleanly without overshoot, but sags below the $1.000\text{ rad}$ target at $q_{\text{ss}} = 1.000 - \frac{\tau_g}{K_p} = 1.000 - \frac{0.60}{4.0} = 0.850\text{ rad}$ ($\text{sag} = 0.150\text{ rad}$).
Unclamped PID ($K_i = 12.0$, no anti-windup): Eliminates sag, but winds up while $u_{\text{raw}} > 1.20\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, causing a massive $0.372\text{ rad}$ overshoot!
Anti-windup PID ($K_i = 12.0$, clamped): Eliminates steady-state sag ($q = 1.000\text{ rad}$) while cutting overshoot nearly $8\times$ down to $0.047\text{ rad}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete the PID update and anti-windup clamp inside sim_pid_arm (TODO 1 and TODO 2) to reproduce the exact PD sag (0.150 rad), unclamped windup overshoot (0.372 rad), and anti-windup overshoot (0.047 rad).
What is real-hardware only: Holding the physical arm shaft with your hand for 3 seconds to feel the integral torque ramp up against your fingers.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Save as pid_spring_damper_antiwindup.py and run python3 pid_spring_damper_antiwindup.py:

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:
Spacing is not graded here: the lines line up because the print statements pad the labels with literal spaces ("Unclamped PID: " carries two, so its final q= starts where "Pure PD (Ki=0): " does) and print every number to three decimals ({q_pd:.3f}, {os_wu:.3f}). The runner ignores indentation, column padding and blank lines and compares your words and numbers, so a ragged print with the right values still passes; the loop itself is checked by the instructor behavioral tests.

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, combine the virtual spring kp e, virtual damper -kd dq, and integral candidate + i_candidate. In TODO 2, freeze i_term (do not update it to i_candidate) whenever anti_windup is True, abs(u_raw) > u_max, and e u_raw > 0.0.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Differentiating error (e - e_prev) / dt instead of position -(q - q_prev) / dt: When target r steps from 0.0 to 1.0 in a single $1\text{ ms}$ tick, (e - e_prev) / dt jumps to $+1000\text{ rad/s}$ (derivative kick), slamming the motor into saturation! Always apply -kd dq on measured velocity.
Enabling high $K_i$ before tuning $K_p$ and $K_d$: Always set $K_i = 0$ first, tune $K_p$ and $K_d$ until step responses are crisp and damped, and only then add a small $K_i$ with anti-windup enabled.

PD gravity sag: If a robot arm experiences a constant gravity torque $\tau_g = 0.60\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and you double the proportional gain from $K_p = 4.0$ to $K_p = 8.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ (with $K_i = 0$), what is the new steady-state gravity sag $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$?
Answer
$e_{\text{ss}} = \frac{0.60}{8.0} = \mathbf{0.075\text{ rad}}$ (doubling stiffness cuts steady-state sag in half).
Critical damping gain $K_d$: For a frictionless joint with inertia $J = 0.02\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ and virtual spring stiffness $K_p = 8.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$, what virtual damper gain $K_d = 2\sqrt{J K_p}$ achieves critical damping ($\zeta = 1.0$)?
Answer
$K_d = 2\sqrt{0.02 \times 8.0} = 2\sqrt{0.16} = 2 \times 0.40 = \mathbf{0.80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}}$.

PD control acts as a virtual mechanical spring ($K_p$) plus a virtual viscous damper ($K_d$), leaving steady-state sag $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$ under constant load $\tau_g$.
Adding Integral action ($K_i$) drives steady-state sag to zero, and anti-windup clamping freezes the integrator during actuator saturation to prevent windup overshoot.

pages.title: Gyroscope Drift, Accelerometer Tilt (atan2) and 2-Line Complementary IMU Fusion

sections.t:
Compare fast but drifting gyroscope integration against drift-free but vibration-noisy accelerometer gravity tilt (atan2), and fuse both in 2 lines of Python using a complementary IMU filter ($\hat{\theta}_k = \alpha(\hat{\theta}_{k-1} + \omega_{\text{gyro}}\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{\text{acc},k}$).
New ideas (max 2):
Gyroscope integration bias drift versus accelerometer gravity tilt (atan2): Why integrating a gyroscope ($\theta \leftarrow \theta + \omega \Delta t$) accumulates constant bias $b_g \cdot t$ over time, while an accelerometer measures gravity angle via atan2(a_y, a_z) without long-term drift.
Complementary IMU filter fusion ($\alpha \cdot \text{gyro} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \theta_{\text{acc}}$): How weighting $98\%$ short-term gyroscope changes with $2\%$ long-term accelerometer gravity reference ($\alpha = 0.98$) cancels both vibration spikes and gyro drift.
New syntax: None (uses math.atan2, for loops, and floating-point arithmetic).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.10: Radians, Rotational Speed & Right-Triangle Trig
Lesson P.11: Reading Time-Series Graphs — Slope & Area
Lesson 01.4: Ground Bounce, Star Grounding & RC Low-Pass Filters
Lesson 05.1: PID Virtual Spring-Damper Control & Integrator Anti-Windup Clamping

sections.h: Idea 1: Gyroscope integration bias drift versus accelerometer gravity tilt (atan2)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Inertial measurement unit ("Operation" & "Errors") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Inertial measurement unit, Operation, and Performance.
What to skip: Skip ring-laser submarine navigation.
Key takeaway: A 6-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU, such as MPU6050) combines a 3-axis gyroscope (measuring angular velocity $\omega$ in rad/s) and a 3-axis accelerometer (measuring linear acceleration plus Earth's $9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ gravity pull). Integrating the gyroscope ($\theta_k = \theta_{k-1} + \omega_{\text{gyro}}\Delta t$) gives smooth fast motion, but even a tiny constant gyroscope bias $b_g = +0.05\text{ rad/s}$ drifts by $0.05 \times 10\text{ s} = 0.50\text{ rad}$ ($28.6^\circ$!) in just 10 seconds. Conversely, computing tilt from gravity via $\theta_{\text{acc}} = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y, a_z)$ never drifts over hours, but shakes whenever the robot frame vibrates.
Alternative resource: SparkFun — Accelerometer Basics [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings What is an Accelerometer? and How to Select an Accelerometer.

Primary resource: Wikipedia — Low-pass filter ("Discrete-time realization") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Low-pass filter and Discrete-time realization (how a recursive weighted average smooths noisy measurements).
What to skip: Skip Butterworth circuit synthesis.
Key takeaway: Because the gyroscope is trustworthy at fast timescales and the accelerometer is trustworthy at slow timescales, a complementary IMU filter blends them in a single line using blending weight $\alpha \in [0.95, 0.995]$ (whose weights $\alpha$ and $1 - \alpha$ sum to $1.0$):
theta_est = alpha (theta_est + omega_gyro dt) + (1.0 - alpha) theta_acc.
Alternative resource: MathsIsFun — Weighted Mean [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review how two weights $\alpha$ and $1 - \alpha$ combine two estimates.

On a balancing robot or mobile base equipped with an MPU6050 IMU, neither sensor works alone: gyroscope integration ($\theta_{\text{gyro}} \leftarrow \theta_{\text{gyro}} + \omega_{\text{gyro}}\Delta t$) responds instantly to fast motion but suffers from unbounded gyroscope bias drift, while accelerometer gravity tilt:
never drifts over long timescales because Earth's gravity vector always points straight down, yet shakes violently whenever motor vibrations accelerate the chassis. The complementary IMU filter combines the best of both sensors in two lines of code at each sample step $\Delta t$:
Here $\tau_c$ is the crossover time constant: for $\Delta t = 0.010\text{ s}$ ($100\text{ Hz}$) and blending weight $\alpha = 0.98$, $\tau_c = \frac{0.98 \times 0.010}{0.02} = 0.490\text{ s}$. Motions faster than $0.49\text{ s}$ come $98\%$ from the clean gyroscope, while over timescales longer than $0.49\text{ s}$ the $2\%$ accelerometer correction anchors the angle to gravity. Even when the gyroscope has a constant offset bias $b_g$, the complementary IMU filter completely stops unbounded runaway drift, bounding steady-state bias error to just $\Delta\theta_{\text{ss}} = \tau_c \cdot b_g$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete accel_tilt_rad (TODO 1) using math.atan2(ay, az) and run_complementary_imu (TODO 2) over a $10.0\text{ s}$ ($1000$-step) stationary hover where the gyroscope has a $+0.05\text{ rad/s}$ bias to verify that pure gyro integration drifts to $+0.500\text{ rad}$ while the $\alpha = 0.98$ complementary filter stays locked at $+0.024\text{ rad}$.
What is real-hardware only: Tapping a physical MPU6050 breakout board on the bench to watch raw accelerometer spikes get rejected by the $\alpha = 0.98$ filter.

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Save as complementary_imu_fusion.py and run python3 complementary_imu_fusion.py:
When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, call math.atan2(ay_m_s2, az_m_s2). In TODO 2, update theta_gyro_only = theta_gyro_only + omega_meas dt and theta_comp = alpha (theta_comp + omega_meas dt) + (1.0 - alpha) theta_acc.
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Using math.asin(ay / 9.81) instead of math.atan2(ay, az): If a vibration bump momentarily makes ay = 9.90 m/s^2, ay / 9.81 > 1.0 crashes math.asin() with a ValueError: math domain error! math.atan2(ay, az) works safely for any finite acceleration vector.
Picking weights that do not add up to 1.0 (e.g., 0.98 and 0.05): If the gyro and accelerometer weights sum to 1.03 instead of 1.00, the filter multiplies the angle by 1.03 on every single tick and diverges to infinity! Always write (1.0 - alpha) for the second weight.

Pure gyro drift: If a gyroscope has a constant zero-rate bias of $b_g = +0.02\text{ rad/s}$, by how many radians does pure gyro integration $\theta = \sum b_g \Delta t$ drift over $60\text{ s}$ (1 minute)?
Answer
$\Delta \theta = 0.02\text{ rad/s} \times 60\text{ s} = \mathbf{1.20\text{ rad}}$ ($\approx 68.8^\circ$!).
Complementary filter time constant: At a loop rate of $f_s = 200\text{ Hz}$ ($\Delta t = 0.005\text{ s}$) with $\alpha = 0.98$, what is the crossover time constant $\tau_c = \frac{\alpha \Delta t}{1 - \alpha}$?
Answer
$\tau_c = \frac{0.98 \times 0.005}{0.02} = \mathbf{0.245\text{ s}}$.

Gyroscope integration is clean at high speed but drifts at $b_g \cdot t$; accelerometer tilt $\theta_{\text{acc}} = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y, a_z)$ is drift-free but sensitive to vibration.
A complementary IMU filter updates $\hat{\theta}_k = \alpha(\hat{\theta}_{k-1} + \omega_{\text{gyro}}\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{\text{acc},k}$ with crossover time constant $\tau_c = \frac{\alpha\Delta t}{1-\alpha}$.

pages.title: Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Feedback, P/I/D Physical Roles & Actuator Saturation

sections.t: This is the bridge module before Step 1.6 (05-control.T1.06). If you command a robot arm joint with a fixed PWM duty cycle (open-loop), gravity, friction, or payload changes will leave it far from the target angle. Closing a feedback loop around encoder error $e(t) = r(t) - y(t)$ turns the motor into a programmable mechanical spring, shock absorber, and gravity compensator (PID control)—and understanding actuator saturation explains why an unclamped integral term causes violent overshoot (integrator windup). Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

Imagine steering a car toward the center of a lane. Open-loop control is closing your eyes and holding the steering wheel at a fixed angle based on a map—the first crosswind blows you off the road. Closed-loop control is looking at your distance from the lane center (the error $e = r - y$) every millisecond:
Proportional ($P$, virtual spring): Pulls harder the farther you are from the target ($K_p e$). Alone, a strong spring overshoots and oscillates, and sags slightly under a steady crosswind or gravity load.
Derivative ($D$, virtual viscous damper): Pushes against velocity ($-K_d \dot{y}$), acting like an oil-filled shock absorber that brakes the joint as it approaches the target so it doesn't overshoot.
Integral ($I$, steady-state bias eliminator): Accumulates past error over time ($K_i \int e\,dt$), steadily ratcheting up torque until steady-state gravity sag is driven to zero. But if the motor hits its $100\%$ voltage limit (saturation), an unclamped integrator keeps ballooning to an enormous number (windup), causing a huge overshoot after reaching the target.

Closed-Loop Tracking Error ($e_k = r_k - y_k$): At discrete control step $k$ with period $\Delta t$ ($\text{s}$), given reference target $r_k$ ($\text{rad}$) and measured position $y_k$ ($\text{rad}$), tracking error is $e_k = r_k - y_k$.
Physical PD Virtual Spring-Damper + Integral Action: Commanded unsaturated control effort $u_{\text{raw},k}$ ($\text{V}$ or $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) with proportional gain $K_p$, integral gain $K_i$, and derivative gain $K_d$ (applied on measurement velocity $\dot{y}_k$ to avoid derivative kick on step changes in $r_k$) is:
Substituting $r_k = 1.0\text{ rad}$, $y_k = 0.6\text{ rad}$ ($e_k = 0.4\text{ rad}$), $\dot{y}_k = 0.5\text{ rad/s}$, $I_k = 0.8\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $K_p = 10.0$, and $K_d = 2.0$ gives $u_{\text{raw},k} = 10(0.4) - 2(0.5) + 0.8 = 3.8\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Actuator Saturation and Clamping Anti-Windup: Physical actuators saturate at $\pm u_{\max}$:
Clamping anti-windup freezes $I_k$ whenever $|u_{\text{raw},k}| > u_{\max}$ and $\operatorname{sign}(e_k) = \operatorname{sign}(u_{\text{raw},k})$ (or clamps $|I_k| \le I_{\max}$).

Predict first (before you run it): The loop below runs $3000$ ticks of $1\ \text{ms}$ on an arm with $J = 0.02\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, $b = 0.05\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$, a gravity load $\tau_g = 0.60\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, a $u_{\max} = 1.20\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ rail and target $r = 1.0\ \text{rad}$. Before you run it, commit to three numbers: where the pure-P run ($K_p = 4.0$, $K_i = 0$) comes to rest, which of the two $K_i = 12.0$ runs overshoots more, and how far past $1.0\ \text{rad}$ the worse one peaks. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: the PD resting angle must sit below $1.0\ \text{rad}$ with a shortfall that multiplies back to exactly $\tau_g = 0.60\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, so resting above the target means the feedback sign is inverted; and the two PID peaks must differ, because equal peaks mean the anti-windup branch never engaged.
Simulate a 1-DOF rotational arm ($J = 0.02\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, $b = 0.05\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$) lifting against a constant gravity torque $\tau_g = 0.60\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ under actuator limit $u_{\max} = 1.20\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ to compare (1) pure P control (leaves steady-state sag), (2) unclamped PID (suffers huge windup overshoot), and (3) anti-windup PID (zero steady-state error and minimal overshoot).
Expected output:

For the arm above with constant gravity load $\tau_g = 0.60\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ under PD control ($K_i = 0$), derive and verify the exact steady-state angle sag $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$ when $K_p = 8.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$. Confirm that sim_arm(kp=8.0, ki=0.0, kd=0.4, anti_windup=False) settles to $q_{\text{ss}} = 0.925\text{ rad}$ ($e_{\text{ss}} = 0.075\text{ rad} \pm 10^{-3}\text{ rad}$).
If your result differs: At steady state ($\dot{q} = \ddot{q} = 0$), the spring torque balances gravity: $K_p e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g \implies e_{\text{ss}} = 0.60 / 8.0 = 0.075\text{ rad}$.

sections.h: Graded package - the spring, the damper, the bias and the rail
sections.t:
exercises/05-control.T1.05a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: tracking_error, control_effort (the spring, the damper on measured velocity, and the integral bias), integral_step, anti_windup_integral (frozen while the demand is past a rail and the error still pushes that way), saturate, steady_state_sag and arm_acceleration. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
53 tests. The demand is checked at the section-3 worked $3.8\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and at the Skip test's $4.0$, in both velocity directions, so a derivative term added instead of subtracted fails; the sag is checked at the exercise's $0.075\text{ rad}$ and $0.925\text{ rad}$, so a sag that multiplies the gain fails; the integral tick is checked at the Gate test's $0.005$, so a missing $\Delta t$ fails; the freeze is checked at $+15\text{ V}$ past a $12\text{ V}$ rail, so an anti-windup that never freezes fails, and at $e = -0.4\text{ rad}$ with the same demand, where the tick must land at $0.7952$ so a rule that freezes on every saturation fails, with the negative rail and the exact $u_{\text{raw}} = \pm u_{\max}$ boundary checked the same way; and the clamp is checked on both rails, so a one-sided clip fails. A closed-loop simulation assembled only from the submission's functions reproduces the section-4 output - PD resting at $0.850\text{ rad}$ (sag $0.150$), anti-windup PID at $<10^{-3}\text{ rad}$ of error with under $0.05\text{ rad}$ of overshoot, and the unclamped integrator overshooting by more than a further $0.10\text{ rad}$. The transfer suite drives the plant's own shoulder: its $0.318825\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ horizontal load sags $0.0319\text{ rad}$ at $K_p = 10$, the $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp is $312.5\text{ rad/s}^2$ over plant.I1, the clamp freezes the integral while the unclamped tick still adds $0.0048$, and one encoder count at the $1\text{ kHz}$ tick is $1.534\text{ rad/s}$, which $K_d = 0.4$ turns into $24.5\%$ of the torque budget. Six planted faults - effort_adds_the_damping, sag_multiplies_the_gain, integral_missing_dt, anti_windup_never_freezes, anti_windup_freezes_any_saturation, saturate_clips_one_rail - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Time-Stepping Loops & Clamping), 00-foundations.T1.00b (Arrays & Plotting), 00-foundations.T1.00e (Mass-Spring-Damper Dynamics), and Legacy Step 1.1 (00-foundations.T1.01) (1st-Order EMA Filtering).
Core Concepts to Review First: Discrete PID virtual spring-damper control, integrator windup clamping & derivative-on-measurement (-Kd (y[k] - y[k-1]) / dt), and complementary IMU sensor fusion $\hat{\theta}_k = \alpha(\hat{\theta}_{k-1} + \omega_{\text{gyro}}\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{\text{acc},k}$ in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Åström & Murray Feedback Systems Ch. 11 (fbsbook.org), Brian Douglas PID Control Lectures, and Track 05 Tier 1 (05-control-and-estimation/README.md).
Expected numbers (the answer): $e_{\text{ss}} = 0.075\ \text{rad}$; $q_{\text{ss}} = 0.925\ \text{rad}$.

Steady state is a spring balance. At rest $\dot q = 0$, so the damper and the integral are both zero and $K_p e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g$: $e_{\text{ss}} = 0.60/8.0 = 0.075\ \text{rad}$, which puts $q_{\text{ss}}$ at $1.0 - 0.075 = 0.925\ \text{rad}$.
The sign of the sag is a check on the whole loop. A settling angle above $1.0\ \text{rad}$ means the feedback sign is inverted; below it by exactly $\tau_g/K_p$ means the loop is right and only the spring is carrying the load.
The damper subtracts velocity, not error. u_raw = kp (r - y) - kd dy + i reproduces the worked example's $3.8\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$; adding + kd dy would give $5.8$ and would drive the joint away from the target as it speeds up.
One tick is one millisecond. With $\Delta t = 0.001$ the integral gains $K_i e \Delta t$ per step; leaving $\Delta t$ out multiplies the accumulator by $1000$ and is the windup the next module is about.
What the suite refuses. control_effort refuses a negative Kp or Kd (a negative gain is positive feedback); integral_step refuses a negative Ki and a non-positive dt; anti_windup_integral refuses a missing or non-positive u_max and a negative i_max; saturate refuses a non-positive rail; steady_state_sag refuses a zero or negative gain; and arm_acceleration refuses a non-positive inertia or a negative damping. All raise ValueError.

Printed: u_raw=3.80 Nm | e_ss=0.0750 rad | q_ss=0.925 rad
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite closes this loop on the plant's own shoulder inertia and damping, and reads one encoder count the way the module does:

Inject: run sim_arm(kp=4.0, ki=12.0, kd=0.4, anti_windup=False) — the worked example's PID with the clamp and the freeze removed, so $I_k$ keeps adding $K_i e\Delta t$ while the demand sits past the $1.20\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ rail.
Symptom: the run reaches the target and sails on to a peak $0.372\ \text{rad}$ above $1.0\ \text{rad}$ instead of the clamped run's $0.047\ \text{rad}$; the pure-P run in the same script is untouched at its $0.150\ \text{rad}$ sag.
Diagnose: only the $K_i = 12.0$ runs are affected, and the two of them differ solely in the clamp and freeze, so the plant, $K_p$ and $K_d$ are ruled out; the PD run still rests $0.150\ \text{rad}$ short, exactly $\tau_g / K_p$, which says the damage is stored in $I_k$ and not in the spring.
Fix: restore anti_windup=True, which clips $\lvert I_k\rvert \le u_{\max}$ and freezes the accumulator while $\lvert u_{\text{raw}}\rvert > u_{\max}$ and $e_k$ still pushes that way; the overshoot then reads $0.047\ \text{rad}$ and the steady-state error falls under $10^{-3}\ \text{rad}$.

Run the Python simulation script above or open Control Loop & Saturation in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) to observe how actuator saturation interacts with closed-loop feedback gains.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Step 1.6 (05-control.T1.06), this exact discrete PID + anti-windup law executes inside the $1\text{ kHz}$ timer ISR on your microcontroller driving the H-bridge or BLDC stage:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: PD steady-state sag equals $\tau_g / K_p = 0.150\text{ rad}$, anti-windup steady-state error $< 0.001\text{ rad}$, and anti-windup overshoot $< 0.05\text{ rad}$.
Pass criteria: score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$) on the Ladder Gate test below to unlock Step 1.6 (05-control.T1.06).

[Recall] [Concept: open_vs_closed_loop_tracking_error] A pure proportional controller ($K_p = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$, $K_i = 0$) holds an arm against a constant gravity torque $\tau_g = 0.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ at steady state ($\dot{q} = \ddot{q} = 0$). Compute the steady-state angle error $e_{\text{ss}} = \tau_g / K_p$ in radians ($\text{rad}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Apply] [Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] Given $r_k = 2.0\text{ rad}$, $y_k = 1.5\text{ rad}$, $\dot{y}_k = 0.4\text{ rad/s}$, $K_p = 10.0$, and $K_d = 2.5$ (with $I_k = 0$), compute the PD control effort $u_k = K_p(r_k - y_k) - K_d \dot{y}_k$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Transfer] [Concept: actuator_saturation_and_integrator_windup] An actuator with voltage rails $\pm 12.0\text{ V}$ has proportional term $P_k = 9.5\text{ V}$, derivative term $D_k = 0.0\text{ V}$, and unclamped integral candidate $I_{\text{cand}} = 6.0\text{ V}$. With anti-windup clamping $I_k \in [-4.0\text{ V}, +4.0\text{ V}]$, compute the saturated actuator output $u_k = \operatorname{clip}(P_k + I_k + D_k, -12.0, +12.0)$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] Which PID term acts as a virtual viscous shock absorber that opposes velocity to damp out oscillations?
A. Proportional ($K_p$)
B. Integral ($K_i$)
C. Derivative ($K_d$)
D. Feedforward gravity torque
[Spaced review -> 00-foundations.T1.00e — Concept: discrete_kinematics_pos_vel_acc] A cart moves at a constant $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ for $0.50\,\text{s}$. Compute the distance travelled in metres (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ ($80\%+$). If you missed Q1, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; if you missed Q2 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; if you missed Q3, study ## 3. Formalization item 3. If you missed Q5, review 00-foundations.T1.00e. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 05 Tier 1 bridge ladder (05-control.T1.05a) before Step 1.6 (05-control.T1.06):
[Concept: open_vs_closed_loop_tracking_error] If target angle is $r = 1.57\text{ rad}$ and measured angle is $y = 1.27\text{ rad}$, compute tracking error $e = r - y$ in $\text{rad}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: open_vs_closed_loop_tracking_error] Why does an open-loop voltage command $V = D \cdot V_{\text{bus}}$ fail to hold a robot arm at a fixed angle when a payload is placed in the gripper?
A. Because open-loop control does not measure angle $y(t)$ and therefore cannot increase torque when the payload pulls the joint downward.
B. Because PWM only works at $0\text{ RPM}$.
C. Because encoders cannot measure negative angles.
D. Because Ohm's law stops holding under load.
[Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] A pure proportional controller ($K_p > 0, K_i = 0, K_d = 0$) on a frictionless inertia $J\ddot{q} = -K_p(q - r)$ behaves like what physical system?
A. An undamped mass-spring oscillator that rings forever around $r$.
B. An overdamped dashpot.
C. A constant-velocity conveyor.
D. An open-loop stepper motor.
[Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] Compute the steady-state integral torque $I_{\text{ss}}$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) when a PID controller holds an arm at zero steady-state error ($e_{\text{ss}} = 0, \dot{q} = 0$) against a constant gravity disturbance $\tau_g = 0.85\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
[Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] Why do production PID loops compute the derivative term on measurement ($-K_d \dot{y}$) rather than on error ($+K_d \dot{e} = K_d(\dot{r} - \dot{y})$) when $r(t)$ is a step command?
A. To avoid derivative kick—an instantaneous step jump in $r(t)$ makes $\dot{r} = \Delta r / \Delta t$ huge for one tick, slamming the actuator into saturation.
B. Because $\dot{y}$ is always zero.
C. Because $r(t)$ cannot be stored in a float.
D. To increase steady-state error.
[Concept: actuator_saturation_and_integrator_windup] Given $u_{\text{raw}} = 18.5\text{ V}$ and supply limit $u_{\max} = 12.0\text{ V}$, compute the saturated output $u = \operatorname{clip}(u_{\text{raw}}, -u_{\max}, +u_{\max})$ in volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: actuator_saturation_and_integrator_windup] Under clamping anti-windup, if $u_{\text{raw}} = +15.0\text{ V} > u_{\max} = 12.0\text{ V}$ and current error is $e_k = +0.4\text{ rad}$ (same sign as $u_{\text{raw}}$), what should happen to the integral accumulator $I_k$ on that tick?
A. Freeze $I_k$ ($I_k = I_{k-1}$; do not add $K_i e_k \Delta t$).
B. Multiply $I_k$ by $10$.
C. Set $K_p = 0$.
D. Reverse the motor polarity.
[Concept: pid_spring_damper_integrator_intuition] Compute the discrete integral update $\Delta I = K_i e_k \Delta t$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $K_i = 20.0$, $e_k = 0.25\text{ rad}$, and $\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $7/8$ ($80\%+$). Remediation: Q1–Q2 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q3–Q5, Q8 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q6–Q7 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 3.

Åström & Murray — Feedback Systems (fbsbook.org, Ch. 11 PID Control, resources/textbooks-and-papers.md): Free textbook chapter on PID physical intuition, derivative filtering, and integrator anti-windup [VERIFIED 2026-10-15].
Track 05 (05-control-and-estimation/README.md): Directly continues into Step 1.6 (05-control.T1.06) [VERIFIED 2026-10-15].

pages.title: Rest-to-Rest Cubic Polynomial Trajectories and Joint-Space Gravity Feedforward

sections.t:
Replace sudden step commands with a smooth rest-to-rest cubic polynomial trajectory ($q_d(t) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)(q_f - q_0)$, $s = t/T$) whose velocity starts and ends at zero, and combine a soft PD spring-damper with gravity feedforward ($\tau_{\text{ff}} = m g L \cos q$) for safe, human-friendly joint-space compliant control.
New ideas (max 2):
Rest-to-rest cubic polynomial trajectories ($q_d(s) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)\Delta q$) with zero endpoint velocity: How scaling normalized time $s = t/T \in [0, 1]$ by $3s^2 - 2s^3$ starts and stops the joint smoothly with $\dot{q}_d(0) = \dot{q}_d(T) = 0$ and peak midpoint speed $\dot{q}_{\max} = 1.5 \frac{\Delta q}{T}$.
Joint-space compliant PD control with gravity feedforward ($\tau = K_p e - K_d \dot{q} + m g L \cos q$): How predicting gravity torque $\tau_g(q) = m g L \cos q$ lets a robot arm hold poses with zero steady-state sag even at low, springy $K_p$ and $K_i = 0$.
New syntax: None (uses Python functions, math.cos, and for loops).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

Lesson P.12: Forces, Newton's Second Law & Lever Torque
Lesson 02.1: 1-Link Planar Forward Kinematics & Coordinate Frames
Lesson 05.1: PID Virtual Spring-Damper Control & Integrator Anti-Windup Clamping

sections.h: Idea 1: Rest-to-rest cubic polynomial trajectories ($q_d(s) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)\Delta q$) with zero endpoint velocity
sections.t:
Primary resource: [Wikipedia — Cubic Hermite spline ("Unit interval [0, 1]")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_Hermite_spline) [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Cubic Hermite spline and Unit interval [0, 1] (notice the basis function $h_{01}(t) = 3t^2 - 2t^3$).
What to skip: Skip cardinal and Catmull-Rom computer-graphics tangents.
Key takeaway: Commanding a sudden step jump (q_des = 1.0 rad at $t = 0$) asks a heavy robot arm to teleport instantaneously, slamming the motor into current saturation and rattling the gears! Instead, for a move of $\Delta q = q_f - q_0$ over duration $T$, define normalized time $s = \operatorname{clip}(t / T,\ 0.0,\ 1.0)$. The cubic polynomial trajectory $q_d(t) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)\Delta q$ and its velocity $\dot{q}_d(t) = \frac{6s(1-s)}{T}\Delta q$ guarantee $\dot{q}_d(0) = 0$, $\dot{q}_d(T) = 0$, and a smooth bell-shaped speed profile peaking at $s = 0.5$ with $\dot{q}_{\max} = 1.5 \frac{\Delta q}{T}$.
Alternative resource: Modern Robotics (Lynch & Park) — Trajectory Generation [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Chapter 9 covers point-to-point cubic time scaling.

sections.h: Idea 2: Joint-space compliant PD control with gravity feedforward ($\tau = K_p e - K_d \dot{q} + m g L \cos q$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Feed forward (control) ("Overview" & "Benefits") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Feed forward (control), Overview, and Benefits.
What to skip: Skip gene-regulatory biological networks.
Key takeaway: In Lesson 05.1, you saw that a pure PD controller sags under gravity unless you either crank $K_p$ very high (making the arm stiff and dangerous around humans) or turn on $K_i$ (which winds up if a human pushes the arm!). Because we already know the exact lever torque of gravity from Lesson P.12 ($\tau_g(q) = m g L_{\text{com}} \cos q$, with $q$ measured from horizontal), we can add gravity feedforward directly to a soft PD controller ($K_i = 0$): the arm floats weightlessly with zero steady-state sag while remaining gentle and compliant if bumped by hand!
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Impedance control [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Impedance control and Principle.

Every collaborative robot arm combines two ingredients inside its $1\text{ kHz}$ control loop: a smooth rest-to-rest cubic polynomial trajectory ($s = \operatorname{clip}(t/T,\ 0,\ 1)$) and joint-space compliant PD control with gravity feedforward:
Why is gravity feedforward superior to an integral term $K_i$ for interactive robot arms that work around humans?
If you set $K_p = 0$ and keep only viscous damping plus gravity feedforward ($\tau_{\text{cmd}} = -K_d \dot{q} + m g L_{\text{com}}\cos q$), the arm enters "Zero-Gravity Lead-Through Teaching Mode": a human operator can grab the gripper, guide the arm smoothly to any pose in space, and release it—and the link stays floating weightlessly wherever you let go!
Even when tracking a trajectory with a gentle, human-safe spring stiffness ($K_p = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$), gravity feedforward cancels $100\%$ of the link weight at horizontal ($q = 0\text{ rad}$), achieving $0.000\text{ rad}$ steady-state sag without any integrator windup when pushed.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete cubic_trajectory (TODO 1) to evaluate $(q_d, \dot{q}_d)$ at $t = 0.0, 0.5, 1.0\text{ s}$ and compliant_gravity_command (TODO 2) to verify that adding $m g L \cos q$ eliminates horizontal gravity sag even with a soft $K_p = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ spring.
What is real-hardware only: Guiding a physical gimbal robot link by hand in Zero-G teaching mode ($K_p = 0$).

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, use (3.0 s2 - 2.0 s3) dq for position offset and (6.0 s (1.0 - s) / duration_T) dq for velocity. In TODO 2, add kp (q_des - q) + kd (dq_des - dq) and mass_kg 9.81 l_com_m math.cos(q).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Forgetting to clamp normalized time s = max(0.0, min(1.0, t / T)) after $t > T$: If $t$ keeps growing past $T$ ($s > 1$), $3s^2 - 2s^3$ turns negative and drives the robot arm backward to $-\infty$! Always clamp $s \in [0.0, 1.0]$ and set $\dot{q}_d = 0$ for $t \ge T$.
Using $\sin q$ instead of $\cos q$ when $q = 0$ is horizontal: Always match your coordinate convention from Lesson P.12 and Lesson 02.1: when $q = 0\text{ rad}$ is horizontal ($+x$-axis), gravity torque is maximum ($\cos 0 = 1$), and when $q = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ is straight up ($+y$-axis), gravity torque is zero ($\cos(\pi/2) = 0$).

Cubic midpoint peak velocity: A robot joint moves $\Delta q = 2.0\text{ rad}$ in $T = 2.0\text{ s}$ along a rest-to-rest cubic polynomial. What is its average speed $\Delta q / T$, and what is its peak speed $\dot{q}_{\max}$ at $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ ($s = 0.5$)?
Answer
Average speed: $\frac{2.0\text{ rad}}{2.0\text{ s}} = \mathbf{1.0\text{ rad/s}}$.
Peak speed at $s = 0.5$: $\dot{q}_{\max} = 1.5 \times 1.0\text{ rad/s} = \mathbf{1.5\text{ rad/s}}$.
Compliant external push deflection: Your joint runs compliant PD + exact gravity feedforward with $K_p = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ ($K_i = 0$). If your hand applies a gentle external torque of $\tau_{\text{hand}} = 0.30\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ against the arm, by how many radians does the arm yield?
Answer
$\Delta q = \frac{\tau_{\text{hand}}}{K_p} = \frac{0.30}{2.0} = \mathbf{0.15\text{ rad}}$ ($\approx 8.6^\circ$), and it springs right back when you let go.

A rest-to-rest cubic polynomial trajectory $q_d(t) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)\Delta q$ ($s \in [0, 1]$) guarantees zero velocity at start and finish with peak midpoint velocity $1.5 \frac{\Delta q}{T}$.
Joint-space compliant PD control with gravity feedforward ($\tau = K_p e + K_d \dot{e} + m g L \cos q$) holds poses without gravity droop while yielding safely like a mechanical spring.

pages.title: 10-Step Smoke-Free Hardware Bring-Up and Single-Tone Sine-Sweep System Identification

sections.t:
Verify encoder-to-actuator sign matching and current-limited power-on safety using the 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up protocol, and extract a motor joint's true viscous friction ($b$) and rotational inertia ($J$) from a two-frequency sine-sweep system identification experiment.
New ideas (max 2):
10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up and encoder-to-actuator sign verification: How unpowered continuity checks, a $100\text{ mA}$ CC/CV current limit, and checking that positive motor command increases measured encoder angle ($\Delta\theta_{\text{meas}} \cdot u_{\text{test}} > 0$) prevent positive-feedback runaway.
Single-tone sine-sweep system identification to measure viscous friction ($b$) and rotational inertia ($J$): How driving $\tau(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t)$ at a slow frequency $f_1$ and a fast frequency $f_2$ extracts $b$ and $J$ from the measured velocity amplitude $|\omega|$.
New syntax: None (uses math.sqrt, math.pi, and conditional safety checks).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

sections.h: Idea 1: 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up and encoder-to-actuator sign verification
sections.t:
Primary resource: SparkFun — How to Use a Multimeter ("Continuity") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Review exact headings Continuity and Measuring Voltage.
What to skip: Skip internal fuse replacement steps.
Key takeaway: Never power a new robot joint from an unfused battery or close a PID loop before checking sensor direction! Our 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up checks unpowered rail continuity (VIN to GND must not beep), powers logic at a $100\text{ mA}$ CC/CV current limit, and performs encoder-to-actuator sign verification: when a small positive open-loop command ($u_{\text{test}} = +0.10$) nudges the motor, the encoder reading $\Delta \theta_{\text{meas}}$ must also be positive ($\Delta\theta_{\text{meas}} \cdot u_{\text{test}} > 0$). If $\Delta\theta_{\text{meas}} < 0$, the encoder is inverted relative to the motor, which turns negative feedback into violent positive-feedback runaway!
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Negative feedback ("Overview") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Compare stabilizing negative feedback against runaway positive feedback.

sections.h: Idea 2: Single-tone sine-sweep system identification to measure viscous friction ($b$) and rotational inertia ($J$)
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — System identification ("Overview") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings System identification and Overview.
What to skip: Skip nonlinear Wiener-Hammerstein Volterra series.
Key takeaway: Instead of guessing your joint's rotational inertia $J$ ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) and viscous damping $b$ ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$) when calculating PID gains ($K_d = 2\sqrt{J K_p}$), you can measure them directly with a single-tone sine-sweep system identification test! For a rotor $J\dot{\omega} + b\omega = A\sin(2\pi f t)$, the steady-state velocity amplitude is $|\omega(f)| = \frac{A}{\sqrt{b^2 + (2\pi f J)^2}}$. At a very slow frequency $f_1 \to 0$, friction dominates so $b \approx \frac{A}{|\omega(f_1)|}$; at a higher frequency $f_2$, inertia dominates and we solve directly for $J = \frac{\sqrt{(A / |\omega(f_2)|)^2 - b^2}}{2\pi f_2}$.
Alternative resource: Wikipedia — Frequency response ("Measurement and plotting") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Read exact headings Frequency response and Measurement and plotting.

Before closing any PID loop on your bench, execute the automated pre-flight checks from the 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up protocol:
Verify unpowered rail resistance $R_{\text{rail}} > 100\ \Omega$ (no short circuit) and CC/CV current limit $I_{\text{limit}} \le 0.15\text{ A}$ for logic bring-up.
Perform encoder-to-actuator sign verification: apply a tiny open-loop pulse $u_{\text{test}} > 0$ and confirm $\Delta\theta_{\text{meas}} \cdot u_{\text{test}} > 0$ (if negative, swap two motor phase wires or flip the encoder DIR pin).
Once open-loop direction is verified, run a two-tone sine-sweep system identification with torque amplitude $A$ (N·m) at low frequency $f_1$ (Hz) and high frequency $f_2$ (Hz). Since total mechanical impedance at angular excitation frequency $\Omega = 2\pi f$ is $Z(\Omega) = \frac{A}{|\omega|} = \sqrt{b^2 + (\Omega J)^2}$:
With $\hat{J}$ and $\hat{b}$ measured from real data, you can compute exact critically damped PD gains without guesswork!

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner): Complete verify_bringup_safety (TODO 1) to catch an inverted encoder sign before closing the loop, and identify_b_and_j (TODO 2) to extract $\hat{b}$ and $\hat{J}$ from two sine-sweep velocity amplitude measurements.
What is real-hardware only: Pressing a physical mushroom E-Stop switch in series with the $+12\text{ V}$ motor supply wire.

When TODO 1 and TODO 2 are completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, check if (u_test dtheta_meas) = 100.0 and psu_limit_a <= 0.50: return "PASS_READY_FOR_CLOSED_LOOP". In TODO 2, compute b_est = amp_nm / omega1_amp, z2 = amp_nm / omega2_amp, and j_est = math.sqrt(z22 - b_est2) / (2.0 math.pi f2_hz).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Closing a PID loop before checking that $+\text{PWM}$ increases encoder angle: This is the #1 cause of violent motor runaway on first power-on. Always run Step 6 of the bring-up checklist (+0.10 open-loop nudge) with the bench PSU current limit capped at $0.3\text{–}0.5\text{ A}$.
Commanding a huge sine-sweep torque amplitude that hits mechanical hard-stops: Keep sine-sweep excitation amplitude $A$ gentle ($10\text{–}20\%$ of rated torque) so the joint oscillates smoothly near the center of its workspace without saturating.

Inverted encoder runaway: What happens when you enable a closed-loop proportional controller $u = K_p(r - \theta_{\text{meas}})$ if positive voltage spins the motor clockwise ($+\theta$) but the encoder counts downward ($-\theta_{\text{meas}}$)?
Answer
As the motor moves toward the target, error $r - \theta_{\text{meas}}$ grows larger instead of smaller (positive feedback), accelerating the joint at full voltage into the mechanical hard-stop!
Low-frequency viscous friction estimate: During a slow sine-sweep test where inertial torque $2\pi f_1 J \approx 0$, a torque amplitude of $A = 0.15\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ produces a peak velocity amplitude of $|\omega| = 3.0\text{ rad/s}$. What is the viscous damping coefficient $\hat{b} = A / |\omega|$?
Answer
$\hat{b} = \frac{0.15\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}{3.0\text{ rad/s}} = \mathbf{0.050\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}}$.

The 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up verifies unpowered continuity, CC/CV current limiting, and positive encoder-to-actuator sign matching ($\Delta\theta_{\text{meas}} \cdot u_{\text{test}} > 0$) before closing any feedback loop.
Single-tone sine-sweep system identification extracts viscous damping $\hat{b}$ at low frequency and rotational inertia $\hat{J}$ at high frequency from $|\omega(f)| = \frac{A}{\sqrt{b^2 + (2\pi f J)^2}}$.
