pages.title: 1D Point-to-Point Motion, Boundary Conditions & Virtual Joint Spring-Damper

sections.t: This is the bridge module before Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07). Feeding an instantaneous step jump ($q_{\text{des}}: 0^\circ \to 90^\circ$ in $0\text{ s}$) into a robot arm controller demands infinite velocity and slams the actuator into saturation. Generating a smooth time-parameterized trajectory $q_d(t), \dot{q}_d(t), \ddot{q}_d(t)$ that starts and ends at zero velocity—and tracking it with a virtual joint spring-damper plus gravity feedforward—lets your arm glide smoothly and yield safely when touched. Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

Imagine an elevator moving from Floor 1 to Floor 5 in $T = 2.0\text{ s}$. A step setpoint is teleporting the target indicator to Floor 5 at $t = 0.001\text{ s}$: the controller panics, sees a massive error, and yanks the cable at $100\%$ torque. A smooth trajectory is a moving ghost cab that accelerates gently from rest ($\dot{q}_d(0) = 0$), cruises smoothly through the middle, and decelerates to a feather-soft stop at Floor 5 ($\dot{q}_d(T) = 0$). Because we have four boundary conditions (start position, start velocity, end position, end velocity), a cubic polynomial $q_d(t) = a_0 + a_1 t + a_2 t^2 + a_3 t^3$ has the exact four knobs $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ needed to satisfy all four! Then, instead of fighting external contact with an infinite-gain integrator, a virtual joint spring-damper $\tau = K_p(q_d - q) + K_d(\dot{q}_d - \dot{q}) + \tau_g(q)$ lets you dial the mechanical stiffness $K_p$ up for precision or down for soft human-safe compliance.

Step Setpoint vs. Time-Parameterized Trajectory: A trajectory generator outputs continuous reference state $(q_d(t), \dot{q}_d(t), \ddot{q}_d(t))$ over $t \in [0, T]$ so tracking error $e(t) = q_d(t) - q(t)$ remains small throughout the move and never saturates the motor.
Rest-to-Rest Cubic Polynomial Boundary Conditions: Requiring $q_d(0) = q_0$, $\dot{q}_d(0) = 0$, $q_d(T) = q_f$, and $\dot{q}_d(T) = 0$ over duration $T$ ($\text{s}$) uniquely determines the cubic polynomial in normalized time $s = t/T \in [0, 1]$:
where $\Delta q = q_f - q_0$ ($\text{rad}$). At the midpoint $t = T/2$ ($s = 0.5$), position is halfway ($q_0 + 0.5\Delta q$), velocity reaches its peak $\dot{q}_{\max} = \frac{1.5\Delta q}{T}$, and acceleration passes through zero. Substituting $\Delta q = 1.0\text{ rad}$ and $T = 2.0\text{ s}$ gives $\dot{q}_{\max} = 0.75\text{ rad/s}$ and $|\ddot{q}(0)| = 1.5\text{ rad/s}^2$.
Virtual Joint Compliance + Gravity Feedforward: Commanding joint torque $\tau$ ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) with stiffness $K_p$ ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$) and damping $K_d$ ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$):
Under an external hand push torque $\tau_{\text{ext}}$ at rest ($\dot{q} = \dot{q}_d = 0$), the joint yields like a physical torsion spring by $\Delta q = \tau_{\text{ext}} / K_p$.

Predict first (before you run it): The block sweeps $q_0 = 0.0\ \text{rad}$ to $q_f = 1.2\ \text{rad}$ in $T = 2.0\ \text{s}$, then computes the yield under a $\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0.50\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ hand push with $K_p = 5.0\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$. Before you run it, commit to three numbers: the position at the midpoint $t = 1.0\ \text{s}$, the peak speed of the move, and the angle the joint gives up to the push. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: the midpoint must be exactly half of $\Delta q$, since $3s^2 - 2s^3 = 0.5$ at $s = 0.5$, so a midpoint near a third means the cubic term was dropped; and the peak speed must be $1.5\times$ the average $\Delta q / T$, so a peak of $0.60\ \text{rad/s}$ means you divided by $T$ and lost the $1.5$.
Generate a rest-to-rest cubic trajectory from $q_0 = 0.0\text{ rad}$ to $q_f = 1.2\text{ rad}$ over $T = 2.0\text{ s}$, verify all four endpoint boundary conditions and the midpoint peak velocity, and compute the compliant deflection under a $\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ hand push when $K_p = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$.
Expected output:

Compute the minimum move duration $T_{\min}$ in seconds ($\text{s}$) required for a rest-to-rest cubic trajectory covering $\Delta q = 2.0\text{ rad}$ if the actuator's maximum speed is $\dot{q}_{\max} = 3.0\text{ rad/s}$ ($\dot{q}_{\max} = \frac{1.5\Delta q}{T_{\min}}$). Verify $T_{\min} = \frac{1.5 \times 2.0}{3.0} = 1.0\text{ s}$ and check that cubic_rest_to_rest(0.5, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0)[1] equals 3.0 $\text{rad/s}$.
If your result differs: Recall that a cubic rest-to-rest profile has peak velocity $1.5\times$ the average velocity ($\frac{1.5\Delta q}{T}$, not $\frac{\Delta q}{T}$) because it spends the first and last halves accelerating and decelerating.

sections.h: Graded package - the moving ghost cab and the spring
sections.t:
exercises/06-robotics.T1.06a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: cubic_rest_to_rest (the clamped cubic, held still past $T$), cubic_coefficients, peak_velocity, min_duration_s, min_duration_for_acceleration, spring_damper_torque and compliance_deflection. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
27 tests. The cubic is checked at all four boundary conditions, at the midpoint, at $t > T$ (held still, not extrapolated) and across 101 samples for overshoot, so a parabola in $s$ fails on arrival speed; the coefficients are evaluated at three times and their endpoint derivatives must vanish; the peak is checked against $1.5\Delta q/T$; both duration limits are checked by substituting the duration back into the profile; the spring-damper is checked at the Gate test's numbers and with the damping acting only on velocity; and the compliance yield is checked against a stiffer spring. The transfer suite feeds the submission the plant's own gains: its spring-damper must equal plant.pd_gravity_torque at three states to $10^{-12}$, a cubic from the plant's current figure-8 pose must land on the next target with zero speed and a $1.5\Delta q/T$ peak, the $1\text{ kHz}$ step setpoint is shown to demand $1000\text{ rad/s}$ where the cubic peaks at $1.5$, and the yield must be the plant's static equilibrium $\tau/K_p$. Five planted faults - cubic_s_squared_only, peak_is_average_speed, min_duration_uses_average, spring_damper_gain_swapped, deflection_times_stiffness - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a (Functions & Loops), 00-foundations.T1.00d (Cosine Gravity Projection), and 00-foundations.T1.00e (Kinematics & Spring Energy).
Prerequisite Bridge Modules: 02-mechanics.T1.02a (2-Link Arm & Lever Torque) and 05-control.T1.05a (PD Virtual Spring-Damper).
Core Concepts to Review First: Rest-to-rest cubic polynomial interpolation $q(t) = q_0 + (3s^2 - 2s^3)\Delta q$ (peak velocity $\frac{3\Delta q}{2T}$), symmetric trapezoidal velocity profiles, and joint-space compliant PD + gravity compensation $\tau = K_p(q_d - q) - K_d\dot{q} + m g L_{\text{com}}\cos q$ in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Lynch & Park Modern Robotics Ch. 9 (hades.mech.northwestern.edu) and Track 06 Tier 1 (06-robotics-and-autonomy/README.md).

The four coefficients. $q(0) = q_0$ and $\dot{q}(0) = 0$ give $a_0 = q_0$, $a_1 = 0$; the two conditions at $t = T$ then give $a_2 = 3\Delta q/T^2$, $a_3 = -2\Delta q/T^3$. For the exercise's $\Delta q = 2.0\ \text{rad}$, $T = 1.0\ \text{s}$ that is $a_2 = 6.0$ and $a_3 = -4.0$, and $q(0.5) = 6(0.25) - 4(0.125) = 1.0\ \text{rad}$ - exactly halfway, as every rest-to-rest cubic is.
Peak speed. $\dot{q}_d = (6\Delta q/T)(s - s^2)$ is a parabola in $s$ with its maximum at $s = 0.5$, where it equals $(6\Delta q/T)(0.25) = 1.5\Delta q/T$. So the same move peaks at $3.0\ \text{rad/s}$, and the $3.0\ \text{rad/s}$ actuator limit is reached by $T_{\min} = 1.5 \times 2.0 / 3.0 = 1.0\ \text{s}$.
When the limit is acceleration. $|\ddot{q}_d|$ is largest at the endpoints, $\ddot{q}_d(0) = -\ddot{q}_d(T) = 6\Delta q/T^2$, so the duration is the square root, $T = \sqrt{6\Delta q/\ddot{q}_{\max}}$ - not $6\Delta q/\ddot{q}_{\max}$.
Holding still, and the spring. Clamping $s$ to $1$ returns $q_f$ with $\dot{q}_d = \ddot{q}_d = 0$; without the clamp $3s^2 - 2s^3$ turns over past $s = 1$ and the arm swings back through its start. For the torque, $K_p$ multiplies the position error and $K_d$ the velocity error, so a $0.80\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ push against $K_p = 4.0\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ yields $0.20\ \text{rad}$.
What the suite refuses. cubic_rest_to_rest refuses a zero move duration; min_duration_s and min_duration_for_acceleration refuse a velocity or acceleration limit at or below zero; spring_damper_torque refuses a negative stiffness or damping gain; and compliance_deflection refuses a zero stiffness, which has no deflection to divide into. All raise ValueError.

Printed: T_min=1.000 s | q(T/2)=1.0000 rad, qd_max=3.0000 rad/s | tau=1.700 Nm | yield=0.2000 rad
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite checks this spring against the plant's own shipped PD+gravity law, term for term, at the plant's gains:

Inject: delete the clamp inside cubic_rest_to_rest so it reads s = t / T, and evaluate the $T = 2.0\ \text{s}$ profile half a second past arrival, at $t = 3.0\ \text{s}$.
Symptom: the arm is no longer at $q_f = 1.2\ \text{rad}$: with $s = 1.5$, $3s^2 - 2s^3 = 6.75 - 6.75 = 0$, so the position reads $0.0\ \text{rad}$ and the velocity $(6 \times 1.2 / 2)(1.5 - 2.25) = -2.7\ \text{rad/s}$ — it swings back through the start at speed instead of holding still.
Diagnose: every sample up to $t = 2.0\ \text{s}$ still matches the worked example (midpoint $0.60\ \text{rad}$, peak $0.90\ \text{rad/s}$), so the coefficients and the gains are right and only the region $t > T$ is wrong; $3s^2 - 2s^3$ stops being monotone past $s = 1$, which localises the fault to the missing clamp rather than to the spring.
Fix: clamp s = max(0.0, min(1.0, t / T)), then re-check the same sample: at $t = 3.0\ \text{s}$ the profile holds $q = 1.2\ \text{rad}$ with $\dot{q}_d = 0.0\ \text{rad/s}$, and the midpoint and peak values are unchanged.

Open URDF / MuJoCo & STO in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev) to compare step setpoints against cubic, trapezoidal, and minimum-jerk profiles interactively.
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.06-robotics.T1.06a, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.
No hardware required for this module (hardware_required: false). In Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07), cubic_rest_to_rest(t, q0, qf, T) runs at $1\text{ kHz}$ on the microcontroller to feed $(q_d(t), \dot{q}_d(t))$ into the joint PD + gravity compensation loop:
Pass/fail verification in simulation: qd_start == 0.0, qd_end == 0.0, qd_mid == 0.90 rad/s, and deflection_rad == 0.10 rad.
Pass criteria: score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/4$) on the Skip test or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$) on the Ladder Gate test below to unlock Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07).

[Recall] [Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] For a rest-to-rest cubic trajectory from $q_0 = 0.0\text{ rad}$ to $q_f = 2.0\text{ rad}$ in $T = 4.0\text{ s}$, compute the midpoint position $q_d(2.0)$ in $\text{rad}$ and peak velocity $\dot{q}_d(2.0) = \frac{1.5\Delta q}{T}$ in $\text{rad/s}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Apply] [Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] Compute the initial acceleration $\ddot{q}_d(0) = \frac{6\Delta q}{T^2}$ in $\text{rad/s}^2$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $\Delta q = 2.0\text{ rad}$ and $T = 2.0\text{ s}$.
[Transfer] [Concept: virtual_joint_compliance_stiffness] A compliant joint controller $\tau = K_p(q_d - q) - K_d\dot{q} + \tau_g(q)$ with $K_p = 4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ is pushed by an external human hand torque of $\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0.80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ at rest. By what angle $\Delta q = \tau_{\text{ext}} / K_p$ in radians (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) does the joint yield?
[Spaced review -> 05-control.T1.05a — Concept: discrete_pid_controller] [Concept: trajectory_vs_step_setpoint] Why do collaborative robots omit the integral term ($K_i = 0$, using PD + gravity feedforward instead) when operating in compliant human-interaction mode?
A. Because $K_i$ is difficult to program in C.
B. Because if a human pushes and holds the arm away from $q_d$, an integral term would wind up to maximum stall torque fighting the human, whereas PD + gravity feedforward yields like a gentle mechanical spring!
C. Because gravity feedforward eliminates inertia.
D. Because cubic trajectories have zero velocity everywhere.
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/4$ ($80\%+$). If you missed Q1 or Q2, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q3 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 1 & 3. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 06 Tier 1 bridge ladder (06-robotics.T1.06a) before Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07):
[Concept: trajectory_vs_step_setpoint] What is the initial tracking error $e(0) = q_d(0) - q(0)$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$ when a rest-to-rest trajectory starts from the robot's current position $q(0) = q_0$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$)?
[Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] How many independent boundary conditions $(q(0), \dot{q}(0), q(T), \dot{q}(T))$ does a cubic polynomial $a_0 + a_1 t + a_2 t^2 + a_3 t^3$ satisfy?
[Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] Compute $q_d(t)$ at $s = t/T = 0.25$ for $q_0 = 0.0\text{ rad}$ and $q_f = 1.0\text{ rad}$ using $q_d = q_0 + \Delta q(3s^2 - 2s^3)$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] Compute the final velocity $\dot{q}_d(T)$ in $\text{rad/s}$ at $s = 1.0$ for any rest-to-rest cubic polynomial (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] Compute the terminal deceleration $\ddot{q}_d(T) = -\frac{6\Delta q}{T^2}$ in $\text{rad/s}^2$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for $\Delta q = 1.5\text{ rad}$ and $T = 3.0\text{ s}$.
[Concept: virtual_joint_compliance_stiffness] Compute the commanded joint torque $\tau = K_p(q_d - q) + K_d(\dot{q}_d - \dot{q}) + \tau_g$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) given $K_p = 10.0, K_d = 1.0, q_d = 0.8\text{ rad}, q = 0.7\text{ rad}, \dot{q}_d = 0.5\text{ rad/s}, \dot{q} = 0.2\text{ rad/s}$, and $\tau_g = 0.4\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
[Concept: virtual_joint_compliance_stiffness] If you reduce virtual stiffness $K_p$ from $20.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ to $2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ while keeping gravity feedforward $\tau_g(q)$ active, how does the arm feel when pushed by hand?
A. Ten times softer (compliant and backdrivable) while still floating weightlessly against gravity.
B. Ten times stiffer.
C. It drops to the table because gravity feedforward is disabled.
D. It spins at constant speed.
[Concept: polynomial_endpoint_boundary_conditions] Why does a cubic polynomial have a discontinuous step jump in acceleration $\ddot{q}_d(0^+) = \frac{6\Delta q}{T^2} \ne 0$ at $t=0$ (infinite jerk), motivating 5th-order polynomials or S-curves in Tier 2?
A. Because a cubic has only 4 coefficients, which are all used up matching position and velocity at $t=0$ and $t=T$, leaving no free parameters to force $\ddot{q}_d(0) = \ddot{q}_d(T) = 0$.
B. Because $3s^2 - 2s^3$ is not differentiable.
C. Because time $T$ is negative.
D. Because velocity is discontinuous at $t=0$.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $7/8$ ($80\%+$). Remediation: Q1 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q2–Q5, Q8 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q6–Q7 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 3.

Kevin Lynch & Frank Park — Modern Robotics (modernrobotics.org, Ch. 9 Trajectory Generation, resources/textbooks-and-papers.md): Free textbook + video lectures on polynomial and trapezoidal time scaling [VERIFIED 2026-10-15].
Track 06 (06-robotics-and-autonomy/README.md): Directly continues into Step 1.7 (06-robotics.T1.07) [VERIFIED 2026-10-15].

pages.title: Industrial State Machines, Cyclic PLC Scan, E-Stop Chains & Sine-Sweep Gain/Phase

sections.t: This is the bridge module before the Tier 1 Boss Capstone (07-systems.T1.08, Step 1.8). Integrating a multi-DOF robot into a workcell requires three system-level skills: structuring supervisory logic around a deterministic Read-Inputs $\to$ Execute-Logic $\to$ Write-Outputs cyclic PLC scan, wiring a fail-safe Normally-Closed (NC) hardware Emergency-Stop chain that cuts motor power even if a wire breaks or the CPU freezes, and measuring your assembled robot's empirical bandwidth via a single-tone sine sweep. Already know this? Read ### Safety notes first, then take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7.

Imagine a factory supervisor who inspects a workcell every $10\text{ ms}$. Instead of letting sensors change halfway through a calculation, the supervisor takes a frozen snapshot of all switches at the top of the cycle (1. Read Inputs), computes the state machine rules on that snapshot (2. Execute Logic), and updates all relays at the end of the cycle (3. Write Outputs)—that is an IEC 61131-3 cyclic PLC scan. Next, why are industrial Emergency-Stop buttons wired Normally-Closed (NC) in series so current must flow continuously to hold the motor power relay closed? Because if a rat chews through an E-stop wire or a connector vibrates loose, the current stops and the machine fails SAFE (stops immediately)—whereas a Normally-Open (NO) wire break would silently leave you with a dead E-stop button that does nothing when pressed! Finally, a sine sweep shakes the joint with one pure sine frequency at a time and compares output amplitude $B$ and lag $\Delta t$ against input amplitude $A$ to plot the real hardware's frequency response.

Cyclic Scan Loop (Read -> Execute -> Write): Each scan cycle $k$ latches input image $I_k$, evaluates pure state transition function $(S_{k+1}, Q_k) = f(S_k, I_k)$, and writes output image $Q_k$. Input changes arriving mid-scan cannot cause race conditions between rungs.
Fail-Safe Normally-Closed (NC) Series E-Stop Chain: For $N$ series NC contacts $E_1, E_2, \dots, E_N \in \{0, 1\}$ (where 1 = closed/healthy and 0 = pressed OR broken wire) and hardware watchdog WD_OK:
Any single open contact or severed wire forces $\text{PWR-ENABLE} = 0$, dropping the motor supply contactor/enable hardware line without relying on software.
Single-Tone Sine-Sweep Gain (dB) and Phase Lag (Self-Contained Logarithm & Decibel Primer):
What $\log_{10}$ and Decibels ($\text{dB}$) Mean: The base-10 logarithm $\log_{10}(x)$ (math.log10(x) in Python) simply asks: "To what power must we raise $10$ to get $x$?" Thus $\log_{10}(1) = 0$ (since $10^0 = 1$), $\log_{10}(0.1) = -1$ (since $10^{-1} = 0.1$), and $\log_{10}(1/\sqrt{2}) \approx \log_{10}(0.7071) \approx -0.1505$. Because mechanical and electrical amplitude ratios $B/A$ span factors of $1000\times$, engineers compress them onto an additive scale called decibels ($\text{dB}$) defined as $20\log_{10}(B/A)$ (and invert back to a linear ratio via $B/A = 10^{\text{dB}/20}$):
$B/A = 1.0 \implies 20\log_{10}(1.0) = 0.0\text{ dB}$ (no attenuation).
$B/A = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.7071 \implies 20\log_{10}(0.7071) \approx -3.01\text{ dB}$ (the $-3\text{ dB}$ bandwidth cutoff).
$B/A = 0.50 \implies 20\log_{10}(0.50) \approx -6.02\text{ dB}$ (half amplitude).
$B/A = 0.10 \implies 20\log_{10}(0.10) = -20.0\text{ dB}$ (one-tenth amplitude).
Empirical Frequency-Response Magnitude & Phase: Injecting $u(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t)$ at frequency $f$ ($\text{Hz}$, period $T = 1/f$) and measuring steady-state response $y(t) = B\sin(2\pi f(t - \Delta t))$ gives empirical magnitude $\lvert G(j2\pi f)\rvert_{\text{dB}}$ (standard shorthand for gain at frequency $f$ in decibels) and phase lag $\angle G(j2\pi f)$:
Substituting $A = 1.0\text{ rad}$, $B = 0.7071\text{ rad}$, $f = 5.0\text{ Hz}$, and peak delay $\Delta t = 0.025\text{ s}$ gives $|G|_{\text{dB}} = -3.01\text{ dB}$ and $\angle G = -360^\circ \times 5.0 \times 0.025 = -45.0^\circ$.

Predict first (before you run it): Two things happen in one block: a cyclic PLC scan walking IDLE -> RUNNING -> ESTOP_LATCHED on a break in estop2_nc, and a $5.0\ \text{Hz}$ sine sweep with input amplitude $A = 1.0\ \text{rad}$, output $B = 0.7071\ \text{rad}$ and a peak delay $\Delta t = 0.025\ \text{s}$. Before you run it, commit to three numbers: the lag in degrees, the gain in decibels, and whether re-closing the snipped wire while Start is still held returns power. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: the lag must be negative, because a peak that arrives after the input is lag, so a positive number means the sign of $\Delta t$ was dropped; and the gain must be negative, because $B < A$, so a positive decibel value means the ratio was inverted or the $20$ became a $10$.
Simulate a cyclic PLC scan controlling a workcell with two series NC E-stop buttons and a guard door interlock (verifying that a broken wire immediately drops motor power and latches FAULT), and compute the empirical Bode gain and phase from a $5.0\text{ Hz}$ sine-sweep measurement.
Expected output:

During a single-tone sine sweep at $f = 8.0\text{ Hz}$ ($T = 0.125\text{ s}$) with input amplitude $A = 0.20\text{ rad}$, the joint encoder output has steady-state amplitude $B = 0.10\text{ rad}$ and its peaks lag the input peaks by $\Delta t = 0.03125\text{ s}$. Compute $\lvert G(j2\pi f)\rvert_{\text{dB}}$ and $\angle G(j2\pi f)$ in degrees. Verify $|G|_{\text{dB}} = -6.0206\text{ dB}$ ($\pm 10^{-3}$) and $\angle G = -90.0^\circ$ ($\pm 10^{-6}$).
If your result differs: Check that $-360^\circ \times 8.0\text{ Hz} \times 0.03125\text{ s} = -90.0^\circ$ (a quarter period of $0.125\text{ s}$) and $20\log_{10}(0.10 / 0.20) = -6.0206\text{ dB}$.

sections.h: Graded package - the scan, the chain and the sweep
sections.t:
exercises/07-systems.T1.07a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds seven holes: scan_frequency_hz, safety_chain_ok (all contacts, never any), plc_scan_step (the latch and the reset), gain_db (20 log10), phase_lag_deg (negative), sine_amplitude (the lock-in) and db_to_ratio. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
32 tests. The scan rate is checked against two different budgets, so seconds-for-milliseconds shows; the chain is checked with one open contact among three, so any fails; the state machine is checked with the chain healthy and Start still held, so a latch that clears itself fails; the gain is checked at half amplitude ($-6.02\text{ dB}$) and at one tenth ($-20\text{ dB}$), so 10 log10 fails; the phase is checked at a quarter period, so a positive lead fails; and the lock-in must recover a known amplitude through a $37\text{ Hz}$ interferer and a DC offset. The transfer suite measures the plant's own figure-8: sine_amplitude must return plant.AX and plant.AY from samples of plant.figure8_target to $10^{-6}$, reject the neighbouring frequency, read the plant's $1\text{ ms}$ budget as its $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, and drop the power enable on the very next scan after a wire break while refusing to restart without a reset. Five planted faults - scan_in_seconds, chain_uses_any, phase_positive_lead, gain_10log, plc_no_latch - each fail the test named for them.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T1.00a–00-foundations.T1.00e (Loops, Trigonometry & SI Units), plus the self-contained inline logarithm and decibel primer in ## 3. Formalization item 3 above (which previews Pass 2 00-foundations.T2.00d).
Prerequisite Bridge Modules: 01-electronics.T1.01c (CC/CV Bench Safety), 01-electronics.T1.01d (RC Cutoff), and 05-control.T1.05a (PID Control).
Core Concepts to Review First: Deterministic IEC 61131-3 PLC cyclic scan (Read -> Execute -> Write), single-tone sine-sweep System Identification ($|G|_{\text{dB}} = 20\log_{10}(B/A)$ and $\angle G = -360^\circ f \Delta t$), and the 10-step smoke-free hardware bring-up checklist in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: OpenPLC IEC 61131-3 Documentation (autonomylogic.com) and Track 07 Tier 1 (07-systems-hil-and-production/README.md).

Expected numbers (the answer): $f_{\text{scan}} = 500.0\ \text{Hz}$ for the $0.40 + 1.10 + 0.50\ \text{ms}$ budget; $|G|_{\text{dB}} = -6.0206\ \text{dB}$ and $\angle G = -90.0^\circ$ at $8.0\ \text{Hz}$ with $\Delta t = 0.03125\ \text{s}$; the chain stays enabled only while all three contacts are closed, and the trip latches until a reset with Start released.

The scan budget is a period. $0.40 + 1.10 + 0.50 = 2.00\ \text{ms}$, so $f_{\text{scan}} = 1000/2.00 = 500\ \text{Hz}$; a result of $0.002$ Hz means the milliseconds were used as seconds.
all, not any. The series chain is $E_1 \land E_2 \land E_3$: with one open contact among three all(...) returns False while any(...) still returns True - exactly the bug that leaves a broken wire looking healthy.
The latch is a state, not a flag. After a trip, state == "ESTOP_LATCHED" must ignore a held Start button; only reset_btn_no and not start_btn_no returns IDLE, and even that scan keeps pwr = False.
Decibels and the lag sign. $20\log_{10}(0.10/0.20) = -6.0206\ \text{dB}$ (the $10\log_{10}$ form would give $-3.0103$), and $-360^\circ \times 8.0 \times 0.03125 = -90^\circ$ is a quarter of the $0.125\ \text{s}$ period, so a positive number means the sign of $\Delta t$ was dropped.
What the suite refuses. scan_frequency_hz refuses a negative stage time on any of the three phases, and a zero or negative total budget (a scan with no period has no rate) - a negative read time can leave a positive sum and still be physically impossible, safety_chain_ok refuses an empty chain and any contact that is not 1/0, plc_scan_step refuses a state name it does not know, gain_db refuses a zero input amplitude or a negative one, phase_lag_deg refuses a negative delay, and sine_amplitude refuses an empty sample list - each with ValueError.

Printed: scan=500.0 Hz | chain=False | state=ESTOP_LATCHED pwr=False, then gain=-6.0206 dB | phase=-90.0 deg | sine_amp=1.0000 rad | ratio=0.5000.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite lock-in-recovers the figure-8's published amplitudes from the plant's own target function, and takes the 1 kHz scan straight from its tick:

Inject: delete the if state == "ESTOP_LATCHED" branch from plc_scan_step, so a healthy chain and a held Start button fall straight through to the state == "IDLE" rule.
Symptom: the worked example's third assertion fails — after the broken-wire scan the state is ESTOP_LATCHED with pwr = False, but the next scan, with estop2_nc repaired and start_btn_no=True, reset_btn_no=False, returns ("RUNNING", True) instead of staying inhibited, so the motor re-energises the instant the mushroom is twisted out.
Diagnose: the fault scan itself still drops power correctly, since $\text{PWR-ENABLE} = E_1 \land E_2 \land E_3$, and the sine-sweep numbers are untouched; the only scan that misbehaves is the one whose input state is ESTOP_LATCHED, which localises the fault to the missing latch branch.
Fix: restore the branch so ESTOP_LATCHED leaves only on reset_btn_no and not start_btn_no; that scan then returns ("ESTOP_LATCHED", False) and the third assertion passes, with pwr False as the expected output shows.

Test the cyclic PLC logic in OpenPLC Editor (resources/open-source-toolchains.md) or open Functional Safety & STO and System Identification in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev).
The graded package is also a workbench entry: Modules -> EX.07-systems.T1.07a, where selfcheck.py is appended below the starter and Verify compares its SELF-CHECK PASS: line. scripts/e2e_pages_bundle.mjs drives it on the built bundle, so the browser path is tested, not assumed.

⚠️ Mandatory Safety Briefing (safety_level: high — read before touching hardware or taking the Skip/Gate test):
Hardware E-Stop Must Break Power Physically: A software if (button_pressed) check inside loop() is never a valid Emergency Stop—if the microcontroller hangs in an infinite loop or a MOSFET shorts failed-closed, software cannot stop the motor. The physical E-stop mushroom switch must directly interrupt the motor power supply (VM) or hardware driver enable (nSLEEP) via Normally-Closed (NC) contacts.
No Automatic Restart After E-Stop Release: Twisting/releasing a latched E-stop mushroom button must never cause the robot to resume motion automatically (ESTOP_LATCHED -> IDLE requires an explicit manual Reset action while Start is not asserted).
Clear Workspace Before Sine Sweep: Keep hands and loose cables outside the manipulator swept volume during sine-sweep excitation, and bound excitation amplitude to $\le 15\%$ of joint travel.

Pass criteria: read ### Safety notes, score $\ge 80\%$ ($4/5$) on the Skip test ($100\%$ on [SAFETY] items), or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$, $100\%$ on [SAFETY] items) on the Ladder Gate test to unlock the Tier 1 Boss Capstone (07-systems.T1.08, Step 1.8).

[Recall] [Concept: single_tone_sine_sweep_gain_phase] A $10.0\text{ Hz}$ sine sweep with input amplitude $A = 0.50\text{ rad}$ produces steady-state output amplitude $B = 0.25\text{ rad}$ with peak time delay $\Delta t = 0.0125\text{ s}$. Compute the phase lag $\angle G = -360^\circ f \Delta t$ in degrees (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Apply] [Concept: cyclic_plc_scan_read_execute_write] An IEC 61131-3 PLC cyclic scan takes $t_{\text{read}} = 0.40\text{ ms}$ to freeze inputs, $t_{\text{exec}} = 1.10\text{ ms}$ to evaluate logic, and $t_{\text{write}} = 0.50\text{ ms}$ to latch outputs. Compute the deterministic scan frequency $f_{\text{scan}} = \frac{1000}{t_{\text{read}} + t_{\text{exec}} + t_{\text{write}}}$ in $\text{Hz}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Transfer] [SAFETY] [Concept: normally_closed_hardware_estop_chain] Why are industrial Emergency-Stop buttons wired with Normally-Closed (NC) contacts in series rather than Normally-Open (NO) contacts in parallel?
A. Because NC switches are cheaper.
B. Because in a series NC chain, continuous current is required to hold power enabled; pressing any E-stop or severing/unplugging any wire drops current to zero and fails safe immediately.
C. Because NO contacts cannot carry $3.3\text{ V}$.
D. To make the motor spin faster.
[Spaced review -> 04-embedded.T1.04b — Concept: finite_state_machine_switch_enum] [SAFETY] [Concept: normally_closed_hardware_estop_chain] When an operator twists and releases a tripped E-stop button, what must the control state machine do?
A. Immediately resume the interrupted trajectory at full speed.
B. Remain inhibited in a safe latched state (ESTOP_LATCHED / IDLE) with motor torque disabled until a deliberate Reset command is issued.
C. Apply $100\%$ reverse PWM.
D. Bypass the current limit.
[Concept: single_tone_sine_sweep_gain_phase] What linear amplitude ratio $B/A$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-3}$) corresponds to the $-3.01\text{ dB}$ closed-loop bandwidth frequency $f_{\text{BW}}$?
Answer key:
Pass mark: $4/5$ overall ($80\%+$) AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on Q3 and Q4 ([SAFETY]). If you missed Q1 or Q5, study ## 3. Formalization item 3; if you missed Q2, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; if you missed Q3 or Q4, study ## 3. Formalization item 2 and ### Safety notes. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 07 Tier 1 bridge ladder (07-systems.T1.07a) before Step 1.8 (07-systems.T1.08):
[Concept: cyclic_plc_scan_read_execute_write] If a PLC cyclic scan runs with period $T_{\text{scan}} = 5.0\text{ ms}$, how many complete scans execute per second ($\text{Hz}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$)?
[Concept: cyclic_plc_scan_read_execute_write] Why does freezing the input image at the start of each PLC scan prevent mid-scan race conditions?
A. Because every logic rung in that scan sees the exact same consistent boolean value for each sensor, even if the physical sensor bounces halfway through the scan.
B. Because it disables all sensors permanently.
C. Because it converts digital inputs to analog voltages.
D. Because it slows the CPU clock down to $1\text{ Hz}$.
[SAFETY] [Concept: normally_closed_hardware_estop_chain] Three NC safety switches (EStop1, EStop2, GuardDoor) are wired in series ($E_1 \land E_2 \land E_3$). If EStop1 = 1, EStop2 = 1, and a cable break sets GuardDoor = 0, what is the boolean state (0 or 1) of the hardware power-enable line?
[SAFETY] [Concept: normally_closed_hardware_estop_chain] Why is a software-only E-stop (if (!digitalRead(ESTOP_PIN)) pwm = 0;) unacceptable as the primary safety disconnect?
A. Because digitalRead takes $10\text{ s}$.
B. Because a firmware hang, stack overflow, ISR deadlock, or shorted power FET would leave the motor energized despite the button press; hardware E-stop must physically remove actuator power/enable.
C. Because GPIO pins cannot read buttons.
D. Because C++ does not support boolean logic.
[SAFETY] [Concept: normally_closed_hardware_estop_chain] After an E-stop event clears (safety_chain_ok == True), why must plc_scan_step check reset_btn_no and not start_btn_no before entering IDLE?
A. To prevent an operator from taping down the Start button and causing immediate motion the instant Reset is pressed.
B. To drain the capacitor bank.
C. To increase baud rate.
D. To invert the encoder direction.
[Concept: single_tone_sine_sweep_gain_phase] Compute the magnitude in decibels $20\log_{10}(B/A)$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-4}\text{ dB}$) when input amplitude is $A = 0.40\text{ rad}$ and output amplitude is $B = 0.04\text{ rad}$.
[Concept: single_tone_sine_sweep_gain_phase] At $f = 4.0\text{ Hz}$ ($T = 0.25\text{ s}$), the output sine wave peaks $\Delta t = 0.0625\text{ s}$ after the input sine wave. Compute the phase lag in degrees (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
[Concept: single_tone_sine_sweep_gain_phase] Why must you discard the first $2\text{–}3$ cycles after stepping to a new frequency in a single-tone sine sweep before measuring amplitude $B$ and phase $\Delta t$?
A. To allow the initial transient response to decay so you measure pure steady-state sinusoidal response.
B. Because the encoder is turned off during the first 2 cycles.
C. Because $\sin(t)$ is zero for the first 3 cycles.
D. To let the resistor cool down.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $7/8$ overall AND $3/3$ ($100\%$) on [SAFETY] questions Q3, Q4, and Q5. Remediation: Q1–Q2 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q3–Q5 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 2 and ### Safety notes; Q6–Q8 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 3.

pages.title: Tier 1 Boss Milestone — 1 kHz 2-DOF Compliant Arm Plant, Figure-8 PD Control & CRC-8 Telemetry

sections.t:
Integrate every skill from Track P, Stage 0, and Pass 1 (Tracks 00–07) into a complete, self-verifying 1,000-step ($1\text{ kHz}$, $\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$) time-stepped 2-DOF Planar Compliant Robot Arm simulation that solves Law-of-Cosines Inverse Kinematics (Lesson 02.3), drives a physical 2-link plant with joint inertia, damping, gravity loading, and a $0.4\text{–}0.6\text{ s}$ payload disturbance using closed-loop PD + 2-link gravity feedforward (Lesson 06.1), measures both kinematic IK$\to$FK round-trip error and actual dynamic arm tip tracking error, and verifies 20-byte polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) telemetry & 8N1 UART ring-buffer bandwidth (Lesson 04.2).
New ideas (max 2):
End-to-end 2-DOF Cartesian figure-8 path generation and Law-of-Cosines IK loop: Mapping a continuous 2D target curve $(x_d(t), y_d(t))$ into desired shoulder and elbow joint angles $(q_{1,d}(t), q_{2,d}(t))$ and finite-difference velocities $(\dot{q}_{1,d}, \dot{q}_{2,d})$ at every $1\text{ kHz}$ tick.
Time-stepped 1 kHz dual-joint compliant PD + gravity feedforward plant with CRC-8 telemetry and 8N1 UART buffering: Driving a time-stepped 2-DOF physical arm plant ($I_1, I_2, b_1, b_2$, gravity, and external disturbance torques) with closed-loop PD + gravity feedforward, measuring true dynamic tip tracking error (mm), and verifying that a $20\text{-byte}$ CRC-8 frame at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($200\text{ kbit/s}$ 8N1) overflows $115.2\text{ kbaud}$ (412 dropped frames) while running with zero dropped frames at $500\text{ kbaud}$.
New syntax: None (capstone integration of math, struct, functions, loops, and assert).
Target time (unmeasured — log yours): Typical: 2.0–2.5 hours | Slow-learner: 3.5–4.5 hours

Lesson 02.2: 2-Link Planar Forward Kinematics
Lesson 02.3: 2-Link Planar Inverse Kinematics (Law of Cosines)
Lesson 04.2: Packed Binary Telemetry Structs, CRC-8 & UART Bandwidth Budgets
Lesson 06.1: Rest-to-Rest Cubic Polynomial Trajectories & Joint-Space Gravity Feedforward
Lesson 07.1: 10-Step Smoke-Free Hardware Bring-Up & Single-Tone Sine-Sweep System Identification

sections.h: Idea 1: End-to-end 2-DOF Cartesian figure-8 path generation and Law-of-Cosines IK loop
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Lemniscate of Gerono ("Parametrization") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Lemniscate of Gerono (a smooth figure-8 curve parameterized by $\sin(\omega t)$ and $\sin(2\omega t)$).
What to skip: Skip algebraic fourth-degree curve duals.
Key takeaway: To test both joints simultaneously inside the workspace of a 2-link planar arm ($L_1 = 0.10\text{ m}, L_2 = 0.10\text{ m}$, reach $0.20\text{ m}$), we command a smooth Cartesian figure-8 path centered at $(x_0, y_0) = (0.12\text{ m}, 0.00\text{ m})$ over $1000$ ticks ($\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$):
$x_d(t) = 0.12 + 0.03\sin(2\pi f t)$ and $y_d(t) = 0.04\sin(4\pi f t)$. At every $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, our Law-of-Cosines Inverse Kinematics (IK) function solves for desired angles $(q_{1,d}, q_{2,d})$ and desired angular velocities $\dot{q}_{i,d} = (q_{i,d}[k] - q_{i,d}[k-1])/\Delta t$. We distinguish kinematic IK$\to$FK round-trip error ($\|\text{FK}(\text{IK}(x_d, y_d)) - (x_d, y_d)\| \approx 0.0000\text{ mm}$) from actual dynamic arm tip tracking error ($\|\text{FK}(q_1(t), q_2(t)) - (x_d(t), y_d(t))\|$).
Alternative resource: Modern Robotics (Lynch & Park) — Inverse Kinematics [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review Chapter 6 analytical 2R planar inverse kinematics.

sections.h: Idea 2: Time-stepped 1 kHz dual-joint compliant PD + gravity feedforward plant with CRC-8 telemetry and 8N1 UART buffering
sections.t:
Primary resource: Wikipedia — Robot kinematics ("Forward kinematics" & "Inverse kinematics") [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]
What to read: Read exact headings Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics.
What to skip: Skip parallel Stewart hexapod legs.
Key takeaway: At every $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, our controller computes 2-link gravity feedforward $\tau_{g2} = m_2 g L_{c2}\cos(q_1 + q_2)$ and $\tau_{g1} = (m_1 L_{c1} + m_2 L_1) g \cos(q_1) + \tau_{g2}$ plus compliant PD feedback $\tau_i = K_{p,i}(q_{i,d} - q_i) + K_{d,i}(\dot{q}_{i,d} - \dot{q}_i) + \tau_{g,i}$, clamped to $\pm 2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. This torque drives a physical 2-DOF plant ($\ddot{q}_i = (\tau_i - \tau_{g,i} + \tau_{\text{dist},i} - b_i\dot{q}_i)/I_i$) subjected to a downward payload disturbance pulse ($\tau_{\text{dist}} = [-0.15, -0.08]\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) during $t \in [0.40, 0.60)\text{ s}$, while streaming a 20-byte polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) frame over a simulated 256-byte UART TX ring buffer.
Alternative resource: Python 3 Documentation — struct [HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py] — Review struct.pack for binary telemetry packets.

In this Tier 1 Boss Milestone, every building block from the Beginner Path runs together inside a genuine $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1000\text{-tick}$, $\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$) time-stepped physical simulation:
Cartesian Figure-8 Trajectory $\to$ Law-of-Cosines IK (Lesson 02.3): At each $1\text{ ms}$ step, solve $(q_{1,d}, q_{2,d}) = \text{IK}(x_d(t), y_d(t))$ with clamped $\cos q_2 \in [-1, 1]$ and compute reference joint velocities $(\dot{q}_{1,d}, \dot{q}_{2,d})$.
Time-Stepped 2-DOF Plant + Closed-Loop Compliant PD + Gravity Feedforward (Lesson 06.1): Apply $\tau_i = \operatorname{clip}(K_{p,i} e_i + K_{d,i} \dot{e}_i + \tau_{g,i}(q),\ -2.5,\ +2.5)$ to the moving arm plant:
Even when a sudden external disturbance torque hits both joints during $0.40\text{ s} \le t < 0.60\text{ s}$, the compliant PD + gravity feedforward loop keeps actual dynamic tip tracking error under $2.5\text{ mm}$ peak ($0.91\text{ mm}$ RMS)!
20-Byte Polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) & 8N1 UART Ring-Buffer Test (Lesson 04.2): A 20-byte <BHffffB packet at $1\text{ kHz}$ requires $20 \times 10 \times 1000 = 200\text{ kbit/s}$ on an 8N1 serial link—overflowing a 256-byte TX buffer at $115.2\text{ kbaud}$ (412 dropped frames) but achieving zero dropped frames at $500\text{ kbaud}$.

What is simulated and in which tool:
In Python 3 (or the in-browser MechaLab Python Runner and the Robot Arm Kinematics & Safety Cutoff lab): Instead of a single monolithic fill-in, complete this capstone in 4 progressive stages:
Stage 1 — Pre-Run Prediction Worksheet (Predict): Before running the code, write down your quantitative predictions for:
Horizontal gravity torque at $(q_1=0, q_2=0)$ with $m_1=0.20\text{ kg}, m_2=0.15\text{ kg}, L_1=0.10\text{ m}, L_{c1}=0.05\text{ m}, L_{c2}=0.05\text{ m}$ ($\tau_{g2} = 0.15 \times 9.81 \times 0.05 = 0.0736\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\tau_{g1} = 0.3188\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$).
Whether a 20-byte frame ($200\text{ bits}$ at 8N1) at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($200\text{ kbit/s}$) will drop frames at $115.2\text{ kbaud}$ vs. $500\text{ kbaud}$.
Repair prediction worksheet: Before you touch TODO 3b–TODO 3e, fill the four-row table below with your estimate of each before/after metric.
Stage 2 — R2 Link Length & Payload Adaptation: Complete ik_2link (TODO 1) and gravity_ff_2link (TODO 2) so they work for any link lengths (l1, l2) and payload mass m2.
Stage 3 — R4 Diagnose Four Broken Capstone Versions: Complete diagnose_capstone_fault (TODO 3) to identify four broken versions from their observable bench symptoms. The signatures are described; the boundaries are yours to choose:
Broken Version A ("gravity_ff_sign_inverted"): The arm sags visibly downward at horizontal; the steady-state joint angle sits well below the commanded zero.
Broken Version B ("wrong_encoder_cpr"): Measured angles are about four times too large; IK/FK position mismatch is huge at every pose, not just under load.
Broken Version C ("missing_anti_windup"): A large step overshoot appears only after the actuator saturates; the integral keeps accumulating while the command is clipped.
Broken Version D ("encoder_zero_offset"): A correctly scaled encoder with a zero offset. The tip is off by a small, roughly constant distance (about $12\text{ mm}$) at every pose, with no sag and no overshoot.
Stage 3b — R4 Repair the zero-offset unit: Complete repair_encoder_offset (TODO 3b) to subtract the constant offset, then prove the corrected FK tip error falls from the measured offset to below $1\text{ mm}$.
Stage 3c — R4 Repair the CPR unit: Complete repair_encoder_cpr (TODO 3c) to divide out the measured $4\times$ scale, then prove the FK tip error falls from about $174\text{ mm}$ to below $1\text{ mm}$ in the bench check.
Stage 3d — R4 Repair the anti-windup unit: Complete repair_integral_update (TODO 3d) to freeze the integral while the command is saturated in the direction of the error, then prove the step overshoot falls from $37.2\%$ to below $5\%$ in the 3000-step bench simulation.
Stage 3e — R4 Repair the gravity-sign unit: Complete repair_gravity_sign (TODO 3e) to flip the inverted feedforward command, then prove the horizontal tip error falls from about $32\text{ mm}$ to below $1\text{ mm}$ at the $K_p = 4$ bench check.
Stage 3f — R4 Diagnose a unit nobody described: A fifth unit came back from the bench with the readings below. None of A–D describes it, and no rule above tells you what it is. Work it out from the readings alone, return the cause as one number with infer_encoder_scale (TODO 6), then correct it with the repair you already wrote (TODO 3c).
No sag and nominal overshoot point away from the loop. The tip error doubles when the pose doubles, which a fixed distance would not do. The tests check your factor on this unit, on an honest encoder, and on a unit whose error is a constant offset: a fix that cannot tell a scale from an offset is a guess, not a diagnosis.
Stage 4 — R5 Blank-Page Trajectory Generator from Spec: Write figure8_target(t_s, x0=0.12, y0=0.0, ax=0.03, ay=0.04, freq_hz=0.5) (TODO 4 — the only blank-page function) from specification: return $(x_d, y_d)$ where $x_d = x_0 + a_x \sin(2\pi f t)$ and $y_d = y_0 + a_y \sin(4\pi f t)$, plus pack_boss_telemetry (TODO 5).
08.1 Four-Fault Bench (in the Python runner): Select Lesson 08.1 and use the bench below the lesson header. It grades your own repair_encoder_offset, repair_encoder_cpr, repair_integral_update and repair_gravity_sign: press Grade my repairs, and each card reports the tip error or overshoot your function actually produces — $174\text{ mm}$, $37.2\%$, $31.8\text{ mm}$ and $12\text{ mm}$ while the TODOs are unfilled, and $0$, $4.7\%$, $0$, $0$ once they are right. A repair that is only close keeps its real error: returning an angle $10\%$ short of the offset leaves $1.2\text{ mm}$ on the card, not a green badge. The zero-offset slider is a separate playground that applies its own manual correction, so you can see the target before writing the function. The bench computes its own two-link FK chord and runs the same 3000-step saturated PI loop as the proof lines below; your fk_2link cannot make a wrong repair look right.
The bench is this lesson's pass condition, not a sidebar: Run & Verify Output marks 08.1 verified only when all four bench cards are at target ($\le 1\text{ mm}$ tip error, $< 5\%$ overshoot). A repair one line short of right keeps its real metric on the card and the lesson stays unverified — a printed repair line cannot carry the capstone on its own.
What is real-hardware only: Assembling the 3D-printed double-shear 608 bearing links and wiring two SimpleFOCMini + AS5600 gimbal joints on your bench (resources/lab-workbench-bom.md).

Before you complete TODO 3b–TODO 3e, estimate each metric from the geometry and the Lesson 05.1 PI result. Write your own numbers first; the reference row is hidden below.
Then open the 08.1 Four-Fault Bench in the Python runner, write each repair function, and press Grade my repairs. Compare the before column within $10\%$ and the after column against the target (below $1\text{ mm}$ or below $5\%$). The zero-offset slider shows what a correct correction looks like; the card above it only turns green when your function does the same.
Reference estimates — check after filling your row

sections.h: Starter Code (runs as-is — fill in the TODOs)
sections.t: Save as tier1_boss_2dof_arm.py and run python3 tier1_boss_2dof_arm.py:
When every TODO is completed, running the script prints:

Hint 1 (Concept nudge)
In TODO 1, review Lesson 02.3 for Law-of-Cosines 2-link IK. In TODO 2, compute tau_g2 = m2 g lc2 math.cos(q1 + q2) and add (m1 lc1 + m2 l1) g math.cos(q1) for tau_g1. In TODO 3, separate the four signatures: a large negative sag is the sign inversion, a huge mismatch is the CPR error, a small constant mismatch is the zero offset, and overshoot after saturation is the missing anti-windup. Pick boundaries that keep nominal_ok nominal. In TODO 3b, subtract the constant offset. In TODO 3c, divide by the measured scale (4.0 here). In TODO 3d, freeze i_term when abs(u_raw) > u_max and e u_raw > 0.0; otherwise keep i_candidate. In TODO 3e, negate the inverted feedforward command. Each repair ends by checking the corrected tip error or overshoot against the true value. In TODO 4, use math.sin(2.0 math.pi freq_hz t_s) and math.sin(4.0 math.pi freq_hz t_s).
Hint 2 (Formula / structure)
Full Solution

Confusing kinematic IK$\to$FK round-trip error (0.0000 mm) with dynamic plant tracking error (2.40 mm peak under disturbance): Evaluating FK(IK(x_d, y_d)) only tests your trigonometry formula—it does not test whether a moving arm with inertia, damping, and payload disturbances actually follows the trajectory! Always step the physical plant state $(q, \dot{q})$ forward at $\Delta t = 1\text{ ms}$ and measure $\|\text{FK}(q_1(t), q_2(t)) - (x_d(t), y_d(t))\|$.
Using $\cos(q_2)$ instead of $\cos(q_1 + q_2)$ for elbow gravity torque $\tau_{g2}$: Gravity pulls straight down in the global world frame, and the forearm's global angle from horizontal is $q_1 + q_2$, not the relative elbow angle $q_2$!
Streaming 20-byte telemetry frames at $1\text{ kHz}$ over $115{,}200\text{ baud}$: A 20-byte frame is $200\text{ bits}$ on an 8N1 UART link ($200\text{ kbit/s}$ at $1\text{ kHz}$), which overflows the TX ring buffer (412 dropped frames in $1\text{ s}$). Configure UART to $\ge 230{,}400$ or $500{,}000\text{ baud}$.

Shoulder vs. elbow gravity load: At horizontal stretch ($q_1 = 0, q_2 = 0$), why is the shoulder gravity holding torque ($\tau_{g1} = 0.3188\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) more than $4\times$ larger than the elbow gravity holding torque ($\tau_{g2} = 0.0736\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$)?
Answer
Because the shoulder must hold up both Link 1 ($m_1$ at $L_{c1}$) and Link 2 ($m_2$ at a longer lever arm $L_1 + L_{c2} = 0.15\text{ m}$), whereas the elbow only holds Link 2 at lever arm $L_{c2} = 0.05\text{ m}$.
Two AS5600 encoders on one MCU: Since every AS5600 I2C magnetic encoder has the same fixed address 0x36, how do you connect both the shoulder and elbow encoders to a single ESP32 or STM32?
Answer
Connect one AS5600 to hardware bus I2C0 (Wire) and the second to hardware bus I2C1 (Wire1), or use an I2C multiplexer / SPI AS5048A encoders with separate Chip-Select (CS) pins.

You combined 2-link Law-of-Cosines IK, a 1,000-step ($1\text{ kHz}$) time-stepped 2-DOF physical arm plant with PD + 2-link gravity feedforward and disturbance rejection, four graded R4 repairs for zero offset, CPR scale, anti-windup, and gravity sign, and 20-byte polynomial CRC-8 (0x07) telemetry + 8N1 UART ring-buffer verification into a complete 2-DOF figure-8 robot arm controller.
Completing all 48 beginner lessons (Track P $\to$ Stage 0 $\to$ Tracks 00–08 Tier 1) prepares you to tackle the Tier 1 Bridge Modules (modules/) or level up to Pass 2 (Tier 2)!

sections.h: You're done with the Pass 1 Beginner Lesson Path when...
sections.t:
Your tier1_boss_2dof_arm.py script prints IK->FK err=0.0000 mm | Dynamic tip err max=2.40 mm, RMS=0.91 mm, tau_g1=0.3188 Nm | tau_g2=0.0736 Nm, and CRC8=0xB2 valid=True | Dropped @115.2k=412, @500k=0.
The four repair lines print 12.00 mm -> 0.0000 mm, 174.0 mm -> 0.0000 mm, 37.2% -> 4.7%, and 31.8 mm -> 0.0000 mm.
All four 08.1 Four-Fault Bench cards read REPAIRED ($0$, $0$, $4.7\%$, $0$). While any card still shows its broken metric — say a repair left at $1.20\text{ mm}$ — the lesson does not verify, because the bench, not the printed line, decides the pass.
infer_encoder_scale names Unit E's cause as $1.5$ from its readings alone, and repair_encoder_cpr brings its report back to $0.305\text{ rad}$; an honest encoder returns $1.0$, and a constant-offset unit cannot be mistaken for either.
You tested your code in the in-browser MechaLab Python Sandbox and explored the real-time physics tabs.

pages.title: System Error/Latency Budgeting, Cross-Domain Interface Contracts & Pre-Bring-Up Safety Sign-Off

sections.t: This is the final bridge module in the entire repository before Step 3.8 (08-capstones.T3.08: Capstone 1 High-Speed Precision Motion Stage, Capstone 2 Balancing Mobility Robot, or Capstone 3 6-DOF Force-Controlled Tele-Impedance Manipulator — the Graduate Goal). Why do so many student and startup robot builds fail during final integration even when the CAD, PCB, firmware, and ROS 2 nodes each worked on their own benches? Because nobody added up the end-to-end spatial error budget ($\sigma_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma_i^2}$), the end-to-end latency & phase-margin erosion budget ($\Delta\phi = \omega_{gc}\sum \tau_i$), or verified a formal Cross-Domain Interface Contract (ICD) & Pre-Bring-Up Safety Sign-Off before energizing the $48\text{ V}$ bus! Already know this? Read ### Safety notes first, then take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7.

When you bolt six joints, six encoders, a camera, a CAN-FD bus, a $1\text{ kHz}$ ros2_control loop, and a $50\text{ Hz}$ learned policy together, errors and delays accumulate across every domain boundary:
Spatial Error Budgeting (RSS vs. Worst-Case): Deterministic systematic offsets $b_i$ (like uncalibrated thermal expansion) add linearly ($\sum |b_i|$), whereas independent random errors $\sigma_i$ (encoder noise, bearing runout, structural deflection, calibration residual) add in Root-Sum-Square (RSS): $\sigma_{\text{rss}} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma_i^2}$. Looking at the RSS breakdown tells you immediately which single subsystem dominates $80\%$ of your error so you don't waste \$1,000 on an ultra-precise encoder when link deflection is $10\times$ larger!
End-to-End Latency & Phase-Margin Budget: Every microsecond of sensor readout delay ($\tau_{\text{enc}}$), CAN-FD wire transport ($\tau_{\text{can}}$), digital filtering ($\tau_{\text{filt}}$), and zero-order hold ($\frac{1}{2}T_s$) adds up to total loop delay $\tau_{\text{total}} = \sum \tau_k$, which steals $\Delta\phi = \omega_{gc}\tau_{\text{total}}\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ degrees of Phase Margin from your servo loop (05-control.T2.05a).
Cross-Domain Interface Control Document (ICD) & Pre-Bring-Up Sign-Off: Before first motion on a multi-DOF capstone robot, every mechanical, electrical, firmware, control, and safety assertion must pass an automated Go / No-Go Sign-Off Checklist.

Combined Systematic + Root-Sum-Square (RSS) Spatial Error Budget: Given $M$ subsystems with residual systematic bias $b_i$ and independent $1\sigma$ random error $\sigma_i$ mapped to end-effector tip displacement via sensitivity $s_i$:
The fractional variance contribution of source $i$ is $w_i = \frac{(s_i \sigma_i)^2}{\sum_j (s_j \sigma_j)^2}$ ($\sum w_i = 1$).
End-to-End Loop Latency & Phase-Margin Erosion Budget: Across sensor delay $\tau_{\text{sens}}$, bus transport $\tau_{\text{bus}}$, filter group delay $\tau_{\text{filt}}$, compute time $\tau_{\text{comp}}$, and Zero-Order Hold $\tau_{\text{zoh}} = \frac{1}{2}T_s$:
Cross-Domain ICD & Pre-Bring-Up Go/No-Go Sign-Off Function: A capstone build is cleared for energized closed-loop testing (GO = True) iff all 5 domain gates hold simultaneously:

Reach for these three budgets at design freeze, and again after any subsystem swap, before a multi-DOF build is energised for the first time: the error budget says which source is worth money, the latency budget says whether the loop is still stable at its crossover, and the sign-off gate says whether it may move at all.
One run on this module's own numbers:
The biases $0.01 + 0.04 + 0.03 + 0.02 = 0.10\text{ mm}$ add linearly; the random terms give $\sqrt{0.03^2 + 0.06^2 + 0.08^2 + 0.03^2} = 0.1086\text{ mm}$, so $e_{3\sigma} = 0.10 + 3(0.1086) = 0.4259\text{ mm} \le 0.50\text{ mm}$. Structural link deflection owns $0.08^2/0.0118 = 54\%$ of the variance and is the only source worth re-engineering.
The delays $20 + 180 + 250 + 150\ \mu\text{s}$ plus half a $1\text{ kHz}$ tick are $\tau_{\text{total}} = 1.10\text{ ms}$, which erodes $150 \times 0.0011 \times 180/\pi = 9.45^\circ$ and leaves $52.55^\circ$: the verdict is GO.
Swap in a 10-tap average ($2550\ \mu\text{s}$) and the same chain is $3.40\text{ ms}$ and $32.78^\circ$; the margin alone fails, so the verdict is NO-GO whatever the other four gates say.
Checks that catch most mistakes: an RSS sum is never larger than the sum of magnitudes; a larger delay must lower the margin; the $3\sigma$ factor multiplies only the quadrature sum and never the biases; the zero-order hold is half a tick, not zero; and a five-way gate is a conjunction - four green lights and one red is red.

Why RSS, and why biases do not cancel. With independent zero-mean errors $\epsilon_i$ mapped to the tip by sensitivity $s_i$, the combined displacement is $e = \sum_i s_i\epsilon_i + \sum_i s_i b_i$. Independence makes every cross term vanish in expectation, so the variance is additive:
The systematic part takes magnitudes because a bias does not average out with more samples: two offsets on opposite sides still move the tip by their sum in the worst case. The factor $3$ is a coverage factor ($99.73\%$ of a normal source), so it belongs on the random term alone. The variance share $w_i = s_i^2\sigma_i^2 / \sum_j s_j^2\sigma_j^2$ is what makes the budget actionable - at $w = 0.54$ a better encoder buys at most the remaining $46\%$.
Why half a tick, and why it becomes degrees. A sample taken at $kTs$ is held until $(k+1)Ts$, so on average it describes the signal $Ts/2$ late; in the frequency domain the hold $(1 - e^{-sTs})/(sTs)$ is $e^{-sTs/2}$ to first order in $s$. A pure delay $\tau$ contributes phase $-\omega\tau$ radians, so at crossover it subtracts directly:
The $17^\circ$ between $62^\circ$ and the $45^\circ$ floor therefore buys $\tau_{\max} = (17\pi/180)/150 = 1.978\text{ ms}$, which the $3.40\text{ ms}$ chain spends nearly twice over.
Extend. Add a vision pipeline and a second encoder to the same capstone: allocate the fixed $0.50\text{ mm}$ and the $17^\circ$ of margin between the new sources, then derive the largest delay the vision stage may add while capstone_signoff still returns GO.

Predict first (before you run it): Commit to four numbers, a dominant source and one verdict. (1) For $1\sigma$ sources of $0.03, 0.06, 0.08, 0.03\text{ mm}$, is $\sigma_{\text{rss}}$ nearer $0.10$ or $0.14\text{ mm}$? (2) With $20 + 180 + 250 + 150\ \mu\text{s}$ plus the zero-order hold, is $\tau_{\text{total}}$ nearer $0.6$ or $1.1\text{ ms}$? (3) At $\omega_{gc} = 150\text{ rad/s}$ and $\text{PM}_0 = 62.0^\circ$, does the loop keep the $45^\circ$ floor? (4) Which source owns most of the variance? Then answer the exercise's verdict after a $10$-tap filter pushes $\tau_{\text{total}}$ to $3.40\text{ ms}$: GO or NO-GO? Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a convention: a systematic term of $0.0548\text{ mm}$ instead of $0.10\text{ mm}$ means the four biases were Root-Sum-Squared like the random errors (they add linearly); and a net margin above $62.0^\circ$ means the erosion was added to the nominal margin instead of subtracted from it.
Evaluate the complete system error budget, latency/phase-margin budget, and 5-domain Pre-Bring-Up Go/No-Go Sign-Off for Capstone 3 (the 6-DOF Tele-Impedance Manipulator with $e_{\text{spec}} = 0.50\text{ mm}$ repeatability, $\omega_{gc} = 150\text{ rad/s}$, and nominal $\text{PM}_0 = 62.0^\circ$).
Expected output:

Suppose an engineer replaces the $250\ \mu\text{s}$ low-pass filter in the $1\text{ kHz}$ loop above with a heavy 10-tap moving-average filter that adds $\tau_{\text{filt,new}} = 2550\ \mu\text{s}$ of delay (so $\tau_{\text{total}}$ increases from $1.10\text{ ms}$ to $3.40\text{ ms}$). Compute the new net Phase Margin $\text{PM}_{\text{net}} = 62.0^\circ - 150.0 \times 0.0034 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ in degrees, and verify whether capstone_signoff returns True or False. Verify $\text{PM}_{\text{net}} = 32.779^\circ < 45.0^\circ$ and capstone_signoff == False.
If your result differs: Multiply $150.0\text{ rad/s} \times 0.0034\text{ s} = 0.51\text{ rad}$, convert to degrees ($0.51 \times 180/\pi = 29.2208^\circ$), and subtract from $62.0^\circ$ ($32.78^\circ < 45^\circ \implies \text{NO-GO}$).

sections.h: Graded package - the error budget, the delay and the sign-off
sections.t:
exercises/08-capstones.T3.07a/ turns this section into a test. starter.py holds nine holes: rss, systematic_sum, error_budget_3sigma, variance_fraction, zoh_delay_us, total_latency_s, net_phase_margin_deg, max_allowable_delay_ms and capstone_signoff. Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:
42 tests. The $3\sigma$ budget is checked at the worked example's $0.4259\text{ mm}$ and the Gate test's $0.35\text{ mm}$, and a $-0.02\text{ mm}$ bias must still add $0.02\text{ mm}$ rather than cancel, so a linear sum or a signed sum each fail; the latency chain is checked at $1100\ \mu\text{s}$ and at the 10-tap filter's $3400\ \mu\text{s}$, so a chain that forgets the $500\ \mu\text{s}$ zero-order hold fails; the phase subtraction is checked in degrees at $52.55^\circ$, $32.78^\circ$ and $48.54^\circ$, so a raw radian result fails; and the sign-off is checked at the 4-of-5 STO case, an out-of-window $50\ \Omega$ bus, and the inclusive boundaries of all five limits. The transfer suite runs the plant: one count of its 12-bit encoder seen at the full $0.20\text{ m}$ reach is $0.3068\text{ mm}$, so $3\sigma$ is $0.9204\text{ mm}$ and the $0.50\text{ mm}$ capstone spec is already lost before any other source is counted; its $1\text{ kHz}$ tick is the worked $1000\ \mu\text{s}$ period and erodes $8.59^\circ$ at $150\text{ rad/s}$; and the $17^\circ$ between the nominal margin and the $45^\circ$ floor buys $1.978\text{ ms}$, which the module's filter swap spends nearly twice over. Five planted faults - rss_adds_linearly, systematic_forgets_abs, latency_forgets_zoh, phase_margin_forgets_radians, signoff_ignores_sto - each fail the test named for them.
The browser bench is this module's pass condition. In the Python runner, a Tier 3 Capstone Budget Bench reports four rows computed by the harness from your functions on a design point this module never prints: the $3\sigma$ spatial budget, the net phase margin through the latency chain, the delay the remaining margin may buy, and how many of the two sign-off verdicts your capstone_signoff gets right. Run & Verify Output marks the lesson verified only when all four rows are at target ($\le 0.50\text{ mm}$, $\ge 45^\circ$, at least the $1.18\text{ ms}$ chain, both verdicts) - a zero-order hold charged a full tick instead of half keeps its real $42.7^\circ$ on the row and leaves the lesson unverified, whatever the printed line says.
Expected numbers (the answer): $\tau_{\text{total}} = 3.40\ \text{ms}$, $\text{PM}_{\text{net}} = 32.779^\circ < 45.0^\circ$, capstone_signoff == False.

The ZOH is half a tick. Six delays, not five: $20 + 180 + 2550 + 150\ \mu\text{s}$ of measured latency plus $\frac{1}{2}T_s = 500\ \mu\text{s}$, which is $3400\ \mu\text{s}$ and not the $2900\ \mu\text{s}$ the measured chain alone gives.
Radians before degrees. $150.0\ \text{rad/s} \times 0.0034\ \text{s} = 0.51\ \text{rad}$ of lag; subtract $0.51 \times 180/\pi = 29.2208^\circ$ from $62.0^\circ$. A net margin near $61.5^\circ$ means the product was treated as degrees already.
Four out of five is NO-GO. The gate is a conjunction: the $3\sigma$ budget ($0.4259\ \text{mm} \le 0.50$), the margin ($32.78^\circ < 45^\circ$), CPU, termination and STO. Here the margin alone already fails, so the verdict is False whatever the other four say.
The $3\sigma$ budget is a magnitude budget. Biases add linearly, so two offsets on opposite sides still add their sizes; only the independent random terms add in quadrature, and only then is the $3\sigma$ factor applied to that quadrature sum.
What the suite refuses. error_budget_3sigma refuses an empty budget and a sensitivity list whose lengths cannot pair, rss refuses a negative sigma, variance_fraction refuses a variance budget summing to zero and an index past its terms, total_latency_s refuses a negative delay or a zero sample period, zoh_delay_us refuses a zero sample period, max_allowable_delay_ms and net_phase_margin_deg refuse a crossover that is not positive (there is no delay budget to divide into), and capstone_signoff refuses an STO flag that is not a bool - each with ValueError.

Printed: PM_net=32.78 deg at tau=3.40 ms | signoff=False, then nominal: tau=1.10 ms, PM_net=52.55 deg, e_3sigma=0.426 mm.
On the shared arm. The Transfer suite prices the plant's own 12-bit encoder and 1 kHz sample period against the capstone's 0.50 mm and $45^\circ$ budgets:

Inject the latency_forgets_zoh fault and diagnose it from the budget alone, keeping $T_s = 1000\ \mu\text{s}$ and $\omega_{gc} = 150\text{ rad/s}$:
Inject: sum the four measured delays and drop the zero-order hold term, i.e. tau_total_s = (tau_sens_us + tau_bus_us + tau_filt_us + tau_comp_us) 1e-6 instead of adding 0.5 ts_us.
Symptom: the worked case reports $0.60\text{ ms}$ and $56.84^\circ$ instead of $1.10\text{ ms}$ and $52.55^\circ$, so it still says GO and a smoke test passes; the exercise's $3.40\text{ ms}$ becomes $2.90\text{ ms}$ and $37.08^\circ$ instead of $32.78^\circ$ (still NO-GO, but $4.3^\circ$ of margin that no longer exists), and the transfer suite's one-plant-tick erosion halves from $8.59^\circ$ to $4.30^\circ$. The error is always exactly $0.5\text{ ms}$ of delay, regardless of which filter is installed.
Diagnose: the constant offset separates it from a sensor or bus latency mistake. A wrong measured delay changes with the hardware and shifts every case by a different amount, whereas a gap that is exactly $\frac{1}{2}T_s$ in all four cases - and that leaves $\text{PM}_0$, the $3\sigma$ budget and the $5$-domain gate untouched - can only be the sampling term, not max_allowable_delay_ms or a degrees/radians slip.
Fix: restore + 0.5 ts_us in the chain and prove it at the two numbers CI checks: $1.10\text{ ms}$ and $52.55^\circ$ for the worked example, $3.40\text{ ms}$ and $32.78^\circ$ for the filter swap, plus the gate's $500\ \mu\text{s}$ ZOH. latency_forgets_zoh must fail test_behavior, and the plant-tick transfer check ($8.59^\circ$ at $150\text{ rad/s}$) must pass.
📚 What to Learn & Resources to Solve This Exercise:
Required Foundations Modules (00-foundations): 00-foundations.T2.00d (Bode Phase Margin), 00-foundations.T2.00f (Root-Sum-Square Variance Summation), and 00-foundations.T3.00a (Multi-Domain Power & Energy Balance).
Prerequisite Tier 3 Modules: 01-electronics.T3.02, 02-mechanics.T3.03, 03-sensors.T3.04, 04-embedded.T3.05, 05-control.T3.06, and 06-robotics.T3.07.
Core Concepts to Review First: End-to-end latency phase erosion $\Delta\phi(\omega_{gc}) = -\omega_{gc}\tau_{\text{total}}\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ and net phase margin $\text{PM}_{\text{net}} = \text{PM}_0 - |\Delta\phi|$, coupled electro-thermo-mechanical power sizing, and ISO 13855 safety stopping distance in ## 3. Formalization and ## 4. Worked example above.
Study Links & Resources: Slocum Precision Machine Design, NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA/SP-2016-6105), and Track 08 Capstones (08-capstone-projects/README.md).

Open URDF / MuJoCo & STO — Capstone 3: 6-DOF Force-Controlled Tele-Impedance Manipulator & System Verification in the MechaLab Workbench (npm run dev), or run the standalone verification script python3 08-capstone-projects/urdf-mujoco-capstone3-6dof/verify_capstone3_kinematics_cbf.py.

⚠️ Mandatory Safety Briefing (safety_level: high — read before energizing any Capstone hardware build or taking the Skip/Gate test):
Mandatory 5-Stage Progressive Bring-Up Sequence: Never power up a newly assembled multi-DOF robot and immediately enable full-torque closed-loop trajectory tracking. Always execute in strict order:
Stage 0 (Power-Off Bench Check): Verify bus resistance (> 10 kOhm +Vbus to GND), CAN termination ($60\ \Omega$), fastener torque witness marks, and mechanical hard stops.
Stage 1 (Current-Limited Logic & Sensor Check): Current-limited bench PSU ($24\text{ V}/48\text{ V}$ at $0.5\text{ A}$), verify encoder counts, joint signs, tf2 tree directions in RViz2, and dual-channel STO cut-off (torque_removed == True).
Stage 2 (Single-Joint Open-Loop / Low-Current FOC Alignment): Align electrical zero angle $\theta_e$ with mechanical load uncoupled or arm supported in a safe cradle.
Stage 3 (Zero-Stiffness Gravity Compensation + Damping Mode): Set $K_p = 0$, $K_d > 0$, $\tau_{\text{ff}} = g(q)$ with $20\%$ torque ceiling; move the arm by hand to verify smooth backdrivability and confirm that pushing each link produces damped resistance (positive damping, not positive feedback!).
Stage 4 (Full Closed-Loop Impedance + CBF Safety Shield + E-Stop Live Test): Enable Cartesian impedance / learned policy only after Stages 0–3 and a live physical E-stop cut test pass.

Pass criteria: read ### Safety notes, score $\ge 80\%$ ($5/6$, $100\%$ on [SAFETY] items) on the Skip test, or score $\ge 80\%$ ($7/8$, $100\%$ on [SAFETY] items) on the Ladder Gate test to unlock Step 3.8 (08-capstones.T3.08).

[Recall] [Concept: rss_and_worst_case_spatial_error_budget] Three independent random error sources have $1\sigma$ end-effector contributions $\sigma_1 = 0.03\text{ mm}$, $\sigma_2 = 0.04\text{ mm}$, and $\sigma_3 = 0.12\text{ mm}$. Compute the combined Root-Sum-Square (RSS) $1\sigma$ error $\sigma_{\text{rss}} = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \sigma_3^2}$ in millimeters ($\text{mm}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
[Apply] [Concept: rss_and_worst_case_spatial_error_budget] In Q1 ($\sigma_1 = 0.03, \sigma_2 = 0.04, \sigma_3 = 0.12\text{ mm}$, so $\sigma_{\text{rss}} = 0.13\text{ mm}$), what fraction of the total error variance $\sigma_3^2 / \sigma_{\text{rss}}^2$ comes from source 3 alone (tolerance $\pm 10^{-4}$)?
[Transfer] [Concept: end_to_end_latency_and_phase_margin_erosion_budget] A servo loop has crossover $\omega_{gc} = 200\text{ rad/s}$, delay-free Phase Margin $\text{PM}_0 = 60.0^\circ$, and total end-to-end loop delay $\tau_{\text{total}} = 0.001\text{ s}$ ($1.0\text{ ms}$). Compute the net Phase Margin $\text{PM}_{\text{net}} = \text{PM}_0 - \omega_{gc}\tau_{\text{total}}\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ in degrees (tolerance $\pm 0.01^\circ$).
[SAFETY] [Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] During Stage 3 of progressive bring-up on a 6-DOF robot arm (before enabling stiff position trajectories), you set $K_p = 0$, $K_d = 1.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$, and $\tau_{\text{ff}} = g(q)$ at a $20\%$ torque limit and gently push Joint 2 by hand. Why is this test mandatory before enabling $K_p > 0$?
A. To polish the aluminum links.
B. It safely verifies at low torque that encoder direction, motor phase sequence, velocity sign ($-K_d\dot{q}$), and gravity vector $g(q)$ all oppose external disturbances rather than accelerating into positive-feedback runaway!
C. Because $K_p$ is never used in robotics.
D. To discharge the battery.
[SAFETY] [Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] If 4 out of 5 pre-bring-up gates pass (e_3sigma = 45 deg, CPU_Util <= 0.70, CAN_Term == 60 Ohm), but the dual-channel Category 3 STO test has not been verified (sto_cat3_ok = False), what integer value must int(all(gates)) return (0 for False / NO-GO, 1 for True / GO, exact integer, tolerance $\pm 0$)?
[Spaced review -> 07-systems.T2.07a — Concept: regenerative_bus_energy_and_chopper_sizing] A $1000\ \mu\text{F}$ bus at $48.0\,\text{V}$ is pushed to $60.0\,\text{V}$ by regeneration. Compute the added energy $\tfrac12 C (V_2^2 - V_1^2)$ in joules (tolerance $\pm 10^{-6}$).
Answer key:
Pass mark: $5/6$ overall AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on Q4 and Q5 ([SAFETY]). If you missed Q1 or Q2, study ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q3, study ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q4 or Q5, study ## 3. Formalization item 3 and ### Safety notes. If you missed Q6, review 07-systems.T2.07a. On pass, proceed to ## 10. Next modules.

Covers the complete Track 08 Tier 3 Capstone Engineering bridge ladder (08-capstones.T3.07a) before Step 3.8 (08-capstones.T3.08):
[Concept: rss_and_worst_case_spatial_error_budget] Compute the $3\sigma$ total error $e_{3\sigma} = |b| + 3\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}$ in millimeters ($\text{mm}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) for systematic bias $b = 0.05\text{ mm}$ and independent random errors $\sigma_1 = 0.06\text{ mm}, \sigma_2 = 0.08\text{ mm}$.
[Concept: rss_and_worst_case_spatial_error_budget] Why is reducing a small error source ($\sigma_1 = 0.02\text{ mm}$) to zero almost useless when another subsystem has $\sigma_2 = 0.20\text{ mm}$?
A. Because in Root-Sum-Square $\sqrt{0.02^2 + 0.20^2} = 0.2010\text{ mm} \to 0.2000\text{ mm}$, the largest variance source ($\sigma_2^2 = 99\%$ of variance) dominates the total RSS sum!
B. Because square roots cannot be computed on small numbers.
C. Because encoders do not affect accuracy.
D. Because systematic bias cancels random noise.
[Concept: end_to_end_latency_and_phase_margin_erosion_budget] In a digital control loop running at sample period $T_s = 1000\ \mu\text{s}$ ($1\text{ kHz}$), what is the effective Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) delay $\tau_{\text{zoh}} = \frac{1}{2}T_s$ in microseconds ($\mu\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$)?
[Concept: end_to_end_latency_and_phase_margin_erosion_budget] Compute the maximum allowable total loop delay $\tau_{\max} = \frac{\Delta\phi_{\max}}{\omega_{gc}}$ in milliseconds ($\text{ms}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-3}\text{ ms}$) if a loop with crossover $\omega_{gc} = 200\text{ rad/s}$ can afford to lose at most $\Delta\phi_{\max} = 0.20\text{ rad}$ ($\approx 11.46^\circ$) of Phase Margin.
[Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] Why must a Cross-Domain Interface Control Document (ICD) explicitly lock down coordinate frame conventions (REP-103 +X fwd, +Y left, +Z up), joint rotation sign (+q right-hand rule about joint axis), and SI units (rad, Nm, A) across Mechanical, Firmware, and ROS 2 teams?
A. Because a single sign inversion or deg/rad unit mismatch across the CAN-FD interface turns negative feedback into violent positive-feedback instability on the very first control tick!
B. To make the README file longer.
C. Because C++ does not support negative numbers.
D. To change the motor winding resistance.
[Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] During Stage 0 (Power-Off Bench Check), what nominal DC resistance in ohms ($\Omega$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) must you measure between CAN_H and CAN_L across a properly terminated 6-joint CAN-FD daisy chain?
[SAFETY] [Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] During Stage 3 bring-up, you push Joint 1 slightly in the $+\theta$ direction and feel the motor push your hand further in the $+\theta$ direction instead of resisting. What is the root cause and immediate action?
A. Hit E-Stop immediately; the encoder direction or motor phase order is inverted relative to the controller sign convention (positive feedback!), and must be flipped and re-tested at low current before proceeding.
B. Increase $K_p$ by $10\times$ to overpower it.
C. Remove the E-stop button.
D. Ignore it and start the neural network policy.
[SAFETY] [Concept: pre_bring_up_interface_and_safety_signoff_gate] Why must the physical hardware E-stop (STO) test in Stage 1 / Stage 4 be tested under actual motion before running autonomous policies?
A. To prove end-to-end that pressing the physical E-stop mushroom immediately removes inverter gate drive power (STO), coasts/brakes the links safely within the stopping distance budget, and latches FAULT until manually reset.
B. To wear in the button spring.
C. To calibrate the camera focal length.
D. To test the Wi-Fi router.
Gate answer key:
Pass mark: $7/8$ overall AND $2/2$ ($100\%$) on [SAFETY] questions Q7 and Q8. Remediation: Q1–Q2 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 1; Q3–Q4 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 2; Q5–Q8 $\to$ ## 3. Formalization item 3 and ### Safety notes.
